stem:
A 38-year-old woman with bipolar I disorder has been stable on lithium carbonate 750 mg at night for 5 years with a steady-state trough level of 0.7 mmol/L. She attends her GP for a routine review. She is well, taking no other medications, with no recent illness. She drinks 2 standard drinks per week and does not smoke. Her last full blood count, electrolytes, urea, creatinine, eGFR, calcium, and TSH were taken 9 months ago and were within normal limits. She wants to know what monitoring she needs from now on while she remains on lithium.

She is not pregnant and is using long-acting reversible contraception.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 72/min, blood pressure 116/74 mmHg, respiratory rate 14/min, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.7°C
data_table.Examination: Well, fine resting tremor of hands, no peripheral oedema
data_table.Investigations: Lithium level 0.7 mmol/L 9 months ago; eGFR 84 mL/min/1.73m2; TSH 2.1 mU/L; calcium 2.42 mmol/L; FBC normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate ongoing monitoring schedule?

options.text: Annual lithium level with electrolytes and renal function only if symptoms of toxicity occur.
options.rationale: Routine surveillance must continue regardless of symptoms because lithium nephrotoxicity and thyroid dysfunction are insidious. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: psychotropic)

options.text: Lithium level every 3 months without further renal or endocrine monitoring needed during stability.
options.rationale: Monitoring lithium without checking eGFR, TSH, and calcium misses the very organ effects routine review is designed to detect. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: psychotropic)

options.text: Lithium level, electrolytes, and TSH every 6 months without parathyroid hormone or calcium tested.
options.rationale: Hypercalcaemia from lithium-induced hyperparathyroidism is a recognised complication that is missed without routine calcium. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: psychotropic)

options.text: Lithium level every 3 months with annual electrolytes, calcium, and TSH long term while on therapy.
options.rationale: Six-monthly is the recommended frequency for the panel when stable; staggering creates gaps in detection. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: psychotropic)

options.text: Lithium level, electrolytes, eGFR, calcium, and TSH every 6 months long term.
options.rationale: Australian Therapeutic Guidelines specify 6-monthly lithium, U+E, eGFR, calcium, and TSH once stable, lifelong. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: psychotropic)

explanation.summary: Long-term lithium therapy requires routine surveillance for the three classical organ effects: chronic kidney disease, hypothyroidism, and primary hyperparathyroidism with hypercalcaemia. Australian Therapeutic Guidelines: psychotropic recommend a steady-state trough lithium level plus electrolytes, eGFR, corrected calcium, and TSH every 6 months once a patient has been stable for at least 6 months, continued lifelong. Earlier monitoring (every 1 to 3 months) is reserved for initiation, dose change, or intercurrent illness with dehydration or new interacting medication.
key_points: Lifelong 6-monthly lithium, U+E, eGFR, corrected calcium, and TSH once stable.
Lithium can cause nephrogenic diabetes insipidus and chronic interstitial nephritis.
Hypercalcaemia from primary hyperparathyroidism is increasingly recognised on long-term lithium.
explanation.pearls: Any new interacting medication (NSAIDs, ACE inhibitors, ARBs, thiazides) or intercurrent illness with vomiting warrants a check at 5 to 7 days because lithium toxicity can develop in days.

stem:
A 24-year-old man with first-episode schizophrenia was commenced on olanzapine 10 mg at night 12 weeks ago by the community mental health team. He has gained 4.5 kg, has settled positive symptoms, and is functionally improving. His baseline metabolic screen at initiation was: BMI 25 kg/m2, fasting glucose 5.0 mmol/L, HbA1c 5.4 percent, total cholesterol 4.8 mmol/L, triglycerides 1.2 mmol/L, prolactin 320 mIU/L, ECG QTc 410 ms. He has no personal or family history of diabetes or cardiovascular disease and does not smoke. He drinks alcohol minimally.

He attends his community mental health appointment today and asks whether any tests are due.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 76/min, blood pressure 122/78 mmHg, respiratory rate 14/min, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.7°C, weight 79 kg (up from 74.5 kg)
data_table.Examination: Well, no abnormal movements; abdominal girth increased; mood euthymic
data_table.Investigations: Baseline 12 weeks ago as listed in stem; no repeat bloods since starting olanzapine

lead_in: What is the most appropriate metabolic monitoring at this visit?

options.text: Repeat fasting glucose, HbA1c, lipid panel, and weight; recheck waist circumference and blood pressure.
options.rationale: RANZCP recommends fasting glucose, HbA1c, lipids, weight, waist, and blood pressure at 12 weeks and then at least annually on second-generation antipsychotics. (Source: RANZCP schizophrenia guideline)

options.text: Repeat only fasting glucose and HbA1c at this 12 week visit because lipids change more slowly.
options.rationale: Lipid abnormalities can emerge within 12 weeks of olanzapine and are part of routine monitoring at this visit. (Source: RANZCP schizophrenia guideline)

options.text: Defer metabolic monitoring until the 6 month review, focusing on symptom response in the meantime.
options.rationale: Twelve week metabolic monitoring is part of the AU schedule precisely because olanzapine commonly causes early metabolic change. (Source: RANZCP schizophrenia guideline)

options.text: Repeat lipid panel only; defer fasting glucose and HbA1c until the 24 week visit later this year.
options.rationale: Insulin resistance can develop early with olanzapine and screening at 12 weeks is recommended. (Source: RANZCP schizophrenia guideline)

options.text: Repeat ECG, prolactin, and metabolic panel together with assessment for tardive dyskinesia today.
options.rationale: Routine 12 week ECG and prolactin are not standard unless symptomatic; tardive dyskinesia surveillance starts later in treatment. (Source: RANZCP schizophrenia guideline)

explanation.summary: Second-generation antipsychotics, especially olanzapine and clozapine, drive weight gain, dyslipidaemia, and impaired glucose tolerance, often within the first 3 months. The RANZCP and Australian Therapeutic Guidelines schedule recommends measuring weight and waist circumference, blood pressure, fasting glucose or HbA1c, and a lipid panel at baseline, 6 weeks, 12 weeks, 6 months, and annually thereafter. Olanzapine and clozapine carry the highest metabolic risk; lurasidone and aripiprazole carry the lowest.
key_points: 12 week monitoring includes weight, waist, BP, fasting glucose or HbA1c, and lipid panel.
Olanzapine and clozapine are the highest-risk antipsychotics for metabolic syndrome.
Switch to a lower-risk agent if HbA1c crosses 6.0 percent or weight gain exceeds 7 percent of baseline.
explanation.pearls: If HbA1c rises by more than 0.5 percent at 12 weeks, prompt a switch consideration rather than waiting for diabetes to develop on top of stable psychotic illness.

stem:
A 42-year-old man with a 25 pack-year history attends his GP wanting to stop smoking 25 cigarettes a day. He has tried nicotine patches twice in the past without success, lapsing back to smoking within 2 weeks each time. He has a quit date in 2 weeks. He has well-controlled hypertension on perindopril 5 mg daily, no significant mental health history, no current depressive symptoms (PHQ-9 score 3), and no history of seizures or eating disorder. He drinks 6 standard drinks per week. He has read about available options online and wants the most effective pharmacotherapy.

He is willing to combine pharmacotherapy with behavioural support through Quitline.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 74/min, blood pressure 128/78 mmHg, respiratory rate 14/min, SpO2 98% on room air, temperature 36.6°C
data_table.Examination: Well, no respiratory distress, mild peripheral cyanosis of fingers from staining; chest clear
data_table.Investigations: Fasting glucose 5.4 mmol/L; HbA1c 5.6 percent; spirometry FEV1/FVC 0.78 predicted

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first-line pharmacotherapy?

options.text: Bupropion sustained release 150 mg daily for 3 days then twice daily, started 1 week before quit date.
options.rationale: Bupropion is second-line when varenicline is contraindicated, declined, or unavailable; varenicline has superior efficacy. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: smoking cessation)

options.text: Varenicline starting at 0.5 mg daily titrated to 1 mg twice daily, started 1 week before quit date.
options.rationale: Varenicline has the highest efficacy as smoking cessation monotherapy in Australia and is first-line for committed quitters without contraindications. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: smoking cessation)

options.text: Combination nicotine replacement therapy with a 21 mg patch plus 4 mg lozenges for breakthrough cravings.
options.rationale: Combination NRT is reasonable but varenicline remains the most effective monotherapy in head-to-head trials. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: smoking cessation)

options.text: Nortriptyline 25 mg at night titrated up to 75 mg over a fortnight to suppress cigarette cravings.
options.rationale: Nortriptyline is a fourth-line option used only if other pharmacotherapies fail or are contraindicated. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: smoking cessation)

options.text: Nicotine inhaler used hourly during waking hours alongside Quitline behavioural counselling sessions.
options.rationale: Monotherapy with a single short-acting NRT is less effective than combination NRT or varenicline. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: smoking cessation)

explanation.summary: Australian Therapeutic Guidelines rank smoking cessation pharmacotherapy by efficacy: varenicline (now considered first-line again following resolution of historical safety concerns) is most effective, then combination nicotine replacement therapy (patch plus short-acting), then bupropion or single NRT, with nortriptyline as a fourth-line option. Varenicline 0.5 mg daily for 3 days, then 0.5 mg twice daily for 4 days, then 1 mg twice daily for 12 weeks, started 1 week before quit date, is the standard schedule. Combine pharmacotherapy with structured behavioural support through Quitline (13 78 48).
key_points: First-line: varenicline.
Second-line: combination NRT (long-acting patch plus short-acting gum or lozenge).
Combine pharmacotherapy with structured behavioural support such as Quitline.
explanation.pearls: If the patient has active major depression or recent suicidal ideation, screen carefully before starting varenicline; current evidence does not show a population-level risk but individual histories warrant caution.

stem:
A 29-year-old female accountant presents to your psychiatry clinic for a second opinion. She describes lifelong difficulty sustaining attention on tasks she finds tedious, frequent careless errors at work, chronic disorganisation, time blindness, and emotional dysregulation. School reports from age 8 documented inattention, daydreaming, and incomplete homework. She has no childhood hyperactivity. Self-report scales show ASRS v1.1 part A six positive items out of six, and the DIVA-5 confirms five inattention symptoms with childhood onset, persistence, impairment in two domains, and exclusion of other better explanations. Her PHQ-9 is 4 and GAD-7 is 6. She has no psychotic symptoms, no current substance use, and her ECG is normal. She drives 30 minutes daily for work.

She has read about treatment options and is asking what comes next.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 72/min, blood pressure 118/74 mmHg, respiratory rate 14/min, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.7°C
data_table.Examination: Well groomed, normal affect, no abnormal movements, normal cardiovascular and neurological exam
data_table.Investigations: ECG QTc 410 ms; TFTs normal; FBC and U+E normal; urine drug screen negative

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Trial atomoxetine 40 mg daily for 6 weeks before considering any stimulant therapy as the first-line option.
options.rationale: Atomoxetine is reasonable when stimulants are contraindicated or declined but is not the routine first-line in adult ADHD. (Source: RANZCP adult ADHD guideline)

options.text: Refer for structured cognitive behavioural therapy alone over 6 months before any consideration of medication.
options.rationale: CBT augments treatment of adult ADHD but is not curative as monotherapy when stimulants are appropriate. (Source: RANZCP adult ADHD guideline)

options.text: Commence lisdexamfetamine 30 mg orally each morning, review in 4 weeks, and advise no driving during titration.
options.rationale: DSM-5 adult ADHD is established; first-line is a long-acting stimulant with driving restriction during titration per AU prescribing advice. (Source: RANZCP adult ADHD guideline)

options.text: Trial methylphenidate immediate release 5 mg three times daily without driving restrictions because doses are small.
options.rationale: Immediate release methylphenidate requires multiple daily doses and AU prescribing still advises driving caution during titration. (Source: RANZCP adult ADHD guideline)

options.text: Defer treatment and reassess in 6 months because her PHQ-9 and GAD-7 scores are too high for stimulant prescribing.
options.rationale: PHQ-9 of 4 and GAD-7 of 6 are not above thresholds that would defer ADHD treatment in this presentation. (Source: RANZCP adult ADHD guideline)

explanation.summary: Adult ADHD diagnosis under DSM-5 requires at least five inattentive or hyperactive-impulsive symptoms (out of nine each), childhood onset before age 12, persistence, impairment in at least two settings, and no better explanation. First-line treatment in Australia is a long-acting stimulant such as lisdexamfetamine 30 mg daily or methylphenidate ER, titrated weekly. Pre-treatment workup includes cardiovascular assessment with resting ECG. Patients must be advised that driving may be impaired during titration or dose changes, and to defer driving until they know their response; ongoing disclosure to the licensing authority is required only if a clinician judges fitness to drive is affected.
key_points: Long-acting stimulant is first-line for adult ADHD in Australia.
Baseline ECG and cardiovascular history are required before initiation.
Patients should not drive during titration or for 2 weeks after each dose change until response is known.
explanation.pearls: Document that the patient understands driving restrictions during titration and the obligation to self-report to the licensing authority if symptoms compromise safe driving; this is a recurrent medicolegal pitfall.

sources.label: Australian Evidence-Based Clinical Practice Guideline for ADHD

stem:
A 32-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department 90 minutes after ingesting an estimated 50 tablets of amitriptyline 25 mg (1250 mg total) with alcohol. She is drowsy but rousable. She has a known history of depression and previous overdose. On examination she is warm and dry with dilated pupils and absent bowel sounds. An ECG taken on arrival 10 minutes ago is on the trolley. She has been intubated for airway protection because of decreasing GCS and her arterial blood gas has returned.

The ED registrar is preparing the next intervention.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 132/min, blood pressure 90/55 mmHg, respiratory rate ventilated at 16/min, SpO2 99% on FiO2 0.4, temperature 37.4°C
data_table.Examination: Sedated, intubated; pupils dilated; warm and dry skin; absent bowel sounds; no focal neurology
data_table.Investigations: ECG: sinus tachycardia, QRS 145 ms, terminal R in aVR 4 mm; ABG pH 7.28, PaCO2 38 mmHg, HCO3 18 mmol/L, lactate 3.2 mmol/L; potassium 3.6 mmol/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next intervention?

options.text: Amiodarone 300 mg intravenous bolus over 10 minutes to terminate the tachyarrhythmia.
options.rationale: Class IA, IC, and III antiarrhythmics are contraindicated in TCA poisoning because they prolong QT and worsen sodium channel blockade. (Source: AU TCA poisoning guideline)

options.text: Flumazenil 0.2 mg intravenously to reverse benzodiazepine-associated sedation contribution.
options.rationale: Flumazenil in mixed overdose risks precipitating seizures, particularly with TCA co-ingestion. (Source: AU TCA poisoning guideline)

options.text: Activated charcoal 50 g via the nasogastric tube without prior bicarbonate therapy considered first.
options.rationale: Charcoal is only useful within 1 to 2 hours of ingestion and does not address sodium channel blockade cardiotoxicity. (Source: AU TCA poisoning guideline)

options.text: Sodium bicarbonate 1 to 2 mmol/kg intravenously over 5 minutes targeting QRS narrowing and pH 7.45 to 7.55.
options.rationale: QRS above 100 ms or terminal R in aVR above 3 mm in TCA poisoning is an indication for sodium bicarbonate. (Source: AU TCA poisoning guideline)

options.text: Intravenous lipid emulsion 1.5 mL/kg as first-line therapy ahead of any other intervention.
options.rationale: Lipid emulsion is a rescue therapy for refractory cardiovascular collapse, not first-line in TCA poisoning. (Source: AU TCA poisoning guideline)

explanation.summary: Tricyclic antidepressant cardiotoxicity is from fast sodium channel blockade in myocardial Purkinje fibres, causing QRS prolongation, hypotension, ventricular arrhythmias, and seizures. The 12-lead ECG features predicting arrhythmia are QRS at or above 100 ms and a terminal R wave in aVR at or above 3 mm. Treatment is sodium bicarbonate 1 to 2 mmol/kg IV boluses repeated to narrow QRS, target arterial pH 7.45 to 7.55, and reverse hypotension. Hyperventilation alkalinisation can be added. Lipid emulsion is rescue therapy for cardiovascular collapse despite bicarbonate.
key_points: QRS at or above 100 ms or terminal R in aVR at or above 3 mm triggers sodium bicarbonate.
Avoid class IA, IC, and III antiarrhythmics in TCA poisoning.
Lipid emulsion is rescue for refractory hypotension despite bicarbonate.
explanation.pearls: Maintain sodium bicarbonate boluses or infusion until QRS narrows below 100 ms and the patient is haemodynamically stable, not until pH returns to normal range.

stem:
A 22-year-old man with a known diagnosis of schizophrenia is brought from his community accommodation by his case manager. Over 5 days he has progressively stopped eating, drinking, and speaking. On examination he is mute, holds postures imposed on him for over a minute (waxy flexibility), and shows echolalia when prompted. He has not eaten in 48 hours. He is on no current antipsychotic having stopped his depot 3 months ago because of side effects. He has no fever. His Bush-Francis catatonia rating scale score is 18. Bedside investigations have just returned.

The team is now planning treatment.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 110/min, blood pressure 138/86 mmHg, respiratory rate 18/min, SpO2 97% on room air, temperature 36.8°C
data_table.Examination: Mute, immobile, waxy flexibility, echolalia, posturing; no rigidity, no clonus; mildly dry mucous membranes
data_table.Investigations: CK 320 U/L; creatinine 95 micromol/L; sodium 138 mmol/L; CRP 6 mg/L; urine drug screen negative; CT brain normal
data_table.Medications: Nil current; last paliperidone depot 3 months ago

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Lorazepam 2 mg intramuscularly as a diagnostic and therapeutic challenge with reassessment at 30 minutes.
options.rationale: Lorazepam 1 to 2 mg IM is the standard catatonia lorazepam challenge: rapid improvement supports diagnosis and confirms first-line treatment. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: psychotropic)

options.text: Restart paliperidone palmitate depot 100 mg intramuscularly today as first-line treatment of the relapse.
options.rationale: Antipsychotics can precipitate or worsen catatonia, particularly malignant catatonia, and are not first-line here. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: psychotropic)

options.text: Refer for urgent electroconvulsive therapy without trialling a benzodiazepine challenge first.
options.rationale: ECT is highly effective in catatonia but is second-line after a trial of lorazepam unless features are life-threatening. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: psychotropic)

options.text: Bromocriptine 5 mg orally three times daily targeting central dopamine receptor agonism over 7 days.
options.rationale: Bromocriptine is used in neuroleptic malignant syndrome, which is excluded here by normal temperature, normal CK, and no rigidity. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: psychotropic)

options.text: Olanzapine 10 mg orally now and reassessment at 24 hours of the catatonic features by the team.
options.rationale: Antipsychotics can precipitate or worsen catatonia and are not the diagnostic or therapeutic step at this stage. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: psychotropic)

explanation.summary: Catatonia is a treatable syndrome of motor and behavioural features (mutism, posturing, waxy flexibility, echolalia or echopraxia, negativism, stereotypy) recognised by Bush-Francis scoring. The lorazepam challenge with 1 to 2 mg IM is both diagnostic and therapeutic: marked improvement within 30 minutes supports the diagnosis and warrants regular lorazepam (often 4 to 16 mg daily in divided doses). Electroconvulsive therapy is second-line if lorazepam fails or for malignant catatonia (fever, autonomic instability, rhabdomyolysis). Antipsychotics may worsen catatonia and are generally avoided in the acute phase.
key_points: Lorazepam 1 to 2 mg IM as the standard catatonia challenge.
Antipsychotics can precipitate or worsen catatonia in the acute phase.
ECT is second-line, and first-line in malignant catatonia with autonomic instability.
explanation.pearls: Catatonia plus fever, autonomic instability, and rising CK should be treated as malignant catatonia and referred for urgent ECT rather than persisting with benzodiazepines.

stem:
A 27-year-old man is referred to your community mental health service. Over the last 3 years he has had two clearly defined manic episodes lasting 4 to 6 weeks with elevated mood, decreased need for sleep, grandiose delusions, and pressured speech, each requiring inpatient admission. Between episodes, in periods totalling over 12 months out of the last 3 years, he has had persistent auditory hallucinations of a derogatory commentary voice and persecutory delusions about being followed by ASIO, without prominent mood symptoms during that time. He is currently euthymic on valproate 1000 mg daily but still hears the voice. Substance use, organic causes, and recent stressors have been excluded.

The team is preparing his diagnosis and treatment plan.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 76/min, blood pressure 124/78 mmHg, respiratory rate 14/min, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.7°C
data_table.Examination: Euthymic, organised speech; reports persecutory belief about being monitored and ongoing voices
data_table.Investigations: FBC, U+E, LFTs, TFTs, B12, folate, and CRP normal; CT brain normal; urine drug screen negative

lead_in: What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.text: Bipolar I disorder with mood-congruent psychotic features confined to episodes of severe mania.
options.rationale: Persistent psychotic symptoms across 12 cumulative months between mood episodes excludes simple bipolar I with psychotic features. (Source: RANZCP schizophrenia guideline)

options.text: Schizoaffective disorder bipolar type, because psychotic symptoms persist outside mood episodes.
options.rationale: DSM-5 schizoaffective disorder requires at least 2 weeks of psychotic symptoms in the absence of major mood symptoms during the lifetime of illness. (Source: RANZCP schizophrenia guideline)

options.text: Schizophrenia with comorbid recurrent major depressive disorder rather than schizoaffective disorder.
options.rationale: Clear discrete manic episodes meeting bipolar criteria favour schizoaffective bipolar type over schizophrenia plus depression. (Source: RANZCP schizophrenia guideline)

options.text: Delusional disorder coexisting with bipolar I disorder, because the delusions are non-bizarre persistent.
options.rationale: Delusional disorder requires functioning outside the delusion to be relatively preserved and excludes prominent hallucinations. (Source: RANZCP schizophrenia guideline)

options.text: Substance-induced psychotic disorder with recurrent affective episodes triggered by past stimulant use.
options.rationale: Urine drug screen is negative and the symptoms persist outside any substance use, excluding this diagnosis. (Source: RANZCP schizophrenia guideline)

explanation.summary: DSM-5 schizoaffective disorder requires (a) an uninterrupted period of illness during which there is a major mood episode (depressive or manic) concurrent with Criterion A of schizophrenia; (b) at least 2 weeks of delusions or hallucinations during the lifetime of illness in the absence of a major mood episode; (c) mood episodes present for the majority of the total duration of illness; (d) not better explained by substance use or other medical condition. Persistent psychosis during 12 cumulative euthymic months distinguishes schizoaffective disorder from bipolar I with psychotic features.
key_points: Schizoaffective bipolar type requires at least 2 weeks of psychosis without mood symptoms in the lifetime.
Mood symptoms must be present for the majority of total illness duration.
Bipolar I with psychotic features confines psychosis to mood episodes.
explanation.pearls: Document the timing of psychosis relative to mood episodes carefully across the lifetime course; the diagnosis hinges on whether psychotic symptoms outlast mood episodes by at least 2 weeks.

stem:
A 31-year-old woman with bipolar I disorder, two prior manic episodes (one with psychotic features), and two prior depressive episodes, has been stable on sodium valproate 1500 mg daily for 4 years with no episodes. She presents to your perinatal psychiatry clinic with a positive home pregnancy test today. Her last menstrual period was 6 weeks ago. She had not been planning pregnancy. She is otherwise well, has no current mood symptoms, takes folate 500 micrograms daily, and lives with a supportive partner. She is well engaged with treatment, has private health insurance, and has no comorbid substance use. She is asking what to do about her medication.

Her most recent bloods are 2 months old.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 78/min, blood pressure 116/72 mmHg, respiratory rate 14/min, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.7°C
data_table.Examination: Euthymic, normal mental state examination; no neurological abnormality
data_table.Investigations: Bedside beta-hCG positive; pelvic ultrasound to be arranged; FBC, U+E, LFTs, and TSH 2 months ago all normal; valproate level 480 micromol/L
data_table.Medications: Sodium valproate 1500 mg daily; folate 500 micrograms daily

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Continue valproate at current dose because abrupt change risks a relapse during organogenesis.
options.rationale: Valproate carries 10% major congenital malformation and 30 to 40% neurodevelopmental disability rates and is contraindicated in pregnancy unless no alternative. (Source: RANZCP perinatal mood disorder guideline)

options.text: Stop valproate abruptly today and reintroduce only if a manic relapse occurs during the pregnancy.
options.rationale: Abrupt cessation of valproate without substitution carries about 50 percent risk of relapse in the first trimester. (Source: RANZCP perinatal mood disorder guideline)

options.text: Cross-titrate valproate to quetiapine over 4 weeks, increase folate to 5 mg daily, and arrange dating scan.
options.rationale: Valproate carries 10% major malformation risk and 30 to 40% neurodevelopmental risk; substitution by a safer mood stabiliser is recommended. (Source: RANZCP perinatal mood disorder guideline)

options.text: Switch to lithium carbonate 750 mg at night during the first trimester then return to valproate later.
options.rationale: Lithium during organogenesis carries a small Ebstein anomaly risk and is generally avoided in the first trimester if a safer alternative exists. (Source: RANZCP perinatal mood disorder guideline)

options.text: Add lamotrigine 25 mg daily to valproate, intending to taper valproate after the first trimester ends.
options.rationale: Valproate strongly inhibits lamotrigine clearance, doubling Stevens-Johnson syndrome risk; combining the two during titration is unsafe. (Source: AMH antiepileptic interactions)

explanation.summary: Sodium valproate has the highest teratogenic and neurodevelopmental risk of any mood stabiliser: approximately 10% major congenital malformations (notably neural tube, cardiac, and craniofacial) and 30 to 40% rate of neurodevelopmental disability including reduced IQ and autism spectrum disorder. Australian and TGA pregnancy prevention requirements mean valproate should not be used in women of childbearing potential unless no alternative works. When unplanned pregnancy occurs, cross-titrate to a safer agent (quetiapine, lamotrigine if not on valproate, or lithium balancing first trimester Ebstein risk against later trimester safety) over 2 to 4 weeks, increase folate to 5 mg daily, arrange dating ultrasound, and refer to perinatal psychiatry.
key_points: Valproate is contraindicated in pregnancy unless no alternative exists.
Cross-titrate over 2 to 4 weeks to avoid relapse; quetiapine and lamotrigine are commonly substituted.
Increase folate to 5 mg daily for 12 weeks of pregnancy on any anticonvulsant.
explanation.pearls: If valproate truly cannot be substituted, the patient must be counselled about the residual risk and offered detailed morphology scanning at 18 to 20 weeks plus paediatric neurodevelopmental follow-up.

stem: A 52-year-old woman with bipolar I disorder has taken lithium 1000 mg nightly for 18 years with excellent mood stability. Her eGFR was 78 mL/min/1.73m2 two years ago and is 48 mL/min/1.73m2 today on a confirmatory repeat four weeks after the first reading. She has no acute illness, is well hydrated, and is on no nephrotoxic medications. Her ACR is 0.8 mg/mmol and renal ultrasound shows mildly bulky kidneys without obstruction. Latest lithium level 0.74 mmol/L (target 0.6-0.8 mmol/L). She has had no manic or depressive episodes for 11 years.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 72, BP 132/82 mmHg, RR 14, SpO2 99%, temperature 36.6°C
data_table.Examination: Body mass index 26, no peripheral oedema, no tremor
data_table.Investigations: eGFR 48 mL/min/1.73m2 (down from 78 two years ago), ACR 0.8 mg/mmol, lithium level 0.74 mmol/L, TSH 2.4 mU/L, calcium 2.36 mmol/L, renal ultrasound bulky kidneys without obstruction
data_table.Medications: Lithium carbonate 1000 mg nocte for 18 years

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Refer to nephrology and psychiatry to discuss switching from lithium to an alternative
options.rationale: Sustained eGFR decline below 60 mL/min/1.73m2 on confirmatory repeat with otherwise unexplained chronic kidney disease in a long-term lithium user prompts joint nephrology and psychiatry review to discuss switching. RANZCP recommends collaborative decision-making with the patient. (Source: RANZCP mood disorders CPG 2020)

options.text: Reduce lithium dose to 500 mg nightly and recheck eGFR in three months
options.rationale: Lower lithium dose does not reverse established interstitial nephritis and risks relapse if the level falls below the therapeutic window. (Source: RANZCP mood disorders CPG 2020)

options.text: Continue lithium unchanged and recheck eGFR every 12 months as usual care
options.rationale: Confirmed eGFR decline to under 60 mL/min/1.73m2 requires escalation in monitoring frequency and consideration of switch, not routine annual review. (Source: RANZCP mood disorders CPG 2020)

options.text: Stop lithium abruptly today and start sodium valproate 500 mg twice daily
options.rationale: Abrupt lithium cessation carries a high relapse risk and valproate is teratogenic; switching is a planned discussion, not an emergency. (Source: RANZCP mood disorders CPG 2020)

options.text: Add amiloride to protect renal function and continue current lithium dose
options.rationale: Amiloride is used for lithium-induced nephrogenic diabetes insipidus, not for chronic interstitial nephropathy with falling eGFR. (Source: RANZCP mood disorders CPG 2020)

explanation.summary: Long-term lithium causes chronic interstitial nephritis in a minority of users, often slowly progressive after 10-15 years. Sustained eGFR decline below 60 mL/min/1.73m2 (CKD G3a) on confirmatory repeat warrants joint nephrology and psychiatry review. Continuing lithium is sometimes the best option for a patient with no alternative mood stabiliser tolerated, but the conversation must occur. Dose reduction does not reverse established nephropathy. Abrupt cessation carries high relapse risk and is contraindicated.
key_points: Lithium nephropathy: progressive interstitial nephritis over 10+ years
Sustained eGFR under 60 mL/min/1.73m2 triggers nephrology/psychiatry joint review
Lithium cessation, if undertaken, is gradual over months
explanation.pearls: The decision to continue lithium with CKD weighs relapse risk (high) against rate of further renal decline (often modest) - shared decision making with both teams is the standard.

subtopic_detail: Valproate in a woman of reproductive age
stem: A 26-year-old woman with bipolar I disorder has been stable on sodium valproate 1000 mg daily for three years after one severe manic episode. She attends review and tells you she has been in a new relationship for four months and would like to stop her copper IUD and try for a pregnancy in the next year. She has no current symptoms of mania or depression. She was previously intolerant of lithium (severe tremor at therapeutic levels) but has never tried other agents. She has no other medical conditions.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 72, BP 116/74 mmHg, RR 14, SpO2 99%, temperature 36.6°C
data_table.Examination: Mental state stable, no thought disorder, mood euthymic, no tremor
data_table.Investigations: Valproate level 380 micromol/L (within therapeutic range), LFTs and FBC normal, beta-hCG negative today

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Continue valproate during conception and counsel on the 10% major malformation risk
options.rationale: Valproate exposure in early pregnancy carries about 10% major congenital malformation rate and about 30-40% neurodevelopmental impairment. It is contraindicated in pregnancy and in women planning pregnancy unless no alternative. (Source: TGA valproate pregnancy prevention program)

options.text: Switch to lamotrigine before conception with gradual cross-titration and high-dose folate
options.rationale: Lamotrigine is the preferred maintenance mood stabiliser in women planning pregnancy who have not tolerated lithium. Cross-titration with valproate is gradual, contraception is continued until stabilisation, and high-dose folate 5 mg daily is added preconception. (Source: RANZCP mood disorders CPG 2020)

options.text: Switch back to lithium and accept the previous tremor as cosmetic only
options.rationale: Severe tremor at therapeutic level was previously intolerable and is not cosmetic; lamotrigine is the more rational option here. (Source: RANZCP mood disorders CPG 2020)

options.text: Stop all mood stabilisers preconception and restart only if a relapse occurs
options.rationale: Untreated bipolar I disorder relapse rate without prophylaxis is high, particularly during pregnancy and postpartum. (Source: RANZCP mood disorders CPG 2020)

options.text: Continue valproate and add quetiapine 300 mg nightly as additional cover
options.rationale: Adding a second agent does not solve the teratogenicity problem; the issue is valproate itself, not the level of cover. (Source: RANZCP mood disorders CPG 2020)

explanation.summary: Sodium valproate is contraindicated in pregnancy and in women planning pregnancy because of a roughly 10% major malformation rate and a 30-40% rate of neurodevelopmental impairment. The TGA pregnancy prevention program requires effective contraception, annual review, and documented counselling. For bipolar maintenance in women planning pregnancy who do not tolerate lithium, lamotrigine is the preferred switch, cross-titrated gradually with continued contraception until stable, and combined with high-dose folate 5 mg daily preconception.
key_points: Valproate: 10% major malformation rate, 30-40% neurodevelopmental impairment
TGA pregnancy prevention program mandates documented annual review
Lamotrigine is the preferred bipolar maintenance in pregnancy planning
explanation.pearls: Folate 5 mg daily preconception is for women on enzyme-inducing antiepileptics or those at high neural tube defect risk - not just 0.5 mg.

stem: A 27-year-old software engineer has been diagnosed by a psychiatrist with adult ADHD combined presentation. She has childhood symptoms documented in school reports, persistent inattention and impulsivity in adulthood, and significant occupational impairment. She has no history of cardiovascular disease, no substance use disorder, and no psychotic disorder. She has well-controlled generalised anxiety on sertraline 100 mg daily. She has a current Australian driver licence and her resting blood pressure is 124/78 mmHg with pulse 72.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 72, BP 124/78 mmHg, RR 14, SpO2 99%, temperature 36.7°C
data_table.Examination: Mental state alert and oriented, no thought disorder, mood mildly anxious but stable
data_table.Investigations: ECG sinus rhythm rate 72, no QT prolongation, no LVH; baseline TFTs normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first-line pharmacotherapy?

options.text: Methylphenidate immediate release titrated against effect and tolerability
options.rationale: Long-acting preparations are preferred first-line in adult ADHD to reduce diversion and improve adherence; immediate release is reserved for top-up. (Source: Australian Evidence-Based Clinical Practice Guideline for ADHD 2022)
source_refs: Australian Evidence-Based Clinical Practice Guideline for ADHD 2022

options.text: Atomoxetine 40 mg daily titrated to 80 mg over four weeks as initial therapy
options.rationale: Atomoxetine is second-line; reserved for stimulant intolerance, contraindication, or substance use disorder concern. (Source: Australian Evidence-Based Clinical Practice Guideline for ADHD 2022)
source_refs: Australian Evidence-Based Clinical Practice Guideline for ADHD 2022

options.text: Long-acting lisdexamfetamine started at 30 mg daily and titrated weekly
options.rationale: Long-acting stimulant (lisdexamfetamine or extended-release methylphenidate) is first-line in adult ADHD in Australia. Lisdexamfetamine has a low abuse potential due to lysine prodrug structure. (Source: Australian Evidence-Based Clinical Practice Guideline for ADHD 2022)
source_refs: Australian Evidence-Based Clinical Practice Guideline for ADHD 2022

options.text: Guanfacine extended release 1 mg daily titrated to 4 mg over six weeks
options.rationale: Guanfacine is third-line in adults and primarily used in children/adolescents. (Source: Australian Evidence-Based Clinical Practice Guideline for ADHD 2022)
source_refs: Australian Evidence-Based Clinical Practice Guideline for ADHD 2022

options.text: Bupropion 150 mg daily titrated to 300 mg over four weeks as monotherapy
options.rationale: Bupropion is not first-line for ADHD; reserved for selected cases or co-existing nicotine dependence. (Source: Australian Evidence-Based Clinical Practice Guideline for ADHD 2022)
source_refs: Australian Evidence-Based Clinical Practice Guideline for ADHD 2022

explanation.summary: Long-acting stimulants (lisdexamfetamine or extended-release methylphenidate) are first-line for adult ADHD per the Australian Evidence-Based Clinical Practice Guideline 2022. Lisdexamfetamine is a lysine prodrug, requiring intestinal conversion to active dexamfetamine, which reduces abuse potential. Baseline cardiovascular assessment (history, blood pressure, pulse, ECG when indicated) is required before initiation. Atomoxetine and guanfacine are second/third-line.
key_points: Long-acting stimulant first-line in adult ADHD in Australia
Baseline BP, pulse, and cardiovascular history are required
Atomoxetine reserved for stimulant intolerance or substance use concerns
explanation.pearls: Most state stimulant prescribing rules require a paediatrician or psychiatrist for initiation; GPs continue care under shared care arrangements.

sources.label: Australian Evidence-Based Clinical Practice Guideline for ADHD 2022

stem: A 22-year-old man with first-episode psychosis is admitted to a psychiatric ward. Over 48 hours he becomes mute, immobile in a wax-flexible posture (he maintains an arm raised when positioned), and resistant to being moved. He has not eaten or drunk for 18 hours and his sodium is 134 mmol/L. He has been receiving risperidone 2 mg daily for four days. He has no fever, normal vitals, no rigidity, no autonomic instability, no rhabdomyolysis. The Bush-Francis Catatonia Rating Scale screen is positive.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 76, BP 122/78 mmHg, RR 14, SpO2 99%, temperature 36.7°C
data_table.Examination: Mute, immobile, waxy flexibility, posturing arm maintained when raised, no rigidity, no fever
data_table.Investigations: Sodium 134 mmol/L, creatine kinase 110 U/L (normal), Bush-Francis screen positive
data_table.Medications: Risperidone 2 mg daily commenced four days ago

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Refer urgently for electroconvulsive therapy without prior medication trial
options.rationale: ECT is highly effective in catatonia but is reserved for failure of lorazepam or for malignant catatonia; lorazepam challenge precedes ECT. (Source: RANZCP psychosis CPG 2016)

options.text: Bromocriptine 2.5 mg three times daily with dantrolene for NMS suspicion
options.rationale: There is no fever, no rigidity, and normal creatine kinase. NMS is unlikely and dopamine agonists are not the first move in catatonia without NMS. (Source: RANZCP psychosis CPG 2016)

options.text: Continue risperidone and add diazepam 5 mg orally three times daily
options.rationale: Antipsychotics can worsen catatonia (and may precipitate NMS); the standard is to pause the antipsychotic and use scheduled lorazepam. Oral diazepam is also slower acting than IV/IM lorazepam in this acute context. (Source: RANZCP psychosis CPG 2016)

options.text: Lorazepam 2 mg IV with reassessment of motor signs after 10 minutes
options.rationale: A lorazepam challenge (1-2 mg IV or IM, sometimes followed by a second dose) is both diagnostic and the first-line treatment for catatonia in adults. Response within 5-15 minutes confirms catatonia and supports scheduled benzodiazepine therapy. (Source: RANZCP psychosis CPG 2016)

options.text: Start IV thiamine 300 mg three times daily for suspected Wernicke onset
options.rationale: Although IV thiamine is appropriate in any unwell, malnourished patient (and should be considered here for nutrition), it does not treat catatonia. (Source: RANZCP psychosis CPG 2016)

explanation.summary: Catatonia is recognised on the Bush-Francis Catatonia Rating Scale and includes mutism, immobility, waxy flexibility, and posturing. The lorazepam challenge (1-2 mg IV or IM) is diagnostic and therapeutic; response within minutes supports scheduled benzodiazepine. Antipsychotic medication is paused because of NMS risk. ECT is reserved for lorazepam failure or for malignant catatonia (fever, autonomic instability, rhabdomyolysis). Thiamine is supportive for nutrition but does not treat catatonia.
key_points: Lorazepam challenge 1-2 mg IV/IM is diagnostic and first-line treatment
Pause antipsychotic medication to avoid NMS precipitation
ECT reserved for lorazepam failure or malignant catatonia
explanation.pearls: If response to first lorazepam dose is partial, a second 2 mg dose 30 minutes later is given before declaring failure - catatonia is benzodiazepine-responsive in roughly 70% of adults.

stem: A 28-year-old woman is brought in by ambulance after deliberate ingestion of an unknown quantity of amitriptyline approximately three hours ago. She is drowsy but rousable, GCS 12 (E3V4M5), with dilated pupils and dry skin. She has had one generalised tonic-clonic seizure on arrival lasting 60 seconds that terminated after IV midazolam 5 mg. Pulse rate 124 sinus, blood pressure 92/58 mmHg, respiratory rate 22, SpO2 96% on 6 L Hudson, temperature 37.4°C. Initial ECG shows sinus tachycardia with QRS 132 milliseconds and a terminal R wave in aVR of 4 mm.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 124 sinus, BP 92/58 mmHg, RR 22, SpO2 96% on 6 L Hudson, temperature 37.4°C
data_table.Examination: GCS 12, dilated pupils, dry skin, hyperreflexia, intact gag reflex
data_table.Investigations: ECG QRS 132 ms with terminal R aVR 4 mm; ABG pH 7.30, pCO2 30 mmHg, HCO3 18 mmol/L, lactate 3.2 mmol/L; paracetamol level negative
data_table.Medications: IV midazolam 5 mg given for seizure; IV access x2 with normal saline 500 mL

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: IV activated charcoal 50 g via nasogastric tube as decontamination measure
options.rationale: Charcoal is considered within one hour of ingestion in alert co-operative patients; at three hours with reduced GCS and seizure risk it is not appropriate. (Source: Toxicology Wiki Calvey TCA 2024)

options.text: IV flumazenil 0.2 mg titrated to reversal of central anticholinergic effect
options.rationale: Flumazenil is contraindicated in TCA co-ingestion because it lowers the seizure threshold; she has already seized. (Source: Toxicology Wiki Calvey TCA 2024)

options.text: IV phenytoin 18 mg/kg loading dose to reduce TCA-induced seizure recurrence
options.rationale: Phenytoin is a class IB agent and worsens TCA cardiotoxicity by adding to sodium-channel blockade. Levetiracetam is the preferred second seizure agent if needed. (Source: Toxicology Wiki Calvey TCA 2024)

options.text: IV lipid emulsion 20% 100 mL bolus then infusion at 0.25 mL/kg/min
options.rationale: Lipid emulsion is reserved for refractory cardiotoxicity (cardiac arrest, persistent shock) after sodium bicarbonate; it is not first-line. (Source: Toxicology Wiki Calvey TCA 2024)

options.text: IV sodium bicarbonate 100 mmol bolus targeting QRS narrowing and pH 7.50-7.55
options.rationale: QRS above 100 ms in TCA overdose indicates sodium-channel blockade requiring sodium bicarbonate. Boluses of 1-2 mmol/kg are repeated until QRS narrows below 100 ms and arterial pH reaches 7.50-7.55. (Source: Toxicology Wiki Calvey TCA 2024)

explanation.summary: TCA overdose causes sodium-channel blockade (widened QRS, right axis deviation, terminal R in aVR) plus anticholinergic features. QRS above 100 ms or aVR R-wave above 3 mm triggers IV sodium bicarbonate 1-2 mmol/kg boluses, repeated until QRS narrows below 100 ms and pH reaches 7.50-7.55. Flumazenil is contraindicated. Phenytoin worsens cardiotoxicity. Lipid emulsion is reserved for refractory toxicity. Activated charcoal is only useful within an hour and only if airway is protected.
key_points: QRS above 100 ms in TCA overdose triggers IV sodium bicarbonate 1-2 mmol/kg
Target arterial pH 7.50-7.55 and QRS below 100 ms
Phenytoin contraindicated; flumazenil contraindicated
explanation.pearls: In TCA overdose, a terminal R wave of 3 mm or more in aVR is a sensitive early marker of cardiotoxicity - check aVR before relying on QRS duration.

stem: A 45-year-old man with major depressive disorder (currently in remission on sertraline 100 mg) attends his GP for smoking cessation support. He has smoked 25 cigarettes daily for 22 years and has tried nicotine patches twice with brief success but relapse within three months each time. He is highly motivated to quit, has no cardiovascular disease, and has no recent suicidal ideation. He asks about the strongest pharmacotherapy option available in Australia.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 76, BP 132/82 mmHg, RR 14, SpO2 98%, temperature 36.7°C
data_table.Examination: Body mass index 26, no neurological deficit, mental state euthymic
data_table.Investigations: Carbon monoxide breath test 16 ppm, fagerstrom test for nicotine dependence score 8

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first-line cessation pharmacotherapy?

options.text: Varenicline titrated over the first 7 days and continued for 12 weeks total
options.rationale: Varenicline has higher cessation rates than NRT or bupropion in network meta-analyses. The 2008 EAGLES trial showed no increased neuropsychiatric event rate in stable depression. RACGP supports varenicline first-line in dependent smokers without recent psychiatric instability. (Source: RACGP smoking cessation guidelines 2021)

options.text: Combination NRT patch plus short-acting gum at routine doses for 12 weeks
options.rationale: Combination NRT is reasonable but historically less effective than varenicline in dependent smokers; he has also failed NRT twice. (Source: RACGP smoking cessation guidelines 2021)

options.text: Bupropion 150 mg twice daily commenced 1-2 weeks before quit date
options.rationale: Bupropion is effective but contraindicated in patients with seizure risk and is less effective than varenicline in head-to-head comparisons. (Source: RACGP smoking cessation guidelines 2021)

options.text: Nortriptyline 75 mg nightly as a second-line antidepressant-based option
options.rationale: Nortriptyline is second-line and rarely used now; not first-line for a stable patient who has options. (Source: RACGP smoking cessation guidelines 2021)

options.text: E-cigarettes via prescription pathway as primary pharmacological strategy
options.rationale: Nicotine vaping is now prescription-only in Australia for cessation when first-line therapy fails; not the primary first-line strategy. (Source: TGA nicotine vaping products 2024)

explanation.summary: Varenicline has the highest cessation success rate in head-to-head trials and is first-line for dependent smokers per the RACGP smoking cessation guidelines, including those with stable depression after the EAGLES trial showed no increased neuropsychiatric event rate. Combination NRT is the alternative when varenicline is unavailable or declined. Bupropion is effective but contraindicated in seizure risk. Nicotine vaping products are now prescription-only second-line in Australia.
key_points: Varenicline first-line in dependent smokers including stable depression
Combination NRT alternative first-line option
Nicotine vaping is prescription-only second-line in Australia
explanation.pearls: Set quit date 7-14 days into varenicline titration; nausea is the most common early side effect and improves with taking the dose after food.

stem: A 24-year-old has had three discrete episodes over 18 months. Two episodes featured elevated mood with reduced need for sleep, grandiose delusions, and pressured speech for two weeks each, and resolved on a mood stabiliser. The third episode (most recent) featured persistent auditory hallucinations and persecutory delusions for four weeks WITHOUT any mood symptoms before mood symptoms (low mood, anhedonia, hopelessness) supervened for the next three weeks. She has had no substance use, no thyroid disease, and a normal MRI brain. She is now stable on lithium and risperidone.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 72, BP 118/74 mmHg, RR 14, SpO2 99%, temperature 36.7°C
data_table.Examination: Currently euthymic, no thought disorder, no first-rank symptoms today
data_table.Investigations: TSH 1.8 mU/L, urine drug screen negative on multiple occasions, MRI brain normal
data_table.Medications: Lithium 750 mg daily, risperidone 2 mg daily

lead_in: What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.text: Bipolar I disorder with mood-congruent psychotic features only
options.rationale: Psychosis persisting for at least two weeks without mood symptoms during the same illness distinguishes schizoaffective from bipolar with mood-congruent psychosis. (Source: DSM-5-TR text revision)

options.text: Schizoaffective disorder bipolar type meeting full DSM-5-TR criteria
options.rationale: Schizoaffective disorder requires a major mood episode concurrent with active-phase schizophrenia symptoms PLUS at least 2 weeks of psychosis without prominent mood symptoms during the same lifetime episode. The bipolar subtype applies because manic episodes have occurred. (Source: DSM-5-TR text revision)

options.text: Schizophrenia with co-existing major depressive disorder of mild severity
options.rationale: Two clear manic episodes preclude a schizophrenia plus MDD construction; the affective component meets bipolar criteria. (Source: DSM-5-TR text revision)

options.text: Brief psychotic disorder followed by an unrelated major depressive episode
options.rationale: Brief psychotic disorder lasts less than one month and does not capture the longitudinal pattern with manic and depressive episodes. (Source: DSM-5-TR text revision)

options.text: Substance- or medication-induced psychotic disorder ruled in on history
options.rationale: Repeated negative urine drug screens and an established pattern over 18 months argue against a substance-induced diagnosis. (Source: DSM-5-TR text revision)

explanation.summary: Schizoaffective disorder requires (a) an uninterrupted period of illness during which a major mood episode is concurrent with criterion-A schizophrenia symptoms, (b) at least two weeks of delusions or hallucinations in the absence of a major mood episode during the same lifetime illness, and (c) mood-episode symptoms present for the majority of the active and residual periods. The bipolar subtype applies when manic episodes occur; the depressive subtype applies when only depressive episodes do.
key_points: Schizoaffective: two-week period of psychosis without mood symptoms is the key discriminator from bipolar with psychotic features
Bipolar subtype if any lifetime manic episode
Substance use and primary medical causes must be excluded
explanation.pearls: Most psychiatrists capture the 'two weeks of pure psychosis' criterion with a detailed week-by-week longitudinal chart of the illness, not a single cross-sectional interview.

subtopic_detail: ECT consent and side effect counselling
stem:
A 58-year-old woman with severe melancholic depression and active suicidal intent has failed two adequate antidepressant trials and one augmentation. She is barely eating and has lost 8 kg in six weeks. The consultant psychiatrist has recommended a course of bilateral electroconvulsive therapy. She is competent to consent. She wishes to understand the most likely adverse effects before signing. She asks specifically about memory.

The registrar is undertaking the consent discussion.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 88, BP 118/76 mmHg, RR 14, SpO2 98%, temperature 36.6°C
data_table.Examination: Psychomotor retardation, flattened affect, no neurological deficit
data_table.Investigations: Bloods within normal limits; ECG normal sinus rhythm; CT brain normal
data_table.Medications: Mirtazapine 45 mg, lithium 750 mg/day, lorazepam 1 mg PRN

lead_in: Which adverse effect should be emphasised as the most common and persistent?

options.text: Memory impairment around the treatment period, usually improving in months
options.rationale: Memory disturbance is the most common ECT side effect and the one most relevant to consent; it usually improves but may persist for some events around treatment. (Source: RANZCP ECT Position Statement 2022)

options.text: Permanent persistent global cognitive impairment in over half of patients
options.rationale: Persistent global cognitive impairment is uncommon; baseline cognition typically returns by 6 months. (Source: RANZCP ECT Position Statement 2022)

options.text: Brain damage with structural MRI changes after every treatment session
options.rationale: There is no evidence of structural brain damage from ECT on MRI or histopathology. (Source: RANZCP ECT Position Statement 2022)

options.text: Cardiac arrhythmia with mortality risk above 1 in 100 sessions
options.rationale: ECT mortality is approximately 2 per 100,000 treatments, similar to general anaesthetic alone. (Source: RANZCP ECT Position Statement 2022)

options.text: Seizure threshold rise that always requires switching to ketamine anaesthesia
options.rationale: Seizure threshold does rise over a course but is managed by adjusting stimulus dose; ketamine substitution is for specific resistant cases. (Source: RANZCP ECT Position Statement 2022)

explanation.summary: Modern ECT is performed under general anaesthetic with muscle relaxation, and remains the most effective treatment for severe depression. The most common adverse effect is cognitive: transient confusion immediately post-treatment, then anterograde and retrograde amnesia mostly for events around the treatment period. Most patients recover baseline cognition within weeks to months. Mortality is comparable to general anaesthetic alone (approximately 2 per 100,000 treatments). Headache and muscle ache occur in around 25%.
key_points: Memory effects are the dominant ECT adverse effect
Mortality is comparable to GA alone
Cognitive recovery typically within months
explanation.pearls: Bilateral ECT has greater cognitive impact than right unilateral; many AU services begin with right unilateral and switch only for non-response after 6 treatments.

stem:
A 24-year-old woman is referred to the community mental health team with a two-year pattern of unstable mood, intense fear of abandonment, repeated self-cutting following arguments with her partner, two previous brief admissions following overdoses, and chronic feelings of emptiness. She meets DSM-5 criteria for borderline personality disorder. She has tried sertraline and quetiapine without sustained benefit. She is currently working part time. She has no current intent.

She asks what she should be offered now.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 76, BP 118/72 mmHg, RR 14, SpO2 99%, temperature 36.6°C
data_table.Examination: Multiple healed superficial forearm scars, mood reactive, no current intent
data_table.Investigations: Bloods within normal limits, urine drug screen negative

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first-line treatment recommendation?

options.text: Structured DBT or mentalisation-based psychotherapy as primary treatment
options.rationale: AU NHMRC and RANZCP guidelines specify structured psychotherapy as the primary treatment for BPD; medications have limited role and are not first-line. (Source: NHMRC BPD Clinical Practice Guideline)

options.text: Lithium 750 mg/day for affective instability as monotherapy
options.rationale: Lithium does not have an evidence base for BPD as monotherapy; psychotherapy is primary. (Source: NHMRC BPD Clinical Practice Guideline)

options.text: Long-term admission to a tertiary inpatient psychiatric unit
options.rationale: Prolonged inpatient care for BPD is associated with regression and dependence; structured outpatient psychotherapy is preferred. (Source: NHMRC BPD Clinical Practice Guideline)

options.text: Increase quetiapine to 300 mg daily as long-term treatment
options.rationale: Antipsychotics have only short-term and symptom-targeted role in BPD; long-term use is not recommended. (Source: NHMRC BPD Clinical Practice Guideline)

options.text: Cease all pharmacotherapy and offer supportive case management only
options.rationale: Supportive management alone is not sufficient when structured psychotherapy is available; AU guidance specifies psychotherapy as primary. (Source: NHMRC BPD Clinical Practice Guideline)

explanation.summary: Borderline personality disorder is best managed with structured evidence-based psychotherapy. AU NHMRC and RANZCP guidelines list DBT, mentalisation-based therapy, schema-focused therapy, and transference-focused psychotherapy as effective. Pharmacotherapy is not first-line; specific target symptoms (impulsivity, mood instability) may be treated symptomatically with short courses. Brief admissions are appropriate for crisis stabilisation but prolonged admissions are not recommended.
key_points: Structured psychotherapy is primary BPD treatment
Medications are symptom-targeted, not core
Avoid prolonged admissions
explanation.pearls: DBT skills training in groups reduces self-harm and emergency presentations by approximately 50% within 12 months when completed.

stem:
A 28-year-old presents with sudden left-sided weakness after a confrontation at work. Neurological examination shows give-way weakness, Hoover sign positive, and inconsistent power on distraction. MRI brain and cervical cord are normal. The patient appears distressed and concerned about the symptoms. There is no clear external incentive identified. She lives independently and is employed. She has no history of inconsistent presentations across hospitals.

The neurology team has referred for opinion.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 84, BP 116/72 mmHg, RR 16, SpO2 99%, temperature 36.7°C
data_table.Examination: Give-way weakness left arm and leg, positive Hoover sign, inconsistent power on distraction
data_table.Investigations: MRI brain and cervical cord normal; routine bloods within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.text: Functional neurological disorder (conversion disorder)
options.rationale: Positive Hoover sign and inconsistent neurology with patient distress and no external incentive support a positive diagnosis of functional neurological disorder. (Source: DSM-5-TR; UK Functional Neurological Disorder consensus)
source_refs: DSM-5-TR; UK Functional Neurological Disorder consensus

options.text: Malingering with an external secondary gain motivation
options.rationale: Malingering requires an external incentive (avoiding work, financial gain, legal); none is present here. (Source: DSM-5-TR; UK Functional Neurological Disorder consensus)
source_refs: DSM-5-TR; UK Functional Neurological Disorder consensus

options.text: Factitious disorder with deliberate symptom fabrication for sick role
options.rationale: Factitious disorder requires conscious symptom fabrication for the sick role; clinical pattern here is involuntary distress without fabrication. (Source: DSM-5-TR; UK Functional Neurological Disorder consensus)
source_refs: DSM-5-TR; UK Functional Neurological Disorder consensus

options.text: Acute ischaemic stroke not yet visible on early imaging
options.rationale: Hoover positive and distractibility are not stroke findings; normal MRI within hours of presentation does not exclude stroke but inconsistent power on distraction is functional. (Source: DSM-5-TR; UK Functional Neurological Disorder consensus)
source_refs: DSM-5-TR; UK Functional Neurological Disorder consensus

options.text: Multiple sclerosis presenting with first demyelinating event
options.rationale: MS would not produce Hoover positive findings or distractibility; MRI is normal. (Source: DSM-5-TR; UK Functional Neurological Disorder consensus)
source_refs: DSM-5-TR; UK Functional Neurological Disorder consensus

explanation.summary: Functional neurological disorder is a positive diagnosis based on internal inconsistency of neurological signs (Hoover sign for leg weakness, tremor entrainment, give-way power, distractibility). It is not a diagnosis of exclusion. Patients are typically distressed and concerned. Malingering and factitious disorder differ by conscious symptom production; only malingering has external incentive. Treatment is multidisciplinary including physiotherapy, psychoeducation, and CBT.
key_points: FND is a positive diagnosis using internal inconsistency
Malingering needs external incentive
Factitious is conscious for sick role
explanation.pearls: Naming the diagnosis clearly using positive signs (Hoover) reduces healthcare utilisation more than ambiguous explanations - patients often improve when given the diagnosis and a referral to FND physiotherapy.

sources.label: DSM-5-TR; UK Functional Neurological Disorder consensus

stem:
A 31-year-old woman presents requesting assessment for autism. She reports lifelong difficulties with social interpretation, sensory sensitivities to noise and clothing, intense special interests in marine biology since childhood, and exhaustion after social interactions that she finds requires extensive preparation. She has high academic achievement and is employed as a librarian. She has previously been diagnosed with social anxiety and persistent depressive disorder. She scores 138 on the CAT-Q (camouflaging autistic traits). The GP letter notes apparent eye contact and conventional conversation in the consult.

The psychiatry registrar is reviewing referral options.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 76, BP 118/74 mmHg, RR 14, SpO2 99%, temperature 36.6°C
data_table.Examination: Mental state with appropriate but rehearsed-feeling social engagement
data_table.Investigations: AQ-50 score 39, CAT-Q 138

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Refer for structured ADOS-2 plus ADI-R assessment by an experienced clinician
options.rationale: AU national autism guideline mandates a structured diagnostic assessment using validated tools by an experienced clinician for adult diagnosis, especially given the masking presentation. (Source: NHMRC National Guideline for Autism Diagnosis 2018)
source_refs: NHMRC National Guideline for Autism Diagnosis 2018

options.text: Reassure that adult diagnosis is not useful and continue treating social anxiety
options.rationale: Adult diagnosis can provide identity, access to NDIS supports, and adjustment of treatment; dismissing the request is not consistent with AU guidance. (Source: NHMRC National Guideline for Autism Diagnosis 2018)
source_refs: NHMRC National Guideline for Autism Diagnosis 2018

options.text: Diagnose ASD based on the AQ-50 and CAT-Q screening results alone
options.rationale: Self-report screens cannot make a diagnosis; structured clinician-administered assessment is required. (Source: NHMRC National Guideline for Autism Diagnosis 2018)
source_refs: NHMRC National Guideline for Autism Diagnosis 2018

options.text: Order genetic chromosomal microarray testing before clinical assessment
options.rationale: Chromosomal microarray is offered after diagnosis when there are features of syndromic autism; it does not precede clinical diagnostic assessment. (Source: NHMRC National Guideline for Autism Diagnosis 2018)
source_refs: NHMRC National Guideline for Autism Diagnosis 2018

options.text: Start risperidone for autism-related symptoms before completing assessment
options.rationale: Risperidone is reserved for severe irritability and aggression in ASD, not core social features; it is never started before diagnosis. (Source: NHMRC National Guideline for Autism Diagnosis 2018)
source_refs: NHMRC National Guideline for Autism Diagnosis 2018

explanation.summary: Adult ASD diagnosis, especially in women, requires a structured assessment to overcome masking and camouflaging. The AU National Guideline recommends use of the ADOS-2 plus a developmental history (ADI-R or 3Di-Adult) by a clinician experienced in adult presentations. Self-report screens (AQ-50, RAADS-R, CAT-Q) are valuable indicators but cannot replace assessment. Diagnosis enables NDIS access and reframes prior misdiagnoses such as social anxiety or BPD.
key_points: Structured ADOS-2 + developmental history is the gold standard
Self-report screens do not diagnose
Female presentation often masks - require experienced clinician
explanation.pearls: Women diagnosed in adulthood have higher rates of co-occurring depression and PTSD than men, and benefit from autism-specific therapy rather than generic CBT.

sources.label: NHMRC National Guideline for Autism Diagnosis 2018

stem:
A 42-year-old man who arrived in Australia from Iraq four months ago presents to the GP with persistent headaches, body aches, palpitations, and disturbed sleep. He fled torture and incarceration in 2021. Through an interpreter, he says his head feels heavy and his chest feels tight. He cannot return to his country. He is supported by an asylum support service. He denies depressed mood when asked directly but reports nightmares and avoiding crowds. He is on a temporary protection visa.

A family member is in the room.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 88, BP 128/78 mmHg, RR 16, SpO2 99%, temperature 36.7°C
data_table.Examination: No focal neurology, cardiovascular and respiratory examinations within normal limits
data_table.Investigations: FBC, UEC, LFTs, TSH, B12, ferritin, vitamin D within normal limits; ECG sinus rhythm

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Professional interpreter (excluding family) and refugee trauma service referral
options.rationale: Refugee somatic complaints often mask PTSD; trauma history requires a professional interpreter without family present, and AU refugee trauma services (e.g. STARTTS, Foundation House) are the appropriate referral pathway. (Source: ASID and Australian Refugee Health Practice Guide)

options.text: Reassure normal investigations and discharge with no further follow-up
options.rationale: Somatic complaints in refugees often signal underlying PTSD; reassurance alone misses the diagnosis. (Source: Australian Refugee Health Practice Guide)

options.text: Use the family member as interpreter to discuss trauma history
options.rationale: Family interpreters compromise confidentiality, miss disclosure, and create harm; a professional interpreter is mandated. (Source: Australian Refugee Health Practice Guide)

options.text: Prescribe diazepam 5 mg three times daily for ongoing anxiety
options.rationale: Benzodiazepines worsen PTSD outcomes and carry dependence risk; they are not first-line. (Source: Australian Refugee Health Practice Guide)

options.text: Refer to general adult mental health service without trauma-informed expertise
options.rationale: Generic services may lack interpreters and trauma-specific therapies; specialist refugee services are the correct AU pathway. (Source: Australian Refugee Health Practice Guide)

explanation.summary: Refugees presenting with somatic complaints commonly have underlying PTSD, depression, or anxiety. Confidential history-taking with a professional (preferably gender-matched) interpreter is essential; family interpreters miss disclosure and may pose safety risks. Australian specialist refugee trauma services (STARTTS NSW, Foundation House VIC, ASeTTS WA, QPASTT QLD) provide trauma-focused therapy with culturally appropriate care. Benzodiazepines worsen PTSD outcomes and are not first-line.
key_points: Refugee somatic complaints can mask PTSD
Professional interpreter required, not family
Refer to specialist refugee trauma service
explanation.pearls: Refugees on temporary protection visas have restricted Medicare and may have no access to PBS-subsidised medications; check eligibility before prescribing.

stem:
A 27-year-old man with schizophrenia, currently on a community treatment order, missed two depot appointments in the past month. His mother phones the community mental health team to report he is increasingly suspicious, not eating well, and has stopped his oral medications. He lives with his parents. He has not contacted the service. He has a history of two prior involuntary admissions following relapse during medication non-adherence. He has not been violent.

The registrar is determining the next clinical step.

data_table.Vital signs: Last recorded 6 weeks ago: pulse 78, BP 124/78 mmHg, RR 14, SpO2 99%, temperature 36.6°C
data_table.Examination: Last MSE 6 weeks ago: stable, well-engaged
data_table.Investigations: Last clozapine level 6 weeks ago therapeutic
data_table.Medications: Paliperidone depot monthly (last dose 5 weeks ago)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first action?

options.text: Urgent home visit (with police if safety risks) to assess under the CTO
options.rationale: CTOs in AU jurisdictions authorise community follow-up and assessment; the first step in suspected relapse is direct clinical assessment, with police only if safety risks. (Source: NSW Mental Health Act 2007)

options.text: Apply immediately for an inpatient involuntary treatment order without further assessment
options.rationale: An inpatient order requires direct assessment of mental state and risk; second-hand report from family does not substitute. (Source: NSW Mental Health Act 2007)

options.text: Reassure the mother and wait until the next scheduled depot appointment in three weeks
options.rationale: Waiting risks deterioration; the relapse pattern of medication non-adherence followed by admission is well-documented for this patient. (Source: NSW Mental Health Act 2007)

options.text: Discharge the patient from the CTO since he has not contacted the service
options.rationale: Non-contact is a sign for follow-up, not for discharge; revoking a CTO without assessment leaves no legal framework for community care. (Source: NSW Mental Health Act 2007)

options.text: Issue a breach notice under the CTO with no further clinical action this week
options.rationale: Breach administration without clinical assessment is not appropriate; the CTO authorises hands-on review. (Source: NSW Mental Health Act 2007)

explanation.summary: Community treatment orders authorise mental health services to follow up, assess, and enforce treatment in the community for patients with severe mental illness who would otherwise relapse. When a carer reports concern, the AU response is direct clinical assessment, usually by home visit with appropriate safety planning. Police may attend if there is risk of harm. Involuntary admission requires mental state examination demonstrating the criteria. Family information is taken seriously but does not replace clinical assessment.
key_points: CTO authorises home visit assessment
Police only if safety risks
Family report is a trigger to assess, not to admit
explanation.pearls: Most AU jurisdictions require a clinical review within 2-3 working days of CTO breach to either restore adherence or escalate to inpatient assessment; document the timeline in clinical notes.

sources.label: RANZCP Mental Health Legislation Position Statement

stem:
A 26-year-old man brought in by police is shouting, threatening staff, and pacing in the assessment room. He has known schizophrenia and has had two previous similar presentations. De-escalation by an experienced clinician and offer of oral medication have failed. He has been started on a section under the Mental Health Act. He has no known cardiac history. He has not received any medication tonight. Body weight is approximately 80 kg. He is medication-naive in the last 24 hours.

The team has the safe area set up and four trained staff present.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 118, BP 148/92 mmHg, RR 22, SpO2 98%, temperature 37.0°C
data_table.Examination: Hyperaroused, pacing, shouting, no focal neurology
data_table.Investigations: ECG and bloods not yet obtainable

lead_in: What is the most appropriate intramuscular regimen?

options.text: Olanzapine 10 mg IM as a single dose, repeated once at 30 minutes
options.rationale: AU acute behavioural disturbance guidelines list IM olanzapine 10 mg as first-line monotherapy when ECG is not available and oral medication declined; midazolam adds respiratory risk. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Acute Behavioural Disturbance)

options.text: Olanzapine 10 mg IM plus midazolam 10 mg IM simultaneously
options.rationale: Combining IM olanzapine with parenteral benzodiazepines is contraindicated by the manufacturer because of risk of cardiorespiratory depression. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Acute Behavioural Disturbance)

options.text: Droperidol 10 mg IM combined with IM midazolam 5 mg as primary regimen
options.rationale: Droperidol monotherapy is an alternative but routine combination with midazolam is reserved for refractory cases; ECG cannot be obtained safely. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Acute Behavioural Disturbance)

options.text: Haloperidol 5 mg IM combined with promethazine 25 mg IM dose
options.rationale: This is the UK NICE preferred combination but in AU droperidol or olanzapine is preferred because of haloperidol QT and EPSE risks. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Acute Behavioural Disturbance)

options.text: Ketamine 200 mg IM as first-line chemical restraint dose
options.rationale: Ketamine is reserved for pre-hospital agitated delirium under retrieval physician oversight, not first-line for ED behavioural emergency. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Acute Behavioural Disturbance)

explanation.summary: Australian acute behavioural disturbance guidelines (eTG and most state mental health pathways) list IM droperidol 10 mg or IM olanzapine 10 mg as first-line single-agent rapid tranquillisation when oral medication has been declined. IM olanzapine and parenteral benzodiazepines should not be combined because of respiratory depression. Continuous monitoring with pulse oximetry is required. ECG is performed when feasible to detect QT prolongation. Reassessment at 30 minutes guides repeat dosing.
key_points: AU first-line: IM olanzapine 10 mg or IM droperidol 10 mg
Do not combine IM olanzapine with parenteral benzodiazepines
Continuous monitoring including SpO2
explanation.pearls: Patients with intoxication, hypovolaemia, or significant medical illness need lower starting doses (e.g. 5 mg olanzapine) and individual airway plans; the standard 10 mg is for a fit adult.

sources.label: RANZCP Acute Behavioural Disturbance Position Statement

stem:
A 17-year-old presents with anorexia nervosa, restrictive subtype. Her BMI is 13.5 kg/m^2. She has lost 11 kg in three months. She has been eating around 600 kcal a day. Bloods: phosphate 0.6 mmol/L (0.8-1.5), potassium 3.0 mmol/L (3.5-5.0), magnesium 0.6 mmol/L (0.7-1.0), albumin 28 g/L (35-50). ECG shows bradycardia with QTc 480 ms (normal less than 450). She is medically admitted overnight.

The paediatric and dietetic teams are planning refeeding.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 38, BP 88/52 mmHg, RR 14, SpO2 99%, temperature 35.6°C
data_table.Examination: Cachexia, lanugo, cold peripheries
data_table.Investigations: Phosphate 0.6 mmol/L, potassium 3.0 mmol/L, magnesium 0.6 mmol/L, albumin 28 g/L, ECG QTc 480 ms

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial refeeding plan?

options.text: 1400-1800 kcal/day with phosphate, potassium, magnesium, and thiamine cover
options.rationale: AU MARSIPAN and ANZAED guidance now favour higher starting calorie ranges (1400-2000 kcal/day) with proactive electrolyte and thiamine cover, rather than the historic 500-1000 kcal/day. (Source: ANZAED Eating Disorders Practice Standards 2022)

options.text: Start oral feeding at 500 kcal/day to avoid refeeding syndrome
options.rationale: Historic 500 kcal/day under-feeds severe AN and prolongs starvation; current AU guidelines support higher calorie start with electrolyte cover. (Source: ANZAED Eating Disorders Practice Standards 2022)

options.text: Insert NGT and feed at full maintenance without electrolyte correction
options.rationale: Feeding without replacement of phosphate and other electrolytes precipitates refeeding syndrome with arrhythmia and seizures. (Source: ANZAED Eating Disorders Practice Standards 2022)
