options.text: Start IV dextrose 10% infusion without thiamine for rapid calorie delivery
options.rationale: Dextrose without prior thiamine in malnourished patients precipitates Wernicke encephalopathy; thiamine must precede any carbohydrate load. (Source: ANZAED Eating Disorders Practice Standards 2022)

options.text: Discharge home with weekly outpatient dietitian review only
options.rationale: Bradycardia, electrolyte abnormalities, prolonged QTc, and BMI 13.5 are medical admission criteria; outpatient is unsafe. (Source: ANZAED Eating Disorders Practice Standards 2022)

explanation.summary: Severe anorexia with bradycardia, electrolyte abnormalities, and a low BMI requires medical admission. Refeeding syndrome (phosphate, potassium, magnesium drop, thiamine depletion, cardiac decompensation) historically led to ultra-low starting calories. Current AU MARSIPAN and ANZAED guidance favours higher starting calories (1400-2000 kcal/day) combined with proactive electrolyte replacement and thiamine 100 mg IV or oral prior to any carbohydrate load. Cardiac monitoring is required during the first week.
key_points: Higher start (1400-2000 kcal/day) with electrolyte and thiamine cover
Thiamine before any carbohydrate
Cardiac monitoring during first week
explanation.pearls: Phosphate below 0.5 mmol/L is the strongest predictor of refeeding-related arrhythmia; replace IV with 9 mmol over 4-6 hours and recheck.

stem:
A 22-year-old presented three months ago with first-episode psychosis precipitated by daily high-potency cannabis use. He was started on risperidone 4 mg and stopped cannabis at admission. His positive symptoms (persecutory delusions, third-person auditory hallucinations) have persisted despite three months of medication adherence and confirmed abstinence on urine toxicology. He has impaired functioning at university and social withdrawal. There is no family history of psychotic illness. He has not had a manic or depressive episode. No other substance use is identified.

The early psychosis team is reviewing the diagnosis.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 78, BP 122/74 mmHg, RR 14, SpO2 99%, temperature 36.7°C
data_table.Examination: Flat affect, residual delusions of persecution, third-person hallucinations
data_table.Investigations: Urine cannabinoid negative on three samples; routine bloods, MRI brain normal

lead_in: What is the most likely diagnosis at this stage?

options.text: Schizophrenia (cannabis was a precipitant in a vulnerable individual)
options.rationale: Substance-induced psychosis is expected to resolve with abstinence; persistence at 12 weeks with confirmed abstinence and ongoing functional decline shifts the diagnosis to a primary psychotic disorder. (Source: DSM-5-TR; RANZCP Early Psychosis)

options.text: Cannabis-induced psychotic disorder, currently ongoing course
options.rationale: Substance-induced psychosis by DSM-5 resolves within 4 weeks of abstinence; 12 weeks of persistent psychosis with confirmed abstinence excludes this. (Source: DSM-5-TR; RANZCP Early Psychosis)

options.text: Brief psychotic disorder lasting longer than one month
options.rationale: Brief psychotic disorder is by definition under 1 month with full return to baseline; this case has lasted 3 months with ongoing impairment. (Source: DSM-5-TR; RANZCP Early Psychosis)

options.text: Schizoaffective disorder, depressive subtype currently
options.rationale: Schizoaffective requires a major mood episode concurrent with psychosis; no mood episode is described. (Source: DSM-5-TR; RANZCP Early Psychosis)

options.text: Schizophreniform disorder still within the 6-month diagnostic window
options.rationale: Schizophreniform is the correct provisional label between 1 and 6 months only when the clinician cannot yet exclude full schizophrenia trajectory; at 3 months with marked functional decline a schizophrenia diagnosis is increasingly likely. (Source: DSM-5-TR; RANZCP Early Psychosis)

explanation.summary: Substance-induced psychotic disorder by DSM-5 is a time-limited diagnosis that resolves within approximately one month of abstinence. Persistence beyond this point shifts the formulation toward a primary psychotic illness, with cannabis having acted as a precipitant in a vulnerable individual. Cannabis use approximately doubles schizophrenia risk in vulnerable individuals; high-potency forms further increase risk. Long-term antipsychotic treatment and early psychosis service involvement are recommended.
key_points: Substance-induced psychosis resolves within ~4 weeks of abstinence
Persistence beyond shifts diagnosis to primary disorder
Cannabis is precipitant in vulnerable people
explanation.pearls: Schizophreniform is a provisional 1-6 month placeholder; reserve for cases where you genuinely cannot predict whether the episode will remit, and re-formulate at 6 months.

stem:
A 30-year-old woman with a documented history of bipolar I disorder (one previous postpartum manic episode three years ago requiring inpatient care) has just delivered her second baby at 39+5. She stopped her lithium six months ago to plan pregnancy and has not restarted. On day 4 postpartum she is irritable, sleeping 1 hour per night, hyperverbal, has religious delusions about the baby, and is intermittently confused. She is breastfeeding. She is currently calm but the family are very concerned. She does not believe she is unwell.

The perinatal team has been called urgently.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 102, BP 128/78 mmHg, RR 18, SpO2 99%, temperature 37.0°C
data_table.Examination: Pressured speech, religious delusions involving baby, intermittent confusion, MMSE 24/30
data_table.Investigations: FBC, UEC, LFTs, TSH, calcium, magnesium, infection screen within normal limits; MRI brain not yet done

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial step?

options.text: Admit to mother-baby unit, olanzapine 5-10 mg, lorazepam PRN, plus brain imaging
options.rationale: Postpartum psychosis is a psychiatric emergency requiring inpatient care, preferably MBU; antipsychotic plus benzodiazepine is first-line, and confusion mandates exclusion of organic mimic. (Source: RANZCP Perinatal Mental Health 2023)

options.text: Restart lithium 250 mg twice daily and discharge with community follow-up
options.rationale: Outpatient management of postpartum psychosis is unsafe given infanticide and suicide risks; admission is required. (Source: RANZCP Perinatal Mental Health 2023)

options.text: Reassure as normal postpartum baby blues and observe at home overnight
options.rationale: Baby blues do not present with delusions, hyperactivity, sleeplessness, or confusion; this is psychosis. (Source: RANZCP Perinatal Mental Health 2023)

options.text: Cease breastfeeding immediately as a prerequisite to any medication
options.rationale: Many psychotropics are compatible with breastfeeding; cessation is a separate decision balanced with treatment needs, not a prerequisite. (Source: RANZCP Perinatal Mental Health 2023)

options.text: Initiate ECT same day before any pharmacological trial at all
options.rationale: ECT is rapidly effective in postpartum psychosis but is reserved for severe cases or non-response after a short pharmacological trial; antipsychotic plus benzodiazepine is the typical first step. (Source: RANZCP Perinatal Mental Health 2023)

explanation.summary: Postpartum psychosis affects 1-2 per 1000 deliveries but recurrence risk in bipolar I with a prior postpartum episode is 25-50%. Stopping mood stabilisers around delivery increases relapse risk substantially. Admission to a mother-baby unit allows treatment while preserving attachment, with antipsychotic plus benzodiazepine as the first pharmacological step. Lithium can be restarted with monitoring, and ECT is reserved for severe or treatment-resistant cases. Prominent confusion mandates organic workup including thyroid, infection, and consideration of autoimmune encephalitis.
key_points: PPP in bipolar I is high-risk: mood stabiliser at delivery prevents relapse
MBU admission preserves mother-infant attachment
Antipsychotic + benzodiazepine is the typical first regimen
explanation.pearls: Postpartum psychosis with prominent confusion warrants exclusion of NMDA receptor encephalitis - send anti-NMDA antibodies and consider EEG.

sources.label: COPE Australian Perinatal Mental Health Guideline

stem:
A 28-year-old presents for a planning visit at 8 weeks gestation in her first pregnancy. She has had recurrent major depressive disorder for 6 years and has been well on sertraline 100 mg daily for 18 months. Two previous depressive episodes responded well to sertraline. She has had no manic or psychotic features.

She is unsure whether to continue medication. She has a supportive partner and a stable job. There is no recent suicidal ideation. Her partner is also concerned about possible fetal risks and asks for evidence-based advice.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 78, BP 116/72 mmHg, RR 14, SpO2 99%, temperature 36.6 °C, fetal HR 160 bpm
data_table.Examination: Mood euthymic, no psychomotor changes, normal reasoning, no suicidal ideation
data_table.Investigations: Booking bloods within normal limits; viability ultrasound shows single intrauterine pregnancy at 8 weeks

lead_in: What is the most appropriate medication recommendation?

options.text: Switch to mirtazapine 15 mg nocte to avoid SSRI exposure to the fetus completely
options.rationale: Mirtazapine has less pregnancy safety data than sertraline and is not preferred when a patient is already responding well to a first-line SSRI. (Source: RANZCP Perinatal Mental Health Clinical Practice Guideline 2023)
source_refs: RANZCP Perinatal Mental Health Clinical Practice Guideline 2023

options.text: Switch to paroxetine 20 mg daily for a smoother antidepressant profile in pregnancy
options.rationale: Paroxetine is associated with a small increased risk of cardiac malformations in first-trimester exposure and is not preferred when other SSRIs are options. (Source: RANZCP Perinatal Mental Health Clinical Practice Guideline 2023)
source_refs: RANZCP Perinatal Mental Health Clinical Practice Guideline 2023

options.text: Cross-taper to fluoxetine 20 mg daily during the first trimester for safety reasons
options.rationale: Fluoxetine has a long half-life and active metabolite that increases neonatal adaptation syndrome risk; sertraline is preferred when already effective. (Source: RANZCP Perinatal Mental Health Clinical Practice Guideline 2023)
source_refs: RANZCP Perinatal Mental Health Clinical Practice Guideline 2023

options.text: Stop sertraline now and offer psychological therapy alone for the entire pregnancy
options.rationale: Stopping a well-controlled SSRI in recurrent depression carries a 60-70% relapse risk within 6 months, with associated obstetric morbidity and infant outcomes. (Source: RANZCP Perinatal Mental Health Clinical Practice Guideline 2023)
source_refs: RANZCP Perinatal Mental Health Clinical Practice Guideline 2023

options.text: Continue sertraline 100 mg daily at the current effective antidepressant dose
options.rationale: Sertraline has the most extensive AU pregnancy evidence base and is the preferred SSRI antenatally; continuing an effective regimen avoids relapse, which is itself a fetal and maternal risk. (Source: RANZCP Perinatal Mental Health Clinical Practice Guideline 2023)
source_refs: RANZCP Perinatal Mental Health Clinical Practice Guideline 2023

explanation.summary: Antenatal antidepressant decisions weigh untreated maternal depression risks (preterm birth, low birth weight, postnatal depression, impaired attachment) against medication risks. The Australian RANZCP perinatal guideline supports continuing an effective SSRI through pregnancy where the woman has a history of recurrent depression. Sertraline is the preferred first-line SSRI in pregnancy; paroxetine is avoided where possible. Fluoxetine is acceptable when already effective but is more associated with neonatal adaptation syndrome. Multidisciplinary perinatal mental health follow-up is standard.
key_points: Sertraline is the preferred SSRI in pregnancy with the largest AU evidence base.
Paroxetine has a small first-trimester cardiac malformation signal; avoid if alternatives.
Stopping in recurrent depression: 60-70% relapse within 6 months.
Multidisciplinary perinatal mental health surveillance is standard.
explanation.pearls: Sertraline is the preferred AU pregnancy SSRI; paroxetine is avoided due to first-trimester cardiac malformation signal.

sources.label: RANZCP Perinatal Mental Health Clinical Practice Guideline 2023
COPE Perinatal Mental Health National Guideline

stem:
A 38-year-old with bipolar I disorder has been stable on lithium carbonate 800 mg nocte for the last 4 years. Last week she developed acute gastroenteritis with vomiting and diarrhoea. She has continued her usual lithium dose and is now in your GP clinic with a mild tremor, mild ataxia, and slurred speech.

She has no other regular medications. Her last lithium level 3 months ago was 0.7 mmol/L on the morning trough (target 0.6-0.8). She has had no recent change in fluid or salt intake apart from the gastroenteritis and is mentally lucid.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 90, BP 112/68 mmHg, RR 14, SpO2 99%, temperature 36.8 °C
data_table.Examination: Coarse tremor, mild gait ataxia, dysarthria, no nystagmus, alert and orientated, no clonus
data_table.Investigations: Bedside only, no lithium level drawn yet

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Withhold the next dose, urgent serum lithium level and UEC at the same blood draw
options.rationale: Acute illness with volume loss reduces lithium clearance and precipitates toxicity; the AU step is to withhold the dose and measure both lithium and renal function immediately because clinical features alone underestimate risk. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Continue full-dose lithium and increase oral fluid intake to flush the drug through
options.rationale: Continuing full-dose lithium in dehydration risks progressive toxicity; oral fluids without dose adjustment or measurement are inadequate. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Reduce the lithium dose by half empirically and review the patient in 2 weeks
options.rationale: Empirical dose halving without a serum level and renal function is unsafe; lithium has a narrow therapeutic window and the level may already be in toxic range. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Stop lithium permanently and start sodium valproate 500 mg twice daily today
options.rationale: Permanent cessation after a single episode of suspected toxicity is excessive; lithium is generally restarted at a reduced dose after the acute illness resolves and renal function recovers. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Refer immediately to the renal team for haemodialysis without measuring the level
options.rationale: Haemodialysis is reserved for levels >2.5 mmol/L, severe neurological features, or renal failure; you cannot triage to dialysis without measuring the lithium level. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

explanation.summary: Lithium toxicity precipitates in dehydration, renal impairment, NSAIDs, ACE inhibitors or thiazide diuretics, low-salt diet, and intercurrent illness. Mild toxicity (1.5-2.0 mmol/L) presents with tremor, ataxia, dysarthria and gastrointestinal symptoms; moderate (2.0-2.5) adds confusion and myoclonus; severe (>2.5) brings seizures, coma, and arrhythmia. Withhold lithium, measure serum level and UEC, treat the underlying volume loss, and arrange admission if symptomatic or level high. Haemodialysis indicated for level >2.5, neurological compromise, or renal failure.
key_points: Lithium toxicity precipitants: dehydration, NSAIDs, ACE inhibitors, thiazides.
Therapeutic 0.6-1.0; toxicity at 1.5+ mmol/L.
Mild: tremor, ataxia, dysarthria. Severe: seizures, coma, renal failure.
Dialysis: level >2.5, severe neurological features, or renal failure.
explanation.pearls: Mild lithium toxicity at 1.5-2.0 mmol/L presents with tremor, ataxia and dysarthria; gastroenteritis is a classic precipitant.

stem:
A 22-year-old presents to the emergency department 90 minutes after ingesting approximately 50 amitriptyline 25 mg tablets in a suicide attempt. She is drowsy but rousable. She has had one self-terminating generalised seizure in the ambulance.

On arrival she is intubated for airway protection. Her ECG shows sinus tachycardia at 130 bpm with a QRS duration of 130 milliseconds and a terminal R wave in aVR of 4 mm. Bedside glucose is normal, paracetamol level is sent, and she has IV access in place.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 130, BP 90/56 mmHg, RR 12 (ventilated), SpO2 98% on 40% FiO2, temperature 36.8 °C
data_table.Examination: Intubated and sedated, GCS prior to intubation 9, dry mucous membranes, sluggish pupils, hyperreflexia
data_table.Investigations: ECG sinus tachycardia QRS 130 ms with aVR terminal R 4 mm, VBG pH 7.30 pCO2 38 mmHg HCO3 19 mmol/L (22-32), sodium 138 mmol/L (135-145), paracetamol pending
data_table.Medications: Currently nil; previously amitriptyline 25 mg prescribed for chronic pain

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next pharmacological intervention?

options.text: Intravenous flumazenil 0.2 mg bolus, repeated every minute to reverse drowsiness
options.rationale: Flumazenil reverses benzodiazepines, not tricyclic antidepressants; it is also contraindicated in TCA co-ingestion because it lowers the seizure threshold. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology)

options.text: Intravenous physostigmine 1 mg bolus to reverse central and peripheral antimuscarinic effect
options.rationale: Physostigmine is contraindicated in TCA overdose because it can precipitate seizures and asystole; it is reserved for isolated pure antimuscarinic toxidromes. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology)

options.text: Intravenous sodium bicarbonate 1-2 mmol/kg bolus, repeated to a target QRS <120 ms
options.rationale: TCA cardiotoxicity from sodium-channel blockade is reversed by sodium bicarbonate boluses; an indication is QRS >100 ms or features such as terminal R wave in aVR >3 mm or refractory hypotension. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology)

options.text: Intravenous activated charcoal 50 g via the nasogastric tube once airway is protected
options.rationale: Activated charcoal in TCA overdose is considered only within 1 hour of ingestion and in an airway-protected patient; at 90 minutes the cardiotoxicity is the priority and bicarbonate should not be delayed. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology)

options.text: Intravenous lidocaine infusion 1 mg/kg load then 1-4 mg/min for tachyarrhythmia control
options.rationale: Class IB antiarrhythmic alone does not address the underlying sodium-channel blockade; lidocaine is a second-line option for ventricular arrhythmias after bicarbonate, not first-line. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology)

explanation.summary: Tricyclic antidepressant overdose causes sodium-channel blockade (wide QRS, terminal R in aVR, hypotension), antimuscarinic effects (mydriasis, urinary retention, ileus), seizures, and CNS depression. The cornerstone of cardiotoxic management is intravenous sodium bicarbonate, indicated when QRS >100 ms, terminal R wave in aVR >3 mm, refractory hypotension, or ventricular arrhythmia. Target QRS <120 ms and serum pH 7.50-7.55. Class IA, IC, and III antiarrhythmics are contraindicated. Refractory cases may require lipid emulsion or VA-ECMO.
key_points: TCA cardiotoxicity: QRS >100 ms, aVR terminal R >3 mm, refractory hypotension.
Sodium bicarbonate 1-2 mmol/kg IV bolus, repeat to target QRS <120 ms.
Target serum pH 7.50-7.55.
Avoid class IA, IC, III antiarrhythmics; avoid physostigmine.
explanation.pearls: TCA overdose: sodium bicarbonate 1-2 mmol/kg when QRS >100 ms or terminal R in aVR >3 mm.

stem:
A 28-year-old with schizophrenia has been on olanzapine 15 mg nocte for 8 months with full symptomatic remission. At his routine review you note he has gained 12 kg, his waist circumference is now 110 cm, fasting glucose is 6.5 mmol/L, and lipids show triglycerides 2.8 mmol/L and HDL 0.8 mmol/L. He is sedentary, eats takeaway most evenings, but does not drink alcohol.

He asks about whether his medication should change. He has had one previous relapse on quetiapine following self-cessation 2 years ago. He has no diabetes, no cardiovascular disease, and no extrapyramidal features.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 86, BP 138/86 mmHg, RR 14, SpO2 98%, temperature 36.7 °C
data_table.Examination: BMI 32 kg/m^2 (baseline 28), waist 110 cm, no EPS, no parkinsonism, no akathisia
data_table.Investigations: Fasting glucose 6.5 mmol/L (3.5-5.4), HbA1c 6.0%, triglycerides 2.8 mmol/L (<2.0), HDL 0.8 mmol/L (>1.0), LDL 3.5 mmol/L, prolactin within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate medication strategy?

options.text: Cross-taper olanzapine to risperidone 4 mg mane to improve the metabolic profile
options.rationale: Risperidone has intermediate metabolic burden and high prolactin elevation; aripiprazole offers a better metabolic profile while preserving efficacy. (Source: RANZCP Antipsychotic Maintenance Guideline 2022)

options.text: Reduce olanzapine dose to 5 mg nocte and continue current lifestyle advice only
options.rationale: Dose reduction may modestly help but a substantial proportion of metabolic burden persists even at lower doses; switching is the AU recommendation when metabolic syndrome is established. (Source: RANZCP Antipsychotic Maintenance Guideline 2022)

options.text: Continue olanzapine at current dose and add metformin 500 mg twice daily for glucose
options.rationale: Metformin addition helps offset weight gain but does not address the dyslipidaemia or the overall metabolic profile; switching to a lower-burden antipsychotic is preferred when relapse risk allows. (Source: RANZCP Antipsychotic Maintenance Guideline 2022)

options.text: Cross-taper olanzapine to aripiprazole 15 mg morning while monitoring relapse risk
options.rationale: Aripiprazole has the lowest metabolic burden among atypicals and is the AU preferred switch for olanzapine-related metabolic syndrome in stable patients with relapse risk balanced by partial dopamine agonism. (Source: RANZCP Antipsychotic Maintenance Guideline 2022)

options.text: Switch to clozapine 12.5 mg daily titrated to maintenance dose with weekly bloods
options.rationale: Clozapine is reserved for treatment-resistant schizophrenia (failed 2 antipsychotics at adequate dose); this patient is well controlled on olanzapine and clozapine has worse metabolic burden anyway. (Source: RANZCP Antipsychotic Maintenance Guideline 2022)

explanation.summary: Atypical antipsychotic metabolic burden ranges from clozapine and olanzapine (highest) through quetiapine and risperidone (intermediate) to aripiprazole, lurasidone and ziprasidone (lowest). Monitor weight, waist, lipids, glucose and prolactin at baseline, 4 weeks, 12 weeks, and annually. When metabolic syndrome develops on olanzapine in a stable patient, the AU preferred switch is to aripiprazole, with a cross-taper over 2-4 weeks because abrupt change risks relapse. Lifestyle interventions, metformin for glycaemic concern, and statin therapy when indicated complement the switch.
key_points: Metabolic burden: clozapine/olanzapine > quetiapine/risperidone > aripiprazole.
Cross-taper olanzapine to aripiprazole over 2-4 weeks.
Add metformin for glycaemic concerns; statin if indicated by AbsCVD risk.
Baseline, 4-week, 12-week, then annual metabolic monitoring.
explanation.pearls: Aripiprazole has the lowest metabolic burden of the atypicals and is the preferred switch when olanzapine causes metabolic syndrome.

stem:
A 26-year-old presents with a 6-week history of elevated mood, reduced sleep need, grandiose plans, and pressure of speech. During this time he believes he is being followed by ASIO operatives and hears their voices commenting on his actions. His mother says these psychotic features have persisted for 3 weeks now without any of the elevated-mood symptoms.

He has had two prior depressive episodes treated by his GP. He has no significant past medical history, no substance use, and no family history of psychosis. His thyroid function and urine drug screen are normal. There is no head trauma history.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 88, BP 122/76 mmHg, RR 14, SpO2 99%, temperature 36.6 °C
data_table.Examination: Currently mood euthymic, mild psychomotor slowing, persistent persecutory delusion, auditory hallucinations, insight partial
data_table.Investigations: TFTs within normal limits, urine drug screen negative, FBC and UEC within normal limits, MRI brain awaiting

lead_in: What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.text: Schizoaffective disorder, bipolar type, current episode with manic features
options.rationale: DSM-5 schizoaffective disorder requires a mood episode concurrent with criterion A psychosis AND at least 2 weeks of psychotic symptoms without prominent mood symptoms; the 3 weeks of pure psychosis here is the discriminator from bipolar with psychotic features. (Source: DSM-5-TR American Psychiatric Association 2022)

options.text: Bipolar I disorder, current episode manic, with mood-congruent psychotic features
options.rationale: Bipolar I with psychotic features confines psychosis to the mood episode; the 3 weeks of psychosis without mood symptoms in this patient excludes this diagnosis. (Source: DSM-5-TR American Psychiatric Association 2022)

options.text: Schizophrenia, paranoid subtype with comorbid recurrent depressive episodes
options.rationale: Schizophrenia requires criterion A symptoms for at least 6 months and mood episodes are time-limited relative to total illness duration; the prominence of mood episodes here makes schizoaffective the better fit. (Source: DSM-5-TR American Psychiatric Association 2022)

options.text: Major depressive disorder, current severe with psychotic features and mixed mania
options.rationale: MDD with psychotic features confines psychosis to mood episodes and excludes manic episodes; this patient has clear manic features with elevated mood and reduced sleep need. (Source: DSM-5-TR American Psychiatric Association 2022)

options.text: Brief psychotic disorder with marked stressor lasting less than one month duration
options.rationale: Brief psychotic disorder is by definition less than 1 month and resolves with return to premorbid functioning; this patient has been symptomatic for 6 weeks with prior mood episodes. (Source: DSM-5-TR American Psychiatric Association 2022)

explanation.summary: Schizoaffective disorder is distinguished from bipolar disorder with psychotic features by the requirement of at least 2 weeks of criterion A psychotic symptoms in the ABSENCE of prominent mood symptoms during the lifetime course of illness. Mood episodes must also be present for the majority of the total illness duration. Bipolar with psychotic features confines all psychotic symptoms to the mood episode. Schizoaffective subtype is bipolar type if any manic episode has occurred, depressive type otherwise. Treatment combines a mood stabiliser or antipsychotic with episode-specific care.
key_points: Schizoaffective requires ≥2 weeks of psychosis WITHOUT mood symptoms.
Bipolar with psychotic features: psychosis only during mood episodes.
Schizophrenia: mood episodes brief relative to total illness duration.
Schizoaffective subtype is bipolar type if any manic episode.
explanation.pearls: Schizoaffective vs bipolar with psychotic features: ≥2 weeks of psychosis without mood symptoms is the schizoaffective discriminator.

sources.label: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines for Schizoaffective and Related Disorders

stem:
A 26-year-old at 16 weeks gestation attends her GP for review. She smokes 15 cigarettes daily and has done so since age 17. She has tried unsuccessfully to quit during the first trimester using behavioural strategies alone. Her partner also smokes but is willing to support her quit attempt.

She has no other psychiatric or medical history, no significant past medical history, and is on no other medications apart from a pregnancy multivitamin. She asks specifically about pharmacological help because she feels behavioural advice has not been enough.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 82, BP 118/74 mmHg, RR 14, SpO2 99%, temperature 36.7 °C, fetal HR 152 bpm
data_table.Examination: Mood euthymic, no anxiety symptoms, no psychomotor changes, weight tracking on the 50th centile
data_table.Investigations: Booking bloods within normal limits, CO breath analyser 18 ppm (smoker range), urine drug screen negative

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next pharmacological option?

options.text: Bupropion sustained-release 150 mg daily for one week then increased to twice daily
options.rationale: Bupropion is contraindicated in pregnancy because of seizure threshold effects and insufficient safety data; intermittent NRT is the AU pregnancy first-line. (Source: RACGP Supporting Smoking Cessation Guideline 2021)

options.text: Varenicline 0.5 mg titrated daily for 12 weeks as the most effective oral agent
options.rationale: Varenicline is contraindicated in pregnancy due to insufficient safety data and a signal for neuropsychiatric effects; AU guidance does not use it antenatally. (Source: RACGP Supporting Smoking Cessation Guideline 2021)

options.text: Intermittent nicotine replacement therapy by 2 mg lozenge as needed for cravings
options.rationale: RACGP and RANZCOG guidance prefers intermittent (not patch) NRT in pregnancy because lozenges and gum allow self-titration to minimum effective dose; varenicline and bupropion are contraindicated in pregnancy. (Source: RACGP Supporting Smoking Cessation Guideline 2021)

options.text: Electronic cigarettes with 12 mg/mL nicotine for use throughout the pregnancy day
options.rationale: AU guidance does not recommend electronic cigarettes in pregnancy because of inhalation product safety concerns and unregulated nicotine doses. (Source: RACGP Supporting Smoking Cessation Guideline 2021)

options.text: Continuous nicotine 21 mg patch for 16 hours daily across the next 8 to 12 weeks
options.rationale: Continuous patches give sustained nicotine that crosses the placenta; AU pregnancy guidance prefers intermittent dosing to minimise fetal nicotine exposure. (Source: RACGP Supporting Smoking Cessation Guideline 2021)

explanation.summary: Smoking in pregnancy increases miscarriage, IUGR, placental abruption, stillbirth and SIDS. Behavioural support is first-line; pharmacotherapy should be considered when behavioural alone fails. Intermittent NRT (lozenges, gum, inhaler) is preferred to patches because it allows lower total nicotine dose and self-titration. Varenicline and bupropion are contraindicated in pregnancy due to safety data gaps. Electronic cigarettes are not recommended. Partner cessation, nicotine replacement counselling, and ongoing CO breath monitoring increase quit success.
key_points: First-line: behavioural support and brief intervention.
Pharmacotherapy: intermittent NRT (lozenges, gum) preferred over patches.
Varenicline and bupropion contraindicated in pregnancy.
Electronic cigarettes not recommended.
explanation.pearls: AU pregnancy NRT: intermittent lozenges or gum over patches because self-titration reduces total fetal nicotine exposure.

stem:
A 24-year-old with a 2-year history of major depression presents to ED brought in by family. He has not spoken for 2 days, refuses food and water, and adopts unusual postures that he maintains for long periods. The family say he was started on no new medications recently and has not been on antipsychotics in the past.

On examination he stares without blinking, allows you to lift his arm into an unusual position which he maintains, and resists passive movement of his other limbs. His temperature is mildly elevated. There are no focal neurological signs. His urine drug screen is negative.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 110, BP 140/86 mmHg, RR 22, SpO2 99% in air, temperature 37.8 °C
data_table.Examination: Mute, posturing with waxy flexibility, negativism, staring without blinking, no focal neurology, hydration moderate to poor
data_table.Investigations: FBC and UEC within normal limits, CK 320 U/L (<170), urine drug screen negative, CT brain unremarkable, lumbar puncture pending if no improvement
data_table.Medications: Sertraline 100 mg mane, no antipsychotic exposure

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate intervention?

options.text: Mechanical ventilation and IV dantrolene 2.5 mg/kg for presumed malignant catatonia now
options.rationale: Dantrolene is for malignant hyperthermia; malignant catatonia treatment is benzodiazepines and ECT, not dantrolene, and pre-emptive intubation is not the first step in this stable patient. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Bilateral electroconvulsive therapy under general anaesthesia within the next 24 hours
options.rationale: ECT is the next escalation if benzodiazepines fail or the patient is malignant catatonia, but lorazepam challenge is the diagnostic and first-line therapeutic step. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Intramuscular haloperidol 5 mg with promethazine 25 mg for rapid behavioural control
options.rationale: Antipsychotics in catatonia risk precipitating neuroleptic malignant syndrome and worsening rigidity; they are not first-line and should be avoided until catatonia is treated. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Empirical IV ceftriaxone 2 g plus acyclovir 10 mg/kg for suspected encephalitis cover
options.rationale: Empirical infectious cover is given when meningoencephalitis is plausible, but unblinking stare with waxy flexibility and negativism in a known depression patient is more likely catatonia; CT and clinical picture do not suggest encephalitis. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Intravenous lorazepam 2 mg over 2 minutes with reassessment of catatonia at 15 minutes
options.rationale: The Bush-Francis lorazepam challenge is the AU first-line approach to catatonia: 1-2 mg IV with response (improved mutism, posturing, rigidity) at 10-15 minutes confirms the diagnosis and informs ongoing therapy. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

explanation.summary: Catatonia is a clinical syndrome (not a discrete diagnosis) characterised by mutism, negativism, posturing, waxy flexibility, stupor or excitement. It is most commonly secondary to mood disorders (especially depression and bipolar), then schizophrenia, then medical causes (autoimmune encephalitis, NMS, drug withdrawal, electrolyte disturbances). The Bush-Francis lorazepam challenge (1-2 mg IV with reassessment in 10-15 minutes) is diagnostic and often therapeutic. Failure of response or malignant features (fever, autonomic instability, rigidity, raised CK) trigger ECT consideration. Avoid antipsychotics during active catatonia because they worsen rigidity and risk NMS.
key_points: Bush-Francis lorazepam challenge: 1-2 mg IV, reassess in 10-15 minutes.
Antipsychotics worsen catatonia and risk NMS - avoid during the syndrome.
Malignant features (fever, instability, rigidity, raised CK) escalate to ECT.
Causes: mood disorders > schizophrenia > medical (autoimmune, electrolytes).
explanation.pearls: Lorazepam 1-2 mg IV is the Bush-Francis challenge for catatonia; response at 10-15 minutes confirms diagnosis and starts treatment.

stem:
A 38-year-old with treatment-resistant schizophrenia has been on clozapine 400 mg nocte for 18 months with sustained remission of positive and negative symptoms. He attends his routine clozapine clinic. He has no fever, no infection, no mucositis, and feels his usual self. He takes no other regular medications.

His weekly FBC today shows a neutrophil count of 1.2 × 10^9/L (lower limit 2.0); his haemoglobin and platelets are within normal limits. Last week his neutrophil count was 2.3 × 10^9/L. A repeat FBC drawn 4 hours later in the same clinic confirms 1.2 × 10^9/L.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 78, BP 122/76 mmHg, RR 14, SpO2 98%, temperature 36.7 °C
data_table.Examination: No oral lesions, no rash, no infection focus, mental state stable, no positive or negative symptoms
data_table.Investigations: Neutrophils 1.2 × 10^9/L on repeat (2.0-7.5), Hb 142 g/L, platelets 280 × 10^9/L, CRP <5 mg/L, no infection focus

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Continue clozapine but increase FBC monitoring to twice weekly with infection precautions
options.rationale: Australian Clopine and Clozaril protocols classify neutrophils 1.0-1.5 × 10^9/L as 'amber' alert: continue clozapine but switch to twice-weekly FBC until neutrophils recover above 2.0, with infection precautions. (Source: ClozapineConnect Australian Treatment Protocol 2024)

options.text: Stop clozapine immediately and refer to haematology for granulocyte colony stimulating factor
options.rationale: Cessation and G-CSF are reserved for 'red' alerts (neutrophils <0.5 × 10^9/L) or symptomatic patients; an amber-level fall in an asymptomatic patient is managed by enhanced monitoring. (Source: ClozapineConnect Australian Treatment Protocol 2024)

options.text: Reduce clozapine dose to 200 mg nocte and review FBC again in one week's time
options.rationale: Dose reduction does not improve haematological recovery because clozapine-induced neutropenia is idiosyncratic, not dose-related, and reduction risks symptomatic relapse. (Source: ClozapineConnect Australian Treatment Protocol 2024)

options.text: Switch to olanzapine 20 mg nocte from tonight without further clozapine dose given
options.rationale: Switching from clozapine in treatment-resistant schizophrenia after an amber alert is premature; the AU protocol allows continuation with enhanced monitoring and saves clozapine for the patient who has responded. (Source: ClozapineConnect Australian Treatment Protocol 2024)

options.text: Admit immediately for IV broad-spectrum antibiotics until neutrophils recover above 2.0
options.rationale: Empirical IV antibiotics are for neutropenic fever or significant infection; this patient is asymptomatic and afebrile, so admission is not indicated. (Source: ClozapineConnect Australian Treatment Protocol 2024)

explanation.summary: Clozapine-induced neutropenia and agranulocytosis is the highest-risk haematological adverse effect, with risk peaking in the first 18 weeks of treatment. Australian clozapine programs (ClozapineConnect, ClopineConnect) use a traffic-light system: green (neutrophils ≥2.0 × 10^9/L, continue and routine monitoring), amber (1.0-1.5, continue with twice-weekly FBC, infection precautions), red (<1.0 or signs of infection, stop clozapine, urgent haematology, possible G-CSF). Patients with confirmed agranulocytosis are usually permanently de-registered; rechallenge requires specialist haematology and psychiatry input.
key_points: Traffic light: green ≥2.0, amber 1.0-1.5, red <1.0 (×10^9/L).
Amber: continue clozapine, twice-weekly FBC, infection precautions.
Red or febrile: stop clozapine, urgent haematology, possible G-CSF.
Rechallenge after agranulocytosis requires specialist haematology and psychiatry.
explanation.pearls: Clozapine amber alert (neutrophils 1.0-1.5): continue dose with twice-weekly FBC and infection precautions; stop only at <1.0 or febrile.

subtopic_detail: Postnatal depression severity and treatment escalation
stem:
A 32-year-old woman is 8 weeks postpartum after a forceps delivery and prolonged second stage. She presents to her GP for the routine 6 to 8 week postnatal check, where she completes an EPDS that scores 18 out of 30, with positive endorsement of question 10 about "thoughts of harming myself have occurred to me" recorded as "sometimes". She describes a 4-week history of low mood, anhedonia, poor sleep beyond the baby's feeding pattern, and decreased appetite with 3 kg weight loss. She is breastfeeding exclusively. She denies plans or intent to harm herself or her baby.

She has no prior psychiatric history and no history of bipolar disorder, postpartum psychosis, or postnatal psychiatric admission in herself or her family.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 78, BP 116/72 mmHg, RR 16, SpO2 99% in room air, temperature 36.7 °C
data_table.Examination: Mood low, affect reactive but constricted, no psychomotor retardation, no psychotic features, no suicidal plans or intent on direct questioning
data_table.Investigations: EPDS 18/30, item 10 positive (sometimes); TSH 1.8 mIU/L (0.4-4.0), Hb 124 g/L (115-160), ferritin 28 micrograms/L (15-200)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Commence diazepam 5 mg twice daily and continue to monitor
options.rationale: Benzodiazepines do not treat depression, accumulate in breast milk, may cause infant sedation, and risk maternal dependence. They are not first-line for PND. (Source: NHMRC Clinical Practice Guideline: Perinatal Mental Health)
source_refs: NHMRC Clinical Practice Guideline: Perinatal Mental Health

options.text: Commence fluoxetine 20 mg orally daily and recommend formula feeding
options.rationale: Fluoxetine is not first-line for the breastfeeding mother because its long half-life and active metabolite norfluoxetine result in higher relative infant dose than sertraline. Stopping breastfeeding is also not required for SSRI initiation. (Source: NHMRC Clinical Practice Guideline: Perinatal Mental Health)
source_refs: NHMRC Clinical Practice Guideline: Perinatal Mental Health

options.text: Refer immediately to mother-baby inpatient unit for admission
options.rationale: Inpatient mother-baby admission is reserved for severe PND with active suicidal intent or plan, psychotic features, or inability to care for baby. She has passive thoughts of harm without intent or plan and is functioning to a degree; community management with safety planning is appropriate. (Source: NHMRC Clinical Practice Guideline: Perinatal Mental Health)
source_refs: NHMRC Clinical Practice Guideline: Perinatal Mental Health

options.text: Commence sertraline 50 mg orally daily and refer for perinatal CBT
options.rationale: EPDS 18 with item 10 positive and 4 weeks of melancholic features defines moderate-to-severe postnatal depression. NHMRC and beyondblue guidance is for combined pharmacotherapy plus psychological therapy for moderate-to-severe PND. Sertraline is first-line for breastfeeding because of the lowest relative infant dose (<2%); the AU SAFEMOM database lists it as compatible with breastfeeding. (Source: NHMRC Clinical Practice Guideline: Perinatal Mental Health)
source_refs: NHMRC Clinical Practice Guideline: Perinatal Mental Health

options.text: Refer for interpersonal therapy only and review in 2 weeks
options.rationale: Psychological therapy alone is reasonable for mild-to-moderate PND (EPDS 10 to 13 without item 10 endorsement) but moderate-to-severe disease with passive suicidal ideation benefits from combined treatment. Waiting 2 weeks risks worsening with active suicidal ideation. (Source: NHMRC Clinical Practice Guideline: Perinatal Mental Health)
source_refs: NHMRC Clinical Practice Guideline: Perinatal Mental Health

explanation.summary: EPDS ≥13 plus item 10 endorsement is the AU community threshold for further assessment and intervention. Moderate-to-severe PND benefits from combined pharmacotherapy (sertraline first-line in breastfeeding) and psychological therapy. Suicidal ideation requires a documented safety plan even when passive, and inpatient admission is reserved for active intent, psychosis, or care impairment.
key_points: EPDS ≥13 with item 10 endorsement is the AU community referral threshold
Sertraline is preferred SSRI in breastfeeding because relative infant dose is <2%
Combined SSRI plus psychological therapy beats either alone for moderate-to-severe PND
explanation.pearls: Always screen for bipolar history before starting SSRI in postpartum women - postpartum unmasking of bipolar with SSRI-induced mania is a recognised risk. EPDS item 10 is the suicide-question; any non-zero response warrants safety planning. Paroxetine has higher discontinuation symptoms; fluoxetine has the longest half-life and active metabolite.

sources.label: NHMRC Clinical Practice Guideline: Perinatal Mental Health

subtopic_detail: First-episode psychosis - organic vs functional discrimination
stem:
A 22-year-old male university student is brought to ED by his parents with a 2-day history of new bizarre behaviour, paranoid statements that strangers are following him, and tactile hallucinations of insects on his skin. He has been recently treated with prednisolone 50 mg daily for 5 days for an asthma exacerbation, finishing 3 days ago. He has had no fever, no headache, no neck stiffness, and no overseas travel. His parents say he attended a music festival 1 week ago.

His usual medications include fluticasone-salmeterol inhaler and a recently completed prednisolone course. He has no other psychiatric history.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 118, BP 142/86 mmHg, RR 22, SpO2 98% in room air, temperature 37.1 °C
data_table.Examination: Disoriented to date but oriented to person and place, fluctuant attention with inability to recite months backwards, mydriatic pupils 6 mm reactive bilaterally, dry warm flushed skin, no focal neurology, no neck stiffness
data_table.Investigations: FBC and CRP within normal limits, UEC and LFTs within normal limits, MRI brain normal, urine drug screen pending, blood ammonia within normal limits, TSH within normal limits, B12 within normal limits, CT head normal
data_table.Medications: Fluticasone-salmeterol; recent prednisolone 50 mg/day for 5 days (last dose 3 days ago)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Send urine drug screen for amphetamines, give lorazepam 1 mg IV, and observe quietly
options.rationale: Fluctuant attention, sympathomimetic features (mydriasis, tachycardia, hypertension, hyperthermia, warm flushed skin), and tactile hallucinations point to delirium - probably from stimulant use at the music festival, not primary psychosis. RANZCP defines first-episode psychosis with these features as needing organic workup completed before functional diagnosis. Antipsychotics in acute stimulant intoxication may worsen hyperthermia; benzodiazepines are first-line. (Source: RANZCP Practice Guidelines)

options.text: Commence intravenous aciclovir 10 mg/kg for HSV encephalitis pending lumbar puncture
options.rationale: HSV encephalitis is a reasonable differential but he is afebrile with normal CRP, normal MRI, no neck stiffness, no headache, and an alternative cause is more likely from history; he also has the toxidrome of stimulants. Empirical aciclovir is not the most appropriate immediate step unless the LP is showing pleocytosis. (Source: RCH CPG: Encephalitis)

options.text: Diagnose corticosteroid-induced psychosis and stop the prednisolone now
options.rationale: Steroid-induced psychosis usually occurs during steroid therapy and at higher doses (typically above 40 to 60 mg prednisolone daily). The prednisolone course has already finished 3 days ago and the sympathomimetic features are not steroid-induced; this is a misattribution. (Source: RANZCP Practice Guidelines)

options.text: Commence olanzapine 10 mg orally and admit to psychiatry as first-episode psychosis
options.rationale: Diagnosing primary psychosis without completing organic workup is the AU sentinel-event lesson learned from missed encephalitis, delirium tropicale and stimulant toxidromes. Olanzapine carries QT prolongation and hyperthermia risk in stimulant toxicity. (Source: RANZCP Practice Guidelines)

options.text: Discharge home with his parents and follow up with his GP in 1 week
options.rationale: An acutely confused agitated patient with sympathomimetic features and disorientation is not safe for discharge. Acute toxic delirium has a measurable mortality if missed. (Source: RANZCP Practice Guidelines)

explanation.summary: First-episode psychosis with delirium features (fluctuant attention, autonomic instability, hallucination modality other than auditory) mandates organic workup before functional diagnosis. Sympathomimetic toxidromes (amphetamines, cocaine, synthetic cannabinoids, MDMA) cause acute psychosis with mydriasis, hyperthermia, tachycardia and diaphoresis - treat with benzodiazepines, not antipsychotics, in the acute phase.
key_points: Tactile hallucinations and visual hallucinations are more suggestive of delirium / intoxication than primary psychosis
Sympathomimetic toxidrome treated with benzodiazepines first-line; avoid antipsychotics that worsen hyperthermia and QT
Steroid-induced psychosis usually occurs at >40 mg prednisolone daily and during, not after, the course
explanation.pearls: Always include a structured organic workup in first-episode psychosis: blood ammonia, B12, TSH, syphilis, HIV, autoimmune (anti-NMDA receptor antibody), MRI, EEG, and urine drug screen including synthetic cannabinoids. Ammonia derangement is the missed diagnosis in young men with new psychosis on valproate.

subtopic_detail: Adolescent anorexia nervosa - refeeding syndrome risk and admission criteria
stem:
A 15-year-old girl is brought to ED by her mother. She has lost 12 kg over the past 6 months and has been restricting food intake to about 600 kcal/day. Her current BMI is 14.8 (below 0.4 percentile for age). She admits to compensatory exercise (running 10 km daily) but denies purging. She has had no menses for 5 months. She is medically stable on initial review.

Her mother is concerned and supportive. The adolescent eating disorder team has been notified.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 42, BP 88/54 mmHg, RR 12, SpO2 98% in room air, temperature 35.6 °C, postural BP drop 22 mmHg from lying to standing
data_table.Examination: Cachectic, dry skin, lanugo, cool peripheries, no proximal weakness, no peripheral oedema
data_table.Investigations: Na 138 mmol/L (135-145), K 3.1 mmol/L (3.5-5.0), Mg 0.62 mmol/L (0.7-1.1), phosphate 0.74 mmol/L (0.8-1.5), glucose 2.8 mmol/L (3.5-7.8), Hb 102 g/L (115-160), platelets 142 x10^9/L (150-400), LFTs ALT 86 U/L (<35), prolonged QTc 480 ms

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Discharge home with daily GP review and oral nutritional supplements
options.rationale: GCS is preserved but cardiovascular instability (HR 42, postural drop, QTc 480) makes home management with daily GP review unsafe. (Source: RANZCP Practice Guidelines)

options.text: Commence sertraline 50 mg orally daily for comorbid depression
options.rationale: SSRIs are ineffective in underweight anorexia nervosa because of serotonergic depletion at low weight; antidepressant trial is deferred until weight is restored. (Source: RANZCP Practice Guidelines)

options.text: Commence olanzapine 5 mg orally daily for appetite stimulation
options.rationale: Olanzapine is not first-line in adolescent anorexia nervosa; weak evidence supports a small weight gain but it does not address the urgent metabolic and cardiac risks. Admission and refeeding are more critical now. (Source: RANZCP Practice Guidelines)

options.text: Refer to outpatient family-based therapy and review in 1 week
options.rationale: Outpatient management is contraindicated when medical-admission criteria are met. Family-based therapy is the appropriate longitudinal therapy but begins after medical stabilisation when she meets admission criteria. (Source: RANZCP Practice Guidelines)

options.text: Admit for cardiac monitoring and cautious refeeding at 20 kcal/kg/day
options.rationale: RANZCP eating disorder guidelines and the ANZAED guidelines have defined medical-admission criteria: pulse under 50, postural BP drop above 20 mmHg, hypothermia, prolonged QTc above 460 ms, glucose under 3.5, refeeding-syndrome risk markers (hypokalaemia, hypophosphataemia, hypomagnesaemia), and BMI under 75% of expected. She meets multiple. Start refeeding cautiously at 20 kcal/kg/day, correcting electrolytes before increasing calories. (Source: RANZCP Practice Guidelines)

explanation.summary: Adolescent anorexia nervosa with bradycardia (HR under 50), postural BP drop above 20 mmHg, hypothermia, prolonged QTc above 460 ms, hypoglycaemia, or refeeding-syndrome risk markers (low K, Mg, phosphate) requires medical admission. Refeed cautiously at 20 kcal/kg/day with daily electrolyte checks. Family-based therapy is the longitudinal psychological therapy after medical stabilisation.
key_points: ANZAED admission criteria: HR<50, BP drop>20, hypothermia, QTc>460, BMI<75% expected, refeeding risk
Start refeeding at 20 kcal/kg/day; daily electrolyte and phosphate checks for first 5 to 7 days
SSRIs are ineffective in underweight anorexia - defer pharmacotherapy until weight restoration
explanation.pearls: Phosphate is the most commonly seen refeeding electrolyte to drop; prophylactic thiamine 200 mg IV before glucose load (Wernicke prevention) is standard. Family-based treatment (Maudsley method) is first-line psychological therapy for adolescents.

subtopic_detail: Adult ADHD pharmacotherapy with anxiety comorbidity and driving
stem:
A 28-year-old man is referred to a psychiatrist by his GP for new diagnosis of adult ADHD using DIVA-5 interview. He has a long history of inattention, distractibility, and forgetfulness. He works as a commercial truck driver and his employer requires fitness-to-drive review for the heavy vehicle category. He has co-existing generalised anxiety disorder partially controlled on escitalopram 20 mg daily. He has no history of substance misuse or cardiovascular disease.

His ECG and cardiology assessment have been completed by his GP.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 68, BP 122/76 mmHg, RR 16, SpO2 99% in room air, temperature 36.7 °C
data_table.Examination: Mood euthymic, mild restlessness, no tremor, no thyroid enlargement, no cardiac murmur
data_table.Investigations: ECG normal sinus rhythm with no QT prolongation, TSH within normal limits, FBC within normal limits, urine drug screen negative

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Commence long-acting methylphenidate after notifying medical assessor
options.rationale: AU Austroads Assessing Fitness to Drive guidance allows commercial driving with stable, supervised stimulant medication for ADHD provided the medication has been stable for at least 4 weeks, the patient is not impaired, and an annual review by the treating psychiatrist confirms ongoing fitness. Long-acting methylphenidate is first-line for adult ADHD in AU. The medical assessor will need to be informed and follow Austroads guidance. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Commence dexamphetamine 20 mg twice daily without medical assessor notification
options.rationale: Notifying the medical assessor is part of the driver's and clinician's responsibility in AU under the Austroads framework; failing to notify breaches mandatory reporting requirements for heavy vehicle medical certification. Twice-daily dexamphetamine in a long-haul driver also risks afternoon waning. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Defer ADHD pharmacotherapy until he stops commercial driving altogether
options.rationale: AU practice does not require stopping commercial driving to treat ADHD; treatment may improve safety. The supervised-stable-medication pathway in Austroads is the standard. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Commence clonidine 50 micrograms orally twice daily as monotherapy
options.rationale: Clonidine is used as adjunct, often for sleep onset or as adjunct to stimulants in children. It is not first-line monotherapy for adult ADHD in AU. It is also sedating and could compromise commercial driving. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Commence atomoxetine 40 mg orally daily because of driving restriction
options.rationale: Atomoxetine is a second-line agent in ADHD with smaller effect size and slower onset (4 to 6 weeks). It is not contraindicated for commercial driving but stimulants are not blanket-prohibited; the Austroads decision is made on clinical stability rather than drug class. Atomoxetine also interacts with escitalopram via CYP2D6. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

explanation.summary: AU first-line for adult ADHD is long-acting methylphenidate or lisdexamfetamine, started by a psychiatrist under Schedule 8 authority. Commercial driving is not contraindicated; Austroads requires stable medication, no impairment, and at least annual clinical review with notification of the medical assessor. SSRI-stimulant combinations are well tolerated; atomoxetine has CYP2D6 interactions with SSRIs.
key_points: Long-acting methylphenidate or lisdexamfetamine is AU first-line for adult ADHD
Austroads allows stimulant ADHD therapy with commercial driving subject to medical assessor notification and stability
Atomoxetine has CYP2D6 interactions with SSRIs; titrate slowly
explanation.pearls: Schedule 8 prescribing requires psychiatrist authority in most jurisdictions; check state-based S8 stimulant rules (NSW vs Vic differ). Cardiovascular screening before starting stimulants is mandatory; ECG only required if family history of sudden cardiac death or personal cardiac history.

stem:
A 52-year-old woman with recurrent unipolar major depressive disorder has failed two adequate antidepressant trials: sertraline 200 mg daily for 8 weeks and venlafaxine XR 225 mg daily for 8 weeks. She remains moderately depressed with PHQ-9 score 16 and has lost 5 kg over the last 3 months. She has had no manic or hypomanic episodes and her sleep is initial insomnia with terminal early-morning waking. She is not psychotic. Her thyroid function is normal.

She is currently on venlafaxine 225 mg and has reasonable adherence. Her psychiatrist is reviewing options.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 78, BP 122/76 mmHg, RR 16, SpO2 99% in room air, temperature 36.7 °C
data_table.Examination: Mood low, congruent affect, no psychomotor retardation, no psychotic features, MMSE 30/30, no manic features ever
data_table.Investigations: TSH 1.9 mIU/L (0.4-4.0), B12 within normal limits, ferritin 78 micrograms/L (15-200), Na 138 mmol/L (135-145), random cortisol within normal limits
data_table.Medications: Venlafaxine XR 225 mg daily (current trial 8 weeks)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Add diazepam 5 mg orally three times daily for symptomatic relief
options.rationale: Benzodiazepines do not treat depression, risk dependence, and may worsen depression chronically. They are not first-line augmentation. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Refer for psychodynamic therapy and stop venlafaxine immediately
options.rationale: Stopping the partially-effective antidepressant before establishing a replacement risks relapse; psychodynamic therapy has weaker evidence than CBT or IPT in moderate-to-severe depression and is not first-line for TRD. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Add aripiprazole 5 mg orally daily while continuing venlafaxine
options.rationale: Treatment-resistant depression (failure of 2 adequate antidepressant trials) is treated by either switching antidepressant class or augmentation; the strongest evidence for augmentation is with second-generation antipsychotics (aripiprazole, quetiapine, olanzapine, brexpiprazole). Aripiprazole 2 to 5 mg has the best metabolic profile and good evidence (CO-MED, AUS DOLPHIN). Lithium augmentation is also evidence-based but requires monitoring; lithium is preferred where there is a family history of bipolar. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Switch to a monoamine oxidase inhibitor with appropriate 2-week washout
options.rationale: MAOIs are effective in TRD but reserved for failure of multiple later-line strategies because of tyramine restrictions and serotonin syndrome risk if switched from serotonergic antidepressants without 2-week washout. Venlafaxine specifically needs 1 to 2 week washout before MAOI. They are not first-step augmentation. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Add St John's wort 900 mg orally daily as augmentation therapy
options.rationale: St John's wort is a CYP3A4 inducer and serotonergic agent; combining with venlafaxine risks serotonin syndrome and unpredictable drug interactions. It is not an evidence-based TRD augmentation. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

explanation.summary: Treatment-resistant depression (failure of 2 adequate antidepressant trials at therapeutic dose for 6 to 8 weeks each) is managed by augmentation with second-generation antipsychotic (aripiprazole, quetiapine, olanzapine) or lithium, or switching antidepressant class. ECT is considered for severe TRD or with psychotic features.
key_points: Aripiprazole 2 to 5 mg is well-tolerated TRD augmentation with the best metabolic profile
Lithium augmentation is evidence-based; preferred where there is family history of bipolar
ECT is indicated for severe TRD, psychotic depression, or active suicidality requiring rapid response
explanation.pearls: Always reassess for bipolarity (mood elevation history) before augmenting; missed bipolar accounts for some treatment-resistant cases. CANMAT and RANZCP guidelines list ketamine, esketamine, and electroconvulsive therapy as options for severe TRD. The STAR*D trial showed remission rates after 4 sequential steps approach 67%.

subtopic_detail: Catatonia diagnosis and lorazepam challenge in elderly inpatient
stem:
A 76-year-old man with a 5-year history of severe recurrent major depression is admitted to the geriatric psychiatry unit after a 2-week deterioration. He has stopped eating and drinking, says nothing in response to questions, and remains motionless in bed. The nursing staff describe "waxy flexibility" when his arm is moved, and he has held an unusual posture for over 30 minutes during the morning. He has not been febrile but his urine output has dropped over the last 24 hours. His usual medications include sertraline 100 mg daily and zopiclone 7.5 mg nocte. He has no recent dose changes and no infection.

The geriatric psychiatry consultant has examined him and the on-call medical registrar has reviewed his blood results.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 96, BP 102/68 mmHg, RR 14, SpO2 98% in room air, temperature 36.9 °C
data_table.Examination: Mute, motionless, waxy flexibility on passive limb movement, prolonged posturing (>30 minutes), no rigidity beyond catalepsy, no tremor, no clonus, no fever
data_table.Investigations: FBC within normal limits, UEC creatinine 132 micromol/L (60-110, baseline 88), CK 1240 U/L (<200), lactate 1.4, CRP 4 mg/L (<5), MRI brain unchanged from 6 months ago, EEG generalised slowing without status epilepticus
data_table.Medications: Sertraline 100 mg daily, zopiclone 7.5 mg nocte

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Increase sertraline to 200 mg orally daily for depressive psychomotor retardation
options.rationale: Increasing SSRI dose does not treat catatonia and may delay the diagnostic test. Catatonia is a syndrome that requires its own treatment first, even when underlying depression is the cause. (Source: RANZCP Practice Guidelines)

options.text: Refer to neurology for autoimmune encephalitis workup before treatment
options.rationale: Autoimmune encephalitis is a differential but the clinical features (catalepsy, waxy flexibility, mutism, in a known severe MDD patient) point first to catatonia; lorazepam challenge is both diagnostic and therapeutic and should not be delayed. Autoimmune workup proceeds in parallel. (Source: RANZCP Practice Guidelines)

options.text: Administer intravenous lorazepam 2 mg as a diagnostic and therapeutic challenge
options.rationale: Catatonia is diagnosed using the Bush-Francis Catatonia Rating Scale (catalepsy, waxy flexibility, mutism, immobility, posturing, stereotypy, and others). A lorazepam challenge of 2 mg IV (or 4 mg) within 10 to 20 minutes is both diagnostic (response within 10 minutes) and the first-line treatment. If no response, ECT is the definitive treatment. CK elevation and rising creatinine here reflect immobility-related rhabdomyolysis and AKI - these add urgency. (Source: RANZCP Practice Guidelines)

options.text: Commence olanzapine 10 mg orally daily for psychomotor agitation
options.rationale: Antipsychotics may precipitate neuroleptic malignant syndrome (NMS) in catatonia or worsen catatonic features; they are contraindicated in pure catatonia until catatonia has resolved with benzodiazepines or ECT. (Source: RANZCP Practice Guidelines)

options.text: Commence intravenous fluids, monitor input and output, and review in 24 hours
options.rationale: Supportive care addresses the AKI but does not treat the catatonia. Delaying lorazepam challenge by 24 hours risks worsening rhabdomyolysis and AKI. (Source: RANZCP Practice Guidelines)

explanation.summary: Catatonia is recognised by mutism, immobility, catalepsy, waxy flexibility and posturing. Lorazepam 2 mg IV is both diagnostic (response within 10 to 20 minutes) and first-line treatment. ECT is the definitive treatment if no response or if life-threatening catatonia (malignant catatonia: fever, autonomic instability, rhabdomyolysis). Antipsychotics are contraindicated until catatonia resolves because of NMS risk.
key_points: Bush-Francis Catatonia Rating Scale: ≥2 features for diagnosis
Lorazepam 2 mg IV challenge is both diagnostic and therapeutic (response in 10-20 minutes)
Antipsychotics contraindicated until catatonia resolves because of NMS risk
explanation.pearls: Malignant catatonia has hyperthermia, autonomic instability and rhabdomyolysis, mimicking NMS, and is a medical emergency treated with ECT. Always check CK, creatinine, and consider DVT prophylaxis given prolonged immobility.

subtopic_detail: Lithium toxicity at therapeutic level with NSAID interaction
stem:
A 45-year-old woman with bipolar I disorder on lithium 750 mg orally daily for 8 years is reviewed for new confusion, tremor and ataxia over the past 5 days. Her serum lithium concentration today is 0.85 mmol/L (target 0.6 to 1.0 mmol/L for maintenance). She has been taking ibuprofen 400 mg three times daily for the past 10 days for shoulder pain prescribed by her GP. She also takes perindopril 5 mg daily for hypertension that was started 6 months ago.

Her last clozapine review documented stable mood for 3 years. She has no recent fever, vomiting or diarrhoea.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 88, BP 132/82 mmHg, RR 16, SpO2 98% in room air, temperature 36.8 °C
data_table.Examination: Mildly drowsy, oriented to person, coarse postural tremor, broad-based gait with truncal ataxia, hyperreflexia, no clonus
data_table.Investigations: Lithium 0.85 mmol/L (0.6-1.0), creatinine 142 micromol/L (60-110, baseline 88), Na 138 mmol/L (135-145), TSH 4.8 mIU/L (0.4-4.0), CRP 6 mg/L (<5), urine output 30 mL/hour over 6 hours, ECG normal QT
data_table.Medications: Lithium 750 mg daily, perindopril 5 mg daily, ibuprofen 400 mg TDS (10 days)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Switch lithium to sodium valproate 500 mg orally twice daily
options.rationale: Switching mood stabiliser while neurotoxic worsens the picture; first address toxicity. Mood-stabiliser substitution during acute toxicity also raises the risk of mood relapse before steady state is achieved. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

options.text: Refer for emergency haemodialysis to remove lithium urgently
options.rationale: Haemodialysis is indicated for severe lithium toxicity: lithium above 4.0 mmol/L, persistent altered consciousness, AKI not responding to fluids, or seizures. She has a borderline-therapeutic level with renal impairment that may respond to fluid resuscitation; HD is excessive at this point. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

options.text: Continue current lithium dose and reassess in clinic in 1 week
options.rationale: Continuing lithium in the face of new neurological signs and rising creatinine risks progression to severe toxicity. Even with serum level in therapeutic range, CNS lithium accumulates over days in chronic toxicity. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

options.text: Restrict free water and add furosemide for renal recovery support
options.rationale: Furosemide increases lithium reabsorption in the proximal tubule by causing volume depletion; it can worsen lithium toxicity. Restricting free water is also counterproductive in dehydration-induced lithium toxicity. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

options.text: Stop ibuprofen and perindopril, hold lithium, give IV fluids, monitor serially
options.rationale: Chronic lithium toxicity can occur at therapeutic-range levels when renal clearance falls due to NSAID and ACE-I inhibition of renal prostaglandin and afferent arteriolar tone. Neurological features (confusion, tremor, ataxia, hyperreflexia) without GI symptoms are the textbook signature. Treatment is to stop precipitants, restore intravascular volume, and watch renal recovery; haemodialysis is reserved for severe toxicity (lithium >4.0, GCS impaired, AKI not responding, seizures). (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

explanation.summary: Chronic lithium toxicity at therapeutic serum levels occurs when renal clearance falls due to NSAIDs, ACE-I, thiazides, dehydration, or new renal impairment. CNS features (confusion, tremor, ataxia, hyperreflexia, dysarthria) dominate over GI symptoms. Treat by stopping precipitants and restoring intravascular volume. Haemodialysis for severe toxicity.
key_points: NSAIDs and ACE-I are the two most common drug precipitants of chronic lithium toxicity
Haemodialysis indicated for lithium >4.0 mmol/L or severe neurotoxicity
Lithium has its own elimination half-life independent of dialysis; rebound after HD is common
explanation.pearls: Long-term lithium monitoring requires 6-monthly lithium levels, 12-monthly UEC, TSH (lithium-induced hypothyroidism), and PTH/calcium (lithium-induced hyperparathyroidism). Educate patients to hold lithium during gastroenteritis and to avoid OTC NSAIDs.

subtopic_detail: Postpartum psychosis treatment escalation - ECT vs lithium
stem:
A 31-year-old woman is admitted to a perinatal mother-baby psychiatric unit 6 days postpartum following her first delivery. She has had 48 hours of severe insomnia, fluctuant mood between elation and confusion, paranoid persecutory delusions about strangers harming her baby, and command auditory hallucinations telling her to "get rid of" the baby. She is breastfeeding. The on-call perinatal psychiatrist has assessed her with the on-call consultant. She has a maternal aunt with bipolar disorder. The baby is being co-cared with her in the mother-baby unit with continuous staff oversight.

She has been started on olanzapine 10 mg orally nocte 48 hours ago with limited response and her delusions have intensified overnight.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 110, BP 134/82 mmHg, RR 18, SpO2 98% in room air, temperature 37.0 °C
data_table.Examination: Disorganised speech, fluctuant mood, persistent delusions and auditory hallucinations, no fever, no focal neurology, no thyroid enlargement
data_table.Investigations: FBC within normal limits, UEC within normal limits, TSH within normal limits, B12 within normal limits, MRI brain not yet performed
data_table.Medications: Olanzapine 10 mg nocte (commenced 48 hours ago); paracetamol prn

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Increase olanzapine to 20 mg nocte and observe for further 72 hours
options.rationale: Dose escalation may eventually help but the time-critical risk to mother and baby makes rapid response necessary. ECT achieves remission in days versus weeks. (Source: NHMRC Clinical Practice Guideline: Perinatal Mental Health)
source_refs: NHMRC Clinical Practice Guideline: Perinatal Mental Health

options.text: Commence lithium 250 mg orally twice daily and discontinue breastfeeding
options.rationale: Lithium is the long-term prophylaxis of choice (recurrence risk above 50% in subsequent pregnancies) but its onset for acute psychosis is slower than ECT. Breastfeeding can continue under specialist supervision with infant monitoring. (Source: NHMRC Clinical Practice Guideline: Perinatal Mental Health)
source_refs: NHMRC Clinical Practice Guideline: Perinatal Mental Health

options.text: Add diazepam 10 mg orally three times daily for symptomatic relief
options.rationale: Benzodiazepines may sedate but do not treat the underlying psychosis; high doses risk respiratory depression and accumulate in breast milk. (Source: NHMRC Clinical Practice Guideline: Perinatal Mental Health)
source_refs: NHMRC Clinical Practice Guideline: Perinatal Mental Health

options.text: Refer to community mental health team for outpatient follow-up
options.rationale: Outpatient management is not appropriate for a psychotic mother with command hallucinations to harm her baby. Postpartum psychosis is a psychiatric emergency. (Source: NHMRC Clinical Practice Guideline: Perinatal Mental Health)
source_refs: NHMRC Clinical Practice Guideline: Perinatal Mental Health

options.text: Refer for urgent electroconvulsive therapy with continued co-care of the baby
options.rationale: Postpartum psychosis with command hallucinations to harm the baby and limited response to antipsychotic at 48 hours is a psychiatric emergency. RANZCP guidance supports ECT as the rapid-onset definitive treatment with very high response rates (over 80%) in postpartum psychosis, especially when there is harm risk to mother or baby and antipsychotic response is limited. Lithium is the maintenance choice, but ECT achieves remission faster than dose escalation. Mother-baby care continues with continuous staff oversight. (Source: NHMRC Clinical Practice Guideline: Perinatal Mental Health)
source_refs: NHMRC Clinical Practice Guideline: Perinatal Mental Health

explanation.summary: Postpartum psychosis (incidence 1 to 2 per 1000) presents in the first 2 weeks postpartum with mood elevation, paranoid delusions, command hallucinations and severe insomnia. It is a psychiatric emergency. AU first-line is high-potency antipsychotic; ECT is preferred for rapid response in severe cases with harm risk. Long-term prophylaxis with lithium is offered because of high recurrence (over 50%) in subsequent pregnancies.
key_points: ECT achieves remission in days for severe postpartum psychosis with command hallucinations
Recurrence in subsequent pregnancies is above 50% - long-term lithium prophylaxis is offered
Mother-baby separation is not mandatory; continuous staff oversight in MBU is the AU model
explanation.pearls: Untreated mortality risk from infanticide (4%) and suicide (5%) makes urgent treatment time-critical. Future pregnancies require pre-pregnancy psychiatric planning with prophylactic lithium often re-introduced in the third trimester or immediately postpartum.

sources.label: NHMRC Clinical Practice Guideline: Perinatal Mental Health

stem:
A 46-year-old woman is reviewed in the community mental health clinic. She has a 14-year history of recurrent major depressive disorder. Her current episode has been ongoing for 11 months. She has previously had two adequate trials: sertraline 200 mg daily for 8 weeks, and venlafaxine XR 225 mg daily for 10 weeks with no significant response. She is currently 8 weeks into a third trial of escitalopram 20 mg daily plus weekly individual CBT with a clinical psychologist. There has been minimal change in her PHQ-9 score (19 baseline, 17 current).

She has no psychotic features and no suicidal plan. She is keen to add a medication rather than switch again. The psychiatry registrar has just completed a thorough history.

data_table.Vital signs: Within normal limits
data_table.Examination: PHQ-9 17/27, MoCA 28/30, no psychotic features, no manic symptoms past or present, no thoughts of self-harm, mild psychomotor slowing
data_table.Investigations: FBC, UEC, LFTs, TSH within normal limits; ECG QTc 410 ms
data_table.Medications: Escitalopram 20 mg daily (week 8), individual CBT weekly

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next pharmacological step?

options.text: Increase escitalopram to 30 mg daily as an off-label high-dose monotherapy trial
options.rationale: Escitalopram doses above 20 mg show no greater antidepressant effect and increase QTc prolongation risk. Australian therapeutic guidance limits the dose at 20 mg in adults and 10 mg in over-65s. Dose-escalation is not the next step in established non-response. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Add aripiprazole 2 to 5 mg daily as a PBS-listed atypical antipsychotic augmenter
options.rationale: After two adequate antidepressant trials without response, treatment-resistant depression criteria are met and augmentation is recommended. Aripiprazole is the most evidence-supported atypical antipsychotic augmenter in Australia (PBS-listed indication), starting at 2 to 5 mg daily and titrating to 10 mg. It is well-tolerated, has low weight-gain and metabolic burden, and has level 1 evidence. Lithium augmentation is an alternative with strong evidence but more monitoring; quetiapine XR is also used. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Add diazepam 5 mg twice daily for the anxious-depressive features experienced
options.rationale: Long-term benzodiazepine use in depression is not recommended; it can worsen depressive cognition, cause dependence and tolerance, and does not have augmentation evidence. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Switch to phenelzine after a 14-day SSRI washout to commence MAOI monotherapy
options.rationale: MAOIs are reserved for atypical or treatment-resistant depression after multiple failures including augmentation. They require dietary restrictions and a longer washout, so are rarely the next step before atypical antipsychotic augmentation. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Refer for transcranial direct current stimulation (tDCS) as an alternative to drugs
options.rationale: tDCS has limited evidence in TRD compared with ECT or rTMS, and is not the first-line escalation when augmentation has not been tried. rTMS may be considered if pharmacotherapy fails or is declined. (Source: RANZCP Practice Guidelines)

explanation.summary: Treatment-resistant depression is defined as failure of two adequate trials of antidepressants from different classes at therapeutic dose for at least 4 to 8 weeks. First-line augmentation options in Australian practice: aripiprazole (PBS-listed, level 1 evidence, 2 to 10 mg), lithium (target 0.4-0.8 mmol/L), or quetiapine XR. ECT is reserved for severe disease, psychotic features, urgent need to respond, or augmentation failure.
key_points: TRD = failure of 2 adequate trials at therapeutic dose for 4-8 weeks
Aripiprazole 2-10 mg is PBS-listed for TRD augmentation
Lithium augmentation alternative; check renal function and thyroid before starting
explanation.pearls: Before declaring TRD, always confirm adherence, rule out occult bipolarity (a positive screen flips the strategy to a mood stabiliser), screen for substance use, and check thyroid function and B12/folate.

subtopic_detail: Lithium chronic toxicity precipitated by ACE inhibitor
stem:
A 58-year-old woman with type 1 bipolar disorder has been stable on lithium carbonate for 14 years. Her most recent lithium level a month ago was 0.7 mmol/L.
