She has a recent diagnosis of hypertension; her GP started perindopril 5 mg daily 12 days ago. She also takes a topical NSAID gel intermittently for shoulder pain. Today her family bring her to the emergency department because she has been increasingly drowsy, has a fine coarse hand tremor, mild slurred speech, and vomited twice this morning.

She is rousable, oriented to person and place, and cooperates with examination. The ED registrar has just taken a focused history and noted the new ACE inhibitor.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 84, BP 142/86 mmHg, RR 16, SpO2 99% in room air, temperature 37.0 °C
data_table.Examination: Drowsy but rousable, coarse intentional hand tremor, mild dysarthria, gait ataxic, no focal weakness, no nystagmus, no seizure activity
data_table.Investigations: Lithium level 2.1 mmol/L (therapeutic 0.6-1.0), creatinine 132 micromol/L (45-90, baseline 78), sodium 136 mmol/L, potassium 4.4 mmol/L, ECG normal QTc, BSL 5.4
data_table.Medications: Lithium carbonate 750 mg nocte (long-term), perindopril 5 mg daily (12 days), topical diclofenac PRN, atorvastatin 20 mg nocte

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial management?

options.text: Continue lithium and add intravenous frusemide to enhance lithium renal excretion
options.rationale: Loop diuretics increase lithium reabsorption proximally by causing volume depletion and aldosterone-driven sodium retention, which paradoxically RAISES lithium levels. Diuretics are contraindicated in lithium toxicity. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

options.text: Withhold lithium and give 50 mL of 50% dextrose for presumed hypoglycaemic cause
options.rationale: BSL is normal; this is not hypoglycaemic encephalopathy. Withholding lithium is correct but glucose administration is not indicated. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

options.text: Stop lithium and ACE, give intravenous saline, and discuss haemodialysis with renal
options.rationale: Chronic lithium toxicity at level 2.1 mmol/L with neurological signs (drowsiness, ataxia, coarse tremor, dysarthria), in a patient on long-term lithium and recently started ACE inhibitor with new renal impairment, warrants withholding the offending drugs, restoring volume status carefully with 0.9% saline to enhance renal excretion, and considering haemodialysis. EXTRIP guidance suggests dialysis is indicated when level above 4.0 mmol/L OR above 2.5 mmol/L with neurological symptoms OR with significant renal impairment. Chronic toxicity (vs acute overdose) develops at lower levels because of tissue lithium accumulation. (Source: BMJ Best Practice)

options.text: Continue lithium at half the current dose and review lithium level in 7 days time
options.rationale: Active neurotoxicity requires lithium suspension, not dose halving and outpatient review. The risk of cerebellar permanent injury (syndrome of irreversible lithium-effectuated neurotoxicity, SILENT) is real. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

options.text: Administer activated charcoal 50 g orally to bind any unabsorbed lithium dose
options.rationale: Lithium is not adsorbed by activated charcoal. Charcoal is ineffective in lithium poisoning. (Source: BMJ Best Practice)

explanation.summary: Lithium toxicity is precipitated by drugs that reduce renal clearance: ACE inhibitors, ARBs, thiazide and loop diuretics, NSAIDs, and dehydration from any cause. Chronic toxicity occurs at lower serum levels than acute overdose because tissue stores are saturated. Withhold the lithium, withhold precipitating drugs, maintain volume status with 0.9% saline, and dialyse when level above 4.0 mmol/L OR above 2.5 mmol/L with neurological symptoms OR significant renal impairment. SILENT (syndrome of irreversible lithium-effectuated neurotoxicity) is a feared permanent cerebellar syndrome.
key_points: ACE inhibitors, ARBs, thiazides, NSAIDs raise lithium levels
Chronic toxicity at lower levels because of tissue accumulation
Dialysis indicated above 4.0 mmol/L or above 2.5 mmol/L with symptoms
explanation.pearls: Counsel all patients on lithium that any new prescription, OTC NSAID or dehydration episode is a trigger to recheck the lithium level within a week; the drug-drug-disease triangle here is particularly common.

stem:
A 30-year-old woman presents to her GP with her 8-week-old son. She has been increasingly tearful since 2 weeks postpartum. She describes low mood most days, loss of pleasure, poor sleep beyond what is needed by the baby, intrusive guilt about being a bad mother, and intermittent thoughts that her baby might be better off without her. She has no specific suicidal plan and no thoughts of harming the baby. She is exclusively breastfeeding and wants to continue. Her partner is supportive but works full time.

She has no prior psychiatric history and no medication allergies. The community child-health nurse completed an EPDS yesterday.

data_table.Vital signs: Within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Tearful, slumped posture, slowed speech, mild concentration difficulty, no psychotic features, EPDS 18/30 (positive screen)
data_table.Investigations: TSH 1.6 mIU/L, ferritin 28 microgram/L (15-200), B12 280 pmol/L, FBC normal, vitamin D 56 nmol/L
data_table.Medications: Iron and vitamin D supplementation since pregnancy

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Refer for involuntary admission to a mother-baby unit under the Mental Health Act
options.rationale: Involuntary admission is reserved for acute severe risk to self or baby with refusal of voluntary care. This woman is engaged in care and has no specific suicidal plan or infanticidal ideation. Voluntary, community-based care is appropriate. (Source: RANZCP Practice Guidelines)

options.text: Initiate fluoxetine 20 mg daily and advise cessation of breastfeeding immediately
options.rationale: Fluoxetine has a long half-life and an active metabolite (norfluoxetine) that accumulates in breast milk, making it less preferred for breastfeeding initiation; advising weaning is also not indicated. Continuing breastfeeding is supported with most SSRIs. (Source: RANZCP Practice Guidelines)

options.text: Initiate diazepam 2 mg twice daily for anxiety symptoms alongside breastfeeding
options.rationale: Benzodiazepines are not first-line for depression, can accumulate in breast milk, and cause sedation and poor feeding in the infant. Dependence and rebound anxiety on cessation are also concerns. (Source: RANZCP Practice Guidelines)

options.text: Initiate sertraline 50 mg daily and refer for CBT or interpersonal psychological therapy
options.rationale: Moderate-severe postnatal depression (EPDS 13+) with functional impairment warrants combined antidepressant plus psychological therapy. Sertraline is the preferred SSRI in breastfeeding because of low transfer to breast milk (relative infant dose less than 2%) and extensive safety data. CBT and interpersonal therapy have the strongest evidence for postnatal depression. (Source: RANZCP Practice Guidelines)

options.text: Watchful waiting alone with an Edinburgh postnatal depression scale recheck in 4 weeks
options.rationale: Moderate-severe depression with intrusive thoughts and EPDS 18 requires active treatment now. Watchful waiting is appropriate only for mild symptoms (EPDS 10-12) and brief duration. (Source: RANZCP Practice Guidelines)

explanation.summary: Postnatal depression with moderate severity (EPDS 13+) requires combined antidepressant and psychological therapy. Sertraline is the preferred SSRI in breastfeeding mothers because of low milk transfer (relative infant dose under 2%) and extensive safety data. Paroxetine is an alternative. Avoid fluoxetine first-line in breastfeeding because of long half-life and active metabolite accumulation. Specifically ask about thoughts of harming the baby - their presence escalates to mother-baby unit admission and urgent psychiatric review.
key_points: EPDS 13+ warrants combined pharmacotherapy and therapy
Sertraline preferred SSRI in breastfeeding (RID <2%)
Always screen for thoughts of harming the baby AND mother
explanation.pearls: Watch for postpartum thyroiditis (transient hyperthyroidism then hypothyroidism) as a mimic of perinatal mood disorder - check TSH at presentation as part of the workup, especially if symptoms include anxiety with tachycardia or fatigue with weight gain.

stem:
A 27-year-old engineering postgraduate is referred to the adult ADHD specialist clinic after a structured assessment by an ADHD-experienced psychiatrist (DIVA-5 plus collateral from a childhood school report). He meets DSM-5 criteria for combined-presentation ADHD with onset of symptoms before age 12. He has trialled 6 months of cognitive behavioural therapy with persistent functional impairment in his postgraduate study and partner relationship. He has no current alcohol or substance use disorder, no cardiovascular disease, no family history of sudden cardiac death, and his last cardiology screen ECG was normal.

He has no history of bipolar disorder, psychosis, or eating disorder. The psychiatrist plans to commence stimulant therapy.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 76, BP 124/78 mmHg, RR 14, SpO2 99% in room air, temperature 36.8 °C
data_table.Examination: No tics, no chorea, normal cardiac auscultation, normal weight and height, MoCA 30/30
data_table.Investigations: ECG normal sinus rhythm with normal QTc, FBC, UEC, LFTs, TSH within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial pharmacological choice?

options.text: Atomoxetine 40 mg daily for 7 days then 80 mg daily as a non-stimulant alternative
options.rationale: Atomoxetine is a non-stimulant alternative for adults with comorbid substance use disorder, tic disorder, or stimulant failure. It is not first-line where stimulants are appropriate. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Modafinil 200 mg in the morning as an off-label wakefulness-promoting alternative
options.rationale: Modafinil is not approved or PBS-listed for ADHD in Australia and is not the first-line agent. It is used off-label only in selected cases of narcolepsy or shift-work sleep disorder. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Clonidine 50 microgram nocte titrated weekly as a non-stimulant alpha-agonist option
options.rationale: Clonidine has supportive evidence for paediatric ADHD with tics or aggression and is sometimes used as an adjunct. It is not first-line monotherapy in an adult. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Bupropion 150 mg daily as a non-controlled antidepressant agent with ADHD evidence
options.rationale: Bupropion has modest evidence in adult ADHD but is not first-line; it is reserved for patients with substance use or contraindications to stimulants. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Methylphenidate immediate-release 10 mg twice daily, transitioning to long-acting
options.rationale: Stimulants (methylphenidate or lisdexamfetamine) are first-line for adult ADHD after confirmed diagnosis. Starting at low-dose immediate-release methylphenidate (10 mg twice daily) and converting to a long-acting formulation once tolerated is standard practice in Australia. Cardiovascular screening with BP, HR and ECG is required before initiation. Drivers must be advised about Austroads requirements - any seizure, sedation, or impairment must be reported, and PBS authority prescription rules apply for stimulants. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

explanation.summary: First-line pharmacotherapy for adult ADHD after a structured diagnostic assessment is a stimulant - methylphenidate or lisdexamfetamine. Initiate at low dose, titrate over 4 to 6 weeks against efficacy and adverse effects (BP, heart rate, sleep, appetite, mood). Cardiovascular screen (BP, HR, ECG when indicated) before starting. Atomoxetine and guanfacine are non-stimulant options for substance-use comorbidity or stimulant intolerance. Driving advice per Austroads applies; private vehicle drivers with adequately treated ADHD can usually drive unconditionally.
key_points: Stimulants (methylphenidate, lisdexamfetamine) are first-line in adult ADHD
Cardiovascular screen mandatory before starting; recheck BP and HR at follow-up
Austroads driving guidance: notify if impairment, sedation or seizures
explanation.pearls: When initiating a stimulant in an adult, expect a 25 to 30% non-response rate to the first agent; switching to the other class (methylphenidate to lisdexamfetamine or vice versa) recovers most non-responders.

subtopic_detail: Schizoaffective vs bipolar I with psychosis
stem:
A 29-year-old man is reviewed at the community mental health clinic 8 weeks after discharge from his second psychiatric admission. He has a 6-year history of recurrent mood episodes with psychotic features. His first episode at age 23 was a manic episode with grandiose delusions that resolved completely with lithium and risperidone. His second admission a year later was a depressive episode with mood-congruent delusions.

Between episodes over the last 4 years he has had ongoing persecutory delusions and paranoid ideation ("the government is monitoring me"), present even when his mood is euthymic. He has had 8 weeks of stable euthymic mood since his last admission but persecutory beliefs persist.

data_table.Vital signs: Within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Euthymic affect, no manic signs, no significant depressive symptoms, persecutory delusional beliefs about government surveillance, no hallucinations currently, insight partial, cognition grossly intact
data_table.Investigations: Recent FBC, UEC, LFTs, TSH within normal limits; urine drug screen negative; recent lithium level 0.7 mmol/L
data_table.Medications: Lithium carbonate 900 mg nocte, olanzapine 10 mg nocte

lead_in: Which diagnosis best fits this longitudinal presentation?

options.text: Schizoaffective disorder, bipolar type, given inter-episode psychotic features
options.rationale: DSM-5 schizoaffective disorder requires (1) an uninterrupted period of illness during which a major mood episode is concurrent with criterion A for schizophrenia, (2) at least 2 weeks of delusions/hallucinations in the ABSENCE of a major mood episode during the lifetime course, and (3) mood symptoms present for the majority of the total duration of the active illness. This man has persistent persecutory delusions during 4 years of inter-episode euthymia - exactly the criterion-2 feature that distinguishes schizoaffective disorder from bipolar I with psychotic features. Bipolar-type is specified because manic episodes have occurred. (Source: RANZCP Practice Guidelines)

options.text: Bipolar I disorder with mood-congruent psychotic features only during episodes
options.rationale: Bipolar I with psychotic features requires psychotic symptoms to occur ONLY during mood episodes. This patient has 4 years of persistent inter-episode persecutory delusions, which excludes pure bipolar I. (Source: RANZCP Practice Guidelines)

options.text: Schizophrenia with secondary mood symptoms arising from the primary psychosis
options.rationale: Schizophrenia is the diagnosis if mood episodes are brief relative to total illness duration. Mood episodes here are prominent, recurrent and meet criteria for major depressive and manic episodes, with mood-congruent and mood-incongruent psychosis. Mood symptoms present for the majority of illness duration favours schizoaffective over schizophrenia. (Source: RANZCP Practice Guidelines)

options.text: Delusional disorder, persecutory subtype, with no major mood episode history
options.rationale: Delusional disorder requires non-bizarre delusions in the absence of prominent hallucinations or formal psychotic symptoms outside the delusion, with preserved overall function. This man has had hallucinations historically and clear mood episodes, which excludes delusional disorder. (Source: RANZCP Practice Guidelines)

options.text: Substance-induced psychotic disorder, with persistent post-cessation features
options.rationale: Substance-induced disorder requires a temporal link to substance use and resolution after sustained abstinence. Urine drug screen is negative and no substance history is given; chronic persistent delusions over 4 years are not consistent with substance-induced disorder. (Source: RANZCP Practice Guidelines)

explanation.summary: Schizoaffective disorder is diagnosed when criterion A schizophrenia symptoms occur concurrent with a major mood episode AND there have been at least 2 weeks of psychotic symptoms in the absence of a major mood episode during lifetime illness, with mood symptoms present for the majority of the total active illness. Bipolar-type or depressive-type specifier depending on whether manic episodes have occurred. Treatment combines mood stabiliser (lithium, valproate, lamotrigine for depressive type) with an antipsychotic.
key_points: Key differentiator from bipolar I with psychosis: 2+ weeks of psychosis without mood episode
Key differentiator from schizophrenia: mood symptoms present for majority of illness
Subtypes: bipolar-type (mania present) vs depressive-type (only major depressive episodes)
explanation.pearls: Longitudinal data are essential - a single cross-sectional review cannot distinguish bipolar I with psychosis from schizoaffective disorder. Collateral history and review of past clinical records covering inter-episode periods are the diagnostic gold standard.

subtopic_detail: Severe postpartum psychosis with catatonic features
stem:
A 28-year-old G1P1 woman is admitted to the mother-baby psychiatric unit on day 8 postpartum. She had been hyperactive, grandiose and not sleeping for 3 days from day 4, then developed disorganised speech and persecutory delusions on day 7. She was started on olanzapine 10 mg yesterday but overnight she became mute, refused food and fluids, and now lies motionless in bed. Her partner is distressed at the bedside. The baby is being cared for by the woman's mother on the unit.

She has no prior psychiatric history. She has a first-degree relative with bipolar disorder. The medical registrar has examined her with the consultant perinatal psychiatrist.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 116, BP 142/88 mmHg, RR 22, SpO2 97% in room air, temperature 37.4 °C, no diaphoresis
data_table.Examination: Mute, motionless, waxy flexibility with limb posturing held over 30 minutes, no rigidity beyond catalepsy, no clonus, no tremor, mild lead-pipe resistance to passive movement, no fever above 37.5
data_table.Investigations: FBC, UEC, LFTs within normal limits except CK 1860 U/L (<200), lactate 1.4, calcium and magnesium normal, BSL 4.6 mmol/L, urine drug screen negative, MRI brain normal, EEG diffuse slowing without status, anti-NMDA receptor antibody pending
data_table.Medications: Olanzapine 10 mg yesterday (one dose), oxytocin postnatally; no fluids/food in 12 hours

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Continue olanzapine and start prophylactic dantrolene 1 mg/kg IV for emerging NMS
options.rationale: Although NMS is a differential, the temperature is only 37.4, there is no severe rigidity, no autonomic instability and no severe diaphoresis. The features (mutism, motionless, waxy flexibility, posturing) point to catatonia after only one dose of olanzapine, which catatonia history actually makes likely. Continuing olanzapine in suspected catatonia risks worsening it; antipsychotics are contraindicated until catatonia resolves. (Source: RANZCP Practice Guidelines)

options.text: Stop olanzapine, give intravenous lorazepam 2 mg challenge and prepare for urgent ECT
options.rationale: Catatonia is diagnosed by 2+ Bush-Francis features (mutism, immobility, waxy flexibility, posturing - all present). Lorazepam 2 mg IV is both diagnostic (response within 10 to 20 minutes) and first-line treatment. Postpartum psychosis with malignant catatonia (mute, dehydrated, CK rising, mild fever) is a psychiatric emergency; ECT is the definitive treatment if lorazepam fails or if malignant features escalate. Antipsychotics worsen catatonia and risk precipitating NMS. Anti-NMDA receptor encephalitis is the critical organic differential and antibody testing should already be in train. (Source: RANZCP Practice Guidelines)

options.text: Switch olanzapine to clozapine 12.5 mg overnight with continuous ECG monitoring
options.rationale: Clozapine initiation in catatonia is dangerous and inappropriate; clozapine is reserved for treatment-resistant schizophrenia and has its own catatonic and NMS risks. (Source: RANZCP Practice Guidelines)

options.text: Refer to neurology for autoimmune encephalitis workup and withhold all psychiatric care
options.rationale: Anti-NMDA receptor encephalitis workup should run in parallel, NOT replace treatment of catatonia. Withholding treatment risks rapid deterioration with dehydration, rhabdomyolysis, aspiration. Lorazepam challenge is safe in either diagnosis. (Source: RANZCP Practice Guidelines)

options.text: Place a nasogastric tube and feed enterally; the mute state will resolve with food
options.rationale: Refeeding addresses hydration but does not treat the underlying catatonia. NG feeding may be needed adjunctively but does not replace lorazepam challenge and ECT preparation. (Source: RANZCP Practice Guidelines)

explanation.summary: Postpartum psychosis is a psychiatric emergency typically beginning in the first 2 weeks postpartum with mood lability, grandiosity, paranoid delusions, disorganisation and rapid progression. Catatonic features can complicate it. Catatonia is diagnosed by 2+ Bush-Francis features (mutism, immobility, waxy flexibility, posturing). Lorazepam 2 mg IV is diagnostic and therapeutic; ECT is definitive if lorazepam fails or malignant features (rhabdomyolysis, autonomic instability, hyperthermia) emerge. Antipsychotics are contraindicated until catatonia resolves because of NMS precipitation risk. Anti-NMDA receptor encephalitis must be excluded.
key_points: Postpartum psychosis: onset typically within 2 weeks, requires urgent admission
Catatonia + recent antipsychotic exposure: high NMS risk, stop the antipsychotic
Lorazepam challenge first; ECT definitive; rule out anti-NMDA encephalitis
explanation.pearls: First-degree relatives with bipolar disorder confer up to 40% lifetime risk of postpartum psychosis after a first delivery; offer prophylactic mood stabiliser planning preconception and intensified perinatal monitoring.

stem:
A 24-year-old woman with bipolar I disorder has been stable on sodium valproate 1000 mg daily for 18 months following a manic episode requiring brief admission. She has had no further episodes. She has presented to the community mental health clinic for a routine review and tells you she and her partner are planning a pregnancy in the next 6 to 12 months. She has heard about sodium valproate and is asking about her options. She has not been using contraception for 3 months.

She has no other comorbidities and is otherwise well.

data_table.Vital signs: Within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Euthymic affect, no manic or depressive features, weight stable, BMI 24.5
data_table.Investigations: Valproate level 480 micromol/L (therapeutic 350-700), FBC, UEC, LFTs within normal limits, beta-hCG negative

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Continue valproate and commence high-dose folic acid 5 mg daily preconceptionally
options.rationale: 5 mg folic acid is appropriate adjunctive advice for any woman of reproductive age on antiepileptic drugs, but it does not mitigate the substantial teratogenic risk of valproate (10% major congenital malformation, 30 to 40% neurodevelopmental disorder). Folic acid alone is not enough to justify continuing valproate. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Continue valproate, advise reliable contraception and review again in 6 months time
options.rationale: She is already planning pregnancy in 6 to 12 months; advising indefinite contraception delays her family planning and ignores her stated preference. The teratogenic profile of valproate makes this an immediate switch decision. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Counsel teratogenic risk, ensure contraception, plan cross-titration to lamotrigine
options.rationale: Valproate is contraindicated in pregnancy and discouraged in women of reproductive potential because of approximately 10% risk of major congenital malformations (especially neural tube defects, cardiac, facial cleft, hypospadias) AND 30 to 40% risk of neurodevelopmental disability in exposed offspring. In any woman of reproductive potential a documented risk discussion and pregnancy-prevention plan are mandatory before continuing valproate. A planned cross-titration to a safer agent (lamotrigine for predominant depressive episodes; lithium with risk-benefit balance for predominant manic episodes) under specialist supervision is the appropriate step, BEFORE conception. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Stop valproate today and start lamotrigine 25 mg daily without titration upward
options.rationale: Abrupt cessation of a mood stabiliser in stable bipolar disorder risks early relapse. Lamotrigine must be titrated slowly (25 mg daily for 2 weeks, 50 mg daily for 2 weeks) to minimise SJS/TEN risk, and the switch should be a planned cross-titration with monitoring. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Continue valproate at 500 mg daily to minimise teratogenic risk in a planned pregnancy
options.rationale: Lower-dose valproate (below 700 mg daily) reduces but does not eliminate teratogenic risk; the risk of major malformations remains substantially above background. Dose reduction is not an acceptable strategy for preconception planning. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

explanation.summary: Valproate is contraindicated in pregnancy and discouraged in women of reproductive potential because of 10% major congenital malformation rate (neural tube defects, cardiac, cleft, hypospadias) AND 30 to 40% neurodevelopmental disability in exposed offspring. Documented risk counselling and contraception are required to continue valproate. Preconception planning requires planned cross-titration to lamotrigine (depressive-predominant bipolar) or lithium (manic-predominant) under specialist supervision. Lithium has approximately 5% risk of cardiac malformations (Ebstein anomaly was historically overstated) and requires fetal echocardiography; lamotrigine has the best pregnancy safety profile of mood stabilisers.
key_points: Valproate: 10% MCM rate + 30-40% NDD rate; contraindicated in pregnancy
Switch to lamotrigine (depressive predominance) or lithium under specialist care preconception
Pregnancy-prevention plan mandatory in any woman of reproductive potential on valproate
explanation.pearls: If valproate continuation is unavoidable, document the risk discussion, the alternatives considered, and use the lowest effective dose; the woman should sign a valproate-specific risk acknowledgement form per Australian therapeutic guidance.

stem:
A 22-year-old university student attends your GP clinic with binge eating followed by self-induced vomiting, occurring 4-5 times per week for the past 18 months. She also exercises excessively after binges and feels intense guilt and disgust afterwards. Her weight has been stable; BMI 22 kg/m^2. She has no purging-related complications such as hypokalaemia or oesophagitis on screening.

She has been engaged in CBT for eating disorders for 12 weeks with a clinical psychologist with partial improvement but ongoing binge-purge episodes 3-4 times per week. She is asking about medication options. She has no history of bipolar disorder, no suicidal ideation, no pregnancy plan in the next 12 months.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 72, BP 116/72 mmHg, RR 14, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.6 °C
data_table.Examination: BMI 22 kg/m^2, dental enamel erosion on the lingual surface of incisors, parotid swelling bilateral, Russell sign over knuckles minimal, no peripheral oedema
data_table.Investigations: Potassium 3.9 mmol/L (3.5-5.0), bicarbonate 27 mmol/L (22-28), amylase 138 U/L (25-125), creatinine 64 micromol/L, magnesium 0.82 mmol/L, ECG sinus rhythm QTc 410 ms

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Switch to interpersonal therapy and avoid pharmacotherapy
options.rationale: IPT is an alternative psychotherapy for bulimia but switching away from a partially effective CBT-ED course and avoiding pharmacotherapy contradicts the evidence base showing additional benefit from fluoxetine at 60 mg. (Source: RANZCP Eating Disorders)

options.text: Continue CBT and add fluoxetine 60 mg orally each morning
options.rationale: RANZCP and NICE eating disorder guidelines support fluoxetine 60 mg daily as adjunctive pharmacotherapy in bulimia nervosa when binge-purge symptoms persist despite a course of CBT-ED. The 60 mg dose is the evidence-supported anti-bulimic dose (higher than typical antidepressant dosing) and reduces binge and purge frequency by approximately 50% in trials. Continue psychotherapy alongside. (Source: RANZCP Eating Disorders)

options.text: Commence topiramate 100 mg twice daily for binge frequency
options.rationale: Topiramate has trial evidence in bulimia but is second-line because of cognitive adverse effects, weight loss in an otherwise weight-stable patient, and teratogenicity in a woman of reproductive age. (Source: RANZCP Eating Disorders)

options.text: Commence bupropion 150 mg daily as the proposed approach
options.rationale: Bupropion lowers seizure threshold and is contraindicated in bulimia nervosa because of an increased risk of seizures associated with purging-related electrolyte derangement. (Source: AMH)

options.text: Admit for inpatient refeeding and intensive psychotherapy
options.rationale: Inpatient admission is reserved for medical instability (severe electrolyte derangement, cardiac compromise) or treatment-resistant cases with safety concerns; this patient has stable physiology and is receiving outpatient psychotherapy. (Source: RANZCP Eating Disorders)

explanation.summary: Bulimia nervosa first-line treatment is CBT-ED. When CBT-ED is partially effective, fluoxetine 60 mg daily is the evidence-supported adjunctive pharmacotherapy and reduces binge-purge frequency by approximately 50%. Topiramate is second-line because of cognitive side effects and teratogenicity. Bupropion is contraindicated in bulimia. IPT is an alternative psychotherapy. Inpatient admission is reserved for medical instability.
key_points: Fluoxetine 60 mg daily is the anti-bulimic dose (NOT 20 mg)
CBT-ED is first-line; pharmacotherapy adjunctive
Bupropion contraindicated due to seizure risk
Topiramate second-line; teratogenic
explanation.pearls: Fluoxetine in bulimia uses the higher 60 mg dose to leverage the serotonergic anti-binge effect; the standard antidepressant 20 mg dose is inadequate for bulimia symptom suppression.

stem:
A 28-year-old man is referred by his GP after a recent confirmed diagnosis of adult ADHD by a consultant psychiatrist using DIVA-5 and confirmatory childhood school records. He reports lifelong difficulty sustaining attention, organisational struggles, and procrastination, with current impairment in his accounting job. He has no history of substance misuse, no cardiovascular disease, normal ECG, BP 124/78 mmHg, and no current depression. He drives a private vehicle for his commute (45 minutes each way).

He attends today to discuss starting pharmacotherapy. He has no insurance disqualifications and no pregnancy considerations. He has not previously trialled any ADHD medication.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 78, BP 124/78 mmHg, RR 14, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.6 °C
data_table.Examination: Mental state normal cognition and mood, no psychotic features, no suicidality
data_table.Investigations: ECG sinus rhythm 78, QTc 408 ms; FBC and UEC within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Commence bupropion 150 mg daily as off-label ADHD therapy as the proposed approach with the proposed clinical action
options.rationale: Bupropion has limited evidence in adult ADHD and is not a first-line agent. RANZCP first-line is stimulants; atomoxetine and guanfacine are non-stimulant alternatives. (Source: RANZCP ADHD)

options.text: Commence atomoxetine 40 mg daily for 1 week then 80 mg daily, no notification required with the proposed clinical action
options.rationale: Atomoxetine is a reasonable non-stimulant first-line where stimulants are contraindicated or there is significant substance misuse risk, but it has lower effect size than stimulants in adult ADHD. Austroads requires notification for any ADHD treatment that affects driving capacity. (Source: RANZCP ADHD)

options.text: Commence lisdexamfetamine 30 mg orally each morning, baseline weight, and counsel on Austroads driving requirement to notify the licensing authority
options.rationale: RANZCP and AU ADHD guidelines recommend stimulants (methylphenidate or lisdexamfetamine) as first-line in adult ADHD without contraindication; lisdexamfetamine has smoother pharmacokinetics and lower abuse potential than immediate-release amphetamines. Austroads 'Assessing Fitness to Drive' requires self-notification to the driver licensing authority for ADHD on stimulant therapy; the condition itself does not disqualify but treatment must be reviewed. Baseline BP, weight, ECG already done. (Source: RANZCP ADHD)

options.text: Refer for CBT for ADHD and defer pharmacotherapy for 6 months as the proposed approach with the proposed clinical action
options.rationale: Psychological therapy alone has smaller effect than pharmacotherapy in adult ADHD with functional impairment; the standard combined approach is medication plus psychological support and skill-building. (Source: RANZCP ADHD)

options.text: Commence methylphenidate immediate-release 10 mg three times daily without driving advice as the proposed approach
options.rationale: Although methylphenidate is a valid first-line stimulant, IR formulations require multiple daily dosing with greater rebound effect; sustained-release or extended-release preparations are preferred for adult work-and-drive lifestyles. Austroads notification is required regardless of agent. (Source: Austroads Assessing Fitness to Drive)

explanation.summary: Adult ADHD first-line pharmacotherapy is stimulants - lisdexamfetamine or extended-release methylphenidate. Atomoxetine and guanfacine are non-stimulant alternatives for stimulant contraindication or substance misuse history. Baseline BP, pulse, ECG, weight, and Austroads notification are required. Combining pharmacotherapy with psychological support gives the best functional outcomes.
key_points: First-line: lisdexamfetamine or extended-release methylphenidate
Atomoxetine if stimulants contraindicated
Austroads requires driver notification on ADHD stimulant treatment
Baseline ECG, BP, pulse, weight before initiation
explanation.pearls: Austroads 'Assessing Fitness to Drive' treats ADHD as a notifiable condition when treatment may affect driving capacity; under-notification is a common practical compliance gap in AU practice.

stem:
A 38-year-old woman with a 15-year history of schizoaffective disorder, depressed type, is brought by her family because she has stopped eating, speaking, and moving for 4 days. She has been on quetiapine 600 mg nocte and sertraline 100 mg morning, both unchanged for 8 months. The family deny any obvious psychosocial trigger, medication change, or substance use.

In the assessment room she sits with one arm raised at shoulder height and maintains the posture when you adjust it. She does not respond to verbal questions, makes intermittent grimacing movements, and resists passive movement of her opposite arm by adopting an oppositional rigidity. Her examination is otherwise unremarkable; bloods including creatine kinase, electrolytes, and inflammatory markers are within normal limits.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 96, BP 118/76 mmHg, RR 18, SpO2 98% on room air, temperature 37.1 °C
data_table.Examination: Mutism, immobility, waxy flexibility, posturing of right arm, intermittent grimacing, gegenhalten of left arm, no rigidity at rest, no clonus, no autonomic instability
data_table.Investigations: Creatine kinase 92 U/L (<200), sodium 138 mmol/L (135-145), white cell count 7.4 x10^9/L (4-11), CRP 4 mg/L (<5), TSH 1.6 mIU/L; urine drug screen negative; CT brain within normal limits
data_table.Medications: Quetiapine 600 mg nocte, sertraline 100 mg morning

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Urgent electroconvulsive therapy referral as first-line without medication trial as the proposed approach
options.rationale: ECT is highly effective for catatonia and is escalated to when lorazepam is inadequate (typically 48-72 hours of 6-9 mg/day) or with malignant catatonia features. The first step is the diagnostic and therapeutic lorazepam challenge. (Source: RANZCP Catatonia)

options.text: Add olanzapine 10 mg IM and continue quetiapine with the proposed clinical action
options.rationale: Adding a second antipsychotic in suspected catatonia risks worsening catatonia and precipitating neuroleptic malignant syndrome. Antipsychotics are generally withheld until catatonia resolves; the first step is the lorazepam challenge. (Source: RANZCP Catatonia)

options.text: Commence dantrolene 1 mg/kg IV and bromocriptine 2.5 mg orally for suspected neuroleptic malignant syndrome
options.rationale: NMS requires hyperthermia, severe rigidity, autonomic instability, and markedly raised CK; this presentation has none of these. Treating presumptive NMS in confirmed catatonia delays correct therapy. (Source: BMJ Best Practice)

options.text: Lorazepam 2 mg IV/IM as a diagnostic challenge with reassessment of catatonia features in 15 minutes
options.rationale: She meets DSM-5 criteria for catatonia (mutism, immobility, waxy flexibility, posturing, grimacing, negativism). The lorazepam challenge - 2 mg IV or IM with reassessment at 5-15 minutes - is both diagnostic and therapeutic; a partial response within minutes confirms catatonia and directs treatment with scheduled lorazepam 2-3 mg three times daily titrated to response. CK is normal and there is no autonomic instability or hyperthermia, making NMS unlikely. (Source: RANZCP Catatonia)

options.text: Restart sertraline at higher dose (200 mg) and observe with the proposed clinical action
options.rationale: Increasing sertraline does not address catatonia and may worsen agitation or precipitate serotonin syndrome with no benefit. The diagnostic challenge with lorazepam is the next step. (Source: RANZCP Catatonia)

explanation.summary: Catatonia meeting DSM-5 criteria requires a lorazepam challenge (2 mg IV/IM, reassess at 5-15 min) which is both diagnostic and therapeutic; response confirms diagnosis and directs scheduled lorazepam 2-3 mg three times daily titrated up. Antipsychotics are generally withheld during active catatonia because of NMS risk and potential to worsen catatonia. ECT is escalated to for inadequate response or malignant features.
key_points: Lorazepam challenge 2 mg IV/IM, reassess 5-15 min
Confirmed catatonia: scheduled lorazepam 2-3 mg TDS titrated
Withhold antipsychotics during active catatonia
ECT for inadequate response or malignant catatonia
explanation.pearls: Catatonia in schizoaffective disorder is dramatic but the diagnostic test is bedside: 2 mg lorazepam within 15 minutes typically loosens posture and restores some speech if catatonia is the cause.

stem:
A 24-year-old woman is brought by ambulance to the emergency department 90 minutes after a deliberate self-poisoning. She reportedly ingested 30 tablets of amitriptyline 25 mg with a bottle of wine. She is drowsy with intermittent agitation. Her airway is patent and she is breathing spontaneously.

On the trolley she has an episode of generalised tonic-clonic seizure lasting 90 seconds, terminating with IV midazolam 5 mg. After the seizure her vital signs and ECG are obtained. The ECG shows sinus tachycardia with a QRS duration of 140 ms and a prominent terminal R wave in aVR.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 132, BP 86/52 mmHg, RR 18, SpO2 96% on 6 L Hudson mask, temperature 37.2 °C
data_table.Examination: GCS 11 (E3V3M5) post-ictal, dilated pupils 6 mm sluggishly reactive, dry mucous membranes, tachycardia, decreased bowel sounds, urinary retention
data_table.Investigations: ECG sinus tachycardia, QRS 140 ms, terminal R in aVR 4 mm, QTc 470 ms; sodium 136 mmol/L, potassium 3.6 mmol/L, bicarbonate 18 mmol/L, lactate 4.6 mmol/L; venous gas pH 7.22, paracetamol level <10 mg/L, ethanol 0.18%
data_table.Medications: Pre-overdose: amitriptyline 50 mg nocte (prescribed for chronic pain)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: IV sodium bicarbonate 8.4% 1-2 mmol/kg bolus, repeated to target QRS narrowing and arterial pH 7.50-7.55
options.rationale: QRS over 100 ms after TCA overdose indicates sodium channel blockade with elevated risk of seizure and ventricular arrhythmia; QRS over 120 ms or a terminal R wave in aVR over 3 mm are independent predictors. Hypertonic sodium bicarbonate (8.4% 1-2 mmol/kg bolus, repeated to narrow QRS or alkalise pH to 7.50-7.55) overcomes sodium channel blockade through both sodium loading and alkalinisation. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines Toxicology)

options.text: IV intralipid 20% bolus 1.5 mL/kg followed by infusion as first-line as the proposed approach
options.rationale: Intralipid is rescue therapy for cardiac arrest or refractory cardiotoxicity unresponsive to sodium bicarbonate, not first-line; sodium bicarbonate is the priority for QRS widening from TCA. (Source: Austin Toxicology Handbook)

options.text: IV amiodarone 300 mg loading dose for QRS widening with the proposed clinical action
options.rationale: Class III antiarrhythmics including amiodarone are contraindicated in TCA toxicity because they prolong QT and can worsen ventricular arrhythmia; class IA agents are also contraindicated. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines Toxicology)

options.text: Activated charcoal 50 g orally now as the proposed approach with the proposed clinical action
options.rationale: Activated charcoal beyond 1-2 hours post-ingestion is generally not effective and adds aspiration risk in a drowsy patient with anticholinergic ileus; this is 90 minutes post-ingestion with a depressed GCS, so airway protection would be required before charcoal. The priority is sodium bicarbonate for cardiotoxicity. (Source: Austin Toxicology Handbook)

options.text: Flumazenil 0.2 mg IV to reverse benzodiazepine sedation with the proposed clinical action
options.rationale: Flumazenil is contraindicated in TCA overdose because it lowers seizure threshold; this patient has already had one TCA-induced seizure and flumazenil would precipitate further seizures. (Source: Austin Toxicology Handbook)

explanation.summary: TCA overdose causes sodium-channel blockade with QRS widening, seizures, hypotension and ventricular arrhythmia. QRS >100 ms increases seizure risk, and >120 ms or terminal R wave in aVR >3 mm increase ventricular arrhythmia risk. Sodium bicarbonate 8.4% 1-2 mmol/kg bolus titrated to QRS narrowing and arterial pH 7.50-7.55 is first-line. Class I/III antiarrhythmics, flumazenil, and physostigmine are contraindicated. Intralipid is rescue for cardiac arrest only.
key_points: QRS >100 ms = seizure risk; >120 ms = arrhythmia risk
Terminal R in aVR >3 mm = arrhythmia risk
NaHCO3 8.4% 1-2 mmol/kg bolus, repeat to pH 7.50-7.55
Avoid Class I/III antiarrhythmics, flumazenil, physostigmine
explanation.pearls: In TCA cardiotoxicity, both the sodium load and the alkalinisation contribute to displacing the drug from sodium channels; targeting arterial pH 7.50-7.55 rather than 'normal' is the AU recommended endpoint.

stem:
A 30-year-old primary school teacher presents to your neurology clinic with a 6-month history of left-sided weakness and intermittent right hand tremor. The symptoms began 2 days after a stressful complaint from a parent at work. The weakness fluctuates and is worse when observed during examination. She has not had falls and has continued to drive.

On examination, Hoover's sign is positive (her left hip extension force normalises when she is asked to flex the contralateral hip against resistance). The right hand tremor entrains to a tapping rhythm she is asked to perform with the left hand. Sensory examination shows a non-anatomical splitting at the midline. Power graded as 3/5 in the left leg drops away with give-way pattern. MRI brain, cervical spine MRI, and nerve conduction studies are reported normal.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 78, BP 116/72 mmHg, RR 14, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.6 °C
data_table.Examination: Hoover sign positive, tremor entrainment positive, midline splitting of sensory level, give-way weakness, normal tone, tendon reflexes preserved, no clonus, plantars downgoing
data_table.Investigations: MRI brain with contrast normal, MRI cervical spine normal, EMG and nerve conduction studies normal, FBC and UEC within normal limits, ANA negative, B12 and folate within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Refer to a forensic psychiatrist to assess for malingering and benefit-seeking behaviour as the proposed approach with the proposed clinical action
options.rationale: Malingering requires identifiable secondary gain and intentional symptom production; FND is involuntary. Diagnosing malingering on the basis of inconsistency is incorrect and stigmatising. (Source: BMJ Best Practice FND)

options.text: Refer for repeat MRI brain in 3 months and observe with no diagnostic label as the proposed approach with the proposed clinical action as the proposed clinical action
options.rationale: Repeat imaging without an evolving clinical picture does not change management and delays appropriate treatment; FND has positive clinical features and can be communicated as a clear diagnosis. (Source: BMJ Best Practice FND)

options.text: Explain that the diagnosis is functional neurological disorder based on positive clinical signs, and refer for symptom-specific physiotherapy and FND-informed psychological therapy
options.rationale: FND is diagnosed by positive features (Hoover sign, tremor entrainment, give-way weakness, non-anatomical sensory level) not solely by exclusion. The explanation as a problem with how the brain controls movement (not imagined or feigned), with referral to symptom-specific physiotherapy and FND-informed psychological therapy, has the strongest evidence base and improves outcomes. (Source: BMJ Best Practice FND)

options.text: Commence amitriptyline 50 mg nocte for somatoform pain as the proposed approach with the proposed clinical action as the proposed clinical action
options.rationale: There is no role for amitriptyline in motor FND; first-line is positive diagnosis, education, and symptom-specific physiotherapy and psychological therapy. (Source: BMJ Best Practice FND)

options.text: Commence prednisolone 50 mg daily for empirical inflammatory neurological treatment as the proposed approach with the proposed clinical action
options.rationale: Steroid therapy has no role in FND and risks adverse effects with no benefit; immunotherapy is reserved for confirmed autoimmune neurological disease. (Source: BMJ Best Practice FND)

explanation.summary: Functional neurological disorder is now a positive-feature diagnosis: Hoover sign, tremor entrainment, give-way weakness, non-anatomical sensory loss, dissociative seizure semiology. Communicating a clear positive diagnosis (not exclusion-by-default) and referring to FND-informed physiotherapy and psychological therapy improves outcomes. Malingering and somatisation are different diagnostic constructs. Imaging surveillance and empirical immunotherapy or amitriptyline have no role.
key_points: FND diagnosed by positive signs, not exclusion only
Hoover sign, tremor entrainment, give-way are highly specific
Treatment: FND physiotherapy + FND-informed psychological therapy
Distinguished from malingering (intentional, secondary gain)
explanation.pearls: Hoover sign: the patient's apparently weak hip extension force normalises when they flex the contralateral hip against resistance, indicating attentional rather than structural weakness.

stem:
A 76-year-old man on the surgical ward day 3 post-emergency laparotomy for perforated diverticulitis becomes increasingly agitated overnight. He pulls at his lines, tries to climb out of bed, and shouts at staff. His past history includes mild cognitive impairment, well-controlled hypertension, and ischaemic heart disease (LVEF 45%, no recent events). Verbal de-escalation and reorientation have not helped, and he has attempted to strike the nurse.

On examination he is disoriented to time and place but recognises his daughter. He has no fever, vitals are stable, and his most recent ECG today shows sinus rhythm with QTc 450 ms. Recent renal function and electrolytes are within normal limits. He is on regular paracetamol, oxycodone 5 mg PRN, ceftriaxone, and metronidazole.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 92, BP 142/86 mmHg, RR 18, SpO2 96% on room air, temperature 36.7 °C
data_table.Examination: Disoriented to time and place, attentional deficit on serial 7s, recognises family, no focal neurology, no nuchal rigidity
data_table.Investigations: Sodium 138 mmol/L (135-145), potassium 4.2 mmol/L, urea 6.0 mmol/L, creatinine 78 micromol/L, glucose 6.4 mmol/L; ECG sinus rhythm QTc 450 ms; chest X-ray no consolidation; urinalysis nitrites positive, leukocytes 2+
data_table.Medications: Paracetamol 1 g 6-hourly, oxycodone 5 mg PRN, IV ceftriaxone 1 g daily, IV metronidazole 500 mg 8-hourly

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next pharmacological step?

options.text: Haloperidol 5 mg intramuscularly now, repeat every 30 minutes as required
options.rationale: High-dose IM haloperidol 5 mg is inappropriate first-line in a frail elderly patient with cardiac history and a QTc of 450 ms; low-dose oral or sublingual antipsychotic is preferred. AU guidelines reserve high-dose IM haloperidol for severe behavioural disturbance in younger patients with no cardiovascular comorbidity. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines Psychotropic)

options.text: Lorazepam 1 mg orally now, repeat after 60 minutes if required
options.rationale: Benzodiazepines worsen delirium in the elderly and increase falls and respiratory depression risk; they are reserved for delirium related to alcohol or sedative withdrawal or where antipsychotics are contraindicated. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines Psychotropic)

options.text: Olanzapine wafer 2.5 mg orally now, repeat after 60 minutes if required
options.rationale: AU Therapeutic Guidelines Psychotropic recommend low-dose oral olanzapine 2.5-5 mg or risperidone 0.25-0.5 mg as first-line pharmacotherapy for acute agitation in delirium when non-pharmacological measures fail and there is risk of harm; the wafer formulation is suitable when oral cooperation is uncertain. Avoid benzodiazepines as monotherapy because they can worsen delirium except in alcohol or sedative withdrawal. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines Psychotropic)

options.text: Promethazine 25 mg intramuscularly now as the proposed approach
options.rationale: Promethazine adds anticholinergic burden and worsens delirium in the elderly; it is not appropriate for behavioural disturbance in this setting. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines Psychotropic)

options.text: Diazepam 10 mg intravenously now as the proposed approach
options.rationale: High-dose IV diazepam in an elderly patient with delirium increases respiratory depression and falls risk and prolongs delirium; not appropriate here. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines Psychotropic)

explanation.summary: Hyperactive delirium in an elderly post-operative patient with cardiovascular comorbidity calls for low-dose oral atypical antipsychotic (olanzapine 2.5 mg wafer or risperidone 0.25-0.5 mg). Benzodiazepines worsen delirium except in alcohol/sedative withdrawal. High-dose IM haloperidol risks QT prolongation and is not first-line in elderly cardiac patients. Address precipitants (sepsis from possible UTI, opioids, environment, sleep).
key_points: Low-dose olanzapine 2.5 mg wafer or risperidone 0.25-0.5 mg first-line
Avoid benzodiazepines unless alcohol/sedative withdrawal
Address precipitants (sepsis, pain, opioids, sensory deprivation)
Reassess QTc and EPS regularly
explanation.pearls: Antipsychotics in delirium are symptomatic only and do not shorten duration; identifying and treating the precipitant (here possibly UTI plus opioids) is the real intervention.

stem:
A 19-year-old woman is on day 3 of inpatient admission for severe anorexia nervosa. Admission BMI was 13.2 kg/m^2 with bradycardia 38, hypothermia 35.4 °C, and an ECG showing sinus bradycardia with prolonged QTc 480 ms. She has been started on the ward refeeding protocol at 20 kcal/kg/day with thiamine, multivitamin, and phosphate supplementation, with daily electrolyte and ECG monitoring.

This morning on day 3 her serum phosphate has dropped from 1.05 to 0.45 mmol/L and her magnesium has fallen from 0.85 to 0.62 mmol/L despite oral replacement. Her ECG today shows QTc 510 ms, sinus rhythm 42. She is alert but reports cramping and mild dyspnoea on minimal exertion. She has been compliant with the meal plan and supervised meals.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 42, BP 92/58 mmHg, RR 18, SpO2 98% on room air, temperature 35.8 °C
data_table.Examination: Cachectic, dry mucous membranes, peripheral pulses palpable, no oedema, tendon reflexes preserved with prolonged relaxation phase
data_table.Investigations: Phosphate 0.45 mmol/L (0.75-1.50), magnesium 0.62 mmol/L (0.70-1.10), potassium 3.3 mmol/L (3.5-5.0), corrected calcium 2.18 mmol/L (2.10-2.60), glucose 4.2 mmol/L, sodium 134 mmol/L, ALT 78 U/L (<40), albumin 32 g/L, ECG sinus bradycardia 42 QTc 510 ms
data_table.Medications: Oral phosphate Sandoz 500 mg twice daily, oral magnesium aspartate 6.5 mmol twice daily, thiamine 300 mg daily, multivitamin, refeeding protocol 20 kcal/kg/day

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Increase caloric intake to 30 kcal/kg/day to ensure adequate refeeding progress as the proposed approach with the proposed clinical action as part of routine inpatient care
options.rationale: Increasing rate during impending refeeding syndrome accelerates phosphate and magnesium drop and increases cardiac arrest risk. Rate is held until electrolytes stabilise. (Source: ANZAED Eating Disorders)

options.text: Stop refeeding entirely and recommence after 24 hours of fasting with electrolyte recheck as the proposed approach with the proposed clinical action as part of routine inpatient care
options.rationale: Stopping refeeding entirely is the wrong branch; cessation drives further metabolic instability through ongoing glycogen depletion and starvation physiology. Electrolyte replacement plus holding rate is the appropriate approach. (Source: ANZAED Eating Disorders)

options.text: Hold caloric advancement at the current rate, give IV magnesium sulfate 10 mmol over 2 hours, IV potassium phosphate (typically 20-30 mmol over 4-6 hours via central line per inpatient pathway), repeat electrolytes 4-hourly, and consult intensive care
options.rationale: Falling phosphate and magnesium with QTc 510 ms and clinical symptoms (cramps, dyspnoea) is impending refeeding syndrome. AU practice is to HOLD caloric advancement (not stop refeeding), aggressively replace IV phosphate and magnesium, monitor electrolytes 4-hourly, and involve intensive care because of cardiac instability risk. Stopping feeds risks further metabolic catastrophe; advancing risks decompensation. The middle branch is the correct one. (Source: ANZAED Eating Disorders)

options.text: Commence olanzapine 5 mg daily to assist weight gain and address anorexia cognitions as the proposed approach with the proposed clinical action as part of routine inpatient care
options.rationale: Olanzapine has modest weight-gain effect in anorexia but is not indicated for acute refeeding syndrome management; the priority is electrolyte stabilisation. (Source: RANZCP Eating Disorders)

options.text: Discharge to outpatient eating disorder day program as her clinical engagement is good as the proposed approach with the proposed clinical action as part of routine inpatient care
options.rationale: Discharge in active refeeding syndrome with QTc prolongation is unsafe; this is the highest-risk window for cardiac arrest and requires close inpatient monitoring. (Source: ANZAED Eating Disorders)

explanation.summary: Refeeding syndrome arises from intracellular shift of phosphate, potassium and magnesium when carbohydrate is reintroduced after starvation. The correct response is to HOLD caloric advancement at current rate (not stop, not advance) and aggressively replace IV phosphate and magnesium with frequent electrolyte and ECG monitoring. ICU involvement is appropriate when QTc lengthens or arrhythmia risk rises. Stopping feeds entirely worsens metabolic instability.
key_points: Refeeding syndrome: ↓phosphate, ↓magnesium, ↓potassium, fluid shifts
Hold caloric rate; do not stop or advance
IV replacement: phosphate 20-30 mmol, magnesium 10-20 mmol
ICU involvement if QTc prolongs or arrhythmia risk
explanation.pearls: The wrong-branch temptations in refeeding syndrome are both 'stop feeds' and 'advance feeds' - the correct branch is 'hold rate, replace IV, monitor 4-hourly'. AU practice mandates a structured protocol with intensive care involvement once QTc lengthens.

stem:
A 31-year-old woman presents to your general practice clinic 4 weeks after the birth of her first child. She tells you 'I cry a few times a day, and I haven't slept more than a few hours straight because the baby feeds every 2 hours'. She describes feeling overwhelmed and irritable, but is bonded with the baby, smiles when interacting, and finds joy in walks with him. She has thoughts that 'it would be easier if I disappeared' but denies active suicidal ideation, plans, or thoughts of harming the baby. There is no past psychiatric history, no substance use, and her partner is supportive.

On examination she is well, well-groomed, with appropriate eye contact and reactive mood. Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale score today is 12 with a score of 1 on the self-harm item. Thyroid function, FBC, and ferritin are within normal limits. Maternal child health nurse review three days ago noted similar sleep deprivation but did not flag concerns.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 78, BP 116/72 mmHg, RR 14, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.6 °C
data_table.Examination: Well groomed, reactive mood, appropriate eye contact, no psychomotor retardation, no thought disorder
data_table.Investigations: EPDS 12 (item 10 self-harm score 1); FBC, ferritin, TSH within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Provide psychoeducation, social and sleep support, and arrange structured general practice review with repeat EPDS in 2 weeks
options.rationale: An EPDS of 12 with retained interest, intact bond, sleep-deprivation context, and no active suicidal ideation does not yet meet the threshold for major depressive disorder. The COPE perinatal pathway advises psychoeducation, social and sleep support, and a structured 2-week review with repeat EPDS, escalating to psychological therapy if symptoms persist or worsen. Item 10 score of 1 is monitored but does not in itself escalate. (Source: COPE Perinatal Guidelines; RANZCP)

options.text: Commence sertraline 50 mg orally daily and arrange routine general practice review in 4 weeks for breastfeeding monitoring
options.rationale: Sertraline is the AU first-line breastfeeding-compatible SSRI when depression is diagnosed; an EPDS of 12 with intact functioning and bonding does not yet meet that threshold. (Source: COPE Perinatal Guidelines; AMH)

options.text: Admit to a mother-and-baby unit for inpatient assessment and care for safety concerns this evening
options.rationale: Inpatient admission is reserved for severe perinatal depression with risk to self or baby, psychosis, or significant functional impairment; her presentation does not meet criteria. (Source: COPE Perinatal Guidelines)

options.text: Refer urgently to perinatal psychiatry within 24 hours for diagnostic interview and pharmacological plan formulation
options.rationale: Urgent psychiatry referral is reserved for higher EPDS scores with active suicidal ideation, psychosis, or risk to infant; structured general practice review with safety net is appropriate first. (Source: COPE Perinatal Guidelines)

options.text: Suggest that she stops breastfeeding and switches to formula to allow her partner to take over feeds at night
options.rationale: Stopping breastfeeding is not part of first-line management and can worsen distress and bonding; partner-supported expressed-milk feeding overnight can help without stopping. (Source: COPE Perinatal Guidelines)

explanation.summary: Postnatal blues occur in around 80% of women between days 3 and 14, are self-limited, and do not require pharmacotherapy. Postnatal depression is differentiated by persistent low mood, loss of interest, impaired functioning, or thoughts of harm beyond 2 weeks. EPDS over 13 raises concern; item 10 (self-harm) of 1 or more is monitored irrespective of total. AU first-line for diagnosed postnatal depression is breastfeeding-compatible SSRI (sertraline first, paroxetine acceptable) with psychological therapy; mother-and-baby unit admission is reserved for severity, risk, or psychosis.
key_points: Blues: days 3-14, self-limited, sleep + support
Depression: EPDS over 13 or persistent impairment past 2 weeks
Item 10 of 1+ on EPDS: explicit safety review even at lower total scores
Sertraline first-line breastfeeding-compatible SSRI; paroxetine acceptable
explanation.pearls: Sertraline 50 mg orally daily is the AU first-line breastfeeding-compatible SSRI when major postnatal depression is established; relative infant dose is well below the 10% safety threshold.

stem:
A 46-year-old man attends your general practice clinic with his partner asking for help to stop drinking. He has been drinking around 12 standard drinks of beer daily for the last 3 years. His most recent drink was 4 hours ago. He says 'my hands get a bit shaky in the mornings until I have my first drink'. He has had no alcohol withdrawal seizures, no delirium tremens, no recent admissions, and no other major medical comorbidity. He is not currently suicidal. His partner is supportive and they live together.

On examination he is anxious with a mild postural tremor. His Clinical Institute Withdrawal Assessment for Alcohol - revised (CIWA-Ar) score is 9 with no autonomic instability. Pulse, blood pressure, and temperature are within normal limits. Bloods show transaminases mildly elevated (AST 60, ALT 50), MCV 102 fL (80-100), and platelet count 142 x10^9/L (150-400). He has a stable home, a willing supporter, no benzodiazepine use, no opioid use, and access to daily review.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 92, BP 138/82 mmHg, RR 16, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.7 °C
data_table.Examination: Anxious, mild postural tremor, no nystagmus, no ataxia, no confusion
data_table.Investigations: CIWA-Ar 9; AST 60 U/L, ALT 50 U/L, MCV 102 fL (80-100), platelets 142 x10^9/L (150-400); UEC and glucose within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Admit to the inpatient acute medical unit for medically supervised withdrawal and intravenous benzodiazepine infusion
options.rationale: Inpatient management is reserved for severe withdrawal, prior withdrawal seizures or delirium tremens, lack of supports, severe medical or psychiatric comorbidity, or polysubstance withdrawal; this patient is at low risk and home-based management is appropriate. (Source: RACP Alcohol Treatment Guidelines)

options.text: Home-based withdrawal with diazepam loading regimen, oral thiamine, daily clinical review, and safety supervision
options.rationale: Low-risk patients (mild withdrawal, no prior seizure or delirium, intact supports, no severe comorbidity) are AU candidates for outpatient withdrawal with diazepam loading (e.g. 20 mg every 2 hours symptom-triggered or fixed-dose regimen) plus oral thiamine. Daily clinical review, dispense control, and a supervising partner reduce diversion and detect escalation. Higher CIWA-Ar (over 15), seizure history, delirium, or unsupported living shifts to inpatient. (Source: RACP Alcohol Treatment Guidelines; Therapeutic Guidelines: Addiction)

options.text: Commence oral disulfiram 200 mg daily immediately without any thiamine cover for prevention of relapse
options.rationale: Disulfiram is a relapse-prevention adjunct after withdrawal completion, requires informed consent and supervised dispensing, and risks severe disulfiram-ethanol reaction; it is not started before withdrawal. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Addiction)

options.text: Prescribe oral acamprosate 666 mg three times daily and advise sudden cessation of alcohol from tonight
options.rationale: Acamprosate is a relapse-prevention agent after withdrawal completion and does not treat acute withdrawal; sudden cessation without benzodiazepine cover risks seizure and delirium tremens. (Source: AMH)

options.text: Reassure that 12 standard drinks daily is not high enough to need withdrawal management and advise abrupt cessation
options.rationale: Twelve standard drinks daily over years is dependence; abrupt cessation without medical support risks seizure, delirium tremens, and Wernicke. (Source: RACP Alcohol Treatment Guidelines)

explanation.summary: Alcohol withdrawal severity is risk-stratified using CIWA-Ar, drinking pattern, prior withdrawal complications, comorbidity, and supports. Home-based withdrawal with diazepam loading and oral thiamine is safe for low-risk patients (CIWA-Ar under 15, no prior seizure or delirium, no major comorbidity, supportive home). Inpatient management is required for high-risk presentations. Thiamine 300 mg orally daily covers most patients; intravenous thiamine 100 mg pre-glucose is essential if Wernicke is suspected. Relapse-prevention agents (naltrexone, acamprosate, disulfiram) are layered after withdrawal completion.
key_points: Outpatient withdrawal safe for low-risk patients with supports
Diazepam loading symptom-triggered or fixed schedule; thiamine cover always
Inpatient: prior seizure or DT, severe withdrawal, unsupported, comorbidity
Relapse prevention starts after withdrawal completion, not during
explanation.pearls: Oral thiamine 300 mg daily for 5 days, then 100 mg daily, accompanies every alcohol withdrawal regardless of setting; intravenous thiamine 100 mg precedes any dextrose-containing fluid if Wernicke is suspected.

stem:
A 28-year-old graphic designer attends your general practice clinic with 18 months of persistent worry about her job security, finances, and relationships. She says 'the worry is always running in the background and I can't switch it off, even when nothing is wrong'. She has poor sleep onset, muscle tension, fatigue, and difficulty concentrating. She avoids social events. She drinks 2-3 standard drinks weekly. She has no past psychiatric history, no substance use disorder, no suicidal ideation, and no medical comorbidity.

On mental state examination she is anxious-appearing with reactive mood and intact reality testing. GAD-7 score is 16. PHQ-9 score is 9 (no anhedonia, no suicidal ideation). Thyroid function, electrolytes, and ECG are within normal limits. She is keen to engage with treatment but has not previously tried psychological therapy.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 84, BP 122/76 mmHg, RR 16, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.6 °C
data_table.Examination: Anxious affect, reactive mood, no thought disorder, intact reality testing, no psychomotor abnormality
data_table.Investigations: GAD-7 16, PHQ-9 9; TSH 1.6 mIU/L; UEC and ECG within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first-line management?

options.text: Diazepam 5 mg three times daily for 6 weeks with weekly general practice clinic reviews for tolerance
options.rationale: Benzodiazepines are not first-line in generalised anxiety disorder because of dependence risk and effect on cognitive performance; reserve for short-term distress crises. (Source: RANZCP CPG Anxiety Disorders; AMH)

options.text: Propranolol 20 mg three times daily as ongoing monotherapy for the persistent worry and tension symptoms
options.rationale: Propranolol addresses peripheral autonomic features of performance anxiety; it is not effective for the cognitive worry of generalised anxiety disorder. (Source: RANZCP CPG Anxiety Disorders)

options.text: Escitalopram 10 mg orally daily commenced alongside cognitive behavioural therapy referral and lifestyle work
options.rationale: Generalised anxiety disorder with significant functional impairment (GAD-7 over 15) is treated with a combination of cognitive behavioural therapy and an SSRI or SNRI; escitalopram and sertraline are AU first-line SSRI options. CBT alone is reasonable for milder severity but combined treatment improves outcomes at this severity. Avoid benzodiazepines and pregabalin first-line. (Source: RANZCP CPG Anxiety Disorders; AMH)

options.text: Pregabalin 75 mg twice daily titrated to 300 mg total daily dose over the next 2 weeks as the first option
options.rationale: Pregabalin is effective for generalised anxiety disorder but is third-line in AU practice due to dependence and divertibility; SSRI plus CBT is first-line. (Source: AMH; RANZCP CPG Anxiety Disorders)

options.text: Mirtazapine 15 mg orally at bedtime as the first-line option given the sleep onset disturbance she reports today
options.rationale: Mirtazapine is not first-line for generalised anxiety disorder; it is reserved for depression with insomnia. Targeting sleep symptoms first does not address the underlying anxiety disorder. (Source: RANZCP CPG Anxiety Disorders)

explanation.summary: Generalised anxiety disorder is treated stepwise. Milder cases respond to psychoeducation, lifestyle, and cognitive behavioural therapy. Moderate to severe presentations (GAD-7 over 15 with functional impairment) combine an SSRI (escitalopram, sertraline) or SNRI (venlafaxine) with CBT. Benzodiazepines and pregabalin are reserved for refractory or short-term symptom relief because of dependence risk. Antidepressants take 4 to 6 weeks for full effect, with transient anxiety worsening possible in the first 2 weeks of SSRI treatment.
key_points: First-line: SSRI plus CBT for moderate-severe GAD
CBT alone reasonable for milder presentations
Benzodiazepines, pregabalin not first-line - dependence risk
Counsel about initial anxiety worsening in first 2 weeks of SSRI
explanation.pearls: Escitalopram 10 mg orally daily is the AU first-line SSRI for generalised anxiety disorder; counsel that anxiety may transiently worsen in the first two weeks before steady-state benefit at four to six weeks.

subtopic_detail: Metabolic syndrome on olanzapine and switch decision
stem:
A 27-year-old man attends your community mental health clinic for 6-month review after his first episode of psychosis. He has been on olanzapine 15 mg orally daily and is symptom-free, working full-time, and adherent. He says 'I feel well on this one, the others gave me side effects'. He has gained 8 kg since starting, and his trousers no longer fit. He has no family history of cardiovascular disease but his maternal grandfather had type 2 diabetes.

On examination his weight is 88 kg (was 80 kg), waist circumference 102 cm, blood pressure 138/86 mmHg, and pulse 80 regular. Fasting glucose today is 7.2 mmol/L (3.5-5.5), HbA1c 6.0% (under 6.5), fasting triglycerides 3.2 mmol/L (under 1.7), HDL 0.9 mmol/L (over 1.0), and LDL 3.0 mmol/L (under 3.5). Liver function tests and renal function are within normal limits. ECG QTc is 420 ms.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 80, BP 138/86 mmHg, RR 14, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.7 °C
data_table.Examination: Weight 88 kg, waist circumference 102 cm, BMI 28; no acanthosis nigricans, no oedema
data_table.Investigations: Fasting glucose 7.2 mmol/L (3.5-5.5), HbA1c 6.0% (under 6.5), triglycerides 3.2 mmol/L (under 1.7), HDL 0.9 mmol/L (over 1.0), LDL 3.0 mmol/L (under 3.5); LFTs and UEC within normal limits; ECG QTc 420 ms

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Continue olanzapine unchanged and review weight, lipid, and glucose parameters again in 12 months without intervening
options.rationale: Findings already meet metabolic syndrome criteria with impaired fasting glucose; deferring intervention 12 months risks progression to type 2 diabetes and cardiovascular event. (Source: RANZCP CPG Schizophrenia; eTG Endocrinology)

options.text: Initiate lifestyle programme, repeat fasting glucose to confirm diabetes, and switch to aripiprazole with cross-titration
options.rationale: Olanzapine has the highest metabolic burden of the second-generation antipsychotics; in first-episode psychosis with emerging metabolic syndrome and impaired fasting glucose, AU practice is to confirm the glucose result (repeat or HbA1c trend), initiate intensive lifestyle programme, and switch to a lower metabolic burden agent (aripiprazole, lurasidone, or amisulpride) via cross-titration. The choice balances metabolic safety against relapse risk. (Source: RANZCP CPG Schizophrenia; AMH)

options.text: Add metformin 500 mg twice daily to olanzapine without changing antipsychotic, weight loss, or lifestyle programme
options.rationale: Metformin can mitigate antipsychotic-associated weight gain but is adjunctive; switching the offending agent and lifestyle programme remain core. (Source: AMH; eTG Endocrinology)

options.text: Stop olanzapine immediately and commence high-dose haloperidol depot intramuscularly with regular community review
options.rationale: Abrupt switching risks relapse and movement disorders; haloperidol carries extrapyramidal burden inappropriate for first-episode psychosis remission. (Source: RANZCP CPG Schizophrenia)

options.text: Refer to bariatric surgery clinic for sleeve gastrectomy assessment given the persisting weight gain on olanzapine therapy
options.rationale: Bariatric surgery referral is premature; switch antipsychotic and trial intensive lifestyle and pharmacotherapy first. (Source: RANZCP CPG Schizophrenia)

explanation.summary: Antipsychotic-associated metabolic syndrome is a major cause of premature cardiovascular mortality in psychosis. Olanzapine and clozapine carry the highest metabolic burden; aripiprazole, lurasidone, ziprasidone, and amisulpride carry low to moderate burden. AU monitoring (weight, waist, BP, lipids, glucose) is at baseline, weekly initially, at 3 months, then yearly. Emerging metabolic syndrome warrants intensive lifestyle programme, switch to lower-burden agent with cross-titration, and consideration of metformin adjunct. Clozapine usually stays despite metabolic cost given relapse risk.
key_points: Olanzapine: highest metabolic burden after clozapine
Switch to aripiprazole or lurasidone via cross-titration for emerging metabolic syndrome
Lifestyle programme + metformin adjunct for weight if switch insufficient
Monitor weight, waist, BP, lipids, glucose at baseline, 3 months, then yearly
explanation.pearls: Aripiprazole 10-15 mg orally daily is the AU preferred switch target from olanzapine for emerging metabolic syndrome in first-episode psychosis given its low metabolic burden and partial dopamine agonism.

stem:
A 19-year-old apprentice presents to your community mental health intake with a 4-week history of persecutory delusions and auditory hallucinations (running commentary, two voices). He had been smoking high-potency cannabis daily for the past 2 years; he stopped 4 weeks ago after the symptoms started. He is brought by his older sister who says 'he won't come out of his room and he thinks the neighbours are tapping the walls'. He denies suicidal ideation but is socially withdrawn and is not sleeping.

On mental state examination he is suspicious, with thought disorder evident as loosening of associations and tangential speech. There is third-person auditory hallucination and persecutory delusion. Insight is impaired. Urine drug screen 3 weeks ago and again today is negative for cannabis metabolites. Blood tests including TSH, vitamin B12, and HIV serology are pending. CT brain (taken at presentation) is normal. He lives with his sister and parents who are supportive.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 88, BP 124/74 mmHg, RR 14, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.6 °C
data_table.Examination: Thought disorder, persecutory delusion, third-person auditory hallucination, impaired insight, no movement disorder
data_table.Investigations: Urine drug screen negative at week 3 and week 4; FBC, electrolytes within normal limits; TSH, vitamin B12, HIV serology pending; non-contrast CT brain normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management plan?

options.text: Reassure that symptoms will resolve once cannabis fully clears the system and arrange community follow-up in 4 weeks
options.rationale: Persisting psychosis 4 weeks after cessation has crossed the substance-induced threshold and requires antipsychotic therapy and structured early intervention; symptoms may not self-resolve. (Source: Orygen; EPPIC; RANZCP)

options.text: Initiate haloperidol 5 mg intramuscularly stat now and admit involuntarily under the state mental health act
options.rationale: Involuntary admission and IM high-potency typical antipsychotic is reserved for risk-driven presentations not amenable to voluntary care; this patient has family support and is engageable. (Source: RANZCP)

options.text: Refer to the gambling and addiction service to address cannabis dependence before any psychotic symptom treatment
options.rationale: Cannabis cessation is essential but does not replace antipsychotic therapy when psychotic symptoms persist; both run in parallel. (Source: Orygen)

options.text: Prescribe clozapine 12.5 mg orally and arrange weekly haematological monitoring as the next pharmacological step
options.rationale: Clozapine is reserved for treatment-resistant schizophrenia (failure of two adequate antipsychotic trials at adequate dose and duration); not first-line in early psychosis. (Source: RANZCP)

options.text: Refer to early psychosis service for assertive care, commence low-dose risperidone, and continue cannabis-cessation work
options.rationale: Persistent psychotic symptoms 4 weeks after cannabis cessation meet criteria for first-episode psychosis. The AU early-intervention model (EPPIC/Orygen) pairs low-dose second-generation antipsychotic (risperidone, aripiprazole, or amisulpride at low dose), structured assertive case management, family education, and ongoing cannabis-cessation support. Early intervention reduces relapse and improves functional outcome. (Source: Orygen; EPPIC; RANZCP)

explanation.summary: First-episode psychosis in young people benefits from assertive multidisciplinary care via early intervention services. Low-dose second-generation antipsychotics (risperidone, aripiprazole, amisulpride, olanzapine) are AU first-line, paired with family work, vocational support, cannabis-cessation work, and psychological therapy.
