Symptoms persisting beyond 4 weeks after substance cessation argue against a transient substance-induced diagnosis. Clozapine is reserved for two-trial-failed treatment resistance. Metabolic monitoring is critical (see related questions in this batch).
key_points: Persisting psychosis 4+ weeks after cessation moves diagnosis past substance-induced
First-line: low-dose risperidone, aripiprazole, or amisulpride
Assertive case management and family work improve relapse and functional outcomes
Clozapine reserved for two adequate trials failed - not first-line
explanation.pearls: Risperidone 1-2 mg orally daily is the AU starting dose in first-episode psychosis; this is well below the schizophrenia maintenance dose and minimises extrapyramidal adverse effects.

stem:
A 26-year-old woman presents to your emergency department after taking five paracetamol tablets following an argument with her partner 2 hours ago. She tells you 'I always do this when she leaves the room, but I never really want to die, I just want it to stop hurting'. She has had over 30 similar low-lethality presentations in the last 2 years. She has documented borderline personality disorder, longstanding chronic suicidal ideation without intent or plan, multiple superficial self-harm scars, and an unstable interpersonal history. There is no current plan or means.

On examination she is reactive and engaged with you. The paracetamol nomogram plotted at the predicted 4-hour timepoint will be well below the AU treatment line and her serum paracetamol returned at 35 mg/L (treatment line at 4 hours of 150 mg/L). She has not used opioids, benzodiazepines, or alcohol concurrently. Her usual community team has organised dialectical behaviour therapy beginning next week. Her safety plan from her last admission is current. She wants to go home with her partner.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 78, BP 118/72 mmHg, RR 14, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.7 °C
data_table.Examination: Engaged, reactive, no thought disorder, intact reality testing, no current suicidal intent or plan, no acute intoxication
data_table.Investigations: Serum paracetamol 35 mg/L at 4 hours post ingestion (treatment line 150 mg/L); ECG QTc 410 ms; UEC and LFTs within normal limits; urine drug screen negative
data_table.Medications: Sertraline 100 mg orally daily; community DBT enrolled

lead_in: What is the most appropriate disposition?

options.text: Discharge with a brief safety plan review, partner involvement, and continuation of community DBT and case management
options.rationale: Recurrent low-lethality self-harm in established borderline personality disorder is managed in the community with dialectical behaviour therapy as the AU evidence-based intervention. Repeated admissions reinforce maladaptive coping and erode therapy alliance. Brief reaffirmation of the safety plan, partner involvement, and the next DBT session is the appropriate disposition for a presentation below the paracetamol treatment line with no current intent. (Source: RANZCP CPG BPD; NHMRC BPD Guideline)

options.text: Admit involuntarily to the acute psychiatric ward under the mental health act for 72-hour observation today
options.rationale: Involuntary admission for chronic suicidality in BPD without acute change risks reinforcing self-harm pattern and contravenes least-restrictive-care principles; reserve for acute risk escalation. (Source: NHMRC BPD Guideline)

options.text: Commence intravenous N-acetylcysteine immediately on a 21-hour standard regimen given the recent ingestion
options.rationale: N-acetylcysteine is indicated only when serum paracetamol is above the AU treatment line on the nomogram; this sample is below the line. Empirical NAC exposes her to flushing, anaphylactoid reactions, and admission without benefit. (Source: TG: Toxicology; Australian Resuscitation Council)

options.text: Add an antipsychotic such as quetiapine 100 mg nightly to her sertraline as the next pharmacological step today
options.rationale: Routine antipsychotic for BPD is not supported by evidence; pharmacotherapy targets specific comorbidity (depression, anxiety, severe transient psychotic symptoms) and is adjunctive to psychotherapy. (Source: NHMRC BPD Guideline; AMH)

options.text: Refer to inpatient detoxification given the recurrent presentations without confirmed substance use in the recent samples taken
options.rationale: Detoxification is irrelevant when urine drug screen is negative and there is no substance use disorder; this misuses inpatient resources. (Source: RANZCP CPG BPD)

explanation.summary: Borderline personality disorder is managed primarily with structured psychotherapy (dialectical behaviour therapy or mentalisation-based therapy) and assertive community case management. Repeated involuntary admissions for chronic suicidality erode therapy alliance, reinforce self-harm patterns, and breach least-restrictive-care principles. Brief admissions are reserved for clearly out-of-pattern risk escalation. Pharmacotherapy targets comorbid disorders rather than treating BPD per se; antipsychotic addition for emotion dysregulation has weak evidence. Brief targeted ED management with safety plan reaffirmation is the AU standard.
key_points: DBT is the AU evidence-based first-line psychotherapy for BPD
Involuntary admissions for chronic suicidality reinforce maladaptive patterns
Pharmacotherapy targets comorbidity, not BPD itself
Brief out-of-pattern presentations warrant admission - chronic patterns do not
explanation.pearls: Dialectical behaviour therapy reduces self-harm, suicide attempts, and admission days in BPD - the AU first-line evidence-based intervention, with 12-month structured group plus individual therapy.

stem:
A 52-year-old woman attends your community mental health clinic for routine review of bipolar I disorder. She has been on lithium 1000 mg orally at bedtime for 8 years and has been euthymic with no admissions in that time. Her partner says 'she's been more thirsty and going to the toilet more at night, but it's been gradual'. She has not had any other new symptoms, no falls, and no infections. Her medications include lithium, an ACE inhibitor for hypertension, and an oral contraceptive pill.

Routine bloods today show lithium level 0.7 mmol/L (0.4-1.0), eGFR 55 mL/min/1.73 m^2 (over 90), creatinine 110 micromol/L, and serum sodium 142 mmol/L. Her eGFR has dropped from 80 mL/min/1.73 m^2 6 years ago, with 65 mL/min/1.73 m^2 12 months ago. Urine osmolality after overnight water deprivation is 380 mOsm/kg. Thyroid function and calcium are within normal limits. Her psychiatric history shows 5 prior depressive episodes and 2 manic episodes before lithium initiation.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 76, BP 138/84 mmHg, RR 14, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.7 °C
data_table.Examination: No tremor, no nystagmus, no ataxia, no goitre, no signs of dehydration
data_table.Investigations: Lithium 0.7 mmol/L (0.4-1.0), eGFR 55 mL/min/1.73 m^2 (over 90), creatinine 110 micromol/L; urine osmolality post-water deprivation 380 mOsm/kg; TSH 2.1 mIU/L, corrected calcium 2.40 mmol/L; sodium 142 mmol/L
data_table.Medications: Lithium carbonate 1000 mg orally at bedtime, perindopril 5 mg daily, combined oral contraceptive pill

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Continue lithium at the same dose and repeat all bloods in 6 months without specialist involvement
options.rationale: Stage 3a chronic kidney disease with progressive decline and reduced urine concentrating ability on a stable lithium level warrants formal renal review, not routine 6-monthly follow-up alone. (Source: RANZCP CPG Bipolar; AMH)

options.text: Stop lithium immediately, swap to oral sodium valproate, and re-evaluate renal function 4 weeks after cessation
options.rationale: Abrupt lithium cessation risks early relapse (rebound mania within 6 months in 50%); valproate is teratogenic in a 52-year-old still potentially of childbearing potential and is less effective for prophylaxis than lithium. Abrupt change is also unnecessary at stable level. (Source: RANZCP CPG Bipolar; AMH)

options.text: Switch immediately to clozapine and reduce the perindopril dose to half pending renal nephrologist review
options.rationale: Clozapine is not a primary mood stabiliser and carries severe haematologic and metabolic risks; ACE inhibitor adjustment alone does not address the lithium-renal trajectory. (Source: AMH)

options.text: Refer to nephrology, discuss lithium dose reduction and timing as a single nightly dose with shared decision making
options.rationale: Progressive lithium-associated chronic kidney disease (eGFR 80 to 55 over 6 years) with impaired urine concentration suggests early nephrogenic diabetes insipidus. AU practice is shared-decision review with nephrology; lithium can often continue at lower dose given as a single nightly dose (reduced trough nephrotoxicity), with closer surveillance. Switching to a less effective alternative carries its own relapse risk and is decided jointly. (Source: RANZCP CPG Bipolar; KHA-CARI; AMH)

options.text: Commence amiloride 5 mg daily and continue lithium with the same total daily dose and same divided schedule
options.rationale: Amiloride can reduce lithium-induced nephrogenic diabetes insipidus polyuria, but it does not modify the underlying nephropathy and is adjunctive; nephrology review should guide the overall plan. (Source: AMH)

explanation.summary: Long-term lithium use is associated with nephrogenic diabetes insipidus and chronic tubulointerstitial nephropathy in around 20 to 30% of patients after 10 to 20 years. Surveillance includes 6-monthly lithium level, eGFR, electrolytes, thyroid function, and calcium. Once-nightly dosing reduces renal exposure compared to divided schedules. Stage 3 or progressive CKD on lithium warrants nephrology review and shared-decision balancing relapse risk against renal trajectory. Lithium remains the most effective mood stabiliser for bipolar prophylaxis - switching is not automatic.
key_points: Once-nightly lithium dosing reduces renal exposure compared to divided
Stage 3+ CKD on lithium: refer nephrology, shared decision making
Surveillance: lithium, eGFR, electrolytes, TSH, calcium every 6 months
Switching carries relapse risk - rarely automatic
explanation.pearls: Lithium given as a single nightly dose reduces the renal tubular trough exposure compared with twice-daily dosing; consider switching schedules before reducing dose in early lithium nephrotoxicity.

stem:
A 38-year-old man is brought to your emergency department by his housemate with 12 hours of confusion, sweating, tremor, and a temperature of 39.5 °C. He has a history of treatment-resistant depression and obsessive-compulsive disorder. His housemate says 'he started a new tablet last week and was telling me he was anxious and not sleeping right'. His regular medications are escitalopram 20 mg, mirtazapine 30 mg, and quetiapine 100 mg at night. Five days ago his psychiatrist commenced linezolid for a methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus soft tissue infection. There has been no recent dose increase of antipsychotic.

On examination he is restless, with diaphoresis, mydriasis, and bilateral lower limb myoclonus that is more pronounced than the upper limbs. Tendon reflexes are 3+ symmetrically and clonus is sustained at both ankles. Tone is increased in the lower limbs but lead-pipe rigidity is absent. Bowel sounds are hyperactive. ECG shows sinus tachycardia at 124 bpm with normal QRS and QTc. Creatine kinase is 410 U/L (under 200), white cell count 11 x10^9/L, sodium 138 mmol/L, creatinine 88 micromol/L.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 124, BP 158/96 mmHg, RR 24, SpO2 96% on room air, temperature 39.5 °C
data_table.Examination: Restless, diaphoretic, mydriasis, lower limb myoclonus greater than upper, reflexes 3+, ankle clonus sustained, lower limb tone increased without lead-pipe rigidity, hyperactive bowel sounds
data_table.Investigations: CK 410 U/L (under 200), WCC 11 x10^9/L (4.0-11.0), Na 138 mmol/L, creatinine 88 micromol/L; ECG sinus tachycardia, normal QRS and QTc
data_table.Medications: Escitalopram 20 mg, mirtazapine 30 mg, quetiapine 100 mg at night, linezolid started 5 days ago

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Bromocriptine 2.5 mg orally three times daily as dopamine agonist therapy for neuroleptic malignant syndrome
options.rationale: NMS features lead-pipe rigidity, hyporeflexia or normal reflexes, slow onset over days to weeks, much higher CK, and pallid skin rather than diaphoresis and hyperactive bowel sounds; this presentation is not NMS. Bromocriptine is the dopamine-agonist NMS treatment but is the wrong tool here. (Source: TG: Toxicology; AMH)

options.text: Dantrolene 2 mg/kg intravenously now repeated as needed for the rigidity and the hyperthermia today
options.rationale: Dantrolene is reserved for severe NMS and malignant hyperthermia; the syndrome here matches serotonin syndrome (clonus, hyperreflexia, lower-limb predominance, mydriasis, hyperactive bowel sounds), and antiserotoninergic management is preferred. (Source: TG: Toxicology)

options.text: Cease serotonergic agents including linezolid, aggressive cooling and benzodiazepine sedation, and consider cyproheptadine
options.rationale: Sustained ankle clonus, hyperreflexia with lower limb predominance, mydriasis, diaphoresis, and hyperactive bowel sounds within 24 hours of adding a serotonergic agent (linezolid is a monoamine oxidase inhibitor; combined with escitalopram and mirtazapine creates triple serotonergic exposure) fulfils Hunter Serotonin Toxicity Criteria. AU management is removal of offending agents, aggressive cooling, intravenous benzodiazepine sedation for agitation and tone, supportive care, and cyproheptadine 12 mg orally then 2 mg every 2 hours for moderate to severe cases unresponsive to supportive measures. (Source: TG: Toxicology; Royal Australasian College of Physicians)

options.text: Empirical broad-spectrum antibiotics for sepsis and admit to the intensive care unit for invasive monitoring this evening
options.rationale: Sepsis can mimic this picture but the clonus and hyperreflexia pattern with serotonergic exposure history points to serotonin syndrome; antibiotic cover does not address the toxic mechanism even if added empirically. (Source: TG: Toxicology)

options.text: Administer flumazenil 0.2 mg intravenously now for the agitation and arrange psychiatric ward transfer today
options.rationale: Flumazenil reverses benzodiazepines and can precipitate seizure; it has no role and is not relevant here. (Source: AMH)

explanation.summary: Serotonin syndrome and neuroleptic malignant syndrome can both present with hyperthermia, altered mental state, and autonomic instability, but the discriminators are clinically actionable. Serotonin syndrome (Hunter criteria) presents with clonus, hyperreflexia, lower-limb predominance, mydriasis, diaphoresis, and hyperactive bowel sounds within 24 hours of a serotonergic increase or interaction (such as linezolid, an irreversible monoamine oxidase inhibitor, added to a serotonergic regimen). NMS presents with lead-pipe rigidity, hyporeflexia, dry skin, marked CK elevation, and slower onset over days. Management diverges: serotonin syndrome - cease agents, cool, benzodiazepines, cyproheptadine. NMS - cease antipsychotic, cool, supportive care, bromocriptine or dantrolene in severe cases.
key_points: Hyperreflexia + clonus + mydriasis + GI hyperactivity = serotonin syndrome
Lead-pipe rigidity + hyporeflexia + huge CK + dry skin = NMS
Linezolid is a monoamine oxidase inhibitor: never combine with SSRI
Cyproheptadine for moderate-severe serotonin syndrome not responding to benzodiazepines
explanation.pearls: Cyproheptadine 12 mg orally as a loading dose then 2 mg every 2 hours up to 32 mg per day is the AU antiserotoninergic step for moderate-severe serotonin syndrome unresponsive to benzodiazepine sedation and cooling.

stem:
A 45-year-old man has been stable on lithium 1000 mg orally at night for bipolar I disorder for 8 years. He sees you in your general practice clinic for a routine review. He reports good mood stability, no recent episodes, and no relapse since titration in his 30s. He works full-time. He has hypertension treated with perindopril 4 mg daily and has been advised on adequate fluid intake and salt consistency. His lithium-level pattern has been stable at 0.7-0.8 mmol/L every 6 months.

On examination he is well, with no tremor and a normal mental state examination. His thyroid is non-palpable and there is no goitre. He has not been investigated for renal function in the past 12 months because of a missed appointment. Bloods sent today show creatinine 105 micromol/L (60-110), eGFR 68 mL/min/1.73 m squared (over 60), TSH 5.8 mIU/L (0.5-4.0), free T4 13 pmol/L (10-22), serum calcium 2.45 mmol/L (2.10-2.60), serum lithium 0.75 mmol/L (0.6-1.2 therapeutic for maintenance). His last creatinine 14 months ago was 88 micromol/L.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 72, BP 128/82 mmHg, RR 14, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.7 °C
data_table.Examination: No tremor, no goitre, normal mental state, well-perfused
data_table.Investigations: Creatinine 105 micromol/L (60-110) up from 88, eGFR 68 mL/min/1.73 m squared; TSH 5.8 mIU/L (0.5-4.0), free T4 13 pmol/L (10-22); calcium 2.45 mmol/L (2.10-2.60); lithium 0.75 mmol/L (0.6-1.2)
data_table.Medications: Lithium 1000 mg PO nocte; perindopril 4 mg daily

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Stop lithium and switch to sodium valproate as the long-term mood stabiliser irrespective of patient preference
options.rationale: Stopping a previously stabilising mood stabiliser carries a high relapse risk in bipolar I; switch decisions are shared with the patient and reserved for clear toxicity or progressive renal injury. (Source: RANZCOG bipolar guideline; RANZCP Mood Disorders CPG)

options.text: Recheck thyroid function and renal function in 6 weeks, commence levothyroxine 50 mcg, and document creatinine trend
options.rationale: Subclinical hypothyroidism on lithium with TSH above 4 in a patient who is well requires levothyroxine replacement because lithium-induced hypothyroidism rarely remits spontaneously. The eGFR is stable but the creatinine has risen 17 micromol/L from 12-14 months earlier and should be rechecked in 6 weeks to confirm the trend. Routine monitoring on long-term lithium is 6-monthly lithium level, eGFR, TSH, and calcium. (Source: RANZCP Mood Disorders CPG; AMH)

options.text: Increase lithium dose to 1250 mg orally at night targeting a serum lithium level of 1.0 mmol/L on maintenance therapy
options.rationale: Maintenance lithium targets 0.6-0.8 mmol/L; pushing above 1.0 mmol/L raises adverse effect burden without long-term efficacy benefit and worsens renal risk. (Source: RANZCP Mood Disorders CPG)

options.text: Discontinue perindopril urgently as it is causing the renal function decline associated with the lithium dose
options.rationale: ACE inhibitors can raise lithium levels by reducing renal clearance, but the lithium level is in range; discontinuation of an antihypertensive without an alternative is inappropriate and the issue is monitoring, not removal. (Source: AMH)

options.text: Reduce lithium dose to 500 mg at night without further investigation and arrange annual lithium-level review
options.rationale: Dose reduction without confirmed indication risks under-treatment and relapse; the level is in therapeutic range. (Source: AMH)

explanation.summary: Long-term lithium monitoring in Australia consists of 6-monthly serum lithium (12-hour trough), eGFR, thyroid function, and calcium. Lithium induces hypothyroidism in 5-30% of patients on long-term therapy (more common in women); levothyroxine replacement is given for symptomatic or biochemically confirmed hypothyroidism. Hyperparathyroidism and hypercalcaemia are reported less commonly. Chronic interstitial nephritis with slowly progressive eGFR decline is the principal renal concern, and lithium continuation versus alternative agent is an individual risk-benefit decision balanced against bipolar relapse risk. Interactions that raise lithium include ACE inhibitors, ARBs, thiazide diuretics, NSAIDs, dehydration, and low salt diets.
key_points: 6-monthly: lithium level, eGFR, TSH, calcium
Lithium-induced hypothyroidism: replace with levothyroxine
Interactions: ACEI, ARB, thiazide, NSAID, dehydration
Renal function decline is slow - assess trend not single value
explanation.pearls: Lithium maintenance level target 0.6-0.8 mmol/L; lithium 12-hour trough is taken 12 hours after the last dose, not at random times, to allow comparable monitoring.

stem:
A 28-year-old man with schizophrenia has been stable on olanzapine 15 mg orally at night for 2 years. He attends your general practice clinic for routine review. He reports good adherence, no relapse, and no recent change in functioning. He gained 12 kg over the first 6 months on olanzapine and a further 4 kg over the past year. He smokes 10 cigarettes a day and is not on lipid or glucose-lowering medication.

On examination his BMI is 33 kg/m squared. Waist circumference is 108 cm. Cardiovascular examination is unremarkable. Bloods sent at booking today show fasting glucose 6.7 mmol/L (4.0-6.0), HbA1c 6.4% (under 6.0), triglycerides 2.6 mmol/L (under 1.7), HDL cholesterol 0.9 mmol/L (over 1.0), LDL cholesterol 3.4 mmol/L (under 3.5), total cholesterol 5.8 mmol/L (under 5.5), ALT 38 U/L (under 35), TSH 2.1 mIU/L (0.5-4.0). Blood pressure today is 138/86 mmHg.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 82, BP 138/86 mmHg, RR 16, SpO2 98% on room air, temperature 36.7 °C
data_table.Examination: BMI 33 kg/m^2, waist 108 cm, no goitre, no acanthosis nigricans
data_table.Investigations: Fasting glucose 6.7 mmol/L (4.0-6.0), HbA1c 6.4% (under 6.0), triglycerides 2.6 (under 1.7), HDL 0.9 (over 1.0), LDL 3.4 (under 3.5)
data_table.Medications: Olanzapine 15 mg PO nocte; nil other regular

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Continue olanzapine unchanged, refer for dietitian and exercise physiology, and review metabolic profile in 12 months
options.rationale: Lifestyle alone is necessary but insufficient when the metabolic profile meets criteria for the dysmetabolic spectrum; antipsychotic switch and metformin are considered. (Source: RANZCP Schizophrenia CPG)

options.text: Discuss switch from olanzapine to aripiprazole and add metformin for impaired glucose and weight management
options.rationale: Olanzapine is the most metabolically active second-generation antipsychotic. With BMI 33, waist 108 cm, prediabetes-range HbA1c, raised triglycerides, low HDL, and BP 138/86 the patient meets metabolic syndrome criteria. Discussing a switch to a metabolically more favourable agent (aripiprazole, lurasidone, ziprasidone) with shared decision-making and adding metformin 500 mg twice daily for olanzapine-induced metabolic disturbance is the AU first-line approach. Lifestyle measures continue. (Source: RANZCP Schizophrenia CPG; AMH)

options.text: Discontinue olanzapine immediately and substitute clozapine to manage the metabolic and weight gain trajectory
options.rationale: Clozapine carries higher metabolic and haematological risk than olanzapine and is reserved for treatment-resistant schizophrenia. It is not appropriate for metabolic side-effect management. (Source: RANZCP Schizophrenia CPG)

options.text: Refer for bariatric surgery without trial of antipsychotic switch or metformin therapy first
options.rationale: Bariatric surgery is considered after failed pharmacological and lifestyle interventions in patients with BMI typically above 35 with comorbidity; first-line steps are antipsychotic switch and metformin. (Source: RACGP Obesity Guidelines)

options.text: Reduce olanzapine to 5 mg at night and accept the increased risk of psychotic relapse for metabolic improvement
options.rationale: Lowering an effective antipsychotic dose risks relapse and is not the AU first-line for metabolic side effects; switch or adjunct metformin is preferred. (Source: RANZCP Schizophrenia CPG)

explanation.summary: Antipsychotic-induced metabolic syndrome is a major contributor to cardiovascular mortality in schizophrenia. Metabolic monitoring schedule: baseline, then 6 weeks, 12 weeks, 6 months, then annually (weight, waist, BP, fasting glucose or HbA1c, lipid profile, ALT). Olanzapine and clozapine cause the greatest weight gain and dyslipidaemia; aripiprazole, lurasidone, and ziprasidone are weight-neutral or favourable. Management: lifestyle measures, antipsychotic switch when appropriate, metformin for weight and glucose, lipid lowering and antihypertensive therapy by AU CVD risk assessment. Smoking cessation is critical.
key_points: Monitoring: baseline, 6 weeks, 12 weeks, 6 months, then annually
Weight-gain hierarchy: olanzapine/clozapine > risperidone/quetiapine > aripiprazole/lurasidone
Metformin 500 mg BD for olanzapine-induced metabolic disturbance
Switch when feasible to weight-neutral agent
explanation.pearls: Metformin 500 mg twice daily added to olanzapine produces a 3-4 kg weight loss compared to placebo at 24 weeks and improves fasting glucose; lifestyle plus metformin is more effective than either alone.

stem:
A 24-year-old woman is brought to your emergency department by ambulance 2 hours after a deliberate overdose of approximately 30 tablets of amitriptyline 25 mg. Her partner says 'she had been arguing with her family, then I found the empty bottle and she was already drowsy'. There is no co-ingestion of alcohol or other agents. She has previously been treated for major depressive disorder.

On examination she is drowsy but rousable, GCS 12. Pupils are 5 mm and equal. She has dry mucous membranes, flushed skin, and a soft non-distended abdomen. Cardiovascular auscultation is unremarkable. Bedside electrocardiogram shows sinus tachycardia at 124 bpm with a QRS duration of 130 ms and a prominent terminal R wave in aVR (over 3 mm). Venous blood gas shows pH 7.30, bicarbonate 18 mmol/L, lactate 2.4 mmol/L. Bedside paracetamol level is undetectable. A urinary pregnancy test is negative.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 124 regular sinus tachycardia, BP 96/58 mmHg, RR 20, SpO2 98% on room air, temperature 37.0 °C
data_table.Examination: GCS 12, dry mucous membranes, flushed skin, mid-dilated pupils, soft abdomen, normal heart sounds
data_table.Investigations: ECG sinus tachycardia QRS 130 ms with terminal R wave aVR >3 mm; VBG pH 7.30 bicarbonate 18 mmol/L lactate 2.4; paracetamol undetectable
data_table.Medications: Amitriptyline 25 mg (regular for depression); ingested approximately 30 tablets

lead_in: What is the single best initial pharmacological step?

options.text: Activated charcoal 1 g/kg orally for gastric decontamination as the single best intervention at this time
options.rationale: Charcoal is considered within 1-2 hours of ingestion in an awake cooperative patient; this patient is drowsy with airway risk and the QRS widening already mandates sodium bicarbonate. (Source: AusPoison Centre TCA Guideline)

options.text: Intravenous sodium bicarbonate 1-2 mmol/kg boluses targeting QRS narrowing and arterial pH 7.50-7.55
options.rationale: QRS duration over 100 ms with a terminal R wave in aVR over 3 mm indicates sodium channel blockade by amitriptyline and is the indication for hypertonic sodium bicarbonate 1-2 mmol/kg IV bolus, repeated to target QRS narrowing and pH 7.50-7.55. Sodium bicarbonate provides a sodium load and alkalosis that displace the drug from sodium channels. Avoid class 1a, 1c, or 3 antiarrhythmics. (Source: AusPoison Centre TCA Guideline; Toxicology Handbook Australia)

options.text: Intravenous diazepam 5 mg as benzodiazepine for any seizure prophylaxis and supportive care alone otherwise
options.rationale: Benzodiazepines treat established seizures and agitation; they do not address sodium channel blockade and do not prevent the arrhythmic deterioration. (Source: AusPoison Centre TCA Guideline)

options.text: Intravenous flumazenil 0.2 mg increments for reversal of the central nervous system depression from co-ingestion
options.rationale: Flumazenil is contraindicated in mixed overdose with proconvulsant agents (TCAs) because it lowers the seizure threshold; it also does not reverse TCA toxicity. (Source: AMH; AusPoison Centre)

options.text: Intravenous lipid emulsion 1.5 mL/kg as first-line lipid rescue for amitriptyline-induced cardiac toxicity
options.rationale: Lipid emulsion is a rescue therapy in TCA cardiotoxicity refractory to sodium bicarbonate and supportive measures; it is not the first-line initial step. (Source: AusPoison Centre TCA Guideline)

explanation.summary: Tricyclic antidepressant overdose causes anticholinergic, sodium channel, and alpha-blocker effects: tachycardia, mydriasis, dry mucous membranes, urinary retention, drowsiness, seizures, and dysrhythmias. Sodium channel blockade widens the QRS, causes a terminal R wave in aVR over 3 mm, and predisposes to ventricular dysrhythmias. Treatment is supportive (airway, breathing, circulation) with hypertonic sodium bicarbonate boluses for QRS over 100 ms, hypotension, or dysrhythmia. Activated charcoal within 1-2 hours of ingestion if airway protected; consider lipid emulsion in refractory cardiotoxicity. Avoid class 1a, 1c, and 3 antiarrhythmics. Avoid flumazenil for mixed overdose.
key_points: Sodium channel blockade: QRS over 100 ms, R wave in aVR over 3 mm
Treatment: hypertonic sodium bicarbonate 1-2 mmol/kg targeting QRS and pH
Avoid class 1a, 1c, 3 antiarrhythmics
Avoid flumazenil in mixed overdose with TCA
explanation.pearls: A terminal R wave in lead aVR over 3 mm at a sinus rate is highly predictive of seizure and ventricular dysrhythmia in TCA overdose and is itself an indication for sodium bicarbonate without waiting for QRS widening.

stem:
A 24-year-old man with a 3-year history of schizophrenia is brought to your emergency department by his sister after 5 days of becoming progressively withdrawn. She says 'he hasn't eaten for two days, he just stares at the wall, and when I tried to move his arm it stayed where I put it'. He has been on risperidone 4 mg orally at night, with intermittent adherence. He had a brief similar episode 12 months ago that resolved spontaneously over 10 days.

On examination he is mute, sitting rigidly upright with his right arm held above his head. He maintains a position into which his arm is passively placed for over 1 minute (waxy flexibility). He grimaces but does not speak or follow commands. There is no tremor. He is afebrile and there is no rigidity beyond catatonic posturing. Bloods show CK 320 U/L (under 200), white cell count 6.4 x10^9/L (4.0-11.0), CRP 4 mg/L (under 5), creatinine 88 micromol/L (60-110), urea normal. Bush-Francis Catatonia Rating Scale is 14.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 90, BP 124/76 mmHg, RR 16, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.9 °C
data_table.Examination: Mute, waxy flexibility, posturing, no rigidity, afebrile, no tremor, no acute neurological focal signs
data_table.Investigations: CK 320 U/L (under 200), WCC 6.4 x10^9/L, CRP 4 mg/L, creatinine 88 micromol/L; CT head no acute findings; LP not yet performed
data_table.Medications: Risperidone 4 mg PO nocte intermittent adherence

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Administer intravenous lorazepam 2 mg as a diagnostic and therapeutic challenge and admit for ongoing treatment
options.rationale: Catatonia is diagnosed with two or more DSM-5 features (mutism, posturing, waxy flexibility, stupor, mannerism, grimacing among others); a lorazepam challenge of 1-2 mg IV is both diagnostic and therapeutic, with a positive response defined as marked symptomatic improvement within 10-30 minutes. Lorazepam is then continued (typically 1-2 mg three times daily titrated). ECT is the next step for refractory catatonia or malignant catatonia. (Source: RANZCP Catatonia Position Statement)

options.text: Increase risperidone to 6 mg at night and commence benztropine for any extrapyramidal side effect emergence
options.rationale: Antipsychotic dose escalation worsens catatonia and risks malignant catatonia or neuroleptic malignant syndrome; benzodiazepines are first-line. (Source: RANZCP Catatonia Position Statement)

options.text: Commence empirical IV ceftriaxone and vancomycin for any unrecognised encephalitis aetiology behind catatonia
options.rationale: Antibiotic empirical cover is reserved for clinical or biochemical features of infection; no fever, normal inflammatory markers, and normal LP findings remove that indication. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Order electroencephalography first and defer any pharmacological treatment until non-convulsive status is excluded
options.rationale: Non-convulsive status is on the differential and EEG is often performed, but lorazepam challenge is diagnostic and therapeutic and can be delivered at the same time without delaying treatment. (Source: RANZCP Catatonia Position Statement)

options.text: Refer immediately for electroconvulsive therapy as the only definitive treatment of catatonia before benzodiazepine trial
options.rationale: ECT is the definitive treatment for catatonia refractory to benzodiazepines or for malignant catatonia; first-line is lorazepam challenge. (Source: RANZCP Catatonia Position Statement)

explanation.summary: Catatonia is a psychomotor syndrome with mutism, posturing, waxy flexibility, stupor, negativism, echolalia, echopraxia, stereotypies, and grimacing. It complicates mood disorders, psychotic disorders, autism spectrum, organic causes (encephalitis, status epilepticus, autoimmune limbic encephalitis), and is precipitated by antipsychotic exposure. The Bush-Francis Catatonia Rating Scale guides diagnosis and monitoring. Treatment is benzodiazepine first (lorazepam 1-2 mg IV challenge); ECT is reserved for refractory or malignant catatonia (catatonia with autonomic instability, fever, rigidity, raised CK). Antipsychotics are reduced or held during the acute phase due to malignant catatonia risk.
key_points: Diagnosis: 2 or more DSM-5 catatonia features
Lorazepam 1-2 mg IV challenge is diagnostic and therapeutic
ECT for refractory or malignant catatonia
Reduce or hold antipsychotic during acute catatonia
explanation.pearls: Malignant catatonia (catatonia with hyperthermia, autonomic instability, severe rigidity, raised CK) is clinically indistinguishable from neuroleptic malignant syndrome and is a medical emergency requiring ECT after benzodiazepine challenge fails.

subtopic_detail: Adult ADHD diagnosis with comorbid anxiety
stem:
A 32-year-old accountant attends your general practice clinic with a 2-year history of worsening concentration, difficulty completing tasks, and missed deadlines. He says 'I have to write down every step or I lose track, my desk looks like an explosion, and I keep losing my keys'. He has also had persistent worry about work performance, initial insomnia, and muscle tension for the past 18 months. School reports from age 8 describe a 'bright but disorganised' boy whose teachers commented on inattention and inability to sit still.

He drinks 4 standard drinks a week and does not use other substances. There is no mood instability, no psychotic symptoms, no recent head injury, and no thyroid history. Thyroid function is normal on bloods this morning. He scored 22 on the Adult ADHD Self-Report Scale (cut-off 14 for probable diagnosis) and 16 on the GAD-7 (cut-off 15 for moderate to severe anxiety). His worry is unrelated to specific objects and is generalised across multiple domains over more than 6 months.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 86, BP 124/76 mmHg, RR 14, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.8 °C
data_table.Examination: Restless during interview, fidgety, frequent loss of train of thought; mental state otherwise unremarkable, no psychotic features
data_table.Investigations: TSH 1.8 mIU/L (0.5-4.0), normal FBC and UEC; ASRS-v1.1 score 22; GAD-7 score 16

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Commence a long-acting stimulant such as lisdexamfetamine for adult ADHD pending psychiatry confirmation later
options.rationale: Stimulant prescribing for adult ADHD in Australia is restricted to authorised prescribers (psychiatrists, paediatricians, and some neurologists depending on state) and requires diagnostic confirmation by a specialist before initiation. (Source: RANZCP Adult ADHD Position Statement; AMH)

options.text: Commence sertraline 50 mg orally daily for generalised anxiety and review in 6 weeks before any ADHD work-up
options.rationale: Treating only the anxiety risks missing or worsening the ADHD; comorbid presentations are best assessed by a specialist with shared diagnostic formulation. (Source: RANZCP Adult ADHD Position Statement)

options.text: Refer to a psychiatrist for adult ADHD assessment, treat anxiety with first-line measures in parallel, and discuss driving safety
options.rationale: Adult ADHD diagnosis requires specialist confirmation in Australia via collateral history (school reports), structured assessment, and exclusion of differentials. Comorbid generalised anxiety disorder is common (over 50% of adult ADHD) and is treated in parallel with first-line CBT or SSRI when symptoms are moderate to severe. Stimulant safety includes a discussion of driving impairment during titration. (Source: RANZCP Adult ADHD Position Statement; ICGP Adult ADHD)

options.text: Order an electroencephalogram and brain magnetic resonance imaging before any further behavioural assessment occurs
options.rationale: EEG and MRI are not part of the routine ADHD work-up and are reserved for atypical features (head injury, focal deficits, paroxysmal symptoms). (Source: RANZCP Adult ADHD Position Statement)

options.text: Provide cognitive behavioural therapy alone for both inattention and anxiety and review at 12 weeks for response
options.rationale: CBT alone for ADHD has modest benefit and is most effective as an adjunct to pharmacotherapy in moderate to severe ADHD; sole CBT delays effective treatment. (Source: RANZCP Adult ADHD Position Statement)

explanation.summary: Adult ADHD presents with persistent inattention, organisational difficulty, restlessness, impulsivity, and emotional dysregulation continuing from childhood. Diagnosis requires evidence of symptoms before age 12, impairment in two or more domains, and exclusion of differentials. Collateral history (school reports, family) supports diagnosis. Comorbid anxiety, depression, substance use disorders, and learning disorders are common and treated in parallel. Stimulants (lisdexamfetamine, methylphenidate) are first-line pharmacotherapy in Australia and require authorised prescriber initiation. Atomoxetine is a non-stimulant option, particularly when stimulant adverse effects emerge or substance misuse risk is significant. Driving safety advice is part of the discussion.
key_points: Specialist confirmation required for adult ADHD diagnosis in Australia
Comorbidity is the rule, not the exception
First-line: long-acting stimulant by authorised prescriber
Driving safety counselling during titration
explanation.pearls: Adult ADHD Self-Report Scale Part A (ASRS-v1.1) of 4 or more positive items raises pre-test probability sufficiently to refer for diagnostic interview; the score itself is a screening tool, not diagnostic.

stem:
A 28-year-old G1P1 woman is brought by her partner to your emergency department on day 9 postpartum. He says 'she hasn't slept for three nights, she's saying the baby has been swapped at the hospital and the radio is sending her messages'. She has had no prior psychiatric history but her mother has bipolar I disorder. She gave birth to a healthy term boy by normal vaginal delivery; the postnatal period was uneventful initially.

On examination she is alert but tangential, with rapid pressured speech and labile affect. She describes the radio referring to her by name and intermittent visual perceptions of 'shadows changing shape'. There is no fever, no rash, and no neck stiffness. She is breastfeeding and her baby is in good health. There is no acute risk identified in the moment but she repeatedly asks 'are they going to take him away because he is the wrong baby?'. Bedside vitals are unremarkable; haemoglobin 124 g/L, white cell count 9.4 x10^9/L, CRP 4 mg/L, TSH 1.8 mIU/L, urinalysis clear.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 92, BP 122/76 mmHg, RR 18, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.9 °C
data_table.Examination: Tangential, pressured speech, labile affect, delusional content (baby identity, radio referential), visual misperceptions; no neck stiffness, no rash
data_table.Investigations: Hb 124 g/L (115-150), WCC 9.4 x10^9/L (4-11), CRP 4 mg/L (under 5), TSH 1.8 mIU/L (0.5-4.0), urinalysis clear

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Commence sertraline 50 mg orally daily for severe postnatal depression and arrange community midwife visit tomorrow
options.rationale: This is postpartum psychosis (psychotic features, sleeplessness, mood lability, abrupt onset within the first weeks postpartum), not postnatal depression. SSRI alone does not treat psychosis. (Source: RANZCP Perinatal Mental Health Position Statement)
source_refs: RANZCP Perinatal Mental Health Position Statement

options.text: Provide reassurance, schedule a 1-week postnatal follow-up review, and continue breastfeeding without pharmacotherapy
options.rationale: Outpatient management of postpartum psychosis is unsafe; suicide and infanticide risks are elevated and admission to a mother-baby unit is the AU standard. (Source: RANZCP Perinatal Mental Health Position Statement)
source_refs: RANZCP Perinatal Mental Health Position Statement

options.text: Refer urgently to a community mental health team for case management without inpatient admission at this stage
options.rationale: Community management is reserved for mild postnatal mental illness with intact reality testing and adequate supports; psychotic features mandate inpatient mother-baby unit care. (Source: RANZCP Perinatal Mental Health Position Statement)
source_refs: RANZCP Perinatal Mental Health Position Statement

options.text: Admit to a mother-baby unit, commence olanzapine, and consider lithium with a breastfeeding shared decision
options.rationale: Postpartum psychosis is a psychiatric emergency with a significant suicide and infanticide risk; admission to a mother-baby unit allows joint care while ensuring infant safety. An antipsychotic (olanzapine or risperidone) is first-line; lithium has strong evidence for prevention of recurrence and acute treatment, with shared breastfeeding decisions about infant lithium monitoring. ECT is considered for severe or refractory cases or when rapid response is needed. (Source: RANZCP Perinatal Mental Health Position Statement; COPE Perinatal Mental Health Guideline)
source_refs: RANZCP Perinatal Mental Health Position Statement

options.text: Arrange outpatient cognitive behavioural therapy for postnatal adjustment and review in 4 weeks at her next visit
options.rationale: CBT does not treat acute psychosis and outpatient settings cannot guarantee infant safety; this is an emergency. (Source: RANZCP Perinatal Mental Health Position Statement)
source_refs: RANZCP Perinatal Mental Health Position Statement

explanation.summary: Postpartum psychosis affects 1-2 per 1000 births, typically within the first 2 weeks postpartum, with abrupt onset of psychotic features, mood symptoms (often manic or mixed), sleeplessness, and confusion. Past or family history of bipolar disorder or previous postpartum psychosis is the strongest risk factor. Differentials include delirium, autoimmune encephalitis, severe postnatal depression with psychotic features, and substance-induced psychosis. Management is admission to a mother-baby unit when available, antipsychotic therapy, lithium for acute and prophylactic indication, and ECT for severe or refractory cases. Suicide and infanticide risks are elevated and the infant is never left alone with the unwell parent during the acute phase.
key_points: 1-2 per 1000 births; first 2 weeks
Family or personal history of bipolar disorder is the major risk
Admit to mother-baby unit (when available)
Risk of suicide and infanticide remains until resolution
explanation.pearls: Women with a history of postpartum psychosis or bipolar I have approximately 50% risk of relapse in a subsequent pregnancy; prophylactic lithium at delivery is the AU recommended preventive intervention in shared planning.

sources.label: RANZCP Perinatal Mental Health Position Statement

subtopic_detail: Schizoaffective vs bipolar with psychotic features
stem:
A 31-year-old man with a 6-year mental health history attends your community psychiatry clinic for diagnostic clarification. His parents say 'when he's high he doesn't sleep, he talks fast, he buys things he can't afford, and he hears voices then'. He has had four hospital admissions: two for manic episodes with psychotic features (delusions of being a religious prophet, persecutory voices) and two for major depressive episodes with mood-congruent psychosis. Between episodes he has been functioning at work part-time.

Review of his records confirms that during 2 distinct periods, each lasting 4 to 6 weeks between admissions, he experienced delusions of telepathic communication and persecutory auditory hallucinations without concurrent prominent mood symptoms (his mood was 'flat but not depressed' and energy was preserved). His insight is generally good now. There is no substance misuse. He is currently on lithium 900 mg at night, lamotrigine 200 mg daily, and risperidone 4 mg at night, and is in partial remission. He asks 'what is my diagnosis?'.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 72, BP 124/76 mmHg, RR 14, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.8 °C
data_table.Examination: Euthymic at presentation, no current psychotic features, MMSE normal, no extrapyramidal signs
data_table.Investigations: Lithium 0.7 mmol/L (0.6-1.2), TSH 2.0 mIU/L (0.5-4.0), eGFR 84 mL/min/1.73 m squared
data_table.Medications: Lithium 900 mg PO nocte; lamotrigine 200 mg PO daily; risperidone 4 mg PO nocte

lead_in: What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.text: Bipolar I disorder with psychotic features confined entirely to mood episodes and no inter-episode psychosis
options.rationale: Bipolar I with psychotic features requires psychotic symptoms occurring only during mood episodes; the documented inter-episode psychosis disqualifies this label. (Source: RANZCP Mood Disorders CPG; DSM-5-TR)

options.text: Schizophrenia with mood episodes secondary to neuroleptic adverse effects and demoralisation
options.rationale: Schizophrenia requires 6 months of disturbance with at least 1 month of active-phase positive symptoms; the prominent and recurrent mood episodes with mood-congruent psychosis are too prominent for schizophrenia. (Source: DSM-5-TR)

options.text: Schizoaffective disorder bipolar type given prominent mood episodes and inter-episode primary psychotic symptoms
options.rationale: This option correctly identifies the schizoaffective construct but uses imprecise terminology; the DSM-5-TR requires the major mood episodes to be present for the majority of the total active illness duration and at least 2 weeks of psychosis without prominent mood symptoms - the question's diagnostic phrasing differs. The intended best option pairs the bipolar type label with the specific 2-week inter-episode psychosis criterion. (Source: DSM-5-TR)

options.text: Delusional disorder mixed type with comorbid bipolar I disorder and substance use diagnostic complication
options.rationale: Delusional disorder requires non-bizarre delusions for at least 1 month without hallucinations or other psychotic features prominent enough to meet schizophrenia criteria; this patient has prominent hallucinations and prior psychotic episodes that exceed that. (Source: DSM-5-TR)

options.text: Schizoaffective disorder bipolar type with documented psychosis lasting at least 2 weeks without prominent mood
options.rationale: Schizoaffective disorder bipolar type requires (1) an uninterrupted period during which there is a major mood episode (depressive or manic) concurrent with criterion A of schizophrenia, (2) delusions or hallucinations for at least 2 weeks in the absence of a major mood episode during the lifetime of the illness, (3) mood symptoms present for the majority of the active and residual phases. This patient meets all three. The bipolar subtype is assigned because manic episodes have occurred. (Source: RANZCP Mood Disorders CPG; DSM-5-TR)

explanation.summary: Schizoaffective disorder is differentiated from bipolar I with psychotic features and from schizophrenia by the temporal relationship between mood and psychotic symptoms. DSM-5-TR requires: (1) major mood episode (depressive or manic) concurrent with criterion A of schizophrenia, (2) delusions or hallucinations for at least 2 weeks without a major mood episode at any time in the lifetime of the illness, (3) mood symptoms present for the majority of the total active and residual periods. Subtypes are bipolar type and depressive type. Management combines antipsychotic with mood stabiliser (lithium, valproate, lamotrigine) and structured psychosocial intervention. Longitudinal records and collateral history are essential to differentiate from bipolar I with psychotic features.
key_points: At least 2 weeks of psychosis WITHOUT major mood episode (lifetime) - the discriminator
Concurrent major mood episode plus criterion A of schizophrenia
Mood symptoms present for the majority of active and residual phases
Subtype by lifetime presence or absence of manic episodes
explanation.pearls: In schizoaffective disorder, mood symptoms occupy the majority of the total active and residual illness; if they occupy a small fraction with chronic psychosis dominating, the diagnosis is schizophrenia with mood episodes.

stem:
A 27-year-old woman presents to your general practice clinic on her own initiative requesting an autism assessment. She says 'I've masked all my life and I'm exhausted and I can't keep doing it'. She describes intense restricted interests since childhood (collecting and cataloguing fossils for 18 years), sensory sensitivities (overwhelmed in supermarkets, prefers seam-free clothing), and significant social exhaustion after work meetings. She has had a long-term partner for 5 years.

She was a high-achieving student through school and university (engineering degree, GPA 6.9/7) and has held the same software engineering job for 3 years. She struggles with workplace small talk and has had two episodes of generalised anxiety (one in second year of university, one this year) treated with cognitive behavioural therapy. She does not meet criteria for current depression (PHQ-9 = 6). Her father has been described as having 'quirky obsessive interests'. She has no history of self-injurious behaviour and her speech and motor milestones were normal in childhood. Her workplace has just transferred her to a new open-plan office, and she has been having panic attacks in the bathroom.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 76, BP 118/74 mmHg, RR 14, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.8 °C
data_table.Examination: Alert, cooperative, normal speech rhythm and prosody, brief intermittent eye contact, no abnormal movements
data_table.Investigations: PHQ-9 = 6 (not depressed), GAD-7 = 14 (moderate-severe anxiety), AQ-50 = 38 (above clinical threshold of 32)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Diagnose generalised anxiety disorder and commence sertraline 50 mg daily with cognitive behavioural therapy referral
options.rationale: Anxiety is a comorbidity and not a substitute for the autism assessment she has requested; anxiety treatment alone misses the developmental diagnosis. (Source: RANZCP CPG ASD; NICE Adult Autism Guideline)

options.text: Reassure her that high-functioning autism is unlikely given her professional success and partnered relationship status
options.rationale: High autonomic load with masking is characteristic of late-recognised autism in women; functional achievement does not exclude autism. (Source: RANZCP CPG ASD)

options.text: Refer to a specialist multidisciplinary diagnostic service experienced in adult autism in women for formal assessment
options.rationale: Adult autism assessment requires multidisciplinary specialist input including a structured developmental interview (ADI-R or equivalent) and an observational assessment (ADOS-2) with attention to female phenotype features (masking, intense restricted interests in socially accepted domains, internalising comorbidity). General practice screening with AQ-50 above threshold supports referral but does not constitute diagnosis. Concurrent anxiety management is appropriate but does not replace the diagnostic pathway. (Source: RANZCP CPG ASD)

options.text: Refer to occupational health for workplace accommodation under the Disability Discrimination Act before any diagnosis
options.rationale: Workplace accommodation under the DDA depends on a formal diagnosis being established or the worker self-identifying as having a disability; assessment is the prerequisite. (Source: Australian Human Rights Commission)

options.text: Initiate intranasal oxytocin trial for autism social cognition difficulties as the first-line pharmacological intervention
options.rationale: Intranasal oxytocin is not a TGA-approved or AU first-line treatment for autism; evidence is mixed and use is restricted to research settings. (Source: TGA)

explanation.summary: Adult autism in women is frequently identified late because of masking (consciously or unconsciously hiding autistic traits in social settings) and restricted interests aligned with socially accepted domains. Diagnosis is by specialist multidisciplinary assessment with a structured developmental interview (parent-informant if possible) and an observational measure. RANZCP guidance acknowledges the female phenotype and the high comorbidity with anxiety and depression. Management is post-diagnosis and includes psychoeducation, occupational input, sensory environment modification, and concurrent treatment of comorbid anxiety or depression. Late diagnosis often produces relief and improved self-understanding for the person.
key_points: Masking and internalising features common in women with late diagnosis
Multidisciplinary assessment with ADI-R/ADOS-2 (or AU equivalents)
High comorbidity with anxiety and depression
Workplace accommodation under DDA requires assessment first
explanation.pearls: The Autism Quotient (AQ-50) is a self-rated screening tool with a clinical cut-off at 32; sensitivity is reasonable but specificity is modest, so a positive screen prompts referral rather than confirming diagnosis.

stem:
A 51-year-old man presents to your general practice clinic for help quitting smoking. He has smoked 25 cigarettes per day for 33 years (pack-years over 40) and has tried unsupported quitting three times. He says 'I really want to stop for my grandkids, but I'm worried because I've been on antidepressants forever'. His major depressive disorder is currently in remission on sertraline 100 mg daily; the last episode was 2 years ago. He scores PHQ-9 = 3 today.

He has stable angina on metoprolol 25 mg twice daily and an ejection fraction of 60% on a recent echocardiogram. He has had no acute coronary syndrome in the last 12 months. He has no history of seizures, alcohol use disorder, or eating disorder. His BMI is 24. He has no suicidal ideation now and no past suicide attempts. He has tried nicotine replacement therapy in two of his prior attempts; he found the patch helpful but discontinued because of vivid dreams. He scores Fagerstrom = 7 (high dependence). Spirometry is mild obstruction (FEV1 78% predicted) with reversibility.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 64, BP 124/76 mmHg, RR 14, SpO2 98% on room air, temperature 36.6 °C
data_table.Examination: Alert, cooperative, no acute distress, mild expiratory wheeze on auscultation
data_table.Investigations: PHQ-9 = 3 (remission); Fagerstrom = 7 (high dependence); FEV1 78% predicted with reversibility
data_table.Medications: Sertraline 100 mg daily, metoprolol 25 mg twice daily

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first-line pharmacotherapy?

options.text: Bupropion 150 mg daily increasing to 150 mg twice daily after 1 week with target quit date in week 2
options.rationale: Bupropion is contraindicated in active seizure disorder and is best avoided in patients with reduced seizure threshold; varenicline has better cessation outcomes in EAGLES and is no longer considered to worsen neuropsychiatric outcomes. (Source: RACGP Supporting Smoking Cessation Guideline)

options.text: Combination nicotine replacement therapy patch plus lozenge as needed with behavioural support and weekly review
options.rationale: Combination NRT is reasonable second-line, but varenicline has the highest single-agent cessation success rates in the EAGLES trial population including stable depression. (Source: RACGP Supporting Smoking Cessation Guideline)

options.text: Nortriptyline 25 mg daily titrated to 75 mg as a TGA-approved off-label smoking cessation aid for resistant cases
options.rationale: Nortriptyline is a third-line agent; it has cardiac and anticholinergic effects that are less favourable than varenicline in stable depression. (Source: RACGP Supporting Smoking Cessation Guideline)

options.text: Clonidine 0.1 mg twice daily as the AU first-line cessation aid in a patient with comorbid hypertension and depression
options.rationale: Clonidine is fourth-line at best and is not the AU first-line; sedation, hypotension, and rebound limit its use. (Source: RACGP Supporting Smoking Cessation Guideline)

options.text: Varenicline starting 0.5 mg daily titrating to 1 mg twice daily over week 1 with quit date day 8 of treatment
options.rationale: Varenicline (alpha-4 beta-2 nicotinic partial agonist) is the AU first-line single agent with the highest cessation rates. The 2016 EAGLES trial demonstrated no increase in neuropsychiatric adverse events in patients with stable psychiatric disorders compared with placebo. Stable depression on SSRI is not a contraindication. The 12-week course is started 8 days before the planned quit date with titration to 1 mg twice daily. Smoking cessation does not reduce SSRI efficacy but smoking cessation does increase plasma levels of some psychotropics (clozapine, olanzapine) through CYP1A2; sertraline is unaffected. (Source: RACGP Supporting Smoking Cessation Guideline; EAGLES trial)

explanation.summary: Australian guidance ranks varenicline as the first-line single agent for nicotine dependence in adults able to take it. The 2016 EAGLES trial demonstrated comparable neuropsychiatric safety in stable psychiatric patients to non-psychiatric controls, leading to removal of the prior FDA boxed warning. Combination NRT (patch plus oral form) is the alternative first-line for those unable to tolerate varenicline. Bupropion is contraindicated in seizure disorder and bipolar disorder. Behavioural support amplifies pharmacotherapy effect. Smoking cessation increases plasma levels of clozapine, olanzapine, theophylline (CYP1A2 induction by tobacco smoke reverses on cessation) and dose review is required; sertraline is not affected.
key_points: Varenicline first-line; safe in stable depression per EAGLES
NRT combination as first-line alternative
Bupropion contraindicated in seizure disorder
Cessation increases CYP1A2 substrate levels (clozapine, olanzapine, theophylline)
explanation.pearls: Smoking cessation increases plasma clozapine concentration by 50-100% within 2-4 weeks through CYP1A2 de-induction; the clozapine dose is reduced by about 30% at cessation with weekly level monitoring.

stem:
A 22-year-old woman presents to your community mental health team for the third time in 6 months after intentional superficial cutting of her forearm. She says 'when my boyfriend pulls away I feel like I'm disappearing and only the cutting brings me back'. She has chronic feelings of emptiness, recurrent self-harm without suicidal intent, intense unstable relationships, and rapidly shifting mood states. She has been on three different SSRIs (sertraline, escitalopram, fluoxetine) over 2 years without sustained benefit.

She has had two brief admissions for self-harm in the last year; she finds inpatient settings escalate rather than calm her. There is no current suicidal plan or intent. There is no current depression by PHQ-9 (= 9, mild). She uses cannabis on weekends and drinks 4 standard drinks twice a week. Her sleep is fragmented. She has no psychotic features and her reality testing is intact. Her family environment in childhood was emotionally invalidating with intermittent neglect; there is no formal trauma history at this assessment. Her GP has been prescribing repeat low-dose quetiapine 25 mg as needed for distress, which she uses two or three times a week.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 78, BP 116/72 mmHg, RR 14, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.6 °C
data_table.Examination: Alert, cooperative, mood labile, no psychomotor agitation, no thought disorder, multiple superficial healed forearm cuts
data_table.Investigations: PHQ-9 = 9 (mild), no current suicidal plan or intent; AUDIT-C = 4
data_table.Medications: Quetiapine 25 mg as needed (used 2-3 times per week); previously sertraline, escitalopram, fluoxetine

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Restart escitalopram 10 mg daily and titrate to 20 mg over 4 weeks aimed at chronic emotional dysregulation
options.rationale: SSRIs are not first-line for BPD core symptoms; the AU guidance reserves psychotropics for clear comorbid depression, anxiety, or short-term crisis use, and removes them for emotional dysregulation alone. (Source: NHMRC BPD Clinical Practice Guidelines; RANZCP CPG Personality Disorder)

options.text: Admit to an inpatient unit for at least 2 weeks of structured behavioural therapy and medication review
options.rationale: Inpatient admission is reserved for acute crisis with imminent risk and short stays (commonly under 72 hours); prolonged admission risks worsening BPD outcomes. (Source: NHMRC BPD Clinical Practice Guidelines)

options.text: Increase the as-needed quetiapine dose to 100 mg with broader availability for breakthrough distress
options.rationale: Routine as-needed antipsychotic for distress is discouraged; structured psychological therapy with crisis planning is the evidence-based treatment. (Source: NHMRC BPD Clinical Practice Guidelines)

options.text: Refer for structured psychological therapy (dialectical behaviour therapy or mentalisation-based therapy) with clear crisis plan
options.rationale: Australian NHMRC and RANZCP guidance position structured psychological therapy (DBT, MBT, schema-focused therapy, transference-focused therapy) as the cornerstone of BPD treatment. Pharmacotherapy is reserved for clearly defined comorbidities or short-term crisis use. A written crisis plan, safety planning, and a relationship with one primary treating clinician reduces hospitalisation and improves outcomes. (Source: NHMRC BPD Clinical Practice Guidelines; RANZCP CPG Personality Disorder)

options.text: Commence lamotrigine 25 mg titrating to 200 mg over 8 weeks for affective instability in personality disorder
options.rationale: Recent trials (LABILE 2018) showed lamotrigine offers no advantage over placebo for BPD affective symptoms; the AU guidance does not recommend it as first-line. (Source: NHMRC BPD Clinical Practice Guidelines)

explanation.summary: Borderline personality disorder responds best to structured psychological therapy. Australian (NHMRC) guidance lists dialectical behaviour therapy, mentalisation-based therapy, schema-focused therapy, and transference-focused therapy as first-line. Pharmacotherapy is reserved for clearly defined comorbidities (current major depression, persistent generalised anxiety, post-traumatic stress disorder) or short-term crisis use; routine SSRI or antipsychotic use for emotional dysregulation alone is discouraged. A written crisis plan with the patient, a primary treating clinician, and a clear pathway for short focused admissions (commonly under 72 hours) is more effective than reactive long-stay admission. The recovery trajectory is more favourable than once thought, with majority remission of BPD criteria over a decade.
key_points: First-line: DBT, MBT, schema therapy, TFP
Pharmacotherapy reserved for comorbidity or short-term crisis
Brief admission only; long-stay risks worsening
Crisis plan, primary clinician, scheduled review
explanation.pearls: The LABILE trial (Lancet Psychiatry 2018) showed no benefit of lamotrigine over placebo for BPD affective symptoms; AU guidance has reduced routine use of mood stabilisers in this population.

subtopic_detail: Schizoaffective vs bipolar with psychotic features
stem:
A 26-year-old man is admitted to your inpatient psychiatry unit on an involuntary order. His sister says 'he's been hearing voices on and off for nearly a year now, even when he's not high or low'. His mood has alternated between two clear depressive episodes (3 and 7 months ago) and one clear manic episode (4 months ago, lasting 2 weeks with reduced sleep, grandiosity, hypersexuality, and pressured speech). Through this period he has had persistent auditory hallucinations of two male voices commenting on his actions, including at least 2 weeks of euthymia between episodes when the voices continued.

He has no substance use disorder. Urine drug screen is negative. There is no medical cause identified on workup (CT brain normal, TSH normal, B12 normal, syphilis serology negative, HIV negative). He has been started on olanzapine 10 mg with reasonable effect on the active psychotic symptoms and was previously on sertraline (currently off it). His insight is limited but improving. The family asks 'what is it actually, doctor?' and his sister insists 'he's not just bipolar'.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 78, BP 122/74 mmHg, RR 14, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.7 °C
data_table.Examination: Alert, cooperative, third-person auditory hallucinations described, normal speech rhythm, no thought disorder, mood currently euthymic
data_table.Investigations: Urine drug screen negative, CT brain normal, TSH 1.8 mU/L (0.5-4.0), B12 410 pmol/L (200-700), HIV and syphilis negative

lead_in: What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.text: Bipolar I disorder with psychotic features confined to mood episodes only and mood-congruent themes
options.rationale: Bipolar I with mood-congruent psychosis has psychosis only during mood episodes; this patient has 2 weeks or more of psychosis during euthymia, which excludes the diagnosis. (Source: DSM-5-TR)

options.text: Substance-induced psychotic disorder with mood symptoms secondary to long-standing cannabis dependence
options.rationale: Urine drug screen is negative and the symptom pattern is not time-locked to substance use; substance-induced disorder requires temporal association with substance exposure. (Source: DSM-5-TR)

options.text: Major depressive disorder with mood-congruent psychotic features in the context of repeated severe episodes
options.rationale: Recurrent severe major depression with psychosis fits some criteria but does not explain the manic episode, which qualifies the patient for bipolar spectrum or schizoaffective consideration. (Source: DSM-5-TR)

options.text: Schizoaffective disorder bipolar type with mood and psychotic symptoms in defined temporal relationship
options.rationale: DSM-5-TR schizoaffective disorder requires: (1) major mood episode (depressive or manic) concurrent with criterion A of schizophrenia for an uninterrupted period; (2) delusions or hallucinations for 2 weeks or more in the absence of a major mood episode at some time during the lifetime duration; (3) major mood episode symptoms present for the majority of the active and residual illness duration; (4) not attributable to substance or medical cause. The 2-week euthymic interval with persistent psychosis distinguishes schizoaffective from bipolar with psychosis. Bipolar subtype is used because of the manic episode. (Source: DSM-5-TR; RANZCP CPG Schizophrenia)

options.text: Schizophreniform disorder with associated mood disturbance from social and occupational consequences of psychosis
options.rationale: Schizophreniform disorder lasts under 6 months; this patient's illness has been at least 1 year and includes prominent mood episodes meeting full criteria. (Source: DSM-5-TR)

explanation.summary: Schizoaffective disorder is distinguished from bipolar disorder with psychotic features by the presence of delusions or hallucinations for 2 weeks or more in the ABSENCE of a major mood episode at some point during the illness. Mood symptoms must be present for the majority of the active and residual illness duration (otherwise primary schizophrenia with mood symptoms is the diagnosis). Bipolar subtype includes manic episodes; depressive subtype includes only depressive episodes. Treatment requires both mood stabilisation (lithium, valproate, or atypical with mood stabilising effect such as quetiapine, olanzapine, aripiprazole) and antipsychotic effect, often via the same atypical agent.
key_points: 2+ weeks of psychosis in absence of mood episode at some point
Mood symptoms majority of active/residual illness duration
Bipolar subtype if manic episode present
Treatment: mood stabiliser plus antipsychotic effect
explanation.pearls: The 2-week criterion of psychosis without mood episode is the cleanest discriminator between schizoaffective disorder and bipolar with psychotic features; a careful longitudinal interval history is essential.

stem:
A 19-year-old university student is admitted to your psychiatry unit with a 4-week history of paranoid delusions (his housemates are spying on him through air vents), third-person auditory hallucinations, and thought broadcasting. His mother says 'he's been smoking strong skunk weed almost every day for the last 2 years'. He has been continuously using high-potency cannabis (estimated 16% THC) daily for 24 months. Urine THC and metabolites are positive on admission.

He was abstinent for 4 weeks during a remote bushwalking trip 6 months ago; his mother says the voices and paranoid ideas continued throughout that abstinent period and only briefly faded when he returned and started using again. His paternal uncle has schizophrenia. He has had functional decline over 12 months (left first-year engineering after one semester) and his negative symptoms (amotivation, social withdrawal, blunted affect) have persisted for 8 months. There is no acute mood episode (PHQ-9 = 7, YMRS = 3). His insight is poor.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 88, BP 124/76 mmHg, RR 16, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.6 °C
data_table.Examination: Alert, paranoid, third-person auditory hallucinations, thought broadcasting, blunted affect, no abnormal movements
data_table.Investigations: Urine THC and metabolites positive, urine other drugs negative, CT brain normal, TSH normal, B12 normal

lead_in: What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.text: Cannabis-induced psychotic disorder that will resolve with abstinence and supportive care alone
options.rationale: Cannabis-induced psychosis resolves within days to weeks of abstinence; persistent psychosis through 4 weeks of abstinence is inconsistent. (Source: DSM-5-TR; RANZCP CPG Schizophrenia)

options.text: Schizotypal personality disorder with eccentric thinking exacerbated by chronic cannabis exposure
options.rationale: Schizotypal personality disorder does not include sustained delusions, hallucinations, or thought broadcasting; this patient's presentation fits frank psychotic illness. (Source: DSM-5-TR)

options.text: Brief psychotic disorder with substance-related precipitation expected to resolve fully within 4 weeks
options.rationale: Brief psychotic disorder lasts under 1 month; this patient's psychotic symptoms have been continuous over 8-12 months with negative symptoms and functional decline. (Source: DSM-5-TR)

options.text: Major depressive disorder with cannabis use complicating mood and producing transient pseudo-psychotic features
options.rationale: His PHQ-9 is in the mild-to-moderate range and there is no acute mood episode; cannabis-related psychosis without mood prominence is not depression. (Source: DSM-5-TR)

options.text: Primary schizophrenia (cannabis use as risk factor) with characteristic features sustained through abstinence
options.rationale: Continuous psychotic symptoms (delusions, hallucinations, thought broadcasting) through 4 weeks of cannabis abstinence, with functional decline over 12 months, sustained negative symptoms over 8 months, family history, and high-potency cannabis use as a risk factor, fits primary schizophrenia. Cannabis use is causally associated (genetic risk and high-potency THC exposure increase schizophrenia odds ratio approximately threefold) but does not redefine the diagnosis when symptoms persist beyond cannabis clearance. Treatment includes atypical antipsychotic and structured substance use disorder care. (Source: RANZCP CPG Schizophrenia; DSM-5-TR)

explanation.summary: Differentiating cannabis-induced psychosis from primary schizophrenia in a young user requires longitudinal assessment of symptoms during abstinence. Cannabis-induced psychotic disorder resolves within days to a few weeks of abstinence; persistent symptoms beyond 4 weeks of demonstrated abstinence, sustained negative symptoms, and functional decline support primary schizophrenia. Cannabis is a risk factor for schizophrenia onset, especially when high-potency, daily, and used in adolescence; the odds ratio is approximately threefold in heavy daily users. Treatment uses an atypical antipsychotic (aripiprazole, olanzapine, risperidone) plus structured substance use disorder management; cannabis cessation is the most modifiable risk for relapse.
key_points: Cannabis-induced psychosis: resolves within days-weeks of abstinence
Persistent psychosis beyond 4 weeks abstinence supports primary psychosis
Cannabis is risk factor (OR ~3) for schizophrenia in heavy users
Cessation is the most modifiable relapse risk
explanation.pearls: High-potency cannabis (>=10% THC) used daily in adolescence is associated with a dose-response increase in schizophrenia risk; an Australian young person presenting with first-episode psychosis should be screened with quantitative cannabis history.

subtopic_detail: ECT in pregnancy with severe depression
stem:
You are the consultation-liaison psychiatry registrar called to a 32-year-old woman at 24+3 weeks gestation admitted under maternity for severe depression with active suicidal ideation. Her husband says 'she's stopped eating and won't get out of bed and she's been telling me the baby would be better off without her'. She has had no oral intake for 5 days and has lost 4 kg in 10 days. She declines to drink water on the ward.

She has had four adequate trials of antidepressants since the diagnosis of major depressive disorder at age 22 (sertraline, venlafaxine, mirtazapine, vortioxetine) without sustained remission. She had three previous ECT courses (two before pregnancy with full remission, one for postpartum depression with her first child with good response). She has no medical contraindication to general anaesthesia. Her capacity to consent has been assessed and documented as intact by your consultant - she understands the diagnosis, the proposed treatment, the alternatives, and the consequences of declining, and her decisions are consistent. She agrees to ECT and signs informed consent in your presence.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 84, BP 96/58 mmHg, RR 14, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.5 °C, fetal HR 152 bpm reassuring
data_table.Examination: Severely depressed mood, no thought disorder, intact capacity, scleral icterus absent, mucous membranes dry, weight loss 4 kg in 10 days
data_table.Investigations: PHQ-9 = 24 (severe), albumin 28 g/L (35-50), urea 9.2 mmol/L (2.5-7.5), creatinine 76 micromol/L (45-90), TSH normal, fetal anatomy normal at 22 weeks
data_table.Medications: Vortioxetine 20 mg daily ongoing; intravenous fluids running

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Defer ECT until after delivery and increase vortioxetine to 30 mg with a trial of augmentation with quetiapine 50 mg
options.rationale: Severe depression with food and fluid refusal in pregnancy carries acute maternal and fetal risk; ECT is the appropriate AU intervention in this context. (Source: RANZCP CPG Mood Disorders)

options.text: Proceed with ECT with obstetric review, left lateral tilt, continuous fetal monitoring, and short-acting anaesthesia
options.rationale: ECT in pregnancy is safe and effective when the depression is severe with refractory features, food/fluid refusal, or active suicidal ideation. The setup requires obstetric review, left lateral tilt to avoid aortocaval compression, continuous fetal monitoring during the procedure, intubation rather than mask ventilation in the second and third trimester, and short-acting anaesthesia (thiopentone or propofol). The 2nd trimester is the lowest-risk window. Consent is established (capacity intact, informed, voluntary). (Source: RANZCP CPG Mood Disorders; RANZCP Position Statement on ECT)

options.text: Refer to the Mental Health Act tribunal for involuntary ECT order even though her capacity has been documented as intact
options.rationale: The Mental Health Act involuntary ECT pathway is for patients without capacity who refuse; this patient has intact capacity and consents. (Source: Victorian Mental Health and Wellbeing Act 2022 + state equivalents)
source_refs: Victorian Mental Health and Wellbeing Act 2022 + state equivalents

options.text: Commence intravenous lithium 600 mg daily augmentation as the AU first-line approach for refractory depression in pregnancy
options.rationale: Lithium is a Category D drug in pregnancy with first-trimester teratogenicity risk (Ebstein's anomaly) and ongoing fetal monitoring requirements; it is not first-line in this clinical scenario. (Source: AMH; RANZCP CPG Mood Disorders)

options.text: Trial intravenous ketamine 0.5 mg/kg infusion as the rapid-acting alternative to ECT in refractory depression in pregnancy
options.rationale: Ketamine is not a TGA-approved intervention for major depressive disorder in pregnancy and is restricted to research or named-patient use; ECT remains the established AU pathway for severe depression in pregnancy. (Source: TGA; RANZCP CPG Mood Disorders)

explanation.summary: Electroconvulsive therapy is the most effective treatment for severe major depressive disorder with food/fluid refusal, persistent suicidal ideation, catatonia, or psychotic features. In pregnancy, ECT is safe with appropriate setup: obstetric review, left lateral tilt to avoid aortocaval compression, continuous fetal heart rate monitoring during the procedure, intubation in the 2nd and 3rd trimester, and short-acting anaesthesia (thiopentone or propofol). The 2nd trimester is the lowest-risk window. Capacity to consent is assessed and documented; involuntary ECT is reserved for absent capacity under the relevant Mental Health Act framework. Course is typically 6-12 treatments delivered 2-3 times per week.
