Over the past 3 days he has developed fever, generalised rigidity, fluctuating consciousness, and autonomic instability. He has had no recent change in medication and no other psychotropic exposure.

On examination he is drowsy with lead-pipe rigidity in all four limbs. He is diaphoretic and his skin feels clammy. His Glasgow Coma Scale fluctuates between 12 and 14. He has been incontinent of urine. He is on no medications other than haloperidol. The intensive care registrar has been called and the bed manager is finding a bed.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 132/min, BP 180/110 mmHg, RR 28/min, SpO2 96% room air, temperature 39.8 °C
data_table.Examination: Drowsy GCS 12-14; lead-pipe rigidity all limbs; diaphoretic; urinary incontinence; pupils equal and reactive
data_table.Investigations: CK 4500 U/L (40-200); WCC 16 x10^9/L (4-11); K 3.6 mmol/L (3.5-5.0); creatinine 142 micromol/L (45-90); ABG metabolic acidosis pH 7.28

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate immediate management bundle?

options.text: Continue haloperidol; active cooling with paracetamol 1 g rectally only
options.rationale: Continuing the precipitating antipsychotic in NMS perpetuates the syndrome and risks fatal hyperthermia, rhabdomyolysis, and arrhythmia; cessation is the foundational step. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Intravenous diazepam 5 mg as first-line therapy plus paracetamol for fever
options.rationale: Benzodiazepines are an adjunct but not a definitive treatment for NMS; the priority is to cease the antipsychotic, cool, hydrate, and add specific therapy (dantrolene or bromocriptine) for severe cases. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Cease haloperidol, commence IV fluids and cooling, give IV dantrolene 1 mg/kg
options.rationale: Severe NMS with rigidity, hyperthermia above 38.5 °C, and rhabdomyolysis is managed by ceasing the antipsychotic, aggressive cooling, IV fluids, dantrolene for muscle rigidity, and ICU admission; bromocriptine is an alternative dopaminergic agent. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Switch to clozapine immediately and continue current psychiatric care plan
options.rationale: Switching antipsychotic during active NMS is contraindicated; reintroduction of any antipsychotic is delayed until full resolution and is specialist-led. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Intravenous cyproheptadine 12 mg empirically for presumed serotonin syndrome
options.rationale: Cyproheptadine is a serotonin antagonist for serotonin syndrome and has no role in NMS; the picture of haloperidol exposure and lead-pipe rigidity points to NMS, not serotonin syndrome. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

explanation.summary: Neuroleptic malignant syndrome is managed by ceasing the offending antipsychotic, aggressive supportive care (IV fluids, cooling), and specific pharmacotherapy with dantrolene for muscle rigidity or bromocriptine as a dopaminergic agent. Severity is graded by temperature, CK, and autonomic instability. ICU admission is appropriate for severe presentations.
key_points: NMS specific agents: dantrolene 1-2.5 mg/kg IV (rigidity) or bromocriptine 2.5 mg orally TDS (dopamine agonist).
Cyproheptadine is for serotonin syndrome, not NMS; the two differ in muscle tone, reflexes, and trigger drug.
Aggressive cooling and IV fluids to limit rhabdomyolysis and renal failure.
Reintroduction of any antipsychotic is delayed at least 2 weeks after resolution and specialist-led.
explanation.pearls: Lead-pipe rigidity with haloperidol exposure is NMS (dantrolene), not serotonin syndrome (cyproheptadine); reflexes are reduced or absent in NMS but brisk in serotonin syndrome.

stem:
You are the consultation psychiatry registrar seeing a 28-year-old woman with bipolar I disorder. She has been stable for 2 years on sodium valproate 1000 mg daily, with no relapse since starting the medication after one severe manic episode requiring inpatient admission. She and her partner attend together to discuss pregnancy planning. She is on the combined oral contraceptive pill currently, with regular cycles when not on the pill.

Her past history includes one episode of mania requiring inpatient admission 4 years ago and one episode of severe postnatal depression after a previous pregnancy with another partner. She is not currently depressed. She has no other medical issues and is otherwise well. Her GP has provided pre-pregnancy folate counselling.

data_table.Vital signs: Within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Euthymic; cognition intact; insight preserved; no current psychotic features
data_table.Investigations: Last valproate level therapeutic; FBC, LFT, UEC within normal limits; pregnancy test negative

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate management plan?

options.text: Continue valproate at current dose with high-dose folate 5 mg daily peri-conceptually
options.rationale: Folate does not abolish the dose-dependent neurodevelopmental and neural tube defect risk of valproate; valproate carries the highest teratogenic burden of mood stabilisers and AU practice avoids it in women planning pregnancy. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic, perinatal section)

options.text: Switch valproate to carbamazepine at therapeutic dose before conception
options.rationale: Carbamazepine is also teratogenic (neural tube defects, cardiac, urinary) and not preferred over lamotrigine or lithium in bipolar pregnancy planning. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Switch to lithium 600 mg daily before conception, accepting Ebstein anomaly risk
options.rationale: Lithium is a reasonable option in pregnancy for bipolar I prophylaxis (especially if previously responsive) but lamotrigine has a more favourable teratogenic profile; lithium is not the universally preferred next agent. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Cross-titrate to lamotrigine and cease valproate before conception
options.rationale: Lamotrigine has the most favourable perinatal safety profile among mood stabilisers and is preferred for cross-titration before conception in stable bipolar disorder; valproate is avoided in women of reproductive age due to teratogenicity and neurodevelopmental impact. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Cease all mood stabilisers and monitor monthly with mental state examination only
options.rationale: Ceasing prophylaxis in bipolar I with previous severe mania and postnatal depression carries an unacceptably high relapse risk; a safer pregnancy-compatible agent should be substituted. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

explanation.summary: Valproate is the most teratogenic mood stabiliser and is contraindicated in women planning pregnancy or of reproductive potential unless other options are ineffective. Lamotrigine has the most favourable perinatal profile and is the preferred alternative for a stable patient with bipolar I disorder. Lithium remains an option in selected cases but carries the small risk of Ebstein anomaly and requires close level monitoring across pregnancy.
key_points: Valproate teratogenicity is dose-dependent and not abolished by folate.
Lamotrigine is preferred for cross-titration before conception when patient is stable.
Lithium remains an option if lamotrigine inadequate; level monitoring intensifies in pregnancy.
Pre-conception planning includes contraception continuation until cross-titration complete.
explanation.pearls: Stable bipolar I on valproate planning pregnancy: cross-titrate to lamotrigine before stopping contraception, not after conception.

stem:
You are the ED registrar reviewing a 24-year-old woman who has presented 2 hours after taking 30 tablets of amitriptyline 25 mg (estimated 750 mg) in an impulsive act after an argument. She was found by her flatmate and brought straight in by ambulance. She is normally on no medications and has no medical comorbidities. There is no other substance involved on history.

On arrival she is drowsy with a Glasgow Coma Scale of 11. Her airway is patent. She has had no seizures. The toxicology consultant has been contacted and you have access to a HDU bed if needed. The ECG strip is showing a widened QRS complex and a prominent terminal R wave in lead aVR. Her potassium is on the low side of normal.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 122/min, BP 92/58 mmHg, RR 18/min, SpO2 96% room air, temperature 36.8 °C
data_table.Examination: Drowsy GCS 11 (E2 V4 M5); airway patent; pupils dilated 6 mm sluggish to light; bowel sounds reduced
data_table.Investigations: ECG QRS 140 ms (under 120 normal), terminal R wave aVR 4 mm; K 3.4 mmol/L (3.5-5.0); Na 138 mmol/L; venous gas pH 7.32, lactate 2.6 mmol/L

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate immediate intervention?

options.text: Intravenous midazolam 2 mg as sole therapy for sedation while observing
options.rationale: Sedation does not reverse TCA cardiotoxicity; the priority is sodium bicarbonate for QRS prolongation and seizure prophylaxis. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology)

options.text: IV flumazenil 0.2 mg to reverse drowsiness while observing for seizure
options.rationale: Flumazenil is contraindicated in mixed overdose or unknown overdose due to seizure risk, and does not reverse TCA toxicity. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology)

options.text: Activated charcoal 50 g via nasogastric tube only after airway protection
options.rationale: Charcoal is of limited value beyond 1 hour post-ingestion and does not reverse established cardiotoxicity; sodium bicarbonate addresses the immediate life-threatening QRS prolongation. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology)

options.text: Whole bowel irrigation with polyethylene glycol via nasogastric tube
options.rationale: Whole bowel irrigation has no role in TCA overdose; sodium bicarbonate is the cardiotoxicity-specific intervention. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology)

options.text: IV sodium bicarbonate 1-2 mmol/kg bolus, target QRS <120 ms and pH 7.5
options.rationale: TCA cardiotoxicity (QRS above 100 ms, terminal R in aVR above 3 mm, hypotension) is treated with IV sodium bicarbonate 1-2 mmol/kg bolus, titrated to QRS narrowing and pH 7.45 to 7.55; the alkalinisation increases protein binding and the sodium load overcomes the sodium channel block. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology)

explanation.summary: TCA cardiotoxicity is identified by QRS prolongation above 100 ms, terminal R wave in aVR above 3 mm, and hypotension. The specific intervention is intravenous sodium bicarbonate boluses to alkalinise and overcome sodium channel block. Seizures, hypotension, and ventricular arrhythmias are the principal causes of death.
key_points: Sodium bicarbonate dose: 1-2 mmol/kg boluses, repeat to QRS under 120 ms and arterial pH 7.45-7.55.
ECG markers of toxicity: QRS above 100 ms, R wave aVR above 3 mm, R:S ratio aVR above 0.7.
Hypokalaemia worsens arrhythmia risk; correct to normal but expect intracellular shifts with bicarbonate.
Lipid emulsion considered in refractory cardiotoxicity after toxicology advice.
explanation.pearls: QRS above 100 ms with a terminal R wave in aVR after TCA overdose is the cue for sodium bicarbonate, not benzodiazepines.

subtopic_detail: ECT for refusing involuntary patient with capacity
stem:
You are the psychiatry registrar reviewing a 67-year-old woman currently admitted involuntarily under the Victorian Mental Health and Wellbeing Act 2022 with severe major depression with psychotic features. Over the past 3 weeks she has refused all oral medications, lost 8 kg, become bed-bound, and is now requiring nasogastric feeding for nutritional support. She voices the wish to die imminently and refuses fluids when not on the NG.

Your consultant psychiatrist has assessed her as competent to make decisions about her treatment but as having severe melancholic depression life-threatening in its trajectory. The family supports treatment with electroconvulsive therapy. She refuses ECT when offered, stating that she does not deserve to be treated. The treating team agrees ECT is life-saving and the only realistic short-term option for response.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 58/min, BP 102/64 mmHg, RR 14/min, SpO2 98% room air, temperature 36.5 °C
data_table.Examination: Melancholic appearance; psychomotor retardation; nihilistic delusion of decay; reduced reactivity to environment
data_table.Investigations: Albumin 28 g/L (35-50); K 3.4 mmol/L (3.5-5.0); ECG normal sinus; ferritin 18 micrograms/L (30-300)

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate next step to enable treatment?

options.text: Apply to the Mental Health Tribunal for an order authorising ECT under the Act
options.rationale: Under Australian state mental health legislation (including Victorian MHWA 2022 and NSW MHA 2007), ECT for an involuntary patient who refuses requires authorisation by the Mental Health Tribunal regardless of the patient's capacity status; emergency provisions exist for life-threatening situations but the Tribunal pathway is the primary route. (Source: Mental Health and Wellbeing Act 2022 Victoria; RANZCP Position Statement on ECT)
source_refs: Mental Health and Wellbeing Act 2022 Victoria

options.text: Two senior doctors co-sign emergency ECT consent without further authorisation
options.rationale: Two-doctor authorisation alone is not the standard pathway for non-emergent ECT for a refusing involuntary patient; tribunal authorisation is required for planned ECT in this group. (Source: Mental Health and Wellbeing Act 2022 Victoria)
source_refs: Mental Health and Wellbeing Act 2022 Victoria

options.text: Treat under common-law necessity without further legal authorisation
options.rationale: Common-law necessity is not the proper route when the Mental Health Act provides a defined statutory pathway for ECT in involuntary patients. (Source: Mental Health and Wellbeing Act 2022 Victoria)
source_refs: Mental Health and Wellbeing Act 2022 Victoria

options.text: Obtain consent from the substitute decision-maker (next-of-kin) and proceed
options.rationale: Substitute consent does not override the statutory consent requirements for ECT under state Mental Health Acts when the patient is involuntary and refusing; tribunal authorisation is required. (Source: Mental Health and Wellbeing Act 2022 Victoria)
source_refs: Mental Health and Wellbeing Act 2022 Victoria

options.text: Discharge after capacity assessment given she retains decisional capacity
options.rationale: She is involuntary, severely depressed, refusing fluids, and at acute risk of death; discharge in this setting breaches duty of care and the criteria for involuntary treatment remain met. (Source: Mental Health and Wellbeing Act 2022 Victoria)
source_refs: Mental Health and Wellbeing Act 2022 Victoria

explanation.summary: ECT for a refusing involuntary patient under Australian state Mental Health legislation requires authorisation by the relevant Mental Health Tribunal, not just senior doctor sign-off, substitute consent, or common-law necessity. Capacity does not bypass this process when the patient is detained as an involuntary patient. Emergency provisions exist for true life-threatening urgency but the standard pathway is the Tribunal.
key_points: Mental Health Tribunal authorisation is required for ECT in refusing involuntary patients across Australian jurisdictions.
Substitute decision-maker consent does not override the Mental Health Act ECT process.
Emergency ECT provisions exist (varying by state) but require strict criteria.
Capacity assessment is documented but does not change the statutory ECT pathway for involuntary patients.
explanation.pearls: An involuntary patient refusing ECT goes to the Mental Health Tribunal, not to two doctors with a consent form; states differ but the principle is uniform.

sources.label: Mental Health and Wellbeing Act 2022 Victoria

stem:
You are the psychiatry registrar reviewing a 23-year-old woman in the medical ward after a new-onset psychiatric presentation 5 days ago. She is mute, immobile, and has been observed maintaining unusual limb postures for over an hour. Examination reveals waxy flexibility and intermittent grimacing. She has not eaten or drunk in 48 hours and has had no exposure to antipsychotic medication. She presented initially with disorganised speech and anxiety which then progressed to her current state.

This morning her temperature has risen to 38.4 °C and her creatine kinase is elevated. Neurology and infectious diseases have been consulted. Brain MRI yesterday was unremarkable. CSF cell count, glucose, and protein were normal but anti-NMDA receptor antibodies have been sent and are pending. The team is asking what to do next while waiting for those results.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 116/min, BP 138/86 mmHg, RR 18/min, SpO2 98% room air, temperature 38.4 °C
data_table.Examination: Mute, immobile; waxy flexibility; sustained limb posturing; intermittent grimacing; reduced oral intake 48 hours
data_table.Investigations: CK 1800 U/L (40-200); FBC and electrolytes within normal limits; brain MRI unremarkable; CSF cell count normal; anti-NMDA receptor antibody result pending

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate immediate diagnostic and therapeutic step?

options.text: Intravenous haloperidol 5 mg as antipsychotic challenge to test for psychosis
options.rationale: Antipsychotics can worsen catatonia and precipitate neuroleptic malignant syndrome; they are not the diagnostic or therapeutic tool of choice for suspected catatonia. (Source: RANZCP Practice Resources: Catatonia)

options.text: IV lorazepam 2 mg as diagnostic and therapeutic challenge, parallel ECT planning
options.rationale: Lorazepam challenge (1-2 mg IV) is both diagnostic (rapid partial response within minutes to hours) and therapeutic for catatonia, regardless of underlying cause; parallel ECT planning is appropriate as ECT is the definitive treatment for refractory catatonia. (Source: RANZCP Practice Resources: Catatonia)

options.text: Intravenous propofol 1 mg/kg for sedation and disimpaction of posturing
options.rationale: Propofol is not used for catatonia treatment; lorazepam challenge is the AU recommended first-line diagnostic-therapeutic approach. (Source: RANZCP Practice Resources: Catatonia)

options.text: Oral bromocriptine 7.5 mg twice daily for presumed neuroleptic malignant syndrome
options.rationale: There is no neuroleptic exposure, so NMS is unlikely; bromocriptine is for NMS-specific management and is not first-line for catatonia of any cause. (Source: RANZCP Practice Resources: Catatonia)

options.text: Intravenous ceftriaxone 2 g empirically while awaiting anti-NMDA receptor antibody
options.rationale: CSF is bland and there is no meningoencephalitis evidence; empirical antibacterial cover is not justified and does not address the catatonia itself. (Source: RANZCP Practice Resources: Catatonia)

explanation.summary: Catatonia is treated with a lorazepam challenge as both diagnostic and therapeutic step, regardless of the underlying cause (psychiatric, medical, or autoimmune). A partial response within minutes to hours confirms the diagnosis; ongoing benzodiazepine and parallel ECT planning are appropriate as ECT is the definitive treatment for refractory or malignant catatonia. Antipsychotics can precipitate NMS and must be avoided.
key_points: Lorazepam 1-2 mg IV is the AU first-line challenge for catatonia.
Avoid antipsychotics during active catatonia (NMS risk).
ECT is the definitive treatment if lorazepam fails or in malignant catatonia.
Investigate underlying cause in parallel (anti-NMDA, medical, structural).
explanation.pearls: Posturing plus waxy flexibility plus fever and elevated CK without neuroleptic exposure is malignant catatonia; the answer is lorazepam now and ECT next, not haloperidol.

subtopic_detail: Serotonin syndrome after MAOI plus tramadol
stem:
You are the ED registrar called to assess a 38-year-old woman with a 4 year history of refractory depression on phenelzine 60 mg daily who has just been brought in. Her GP prescribed tramadol 100 mg for a severe migraine 4 hours ago, unaware of the MAOI. She took 1 tablet and has rapidly developed agitation, sweating, and shivering. Her husband reports she has been increasingly hot and jittery and she has been vomiting twice.

On examination she is restless and confused with marked diaphoresis. She has rhythmic horizontal eye movements (ocular clonus), hyperreflexia particularly in the lower limbs with sustained ankle clonus, and increased lower limb tone. Pupils are dilated. She is on no other psychotropics and has no infective contacts. She has had no antipsychotic exposure. Phenelzine has been ceased today.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 122/min, BP 162/98 mmHg, RR 24/min, SpO2 97% room air, temperature 39.1 °C
data_table.Examination: Restless, confused; ocular clonus; lower limb hyperreflexia with sustained ankle clonus; pupils dilated; bowel sounds increased; lower limb hypertonia greater than upper limb
data_table.Investigations: CK 1200 U/L (40-200); K 3.4 mmol/L (3.5-5.0); creatinine 96 micromol/L (45-90); venous gas pH 7.36, lactate 2.8 mmol/L; FBC and coags pending

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Intravenous haloperidol 5 mg plus surface cooling with cold packs only
options.rationale: Haloperidol increases the risk of NMS and worsens hyperthermia in serotonin syndrome; antipsychotics should be avoided in the acute setting. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology)

options.text: Intravenous dantrolene 1 mg/kg as first-line agent for hyperthermia
options.rationale: Dantrolene is used in NMS or malignant hyperthermia, not as first-line in serotonin syndrome; benzodiazepines and supportive care are the AU first-line. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology)

options.text: Cease both agents, give IV benzodiazepines plus cooling plus IV fluids
options.rationale: AU management of serotonin syndrome is cessation of the offending agents, IV benzodiazepines as first-line for agitation and hyperthermia, aggressive cooling and IV fluids; cyproheptadine (PO only, no IV preparation in Australia) is reserved as adjunct in moderate-severe non-responders. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology)

options.text: Intravenous cyproheptadine 32 mg loading dose immediately as primary therapy
options.rationale: There is no parenteral cyproheptadine available in Australia; oral or NG cyproheptadine is the only route, and benzodiazepines come first. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology)

options.text: Intravenous sodium bicarbonate 1 mmol/kg for presumed TCA-like cardiotoxicity
options.rationale: Tramadol and phenelzine together cause serotonin syndrome, not sodium channel block; sodium bicarbonate has no role here. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology)

explanation.summary: Serotonin syndrome from a MAOI plus tramadol is managed by ceasing offending agents, supportive care with IV benzodiazepines, aggressive cooling and IV fluids, with cyproheptadine reserved as an oral adjunct in moderate to severe non-responders. Antipsychotics are avoided as they may worsen hyperthermia and confuse the clinical picture with NMS. The discriminator from NMS is hyperreflexia (especially lower limbs) and clonus, versus rigidity and reduced reflexes in NMS.
key_points: Distinguishing features: serotonin syndrome causes hyperreflexia and clonus (lower limb predominant); NMS causes lead-pipe rigidity and reduced reflexes.
Cyproheptadine is oral only in Australia; no IV preparation.
Antipsychotics worsen serotonin syndrome and risk diagnostic confusion with NMS.
MAOIs plus serotonergic agents (SSRI, SNRI, tramadol, pethidine, linezolid) are the highest-risk combinations.
explanation.pearls: Lower limb clonus with diaphoresis after a MAOI plus tramadol is serotonin syndrome; the answer is benzodiazepines and cooling, with oral cyproheptadine as a backup.

subtopic_detail: Valproate in women of childbearing potential - switch planning
stem:
A 22-year-old woman with bipolar I disorder is reviewed in the psychiatry outpatient clinic. She has been stable on sodium valproate 1000 mg daily for the past 3 years with full remission. Her past episodes were all manic with psychotic features, with no significant depressive episodes recorded. She has recently become engaged and discloses that she would like to conceive within the next 1-2 years.

She has read about valproate-associated congenital malformations and neurodevelopmental effects and asks how to plan ahead safely. She has never had a trial of lithium or atypical antipsychotic monotherapy. She drinks no alcohol, does not smoke, and her thyroid function and renal function are within normal limits. There is no family history of bipolar disorder treatment failure.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 72/min, BP 122/78 mmHg, RR 14/min, SpO2 99% room air, temperature 36.7 °C
data_table.Examination: Euthymic; well groomed; no psychomotor disturbance; insight intact; future-oriented goals appropriate to current life stage
data_table.Investigations: Valproate level 410 micromol/L (350-700); TSH 1.6 mIU/L (0.4-4.0); creatinine 65 micromol/L (45-90), eGFR >90 mL/min/1.73 m²; BHCG negative this morning at clinic

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in medication planning?

options.text: Continue current dose of valproate with high dose folate 5 mg daily, detailed pre-conception counselling about teratogenic and neurodevelopmental risks, and proceed to conception when ready
options.rationale: Valproate has the highest teratogenic risk (10% major malformation, 30-40% neurodevelopmental impact); folate does not abolish that risk and continuation in WOCBP is contraindicated where alternatives exist. (Source: RANZCP Bipolar Disorder Clinical Practice Guideline)
source_refs: RANZCP Bipolar Disorder Clinical Practice Guideline

options.text: Cease valproate abruptly now and observe medication free for the next 6 months to confirm stability before any other agent is introduced or pregnancy is planned by the patient
options.rationale: Abrupt cessation of valproate in bipolar I with manic-psychotic episodes carries high relapse risk; switch under cover to an alternative agent before stopping, do not leave untreated. (Source: RANZCP Bipolar Disorder Clinical Practice Guideline)
source_refs: RANZCP Bipolar Disorder Clinical Practice Guideline

options.text: Switch directly to carbamazepine 200 mg twice daily as the primary alternative mood stabiliser with the same efficacy profile and a more favourable pregnancy safety profile than valproate
options.rationale: Carbamazepine is also a category D teratogen (neural tube defects, craniofacial defects) and is no safer than valproate in pregnancy; not appropriate first choice. (Source: RANZCP Bipolar Disorder Clinical Practice Guideline)
source_refs: RANZCP Bipolar Disorder Clinical Practice Guideline

options.text: Switch to olanzapine 10 mg orally nocte as the maintenance agent for mania-predominant bipolar I with planned pregnancy in the next 2 years, with monthly mental state and metabolic monitoring
options.rationale: Olanzapine is acceptable in pregnancy but lithium is the AU first-line for mania-predominant bipolar with planned pregnancy due to superior anti-manic prophylaxis and well characterised pregnancy data. (Source: RANZCP Bipolar Disorder Clinical Practice Guideline)
source_refs: RANZCP Bipolar Disorder Clinical Practice Guideline

options.text: Switch under specialist supervision to lithium with serum level and mood monitoring, confirm stability for at least 6 months on the new agent before conception, and arrange fetal echocardiography in pregnancy
options.rationale: Lithium is RANZCP first-line for mania-predominant bipolar in WOCBP planning pregnancy; absolute Ebstein anomaly risk is approximately 1 in 1000; switch under cover, confirm stability 6 months before conception, and arrange fetal echocardiography at 18-20 weeks. (Source: RANZCP Bipolar Disorder Clinical Practice Guideline)
source_refs: RANZCP Bipolar Disorder Clinical Practice Guideline

explanation.summary: Sodium valproate has the worst teratogenic and neurodevelopmental profile of all antiepileptics and mood stabilisers (major malformation rate 10%; 30-40% neurodevelopmental impact). The TGA has issued a black-box restriction on valproate in women of childbearing potential without a Pregnancy Prevention Programme. For bipolar with predominantly manic episodes, lithium is the AU first-line alternative for women planning pregnancy because of superior anti-manic prophylaxis; the absolute Ebstein anomaly risk is around 1 in 1000 (recent data revise the originally cited 1 in 100). Switch is performed under specialist supervision with at least 6 months of stability on lithium before conception, fetal echocardiography at 18-20 weeks, third-trimester lithium dose review, and discussion of breastfeeding (lithium is relatively contraindicated). Lamotrigine is preferred for depression-predominant bipolar.
key_points: Valproate is contraindicated in WOCBP without a Pregnancy Prevention Programme (TGA).
Lithium first-line for mania-predominant bipolar planning pregnancy.
Absolute Ebstein anomaly risk on lithium ~1 in 1000.
Confirm 6 months of stability before conception attempts.
Lamotrigine first-line if depression-predominant bipolar.
explanation.pearls: Ebstein anomaly absolute risk on lithium is about 1 in 1000 - the historical 1 in 100 figure overstated risk and modern RANZCP guidance favours lithium over valproate for mania-predominant bipolar in WOCBP.

sources.label: RANZCP Bipolar Disorder Clinical Practice Guideline
Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic - Bipolar in pregnancy

stem:
A 28-year-old male software developer is reviewed in the general adult psychiatry outpatient clinic with 6 months of persistent inattention, distractibility, restlessness and difficulty completing tasks at work. School reports document similar features from age 7. ASRS-v1.1 screener is 6 of 6 positive. He requests stimulant treatment after researching options online.

His mother had a myocardial infarction at age 55. His father has hypertension on amlodipine. He has no personal history of cardiac symptoms, syncope, palpitations or exercise intolerance. He drinks 4 standard drinks per week and uses no illicit drugs. His weight is 75 kg and BMI 24. There are no features of psychosis or current mood disorder. He has not previously trialled stimulants or atomoxetine.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 72/min, BP 120/78 mmHg, RR 14/min, SpO2 99% room air, temperature 36.7 °C
data_table.Examination: Mental state appropriate to interview; affect reactive; no psychomotor disturbance; cardiac auscultation dual heart sounds no murmurs; no signs of anxiety disorder beyond ADHD-attributable restlessness
data_table.Investigations: FBC, electrolytes, thyroid function, liver function within normal limits; urine drug screen negative; no ECG or cardiac investigations performed to date

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step before initiating treatment?

options.text: Perform 12-lead ECG and obtain a focused personal and family cardiovascular history with examination before commencing stimulant therapy and arrange a 3 month BP and HR review on treatment
options.rationale: RACGP, AADPA and RANZCP recommend baseline 12-lead ECG plus focused CV history and exam (palpitations, syncope, exercise intolerance, family history of sudden death <40 years) before initiating stimulants; routine cardiology referral is not required without abnormal findings. (Source: AADPA Adult ADHD Clinical Practice Guideline)
source_refs: AADPA Adult ADHD Clinical Practice Guideline

options.text: Commence methylphenidate immediate release 10 mg orally twice daily immediately and arrange a follow up review in 4 weeks to assess clinical response and tolerability to the stimulant therapy
options.rationale: Skipping baseline ECG and CV history is below AU standard for stimulant initiation; baseline ECG is recommended in adults before starting any stimulant. (Source: AADPA Adult ADHD Clinical Practice Guideline)
source_refs: AADPA Adult ADHD Clinical Practice Guideline

options.text: Refer to cardiology for a stress echocardiogram and 24 hour Holter monitor before any consideration of starting a stimulant medication, due to family history of myocardial infarction in mother at 55
options.rationale: Late-onset MI in a parent (mother >50) does not mandate cardiology workup beyond baseline ECG; this is over-investigation that delays treatment without evidence base. (Source: AADPA Adult ADHD Clinical Practice Guideline)
source_refs: AADPA Adult ADHD Clinical Practice Guideline

options.text: Recommend cognitive behavioural therapy alone without medication for the next 6 months given the family history of cardiovascular disease, then reassess for pharmacotherapy after the behavioural trial
options.rationale: Stimulants are first-line pharmacotherapy in adult ADHD with strong evidence; CBT is adjunctive. Family CV history alone does not contraindicate stimulants - baseline screen is enough. (Source: AADPA Adult ADHD Clinical Practice Guideline)
source_refs: AADPA Adult ADHD Clinical Practice Guideline

options.text: Trial of atomoxetine 40 mg orally daily without further investigation as a non-stimulant first-line agent that avoids any cardiovascular concerns associated with stimulant medications for adult ADHD
options.rationale: Atomoxetine also requires baseline BP and HR (and has its own CV considerations); the appropriate first step is baseline ECG plus screening, not bypassing stimulants. (Source: AADPA Adult ADHD Clinical Practice Guideline)
source_refs: AADPA Adult ADHD Clinical Practice Guideline

explanation.summary: The Australian Evidence-Based Clinical Practice Guideline for ADHD (AADPA, 2022) recommends, before initiating any stimulant or non-stimulant pharmacotherapy in adults: (1) baseline 12-lead ECG, (2) baseline blood pressure and heart rate, (3) focused personal and family cardiovascular history (syncope, palpitations, exercise intolerance, sudden death <40 years, congenital heart disease, hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, long QT), and (4) cardiac examination. Routine cardiology referral is NOT required unless abnormalities are identified. Stimulants are first-line; methylphenidate and dexamfetamine/lisdexamfetamine are accessed via psychiatrist or appropriately authorised paediatrician/GP under state regulations.
key_points: Baseline 12-lead ECG, BP, HR, focused CV history before stimulant.
Routine cardiology referral NOT required without abnormal findings.
Sudden cardiac death family history <40 years is the relevant family screening question.
Monitor BP and HR at 1 month, then 3 monthly on stimulants.
Stimulants are first-line; atomoxetine and guanfacine are second-line.
explanation.pearls: Family history of late MI (parent over 50) does not require cardiology referral before stimulants - the screening question is sudden cardiac death under 40, hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, or long QT syndrome.

sources.label: AADPA Adult ADHD Clinical Practice Guideline

subtopic_detail: Borderline PD recurrent self-harm community management
stem:
A 24-year-old woman with a 3-year diagnosis of borderline personality disorder presents to the emergency department for the fourth time this month following superficial cutting of her left forearm. She denies any current suicidal intent. She lives alone in stable accommodation and is engaged with a community case manager and a weekly dialectical behaviour therapy group. Her last admission to hospital was 8 months ago.

On examination she is calm but distressed, asking to be admitted overnight because she does not feel safe at home tonight. The wounds are superficial and have been cleaned and steri-stripped. She has no acute mood or psychotic symptoms. Her case manager is contactable and there is a written safety plan from her DBT therapist in her file. She has no substance intoxication.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 84/min, BP 118/76 mmHg, RR 16/min, SpO2 99% room air, temperature 36.7 °C
data_table.Examination: Calm but distressed; no psychomotor agitation; no thought disorder; denies current suicidal intent or plan; superficial cuts cleaned and dressed; no active substance intoxication
data_table.Investigations: Routine bloods unremarkable; urine drug screen negative; ECG sinus rhythm rate 84; written safety plan from DBT therapist available in file

lead_in: What is the most appropriate disposition for this patient?

options.text: Voluntary inpatient admission to the acute psychiatric ward for at least 72 hours of observation, milieu support, daily medical review and intensive behavioural and pharmacological intervention monitoring
options.rationale: Repeated brief admissions in BPD without active suicidality, psychosis or severe self-injury are iatrogenic (reinforce help-seeking via crisis, foster dependency); community supports with safety plan review are first-line. (Source: NHMRC Clinical Practice Guideline for Borderline Personality Disorder)
source_refs: NHMRC Clinical Practice Guideline for Borderline Personality Disorder

options.text: Discharge home with same-day contact to community case manager, safety plan review, DBT crisis skills coaching call within 24 hours, and a planned follow-up DBT group within 72 hours by current therapy provider
options.rationale: NHMRC BPD guideline emphasises community-based crisis support, safety plan review, and DBT skills application rather than admission; ED discharge with rapid community follow-up is the AU evidence-based standard. (Source: NHMRC Clinical Practice Guideline for Borderline Personality Disorder)
source_refs: NHMRC Clinical Practice Guideline for Borderline Personality Disorder

options.text: Compulsory admission under the Mental Health Act to a closed ward for 7 days observation given the frequency of recurrent ED presentations with deliberate self-harm despite community supports being in place
options.rationale: Compulsory admission requires risk of serious harm AND mental illness amenable to treatment; superficial self-harm in BPD with no current suicidal intent or psychosis does not meet AU Mental Health Act criteria. (Source: NHMRC Clinical Practice Guideline for Borderline Personality Disorder)
source_refs: NHMRC Clinical Practice Guideline for Borderline Personality Disorder

options.text: Referral to community addictions service for substance use assessment and treatment as the primary intervention rather than ongoing mental health and dialectical behaviour therapy follow up arrangements
options.rationale: There is no evidence of substance use disorder (urine screen negative, no history); inappropriate referral diverts from evidence-based BPD care. (Source: NHMRC Clinical Practice Guideline for Borderline Personality Disorder)
source_refs: NHMRC Clinical Practice Guideline for Borderline Personality Disorder

options.text: Increase quetiapine to 200 mg orally at night as a sleep and behavioural stabilising medication to reduce her impulsivity, with weekly mental health team review of mood and self-harm behaviour
options.rationale: Pharmacotherapy in BPD is symptomatic only and adjunct to psychological treatment; escalating sedative antipsychotic in ED without specialist input is below standard. (Source: NHMRC Clinical Practice Guideline for Borderline Personality Disorder)
source_refs: NHMRC Clinical Practice Guideline for Borderline Personality Disorder

explanation.summary: The NHMRC Clinical Practice Guideline for Borderline Personality Disorder (Project Air) emphasises that admission for self-harm in BPD without active suicidal intent, psychosis, or severe medical injury is iatrogenic and tends to reinforce maladaptive coping. Community-based crisis management with rapid follow-up by the existing care team (case manager, DBT therapist) is the evidence-based AU standard. Brief admissions (24-72 hours) may be considered for safety stabilisation in carefully selected cases but should not be the default. Pharmacotherapy is symptomatic and adjunct to psychological therapy (DBT, MBT, schema therapy, transference-focused psychotherapy). Compulsory admission is reserved for active suicidality with intent and plan plus inability to engage with safety planning.
key_points: Routine admission for BPD self-harm without active suicidality is iatrogenic.
Community-based crisis support with safety plan review is first-line.
DBT is the primary evidence-based psychotherapy.
Pharmacotherapy is symptomatic only; no specific licensed agent.
Compulsory admission requires active suicidality plus inability to safety plan.
explanation.pearls: For BPD self-harm without intent, planned community follow-up within 72 hours and DBT skills coaching outperforms 72-hour observational admissions, which can reinforce help-seeking via crisis.

sources.label: NHMRC Clinical Practice Guideline for Borderline Personality Disorder

subtopic_detail: Alcohol withdrawal in decompensated liver disease - benzodiazepine choice
stem:
A 58-year-old man is admitted to the gastroenterology ward 8 hours ago for management of acute alcohol withdrawal. He drinks approximately 350 g of alcohol per day (35 standard drinks) and has not had a drink for 18 hours. He has known biopsy-proven cirrhosis (Child-Pugh class B) with ascites managed by spironolactone, and is being worked up for liver transplantation.

He is tremulous, diaphoretic, and anxious. He is fully oriented to person, place and time, with no current hallucinations and no seizures. CIWA-Ar score is 22. He has had thiamine 300 mg intravenously already. There is no acute infection. He has not yet had any benzodiazepine. He has had no withdrawal seizures in the past.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 110/min, BP 158/95 mmHg, RR 22/min, SpO2 97% room air, temperature 37.0 °C
data_table.Examination: Tremulous and diaphoretic; oriented to person/place/time; no hallucinations; no asterixis; abdomen distended with mild ascites; no encephalopathy
data_table.Investigations: INR 1.8 (0.9-1.2), albumin 28 g/L (35-50), bilirubin 45 micromol/L (<20), ALT 80 U/L (<40), platelets 90 x10⁹/L (150-400); ammonia 60 micromol/L (<35); ethanol level negative

lead_in: What is the most appropriate benzodiazepine regimen?

options.text: Diazepam 10 mg orally on a symptom triggered regimen every 1 to 2 hours titrated to CIWA-Ar below 8 with target dose ceiling of 80 mg in 24 hours and clinical review thereafter
options.rationale: Diazepam undergoes hepatic oxidation with long-acting active metabolites (desmethyl diazepam); in Child-Pugh B cirrhosis it accumulates causing prolonged sedation and precipitating hepatic encephalopathy. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic - Alcohol withdrawal)

options.text: Lorazepam 1 mg orally on a regular regimen with continuous intravenous midazolam infusion as background sedation to control acute autonomic withdrawal symptoms over the first 24 hours
options.rationale: Midazolam infusion is reserved for refractory delirium tremens requiring ICU; first-line is symptom-triggered oral lorazepam or oxazepam; combining with infusion is over-sedation risk. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic - Alcohol withdrawal)

options.text: Oxazepam 15 to 30 mg orally on a symptom triggered regimen every 1 to 2 hours titrated to CIWA-Ar below 8 with clinical reassessment and downward titration once acute autonomic symptoms settle
options.rationale: Oxazepam undergoes glucuronidation without phase I hepatic oxidation, avoiding accumulation in cirrhosis; symptom-triggered dosing is superior to fixed-schedule in moderate withdrawal. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic - Alcohol withdrawal)

options.text: Chlordiazepoxide 50 mg orally every 6 hours on a fixed schedule for 5 days followed by tapering over the next 3 days regardless of clinical course of withdrawal during the first 48 hours
options.rationale: Chlordiazepoxide is hepatically oxidised and accumulates in cirrhosis (similar to diazepam); fixed schedule over-sedates compared with symptom-triggered approach. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic - Alcohol withdrawal)

options.text: Phenobarbital 30 mg orally three times daily as a primary first line agent and arrange referral to addiction medicine for ongoing outpatient relapse prevention follow up after discharge
options.rationale: Phenobarbital is third-line for benzodiazepine-resistant withdrawal in ICU settings; not first-line in any AU outpatient or general ward setting for alcohol withdrawal. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic - Alcohol withdrawal)

explanation.summary: Benzodiazepine choice in alcohol withdrawal is dictated by hepatic function. In NORMAL hepatic function, diazepam (long-acting, self-tapering) is first-line. In SIGNIFICANT hepatic impairment (cirrhosis, Child-Pugh B or C), oxazepam, lorazepam, or temazepam (the LOT drugs) are preferred because they are glucuronidated (phase II metabolism) without prior oxidation - they do NOT accumulate in liver disease. Symptom-triggered dosing (CIWA-Ar guided) reduces total benzodiazepine use, length of stay, and incidence of complications versus fixed-schedule regimens. Thiamine (high-dose IV) must be given before any glucose load to prevent Wernicke encephalopathy. Phenobarbital and continuous infusion benzodiazepines are reserved for benzodiazepine-resistant delirium tremens in ICU.
key_points: Cirrhosis: use oxazepam, lorazepam, or temazepam (LOT) - glucuronidated.
Normal liver: diazepam first-line (long-acting, self-tapering).
Symptom-triggered (CIWA-Ar) reduces total dose and complications.
Parenteral thiamine before any glucose to prevent Wernicke.
Phenobarbital / midazolam infusion: ICU-level refractory withdrawal.
explanation.pearls: LOT drugs (lorazepam, oxazepam, temazepam) are glucuronidated and do not accumulate in cirrhosis - choose oxazepam in any patient with Child-Pugh B or C to avoid encephalopathy from diazepam metabolites.

sources.label: RACP Australian guidelines for the treatment of alcohol problems

subtopic_detail: Refeeding syndrome detection on day 2 of refeed
stem:
A 17-year-old girl has been admitted to the adolescent medicine ward with severe anorexia nervosa. Her BMI is 13.2 kg/m² with 28% weight loss over the past 6 months. She has been eating minimally for the past 4 months. Initial admission bloods: K 3.0 mmol/L (3.5-5.0), Mg 0.65 mmol/L (0.7-1.0), PO4 0.7 mmol/L (0.8-1.5), albumin 30 g/L (35-50). ECG shows QTc 460 ms. Refeeding was commenced 36 hours ago at 1200 kcal/day with thiamine 300 mg IV and oral multivitamin supplementation.

This morning's repeat bloods (day 2 of refeeding) show: K 2.7, Mg 0.55, PO4 0.4. Calcium 2.20 mmol/L (2.10-2.55) corrected. She is asymptomatic with no peripheral oedema, no Chvostek or Trousseau sign, normal cardiac auscultation, and ambulating well. Vital signs are unchanged from admission.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 56/min, BP 95/60 mmHg, RR 16/min, SpO2 99% room air, temperature 36.2 °C
data_table.Examination: Cachectic; alert, oriented; no peripheral oedema; Chvostek and Trousseau negative; normal cardiac auscultation; weight 36 kg (admission 36 kg)
data_table.Investigations: Day 2 K 2.7 mmol/L (3.5-5.0), Mg 0.55 mmol/L (0.7-1.0), PO4 0.4 mmol/L (0.8-1.5), corrected Ca 2.20 mmol/L (2.10-2.55), albumin 28 g/L (35-50); ECG QTc 470 ms; bedside glucose 4.4 mmol/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate adjustment to her refeeding plan?

options.text: Continue the current 1200 kcal/day caloric target as planned and supplement potassium, phosphate and magnesium orally only, with serial bloods every 24 hours for the next 4 days while on the ward
options.rationale: Continuing same calories with falling electrolytes risks symptomatic refeeding syndrome (cardiac arrhythmia, weakness, encephalopathy); reduction of calories AND IV replacement of phosphate, K and Mg are required. (Source: ANZAED Clinical Practice Guideline: Eating disorders)
source_refs: ANZAED Clinical Practice Guideline: Eating disorders

options.text: Increase caloric intake to 1800 kcal/day to better restore body weight quickly and add a multivitamin tablet daily, with daily bloods monitored on the adolescent medicine ward for the first week
options.rationale: Increasing calories in falling electrolytes accelerates refeeding syndrome; the principle is to slow caloric advancement when biochemistry deteriorates, not accelerate. (Source: ANZAED Clinical Practice Guideline: Eating disorders)
source_refs: ANZAED Clinical Practice Guideline: Eating disorders

options.text: Stop refeeding entirely for the next 48 hours and reassess electrolytes and weight before recommencing nutritional support to allow the metabolic disturbance to fully correct prior to nutrition
options.rationale: Stopping refeeding entirely is not appropriate; the principle is to reduce caloric load, replace electrolytes, and continue nutrition. Stopping in severely malnourished patients carries its own risk of further deterioration. (Source: ANZAED Clinical Practice Guideline: Eating disorders)
source_refs: ANZAED Clinical Practice Guideline: Eating disorders

options.text: Reduce caloric intake to maintenance level, replace phosphate, potassium and magnesium intravenously with thiamine 300 mg IV continued, and monitor electrolytes 6 hourly with continuous cardiac monitoring
options.rationale: Biochemical refeeding syndrome (falling K, Mg, PO4 within 72 hours of feeding start) mandates calorie reduction, IV electrolyte replacement, continued thiamine, and 6-hourly monitoring with cardiac telemetry until biochemistry stabilises. (Source: ANZAED Clinical Practice Guideline: Eating disorders)
source_refs: ANZAED Clinical Practice Guideline: Eating disorders

options.text: Transfer the patient to intensive care now and commence total parenteral nutrition with insulin to manage glucose homeostasis during refeeding and intubate for airway protection given her cachexia
options.rationale: ICU and TPN are not first-line; oral or NG refeeding with monitored electrolyte replacement on the adolescent medicine ward is the AU standard for refeeding syndrome. Intubation is unjustified. (Source: ANZAED Clinical Practice Guideline: Eating disorders)
source_refs: ANZAED Clinical Practice Guideline: Eating disorders

explanation.summary: Refeeding syndrome is a constellation of metabolic disturbances (hypophosphataemia, hypokalaemia, hypomagnesaemia, thiamine deficiency, fluid overload) precipitated by reintroduction of carbohydrate-containing nutrition after prolonged starvation, due to intracellular shifts of phosphate, potassium and magnesium driven by insulin. It occurs within 24-72 hours of refeeding commencement. Detection at the biochemical stage (asymptomatic falling electrolytes) requires slowing of caloric advancement, IV electrolyte replacement, continued high-dose thiamine, and intensive monitoring (6-hourly bloods, continuous ECG). Risk factors: BMI <16, weight loss >15% in 3 months, minimal intake >5 days. Symptomatic refeeding syndrome may cause cardiac arrhythmia, respiratory failure, seizures, rhabdomyolysis, and death.
key_points: Refeeding within 24-72 hours: hypophosphataemia, hypokalaemia, hypomagnesaemia.
Detection at biochemical stage: reduce calories, IV replacement, continue thiamine.
Continuous ECG monitoring while electrolytes deranged.
Thiamine 300 mg IV before any carb load (Wernicke prevention).
Stopping refeeding entirely is also dangerous in severe malnutrition.
explanation.pearls: Biochemical refeeding syndrome (PO4 dropping below 0.5 on day 2-3) is a slow-the-feed signal - reduce kcal to maintenance, replace PO4/K/Mg IV, keep thiamine going, and monitor every 6 hours.

sources.label: ANZAED Clinical Practice Guideline: Eating disorders
RCH CPG: Eating disorders - inpatient management

subtopic_detail: Postpartum psychosis with infant-directed command hallucinations
stem:
A 31-year-old G1P1 woman is brought to the emergency department by her husband on day 6 postpartum because she is making no sense and has not slept for 3 days. She believes the baby is dead inside and that she must send him back. She has had a previous diagnosis of bipolar I disorder with manic-only episodes, well controlled on lithium 750 mg nocte which she ceased 6 months prior to conception under specialist advice.

The baby is currently being cared for by the patient's mother at home and is well. The patient is currently exclusively breastfeeding. On mental state examination she is agitated with disorganised speech, with auditory hallucinations telling her to send the baby back, and persecutory delusions about hospital staff. There are no focal neurological signs and no signs of sepsis.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 105/min, BP 130/82 mmHg, RR 18/min, SpO2 99% room air, temperature 36.8 °C
data_table.Examination: Agitated, disorganised, command auditory hallucinations directed at infant; persecutory delusions; no focal neurology; reflexes symmetric; no neck stiffness; perineum healing well
data_table.Investigations: FBC, electrolytes, calcium, magnesium, glucose, LFTs within normal limits; TSH 1.8 mIU/L (0.4-4.0); urine drug screen negative; B12 and folate within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Olanzapine 10 mg orally now and discharge home with husband supervision, with outpatient psychiatry review within 24 hours and community mental health team contact within the working day
options.rationale: Command hallucinations directed at infant in postpartum psychosis is a psychiatric emergency with high infanticide risk; discharge home with supervision is inadequate. (Source: COPE Mental Health Care in the Perinatal Period)
source_refs: COPE Mental Health Care in the Perinatal Period

options.text: Recommence sertraline 50 mg orally daily as postpartum depression treatment with weekly community mental health team review for ongoing assessment and supportive management in the home environment
options.rationale: This is postpartum psychosis (psychotic features, mood-incongruent delusions, infant-directed harm risk), not postpartum depression; SSRI alone is inadequate and delays antipsychotic treatment. (Source: COPE Mental Health Care in the Perinatal Period)
source_refs: COPE Mental Health Care in the Perinatal Period

options.text: Same-day electroconvulsive therapy in the emergency department with brief consent process before any transfer to inpatient psychiatric care or mother baby unit elsewhere in the regional health network
options.rationale: ECT may have a role in refractory or severe puerperal psychosis but is not the immediate ED first step; admission with antipsychotic and lithium reinstatement first-line, ECT if response inadequate. (Source: COPE Mental Health Care in the Perinatal Period)
source_refs: COPE Mental Health Care in the Perinatal Period

options.text: Compulsory admission to a general medical ward for overnight observation, pending formal psychiatry review in the morning, with husband requested to remain at bedside throughout for safety and support
options.rationale: General medical ward lacks psychiatric monitoring, security, and infant access; admission to psychiatric inpatient unit (ideally Mother-Baby Unit) is the AU standard. (Source: COPE Mental Health Care in the Perinatal Period)
source_refs: COPE Mental Health Care in the Perinatal Period

options.text: Involuntary admission to a Mother-Baby Unit with olanzapine, lithium reintroduction with breastfeeding cessation, and ECT consideration if response is inadequate within 48 to 72 hours of admission
options.rationale: Postpartum psychosis with command hallucinations re infant requires involuntary admission; MBU preserves mother-infant attachment where capacity allows; olanzapine plus lithium reintroduction (lithium contraindicated in breastfeeding so cease) is AU first-line; ECT for inadequate response. (Source: COPE Mental Health Care in the Perinatal Period)
source_refs: COPE Mental Health Care in the Perinatal Period

explanation.summary: Postpartum psychosis (puerperal psychosis) is a rare (1 in 1000 births) but severe psychiatric emergency presenting within 2 weeks of delivery with mood symptoms (most commonly mania, sometimes mixed or depressive), psychotic features, disorganisation and confusion. Women with a history of bipolar I disorder (especially those who discontinue mood stabilisers preconception) are at the highest risk - approximately 1 in 4 will develop puerperal psychosis. Infanticide and suicide risk are high. Management is involuntary admission to a Mother-Baby Unit (or general psychiatric inpatient unit with infant access where MBU unavailable), antipsychotic (olanzapine is well-studied in postpartum), reinstatement of lithium (which is incompatible with breastfeeding, so support cessation), and consideration of ECT for rapid response in severe cases. Long-term plan includes mood stabiliser prophylaxis through any future pregnancies.
key_points: Onset within 2 weeks postpartum; mania most common syndrome.
Bipolar I women off mood stabilisers preconception have ~25% risk.
Involuntary admission to MBU (or adult psych unit) for safety and treatment.
Olanzapine first-line acute; lithium reintroduction once breastfeeding ceased.
ECT considered for severe or refractory presentations within 48-72 hours.
explanation.pearls: Bipolar I women who stop lithium before conception carry a 1 in 4 risk of postpartum psychosis - the priority on representation is MBU admission, antipsychotic, and lithium reintroduction with breastfeeding cessation.

sources.label: COPE Mental Health Care in the Perinatal Period
RANZCP Perinatal Mental Health Position Statement

stem:
A 54-year-old man with a 20-year history of bipolar I disorder is brought to a metropolitan emergency department by his wife. He has been increasingly tremulous and unsteady on his feet over the past 4 days. He vomited twice this morning before presentation. He is normally maintained on lithium carbonate 800 mg nightly, with the last serum lithium level at 0.7 mmol/L two months ago. His wife notes that he began ramipril 5 mg daily 3 weeks ago for newly diagnosed hypertension by his GP.

On examination he is awake but drowsy and has coarse hand tremor and ataxia on standing. He is oriented to person but not place or date. Speech is dysarthric. Deep tendon reflexes are brisk with sustained ankle clonus. The abdomen is soft, mucous membranes dry. His regular lithium dose was taken this morning at home. A bedside ECG shows sinus rhythm with QTc 460 ms; no T wave changes. Vital signs are stable. The toxicology service has been contacted.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 96/min, BP 138/86 mmHg, RR 16/min, SpO2 99% room air, temperature 36.8 °C
data_table.Examination: Drowsy, coarse hand tremor, dysarthria, brisk reflexes with sustained ankle clonus, ataxia on standing; mucous membranes dry; abdomen soft
data_table.Investigations: Serum lithium 2.4 mmol/L (0.4-1.0), sodium 144 mmol/L, potassium 4.0 mmol/L, urea 12.4 mmol/L (2.5-7.5), creatinine 165 micromol/L (baseline 78); TSH within normal limits; bicarbonate 22 mmol/L; ECG sinus rhythm QTc 460 ms

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Hold the next dose of lithium and recheck serum lithium level in 12 hours while continuing oral fluids and rest at home with the wife monitoring symptoms
options.rationale: Outpatient management is unsafe with neurological toxicity, lithium of 2.4 mmol/L, and AKI; severe lithium toxicity requires admission and IV rehydration with consideration of dialysis. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology)

options.text: Stop lithium and ramipril, give intravenous 0.9% saline at 1.5 to 2 times maintenance and refer urgently to nephrology for consideration of haemodialysis
options.rationale: Lithium 2.4 mmol/L with neurological toxicity (drowsiness, ataxia, dysarthria, clonus) and AKI meets EXTRIP criteria for haemodialysis; saline and stopping lithium and the precipitant (ACE inhibitor) are essential immediate steps. (Source: EXTRIP Lithium Workgroup Recommendations; Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology)

options.text: Administer activated charcoal 50 g orally now as a single dose to reduce lithium absorption and to limit further increases in serum lithium concentration
options.rationale: Activated charcoal does NOT bind lithium and has no role in lithium toxicity; whole bowel irrigation has a role in massive ingestion of sustained-release lithium only. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology)

options.text: Administer intravenous sodium bicarbonate 1 mmol/kg now and aim to alkalinise the urine to a pH greater than 7.5 to increase the renal elimination of lithium
options.rationale: Urinary alkalinisation does not enhance lithium elimination; saline rehydration and dialysis are the mainstays. Bicarbonate is used for tricyclic antidepressant and salicylate toxicity. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology)

options.text: Substitute oral lithium with intravenous sodium valproate loading dose 20 mg/kg to maintain mood stabilisation throughout the management of his lithium toxicity
options.rationale: Acute toxicity is a separate problem from maintenance bipolar therapy; switching to valproate during the toxicity admission is not the priority and is decided by psychiatry after recovery. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology)

explanation.summary: Lithium toxicity is graded by neurological features rather than serum level alone because tissue distribution lags serum. Mild toxicity (1.5-2.0 mmol/L) gives tremor and GI symptoms; moderate (2.0-2.5) adds dysarthria, ataxia, clonus, drowsiness; severe (over 2.5 or any level with seizures, coma, severe symptoms) requires dialysis. Precipitants include ACE inhibitors, ARBs, thiazides, NSAIDs, dehydration, and renal impairment. EXTRIP recommends haemodialysis for severe neurological toxicity, level above 4.0 mmol/L (or 2.5 with renal impairment), seizures, or coma. Intermittent haemodialysis is preferred over CRRT for faster lithium removal.
key_points: Tissue lithium lags serum level; neurology guides severity
Precipitants: ACE inhibitors, ARBs, thiazides, NSAIDs, dehydration, AKI
Charcoal does not bind lithium; whole bowel irrigation only for massive SR ingestion
EXTRIP threshold for dialysis: severe neurology, level above 4.0 (or 2.5 with AKI), seizures, coma
Stop lithium, IV saline, stop precipitant, dialysis
explanation.pearls: Lithium level alone does not classify severity; coarse tremor, ataxia, dysarthria, drowsiness, and clonus in a chronic user trigger EXTRIP dialysis criteria even at lower levels because tissue lithium lags serum.

stem:
A 24-year-old man with treatment-resistant schizophrenia has been on clozapine for 18 days, currently titrated to 200 mg nightly. He attends his community mental health clinic for routine review and reports 4 days of intermittent fevers up to 38.4 °C, fatigue, and one episode of palpitations the night before. He denies cough, dysuria, or rash. His neutrophil count remains within range on weekly FBC monitoring.

On examination he appears tired but alert. He has resting tachycardia at 116/min and warm peripheries. Heart sounds are dual, no murmurs are audible. Chest is clear. There is no calf tenderness or rash. The clinic nurse has obtained the standard week-2 clozapine screening bloods earlier today. He is otherwise compliant with his medication and lives with his mother who reports no concerning behaviours. He has had no recent overseas travel.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 116/min, BP 124/74 mmHg, RR 18/min, SpO2 99% room air, temperature 38.2 °C
data_table.Examination: Tachycardic regular rhythm, no murmurs, no pericardial rub, no lower limb oedema; clear chest; no rash; warm peripheries
data_table.Investigations: Neutrophils 3.6 x10^9/L (1.5-7.5); CRP 86 mg/L (<5); troponin I 65 ng/L (<14); ALT within normal limits; bedside ECG sinus tachycardia, no ST changes, no T wave inversion; viral swab not yet sent

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Withhold the next clozapine dose, refer urgently to the emergency department for transthoracic echocardiography and same-day cardiology review including repeat troponin
options.rationale: Onset of fever, tachycardia, and elevated troponin and CRP within 4 weeks of clozapine initiation is the classical clozapine-induced myocarditis triad; the AU clozapine screening protocol mandates urgent ED referral with TTE and cardiology. (Source: RANZCP Position Statement: Clozapine-induced Myocarditis; AMH)

options.text: Continue clozapine at the same dose, start oral paracetamol for the fever and recheck inflammatory markers and troponin in 5 days at the next routine clinic appointment
options.rationale: Outpatient observation with rising troponin and CRP during the high-risk first 4 weeks of clozapine misses myocarditis which can progress rapidly to cardiogenic shock; this needs same-day specialist assessment. (Source: RANZCP Position Statement: Clozapine-induced Myocarditis)

options.text: Switch from clozapine to olanzapine immediately at an equivalent dose and arrange a routine follow up appointment with his community psychiatrist within 2 weeks
options.rationale: Switching antipsychotics does not address the immediate concern of possible myocarditis which needs ED workup; only after exclusion of myocarditis can clozapine be ceased and an alternative discussed. (Source: RANZCP Position Statement: Clozapine-induced Myocarditis)

options.text: Repeat the full blood count and inflammatory markers urgently and only refer to the emergency department if the absolute neutrophil count drops below 1.5 x10^9/L this morning
options.rationale: Neutropenia is a separate clozapine adverse effect; the current concern (fever plus tachycardia plus troponin rise plus CRP rise) is myocarditis, not neutropenia. ANC is currently normal. (Source: RANZCP Position Statement: Clozapine-induced Myocarditis)

options.text: Withhold clozapine and commence oral roxithromycin 300 mg daily for 7 days empirically for atypical respiratory infection given the fevers, tachycardia and elevated CRP
options.rationale: Atypical pneumonia is in the differential but troponin rise on a normal chest examination and clear chest x-ray points more strongly to myocarditis; empirical antibiotics alone are inadequate. (Source: RANZCP Position Statement: Clozapine-induced Myocarditis)

explanation.summary: Clozapine-induced myocarditis occurs in around 1% of new initiators and usually presents within the first 4 weeks of treatment. The screening protocol mandates baseline and weekly troponin, CRP, and ECG for the first 4 weeks. Any fever, tachycardia, chest pain, dyspnoea, troponin rise (any value), or CRP above 100 mg/L triggers same-day cardiology referral with echocardiography. Mortality is around 10% without intervention. Clozapine is permanently ceased once myocarditis is confirmed; alternatives include olanzapine or risperidone but neither matches clozapine's efficacy in treatment-resistant schizophrenia. Neutropenia is monitored separately with weekly FBC.
key_points: Clozapine myocarditis usually presents within the first 4 weeks
Screening: weekly troponin, CRP, ECG for 4 weeks
Trigger thresholds: fever, tachycardia, any troponin rise, CRP above 100 mg/L
Mortality 10% without intervention; cardiology and echo same-day
Clozapine permanently ceased once myocarditis confirmed
explanation.pearls: Clozapine-induced myocarditis classically presents within 4 weeks of starting; ANY troponin rise plus fever plus tachycardia is the trigger to refer to ED for echocardiography even when the chest examination is unremarkable.

subtopic_detail: SSRI choice in early pregnancy with prior remission
stem:
A 31-year-old G2P1 woman attends her GP at 7 weeks gestation. She has been in remission from a moderate major depressive episode for the past 18 months on paroxetine 20 mg daily. Her first child is now 3 years old; she had antenatal anxiety but no significant relapse during that previous pregnancy on the same medication. She and her partner planned this pregnancy and were aware that paroxetine has a different safety profile in pregnancy.

She is currently euthymic with stable mood, sleep, and appetite. She has no suicidal ideation. She had one mild relapse during a previous attempt to discontinue paroxetine 2 years ago. Her medical history is otherwise unremarkable and she is on no other medications. Folate 5 mg daily was started by her GP at preconception counselling. The GP has asked your community perinatal mental health service for an opinion on the medication.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 78/min, BP 116/72 mmHg, RR 14/min, SpO2 99% room air, temperature 36.6 °C
data_table.Examination: Euthymic affect, full range; no psychomotor change; no psychotic features; no thoughts of self harm; abdomen soft non-tender
data_table.Investigations: FBC, electrolytes, thyroid function, vitamin D within normal limits; bhCG positive (date-concordant); fetal ultrasound at 6 weeks confirmed single intrauterine pregnancy with cardiac activity

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in her antidepressant management?

options.text: Cease paroxetine immediately and review her in 4 weeks for symptomatic relapse and consider non-pharmacological therapy if symptoms recur during her pregnancy
options.rationale: Abrupt cessation of paroxetine carries a high risk of relapse (relapse rate 60% if antidepressants stopped in pregnancy) and risks fetal SSRI withdrawal; planned cross-taper is safer. (Source: COPE Mental Health Care in the Perinatal Period National Clinical Guideline)
source_refs: COPE Mental Health Care in the Perinatal Period National Clinical Guideline

options.text: Refer to perinatal psychiatry for an inpatient assessment and consideration of electroconvulsive therapy because she has a relapsing major depressive episode in pregnancy
options.rationale: ECT is reserved for severe, treatment-resistant, or life-threatening perinatal depression with psychosis or imminent suicide risk; this woman is currently euthymic. (Source: COPE Mental Health Care in the Perinatal Period National Clinical Guideline)
source_refs: COPE Mental Health Care in the Perinatal Period National Clinical Guideline

options.text: Continue paroxetine 20 mg daily as her current effective treatment given the risks of relapse outweigh any small concerns regarding paroxetine in pregnancy outcomes
options.rationale: Paroxetine has a small but real association with first-trimester cardiac defects (especially ventricular septal defects); switching to sertraline is preferable when remission has been stable and a safer alternative exists. (Source: COPE Mental Health Care in the Perinatal Period National Clinical Guideline)
source_refs: COPE Mental Health Care in the Perinatal Period National Clinical Guideline

options.text: Switch paroxetine to mirtazapine 15 mg nightly with reassessment in 4 weeks given mirtazapine has a better established safety profile in pregnancy than the SSRI class
options.rationale: Mirtazapine is not first-line in pregnancy and the safety database is smaller than for SSRIs; sertraline has the most pregnancy and lactation evidence in the AU setting. (Source: COPE Mental Health Care in the Perinatal Period National Clinical Guideline)
source_refs: COPE Mental Health Care in the Perinatal Period National Clinical Guideline

options.text: Cross-taper from paroxetine to sertraline 50 mg daily over 2 weeks and continue throughout pregnancy and lactation given her history of relapse on discontinuation
options.rationale: Sertraline is the preferred SSRI in pregnancy due to low transplacental and breast milk levels; cross-tapering avoids relapse and the small increased risk of cardiac defects with first-trimester paroxetine. (Source: COPE Mental Health Care in the Perinatal Period National Clinical Guideline)
source_refs: COPE Mental Health Care in the Perinatal Period National Clinical Guideline

explanation.summary: COPE guidelines recommend continuing antidepressants in pregnancy when there has been a prior moderate-severe episode and remission depends on medication; relapse risk on cessation is around 60%. Sertraline is the preferred SSRI in pregnancy and lactation because of low transplacental and breast milk transfer and the largest reassuring evidence base. Paroxetine carries a small first-trimester association with cardiac malformations (especially ventricular septal defects). Fluoxetine has the longest half-life and higher breast milk transfer. Cross-tapering from one SSRI to another over 1-2 weeks is the standard transition method. Non-pharmacological therapies (CBT, IPT) are adjuncts, not substitutes, when relapse risk is high.
key_points: Sertraline is the preferred SSRI in pregnancy and lactation in Australia
Paroxetine first-trimester carries small VSD association
Stopping antidepressants in pregnancy has 60% relapse rate
Cross-taper over 1-2 weeks is the standard transition
ECT reserved for severe perinatal depression with psychosis or imminent risk
explanation.pearls: Sertraline is the preferred SSRI in pregnancy and lactation because of low breast milk transfer (under 2% relative infant dose) and the largest reassuring safety dataset; cross-taper from paroxetine over 1-2 weeks before week 8 of gestation.

sources.label: COPE Mental Health Care in the Perinatal Period National Clinical Guideline
RANZCP Perinatal Mental Health Clinical Practice Guideline

stem:
A 45-year-old woman with bipolar I disorder is admitted to a general medical ward after her family found her standing in the kitchen at home, not moving and not responding for 4 hours. She had stopped eating and drinking 36 hours earlier. Her usual medications are lithium and quetiapine. Her last manic episode was 3 years ago; she has had two previous similar episodes which the family describes as periods of complete withdrawal. There is no recent fever, illness, or drug use.

On arrival she is mute, with a fixed waxy posture of her arms held above the head when placed by the examiner, which she maintains for over 5 minutes. She does not respond to verbal command but tracks the examiner with her eyes. She has rigidity without tremor. Bedside fluids and an indwelling urinary catheter have been placed. Her recent lithium level was therapeutic. Bloods are unremarkable. CT head shows no acute findings. Bush-Francis Catatonia Rating Scale score is 16.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 102/min, BP 124/78 mmHg, RR 18/min, SpO2 99% room air, temperature 37.0 °C
data_table.Examination: Mute, waxy flexibility (catalepsy), arms maintained above head over 5 minutes; tracking with eyes; rigidity without tremor; no fever, no clonus, no rash
data_table.Investigations: Sodium 138 mmol/L, potassium 4.1 mmol/L, urea and creatinine within normal limits; CK 168 U/L; lithium level 0.8 mmol/L; venous blood gas pH 7.40; CT head no acute findings; bush-Francis Catatonia Rating Scale 16

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Commence intravenous dantrolene 1 mg/kg in addition to her usual psychiatric medications targeting the rigidity component present on her clinical examination today
options.rationale: NMS classically has hyperthermia, autonomic instability, marked CK rise (often above 1000), and altered consciousness; her CK is only 168 and she has no fever or autonomic instability - this points to catatonia, not NMS. (Source: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines: Mood Disorders)
source_refs: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines: Mood Disorders

options.text: Refer urgently for unilateral right-sided electroconvulsive therapy under general anaesthesia at the next available list before any pharmacological intervention is trialled first
options.rationale: ECT is highly effective in catatonia (especially malignant or lorazepam-non-responsive) but the diagnostic lorazepam challenge precedes ECT in most protocols. (Source: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines: Mood Disorders)
source_refs: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines: Mood Disorders

options.text: Increase her quetiapine to 600 mg daily for better antipsychotic cover and continue supportive care with intravenous fluids and nasogastric feeding for nutrition
options.rationale: Antipsychotic dose escalation in catatonia worsens it and can precipitate neuroleptic malignant syndrome; antipsychotics are deprescribed and benzodiazepines are first-line. (Source: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines: Mood Disorders)
source_refs: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines: Mood Disorders

options.text: Administer lorazepam 2 mg intravenously as a diagnostic and therapeutic challenge and reassess catatonic features and Bush-Francis score within 30 to 60 minutes
options.rationale: Lorazepam 1-2 mg IV is the AU and international first-line diagnostic challenge for suspected catatonia; over 70% of patients respond within 30-60 minutes and this is both diagnostic and therapeutic. (Source: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines: Mood Disorders; UpToDate Catatonia)
source_refs: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines: Mood Disorders

options.text: Hold lithium and quetiapine for 24 hours and reassess catatonic features tomorrow morning with the consultant psychiatry team before any further therapeutic intervention
options.rationale: Stopping lithium risks bipolar relapse and does not address the immediate catatonic state; benzodiazepine challenge plus supportive care is the priority. (Source: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines: Mood Disorders)
source_refs: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines: Mood Disorders

explanation.summary: Catatonia is a syndrome of motor, behavioural, and autonomic disturbance occurring in primary psychiatric (mood disorders most commonly), neurological (encephalitis, NMDA receptor antibody), and medical (electrolytes, infection) contexts. Diagnostic criteria require 3 or more of 12 features (stupor, catalepsy, waxy flexibility, mutism, negativism, posturing, mannerism, stereotypy, agitation, grimacing, echolalia, echopraxia). Lorazepam 1-2 mg IV is the diagnostic and therapeutic challenge; over 70% respond within 30-60 minutes. ECT is the next-line if lorazepam fails or for malignant catatonia (hyperthermia, autonomic instability). Antipsychotics worsen catatonia and risk NMS; benzodiazepine titration up to 6-8 mg lorazepam daily is often required. The condition is reversible when recognised; missed catatonia carries high morbidity from immobility complications.
key_points: Bush-Francis Catatonia Rating Scale is the standard severity tool
Lorazepam 1-2 mg IV is the diagnostic and therapeutic challenge
Over 70% of patients respond within 30-60 minutes
Antipsychotics worsen catatonia and risk NMS
ECT is first-line for lorazepam-non-responsive or malignant catatonia
explanation.pearls: The lorazepam challenge (1-2 mg IV) is both diagnostic and therapeutic in catatonia; over 70% improve within 30-60 minutes, and persistent benzodiazepine cover plus deprescribed antipsychotics is the standard maintenance approach.

sources.label: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines: Mood Disorders

subtopic_detail: Smoking cessation pharmacotherapy in MDD remission
stem:
A 42-year-old man attends his GP requesting help to quit smoking. He has smoked 25 cigarettes daily for 25 years (about 30 pack years). He has tried nicotine patches twice with relapse within 2 weeks. He has a history of major depressive disorder with one suicide attempt at age 28; he has been in stable remission for the past 7 years on sertraline 100 mg daily. There is no current depression.
