His Heaviness of Smoking Index is 5 of 6 (smokes within 5 minutes of waking, over 30 cigarettes per day). Mood remains stable, with no recent psychosocial stressors. He has no history of seizures, alcohol dependence, or eating disorder. He has no cardiovascular disease and a recent ECG was normal. He is otherwise systemically well. His asthma is well controlled on a low-dose ICS-LABA. He has been screened with the PHQ-9 today which is 3 of 27 indicating no current depression.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 76/min, BP 124/78 mmHg, RR 14/min, SpO2 97% room air, temperature 36.7 °C
data_table.Examination: Mild bilateral wheeze on forced expiration; no clubbing; cardiovascular examination unremarkable; mental state examination euthymic, no suicidal ideation
data_table.Investigations: FBC, electrolytes, LFTs within normal limits; ECG sinus rhythm normal axes and intervals; eGFR over 60 mL/min/1.73m2; PHQ-9 score 3 of 27

lead_in: What is the most appropriate single best initial pharmacotherapy to recommend?

options.text: Bupropion sustained-release 150 mg daily for 3 days then 150 mg twice daily for 7 to 12 weeks with set quit day 1 week into the titration and review at 4 weeks
options.rationale: Bupropion is a reasonable alternative but reduces seizure threshold and interacts with sertraline (CYP2D6 and serotonergic effects); in a stable depression patient on SSRI, varenicline is preferred. (Source: RACGP Supporting Smoking Cessation)

options.text: Combination nicotine replacement therapy with 21 mg patch daily plus a 4 mg gum or lozenge as needed and review the patient again in 2 weeks for clinical follow up
options.rationale: Combination NRT is a reasonable alternative but he has already failed monotherapy NRT twice and his heaviness of smoking suggests pharmacotherapy with the highest efficacy is justified; varenicline outperforms combination NRT. (Source: RACGP Supporting Smoking Cessation)

options.text: Varenicline 0.5 mg daily for 3 days then 0.5 mg twice daily for 4 days then 1 mg twice daily for 12 weeks with set quit day 1 week into the titration
options.rationale: Varenicline is the most efficacious AU first-line pharmacotherapy for moderate-heavy dependence; the EAGLES trial showed it does NOT increase neuropsychiatric events in stable mood disorders. (Source: RACGP Supporting Smoking Cessation: A Guide for Health Professionals; AMH)

options.text: Nortriptyline titrated up to 75 to 100 mg nightly for 12 weeks with set quit day 1 week into the titration after careful baseline ECG and serum nortriptyline level taken
options.rationale: Nortriptyline is a second-line agent for smoking cessation, has significant anticholinergic side effects, and combines with SSRI increases serotonergic risk; varenicline is safer and more effective. (Source: RACGP Supporting Smoking Cessation)

options.text: Behavioural counselling via Quitline alone without pharmacotherapy as initial approach given his prior history of major depressive disorder and concern about pharmacotherapy
options.rationale: Counselling alone has lower quit rates than counselling plus pharmacotherapy; with high dependence and prior NRT failures, behavioural treatment alone is inadequate. (Source: RACGP Supporting Smoking Cessation)

explanation.summary: First-line pharmacotherapy options for smoking cessation in Australia are varenicline, combination NRT (patch plus oral), or bupropion SR. Varenicline is the most effective single agent with around 25% 1-year quit rates. The EAGLES trial demonstrated no increased neuropsychiatric events in stable psychiatric patients, including those with stable depression. Bupropion lowers seizure threshold, is contraindicated in eating disorders and recent alcohol withdrawal, and interacts with SSRIs. NRT combination (patch plus short-acting) is equivalent to varenicline in some studies and is the preferred choice in pregnancy. Counselling plus pharmacotherapy is the additive standard.
key_points: Varenicline is the most effective single AU first-line agent
EAGLES trial - varenicline is safe in stable mood disorders
Bupropion lowers seizure threshold and interacts with SSRIs
Combination NRT (patch plus oral) is equivalent to varenicline
Counselling plus pharmacotherapy beats either alone
explanation.pearls: Varenicline 1 mg twice daily for 12 weeks following a 1-week titration produces around 25% 1-year quit rate in heavy smokers; EAGLES showed no neuropsychiatric signal in stable mood disorders despite older PBS warnings.

subtopic_detail: Adult ADHD pharmacotherapy choice in cocaine history
stem:
A 28-year-old man self-refers to a private psychiatry practice for assessment of attention deficit hyperactivity disorder. He describes lifelong distractibility, difficulty completing tasks, hyperactivity, and emotional dysregulation. Symptoms started before age 12 and have impaired schooling, employment, and relationships. A teacher-completed Vanderbilt scale from his year 4 school report flags 7 of 9 inattentive items.

He is currently a software developer but has been performance managed twice in the last 12 months. He drinks 4 standard drinks weekly. He used cocaine recreationally for 4 years and stopped 18 months ago after a near-fatal cardiac arrhythmia event in a nightclub. He has no current substance use. He has no other psychiatric history. ECG shows sinus rhythm with QTc 410 ms and otherwise normal. Echocardiogram (recent) was normal. He is asking specifically about medication options.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 72/min, BP 124/76 mmHg, RR 14/min, SpO2 99% room air, temperature 36.7 °C
data_table.Examination: Mental state examination - mood euthymic, attention impaired during interview, no psychotic features, no suicidal ideation
data_table.Investigations: FBC, electrolytes, LFTs, thyroid within normal limits; urine drug screen negative; ECG sinus rhythm QTc 410 ms; echocardiogram normal LV function; ASRS-v1.1 score 6 of 6 positive screening items

lead_in: What is the most appropriate single best initial pharmacotherapy to recommend?

options.text: Methylphenidate immediate-release 5 mg twice daily titrated weekly as first-line stimulant therapy given his clear positive screening and lifelong impairment
options.rationale: Stimulants are relatively contraindicated in patients with a history of stimulant-induced cardiac arrhythmia; non-stimulant therapy is safer first-line in this specific context. (Source: RANZCP Practice Guideline 23: Assessment and Treatment of ADHD; AADPA Australian Evidence-Based Clinical Practice Guideline for ADHD)
source_refs: RANZCP Practice Guideline 23: Assessment and Treatment of ADHD
AADPA Australian Evidence-Based Clinical Practice Guideline for ADHD

options.text: Lisdexamfetamine 30 mg daily titrated weekly as a long-acting prodrug stimulant with smoother pharmacokinetics and lower diversion potential than other stimulants
options.rationale: Although lisdexamfetamine has a smoother profile than dexamphetamine, all stimulants share cardiac effects; with a documented arrhythmia event on cocaine, non-stimulant alternatives are first-line. (Source: AADPA Australian Evidence-Based Clinical Practice Guideline for ADHD)
source_refs: AADPA Australian Evidence-Based Clinical Practice Guideline for ADHD

options.text: Guanfacine extended-release 1 mg daily titrated weekly to 4 mg daily as a non-stimulant alpha-2 agonist given his history of stimulant-induced cardiac arrhythmia event
options.rationale: Guanfacine XR is approved for paediatric ADHD in Australia and is not first-line in adults; atomoxetine has the strongest adult AU evidence and is the recommended non-stimulant when stimulants are contraindicated. (Source: AADPA Australian Evidence-Based Clinical Practice Guideline for ADHD)
source_refs: AADPA Australian Evidence-Based Clinical Practice Guideline for ADHD

options.text: Bupropion sustained-release 150 mg daily for 3 days then 150 mg twice daily for ADHD as an off-label noradrenergic-dopaminergic option given his stimulant contraindication
options.rationale: Bupropion has some evidence in adult ADHD but is not first-line in Australia and lowers seizure threshold; atomoxetine is the AADPA-recommended non-stimulant. (Source: AADPA Australian Evidence-Based Clinical Practice Guideline for ADHD)
source_refs: AADPA Australian Evidence-Based Clinical Practice Guideline for ADHD

options.text: Atomoxetine 40 mg daily titrated to 80 mg after 1 week as a non-stimulant first-line agent given his history of stimulant-induced cardiac arrhythmia and current ADHD diagnosis
options.rationale: Atomoxetine is the AU first-line non-stimulant for ADHD; AADPA recommends it as the first-line drug when stimulants are contraindicated, including patients with prior stimulant-induced arrhythmia. (Source: AADPA Australian Evidence-Based Clinical Practice Guideline for ADHD; RANZCP Practice Guideline 23)
source_refs: AADPA Australian Evidence-Based Clinical Practice Guideline for ADHD
RANZCP Practice Guideline 23: Assessment and Treatment of ADHD

explanation.summary: Adult ADHD diagnosis requires DSM-5-TR criteria with onset before age 12, persistence into adulthood, impairment in 2 or more settings, and exclusion of other mental health conditions causing the symptoms. AADPA Australian Evidence-Based Clinical Practice Guideline recommends stimulants (methylphenidate or lisdexamfetamine) as first-line for adults without contraindications. Cardiac contraindications include structural heart disease, prior stimulant-induced arrhythmia, uncontrolled hypertension, and concurrent stimulant misuse. Atomoxetine is the first-line non-stimulant. Driving advice and S8 prescribing rules (state-specific authority required) apply. Baseline ECG, BP, HR, and weight are mandatory; follow-up every 3 months in the first year.
key_points: AADPA guidance: stimulants first-line in adults without contraindication
Prior stimulant-induced arrhythmia is a relative contraindication
Atomoxetine is the first-line non-stimulant in adults
Baseline ECG, BP, HR mandatory before starting stimulants
State-specific authority prescription required for S8 stimulants
explanation.pearls: Atomoxetine takes 4-6 weeks to reach full effect; the dose ceiling in adults is 100 mg daily and the gain over stimulants is the absence of abuse liability and cardiac safety in patients with prior stimulant-induced events.

sources.label: AADPA Australian Evidence-Based Clinical Practice Guideline for ADHD
RANZCP Practice Guideline 23: Assessment and Treatment of ADHD

subtopic_detail: Schizoaffective vs bipolar with psychotic features
stem:
A 30-year-old woman is reviewed in a community psychiatry clinic with an established treating psychiatrist. She has had three episodes of significant mood disturbance over the last 8 years: two manic-like episodes with grandiose delusions and one major depressive episode with mood-congruent persecutory delusions. Between the second manic episode and the major depressive episode 18 months later, she had a continuous 12-week period of clear-cut auditory hallucinations and persecutory delusions without prominent mood symptoms; her mood was reported as euthymic by her partner and family throughout that interval.

She has been on olanzapine 15 mg nightly during episodes and has had remission of psychosis after each episode. She has not used substances. Family history includes a maternal aunt with schizophrenia and a paternal grandfather with bipolar I disorder. Current mental state is euthymic with no psychotic features. The clinic is considering revising her diagnostic formulation. Cognition is intact, no neurological signs.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 78/min, BP 122/76 mmHg, RR 14/min, SpO2 99% room air, temperature 36.7 °C
data_table.Examination: Mental state - euthymic, no psychomotor change, no psychotic features, no suicidal ideation; cognition intact on MMSE 30 of 30
data_table.Investigations: Bloods - FBC, electrolytes, LFTs, TSH, vitamin B12 within normal limits; urine drug screen negative; CT brain (historical, 4 years ago) normal; MRI brain (historical, 18 months ago) normal

lead_in: Based on the longitudinal course described, what is the most likely DSM-5-TR diagnosis?

options.text: Bipolar I disorder with mood-congruent psychotic features in the most recent depressive episode and grandiose features in the prior manic episodes during the illness history
options.rationale: Bipolar I with psychotic features requires that psychotic symptoms only occur during mood episodes; the 12-week interval of psychosis in the absence of mood symptoms excludes this. (Source: DSM-5-TR; RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines: Schizophrenia and Related Disorders)
source_refs: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines: Schizophrenia and Related Disorders

options.text: Schizoaffective disorder bipolar type with the lifetime presence of a major mood episode concurrent with criterion A schizophrenia symptoms and 2 or more weeks of psychotic symptoms without prominent mood symptoms
options.rationale: DSM-5-TR requires (a) a major mood episode (manic or major depressive) concurrent with criterion A of schizophrenia, (b) delusions or hallucinations for 2 or more weeks in the absence of a major mood episode, (c) mood symptoms present for the majority of total illness duration. All three are met. (Source: DSM-5-TR)

options.text: Schizophrenia with comorbid recurrent major depressive disorder and manic features attributable to substance use because the diagnosis of psychosis is supported by clear hallucinations
options.rationale: Schizophrenia with comorbid mood disorder requires mood symptoms to be present for a MINORITY of the total illness duration; her mood episodes are prominent and recurrent rather than residual. (Source: DSM-5-TR)

options.text: Schizophreniform disorder with affective features and a brief duration of mood symptoms within the context of a primary psychotic illness over the last 8 years of her psychiatric history
options.rationale: Schizophreniform is defined by total psychotic illness duration of less than 6 months; the 8 year course makes this diagnosis inapplicable. (Source: DSM-5-TR)

options.text: Delusional disorder mixed type with secondary mood symptoms occurring intermittently and the longitudinal course best characterised by persistent encapsulated non-bizarre delusions
options.rationale: Delusional disorder requires criterion A delusions for 1 month or longer without prominent hallucinations or disorganised speech; this patient has clear hallucinations and mood episodes, which rules it out. (Source: DSM-5-TR)

explanation.summary: DSM-5-TR criteria for schizoaffective disorder are: (A) an uninterrupted period of illness during which there is a major mood episode (major depressive or manic) concurrent with criterion A of schizophrenia (delusions, hallucinations, disorganised speech, grossly disorganised behaviour, or negative symptoms); (B) delusions or hallucinations for 2 or more weeks in the absence of a major mood episode during the lifetime duration of the illness; (C) mood-episode symptoms present for the majority of the total illness duration; (D) not attributable to a substance or medical condition. Bipolar type is subtyped when mania has occurred; depressive type when only major depressive episodes have occurred. Treatment combines antipsychotic with mood stabiliser or antidepressant (depending on subtype); long-term prognosis is intermediate between schizophrenia and bipolar disorder.
key_points: DSM-5-TR schizoaffective requires 2 or more weeks of psychosis without mood symptoms
Mood symptoms must be present for the MAJORITY of total illness duration
Bipolar type if mania ever occurred; depressive type if only MDD
Differential from bipolar with psychosis hinges on inter-episode psychosis-only periods
Treatment combines antipsychotic plus mood stabiliser (bipolar type) or antidepressant (depressive type)
explanation.pearls: The 2-week rule (psychosis without mood symptoms) is the key discriminator between schizoaffective disorder and bipolar disorder with psychotic features; missing this transition window causes most diagnostic errors in this differential.

sources.label: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines: Schizophrenia and Related Disorders

subtopic_detail: Serotonin syndrome with linezolid and SSRI
stem:
A 38-year-old man with chronic recurrent diabetic foot osteomyelitis is admitted to a metropolitan hospital for intravenous antibiotic therapy. He has been taking sertraline 100 mg daily for 6 years for major depressive disorder; mood is in remission. The infectious diseases team commenced intravenous linezolid 36 hours ago for MRSA cover after culture results returned. He was previously stable on oral sertraline through the admission process.

This morning he becomes agitated, confused, and hyperthermic. Nursing staff document inducible clonus in both lower limbs, hyperreflexia worse in the lower limbs than upper, mydriasis, diaphoresis, and a tremor. Sodium and bicarbonate are normal. There is no neck stiffness, no rash, no photophobia. He has had no sympathomimetic medications. The Hunter Serotonin Toxicity Criteria are met. The medical team are calling for advice on management.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 138/min, BP 168/96 mmHg, RR 26/min, SpO2 98% room air, temperature 39.4 °C
data_table.Examination: Agitated and confused, lower-limb-dominant hyperreflexia and inducible clonus, mydriasis, diaphoresis, fine tremor; no neck stiffness; no rash
data_table.Investigations: Sodium 140 mmol/L, potassium 4.2 mmol/L, urea and creatinine within normal limits; CK 1820 U/L; venous blood gas pH 7.34, lactate 3.8 mmol/L (0.5-2.2); CT brain unremarkable

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate immediate management priority alongside ICU referral and active cooling?

options.text: Administer intravenous bromocriptine 2.5 mg three times daily as a dopaminergic rescue for the hyperthermic syndrome and continue the linezolid and sertraline at full dose throughout
options.rationale: Bromocriptine is used as dopaminergic rescue in neuroleptic malignant syndrome, not serotonin syndrome; the antidote concept here is cyproheptadine (5-HT2A antagonist), not a dopamine agonist. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology)

options.text: Commence intravenous dantrolene 1 mg/kg as muscle relaxation for the hyperthermia and rigidity and continue both linezolid and sertraline because the infection requires ongoing treatment
options.rationale: Dantrolene is used in malignant hyperthermia and neuroleptic malignant syndrome; in serotonin toxicity, benzodiazepines are first-line. Continuing the precipitants is the major management error. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology)

options.text: Switch linezolid to vancomycin and continue sertraline because vancomycin does not interact with selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors and infection treatment must continue
options.rationale: Vancomycin substitution is a sensible eventual antibiotic plan but the IMMEDIATE priority is to stop BOTH serotonergic agents and provide supportive care; sertraline cessation also matters because its half-life is long. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology)

options.text: Stop linezolid and sertraline, give intravenous benzodiazepines for agitation and rigidity, and consider cyproheptadine 12 mg orally if features persist after first-line measures
options.rationale: Serotonin toxicity is a clinical diagnosis (Hunter criteria); treatment is removal of serotonergic agents, supportive care with benzodiazepines, active cooling, and cyproheptadine for refractory cases. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology; Hunter Serotonin Toxicity Criteria; UpToDate)

options.text: Administer intravenous flumazenil 0.2 mg slow injection for the agitation and confusion and continue current medications while waiting for the toxicology consultant review
options.rationale: Flumazenil is a benzodiazepine antagonist; agitation in serotonin syndrome benefits from benzodiazepines, NOT flumazenil. Flumazenil also lowers seizure threshold and worsens autonomic instability. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology)

explanation.summary: Linezolid is a weak reversible MAOI; co-prescription with SSRIs, SNRIs, MAOIs, tramadol, fentanyl, pethidine, dextromethorphan, lithium, triptans, methylene blue, or recreational MDMA can precipitate serotonin syndrome. The Hunter Serotonin Toxicity Criteria require ingestion of a serotonergic agent plus one of: spontaneous clonus, inducible clonus with agitation or diaphoresis, ocular clonus with agitation or diaphoresis, tremor with hyperreflexia, hypertonia plus temperature above 38 °C with ocular or inducible clonus. Treatment is removal of all serotonergic agents, benzodiazepines for agitation and clonus, active cooling, and cyproheptadine 12 mg orally followed by 2 mg every 2 hours (max 32 mg/day) for refractory cases. Severe cases require ICU and intubation with non-depolarising muscle relaxants. Recovery is usually within 24-72 hours.
key_points: Hunter criteria diagnose serotonin syndrome clinically
Linezolid is a weak reversible MAOI that combines dangerously with SSRIs
Stop ALL serotonergic agents, supportive care with benzodiazepines, active cooling
Cyproheptadine 12 mg orally for refractory cases
Bromocriptine and dantrolene are NMS, NOT serotonin toxicity, treatments
explanation.pearls: Lower-limb-dominant hyperreflexia, inducible clonus, mydriasis, and hyperthermia in the context of serotonergic co-prescription distinguish serotonin syndrome from NMS; antidote is cyproheptadine 12 mg PO, NOT bromocriptine or dantrolene.

stem:
A 38-year-old woman with bipolar I disorder has been stable on lithium 750 mg at night for the past 18 months following hospitalisation for a manic episode. She is reviewed in the community mental health clinic.

She has had no mood episodes, no medication side effects, and has been working full time. Her last serum lithium level was 0.7 mmol/L (target 0.6 to 0.8 for maintenance) six months ago. Her last full set of monitoring bloods was at the time of initiation 18 months ago, which she completed without prompting. She brings printed copies of those baseline results, all of which were within normal limits including TSH, calcium, creatinine, and full blood count.

data_table.Vital signs: within normal limits
data_table.Examination: no fine tremor, no goitre, euthymic mood, no peripheral oedema
data_table.Investigations: last lithium level 0.7 mmol/L six months ago; no monitoring bloods done since initiation 18 months ago

lead_in: What is the most appropriate ongoing monitoring schedule?

options.text: Lithium level annually with TSH, creatinine and calcium only if symptomatic
options.rationale: Annual lithium and selective biochemistry under-monitors a drug with narrow therapeutic index and predictable renal and thyroid effects, and would miss subclinical change before symptoms develop. (Source: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines for Mood Disorders)
source_refs: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines for Mood Disorders

options.text: Lithium level monthly and TSH plus creatinine 3-monthly indefinitely
options.rationale: Monthly lithium levels are appropriate during titration and the first 6 months; ongoing maintenance does not require this frequency in a stable patient and over-investigates without clinical benefit. (Source: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines for Mood Disorders)
source_refs: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines for Mood Disorders

options.text: Lithium level only when dose changes or symptoms suggest toxicity or relapse
options.rationale: Reactive-only monitoring misses asymptomatic level drift from dehydration, NSAIDs, ACE inhibitors, and dose-adherence change. RANZCP requires routine surveillance even in stable patients. (Source: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines for Mood Disorders)
source_refs: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines for Mood Disorders

options.text: Lithium level 6-monthly with full blood count alone every 12 months
options.rationale: FBC alone misses the key targets of TSH (lithium causes hypothyroidism in 5 to 35 percent over time) and creatinine (cumulative renal injury), and would leave thyroid and renal change undetected. (Source: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines for Mood Disorders)
source_refs: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines for Mood Disorders

options.text: Lithium level 6-monthly; TSH and creatinine 6-monthly; calcium and FBC 12-monthly
options.rationale: RANZCP guidelines for stable maintenance lithium specify level every 6 months, TSH and creatinine every 6 months, and calcium with FBC annually to detect hypothyroidism, renal decline, and hyperparathyroidism. (Source: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines for Mood Disorders)
source_refs: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines for Mood Disorders

explanation.summary: Long-term lithium monitoring targets three predictable adverse effects: thyroid dysfunction (5 to 35 percent develop hypothyroidism over years), renal impairment (cumulative tubular and interstitial injury), and primary hyperparathyroidism (raised calcium with inappropriately normal or elevated PTH). RANZCP recommends serum lithium every 6 months once stable (more often if dose changed, dehydration, new interacting medication), TSH and creatinine every 6 months, and calcium with FBC annually. ACE inhibitors, ARBs, NSAIDs, thiazides, and dehydration all raise lithium levels and prompt earlier rechecking.
key_points: Stable maintenance: lithium level + TSH + creatinine 6-monthly
Calcium and FBC annually (detect hyperparathyroidism, marrow effects)
Recheck level promptly if dehydration, NSAIDs, ACEi/ARB, or thiazide added
Lithium hypothyroidism affects 5 to 35 percent of long-term users
explanation.pearls: Lithium maintenance monitoring: level + TSH + creatinine every 6 months and calcium annually to detect hypothyroidism, renal decline, and hyperparathyroidism.

sources.label: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines for Mood Disorders

stem:
A 24-year-old man with first-episode psychosis was commenced on olanzapine 10 mg nightly two months ago after presenting to the early psychosis intervention service. He has responded well: persecutory delusions have resolved and he is sleeping consistently. He has no past medical history, does not smoke, and drinks alcohol once or twice a month.

Baseline assessment at the time of starting olanzapine included weight 78 kg, BMI 24, BP 122 by 78 mmHg, fasting glucose 4.8 mmol/L (3.0-5.4), total cholesterol 4.2 mmol/L (less than 5.5), LDL 2.4 mmol/L, HDL 1.3 mmol/L, triglycerides 1.0 mmol/L, and a normal ECG. He attends a routine community follow-up appointment.

data_table.Vital signs: within normal limits
data_table.Examination: no extrapyramidal signs, no postural drop
data_table.Investigations: baseline weight 78 kg BMI 24, fasting glucose 4.8 mmol/L (3.0-5.4), cholesterol 4.2 mmol/L, LDL 2.4, HDL 1.3, triglycerides 1.0, ECG normal

lead_in: When is the next set of antipsychotic-related metabolic monitoring bloods due?

options.text: At 12 weeks from initiation (around 4 weeks from now), then annually if stable
options.rationale: The RANZCP and Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic schedule for second-generation antipsychotic monitoring is baseline, then 12 weeks, then annually for fasting glucose and lipids, with weight at every visit and BP at every visit. (Source: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines; Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)
source_refs: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines for Schizophrenia

options.text: At 6 weeks from initiation, then 12 weeks, then annually if stable on therapy
options.rationale: A 6-week check is not part of the RANZCP or AMH schedule for routine metabolic monitoring; the first repeat is at 12 weeks. Adding a 6-week point does not change management. (Source: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines)
source_refs: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines for Schizophrenia

options.text: At 6 months from initiation, then annually if metabolic measures remain stable
options.rationale: A 6-month first repeat misses the early window for olanzapine-related weight gain and dyslipidaemia, where intervention (switch agent or commence metformin) is most effective. (Source: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines)
source_refs: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines for Schizophrenia

options.text: At 12 months from initiation if asymptomatic, then yearly thereafter on therapy
options.rationale: Annual monitoring alone misses early metabolic side effects that emerge within the first 3 months on olanzapine in particular. RANZCP specifies the 12-week timepoint. (Source: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines)
source_refs: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines for Schizophrenia

options.text: Only if weight gain, hypertension, or new symptoms develop on therapy
options.rationale: Reactive-only monitoring misses asymptomatic dyslipidaemia and impaired fasting glucose, which are the targets of antipsychotic metabolic screening. (Source: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines)
source_refs: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines for Schizophrenia

explanation.summary: Second-generation antipsychotics (especially olanzapine and clozapine) cause weight gain, dyslipidaemia, and impaired glucose tolerance early in treatment. Australian monitoring per RANZCP and Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic is structured to detect this window. Baseline assessment includes weight, BMI, waist circumference, BP, fasting glucose, fasting lipids, and ECG. Repeat fasting glucose and lipids at 12 weeks (the first checkpoint), then annually thereafter if stable. Weight and BP are checked at every visit. Prolactin is checked if symptomatic.
key_points: Antipsychotic metabolic monitoring schedule: baseline, 12 weeks, then annually
Weight and BP every visit; fasting glucose and lipids per schedule
Olanzapine and clozapine carry the highest metabolic burden
Switch agent or add metformin if early dyslipidaemia or weight gain
explanation.pearls: Antipsychotic metabolic screen: baseline, 12 weeks, then yearly for fasting glucose and lipids; weight and BP every visit.

sources.label: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines for Schizophrenia

subtopic_detail: Pharmacological management of acute behavioural disturbance
stem:
A 28-year-old man is brought to the emergency department by paramedics under a section of the Mental Health Act after threatening neighbours with a baseball bat. He has a documented history of schizophrenia and methamphetamine use. He has not taken any prescribed medications for the past two weeks.

In the resuscitation cubicle he is shouting, pacing, and intermittently striking the walls. Verbal de-escalation by experienced mental health nurses for 20 minutes has failed. Security staff are present. Pulse is 110, blood pressure 138 by 84 mmHg, respiratory rate 22, SpO2 99 percent on room air, temperature 37.0 degrees Celsius. He weighs approximately 80 kg. He is now physically restrained. There is no history of cardiac disease, no QT-prolonging medications, and no opioid use.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 110, BP 138/84, RR 22, SpO2 99% room air, temperature 37.0 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: agitated, mydriasis, no diaphoresis, no clonus, no rigidity
data_table.Investigations: weight approximately 80 kg; no ECG yet; no recent QT-prolonging medications

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first-line pharmacological intervention?

options.text: Diazepam 10 mg orally with continued verbal de-escalation effort
options.rationale: Oral diazepam is unlikely to be safely administered to an actively combative patient under physical restraint, and onset is too slow for the immediate safety risk. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic - Acute behavioural disturbance)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic - Acute behavioural disturbance

options.text: Intramuscular olanzapine 10 mg with separated benzodiazepine if needed later
options.rationale: Therapeutic Guidelines recommend IM olanzapine 10 mg as first-line for severe acute behavioural disturbance without contraindication, with strict avoidance of co-administration with parenteral benzodiazepines due to respiratory depression risk. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic - Acute behavioural disturbance)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic - Acute behavioural disturbance

options.text: Combined IM haloperidol 10 mg plus IM lorazepam 2 mg given simultaneously now
options.rationale: Co-administration of IM olanzapine or IM haloperidol with parenteral benzodiazepines is associated with respiratory depression and hypotension; this combination is no longer recommended as first-line in Australia. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic - Acute behavioural disturbance

options.text: Oral quetiapine 300 mg with continued seclusion until adequate sedation occurs
options.rationale: Oral quetiapine in this dose has slow onset and is impractical to administer to an actively restrained agitated patient; parenteral therapy is needed for immediate safety. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic - Acute behavioural disturbance)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic - Acute behavioural disturbance

options.text: Continue physical restraint and seclusion only without pharmacological intervention
options.rationale: Prolonged physical restraint without pharmacological calming is associated with rhabdomyolysis, asphyxia, and increased death rate; chemical restraint is part of the standard of care once verbal de-escalation has failed. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic - Acute behavioural disturbance

explanation.summary: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic recommends IM olanzapine 10 mg (5 mg if elderly or frail) as first-line monotherapy for severe acute behavioural disturbance unresponsive to verbal de-escalation. IM droperidol 10 mg is an acceptable alternative (with QT assessment if possible). Combined parenteral antipsychotic plus benzodiazepine carries a respiratory-depression risk and should be separated by at least 1 hour. Continue monitoring including pulse oximetry, BP, and sedation level (RASS) after administration. Physical restraint alone is associated with worse outcomes than appropriate chemical calming.
key_points: First-line: IM olanzapine 10 mg (or IM droperidol 10 mg) monotherapy
Avoid simultaneous parenteral antipsychotic plus parenteral benzodiazepine
Reduce dose in elderly, frail, or naive patients
Continue vital sign and sedation-score monitoring after dose
explanation.pearls: Acute behavioural disturbance first-line in Australia is IM olanzapine 10 mg; never co-administer parenterally with a benzodiazepine because of respiratory depression risk.

sources.label: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic - Acute behavioural disturbance

subtopic_detail: Tricyclic antidepressant overdose with QRS prolongation
stem:
A 42-year-old woman with major depressive disorder is brought to the emergency department by her partner approximately two hours after ingesting an unknown quantity of her amitriptyline 50 mg tablets in a deliberate self-poisoning event. The original 100-tablet bottle is now empty.

On arrival she is drowsy with GCS 11 (E3 V3 M5), pulse 128, blood pressure 92 by 58 mmHg, respiratory rate 14, SpO2 96 percent on room air, temperature 36.5 degrees Celsius. Pupils are 6 mm bilaterally and reactive. She has dry mucous membranes and absent bowel sounds. The 12-lead ECG demonstrates sinus tachycardia with a QRS duration of 132 ms and a terminal R wave of 4 mm in lead aVR. Venous blood gas shows pH 7.30, bicarbonate 19 mmol/L (22-32). Potassium is 3.7 mmol/L (3.5-5.0). Paracetamol level is undetectable.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 128, BP 92/58, RR 14, SpO2 96% room air, temperature 36.5 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: GCS 11 (E3V3M5), dry mucous membranes, absent bowel sounds, pupils 6 mm reactive
data_table.Investigations: ECG sinus tachycardia, QRS 132 ms, terminal R wave aVR 4 mm; pH 7.30, bicarbonate 19 mmol/L (22-32), K 3.7 mmol/L (3.5-5.0); paracetamol undetectable

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate pharmacological intervention?

options.text: Activated charcoal 50 g orally with intravenous fluids and observation only
options.rationale: Two hours post-ingestion with depressed conscious state, charcoal has limited benefit and aspiration risk is meaningful. More importantly, the widened QRS and metabolic acidosis demand active sodium-channel-blockade reversal. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology; Murray TCA overdose)

options.text: Intravenous flumazenil 0.2 mg followed by intravenous fluid resuscitation
options.rationale: Flumazenil is contraindicated in mixed overdose including TCA because it can precipitate seizures, and there is no benzodiazepine indication anyway. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology)

options.text: Intravenous sodium bicarbonate 1 to 2 mmol/kg bolus, then titrate to pH 7.5
options.rationale: QRS more than 100 ms after TCA overdose indicates fast-sodium-channel blockade and predicts arrhythmia and seizures. IV sodium bicarbonate (1 to 2 mmol/kg bolus, then infusion or repeat boluses to target arterial pH 7.50 to 7.55) is the antidote and reverses sodium-channel block. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology; Murray TCA overdose)

options.text: Intravenous magnesium sulfate 2 g bolus over 15 minutes for arrhythmia prevention
options.rationale: Magnesium is appropriate for polymorphic VT or torsades but the live problem here is sodium-channel blockade, which responds to sodium bicarbonate not magnesium. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology)

options.text: Intravenous lidocaine infusion at 1 to 4 mg/min for ventricular arrhythmia prevention
options.rationale: Lidocaine is a sodium-channel blocker itself and worsens the TCA toxicity; class IA and IC antiarrhythmics are contraindicated. Sodium bicarbonate is the answer. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology)

explanation.summary: Tricyclic antidepressant overdose causes fast sodium channel blockade, anticholinergic toxidrome, and alpha-1 antagonism. The cardinal ECG indicator is QRS prolongation; thresholds of more than 100 ms predict seizures and more than 160 ms predict ventricular arrhythmias. A terminal R wave in aVR of more than 3 mm is another marker. IV sodium bicarbonate 1 to 2 mmol/kg bolus, repeated to maintain arterial pH 7.50 to 7.55, reverses sodium-channel block. Avoid class I antiarrhythmics. Hypotension is treated with fluids then noradrenaline (alpha-1 agonist counters the alpha-1 blockade). Lipid emulsion is rescue therapy.
key_points: QRS more than 100 ms after TCA overdose predicts seizures and arrhythmia
Terminal R wave aVR more than 3 mm is another marker of toxicity
IV sodium bicarbonate 1 to 2 mmol/kg, repeat to pH 7.50 to 7.55
Avoid class I antiarrhythmics; flumazenil contraindicated in mixed overdose
explanation.pearls: TCA overdose with QRS more than 100 ms: IV sodium bicarbonate 1 to 2 mmol/kg bolus, titrate to arterial pH 7.50 to 7.55; class I antiarrhythmics and flumazenil are contraindicated.

subtopic_detail: Valproate use in women of childbearing potential
stem:
A 27-year-old woman with bipolar I disorder has been stable on sodium valproate 1000 mg daily for two years. Prior to valproate she had three manic episodes requiring hospitalisation, two of which were precipitated by lithium discontinuation due to renal concerns at the time (creatinine has since normalised). Her current valproate level is 500 micromol/L (350-700) and her last manic episode was three years ago.

She attends her psychiatry follow-up to share that she and her partner are planning to conceive within the next 6 to 12 months. She has been using a contraceptive intrauterine device since starting valproate. There is no relevant family history, no medical comorbidity, and she takes no other medications.

data_table.Vital signs: within normal limits
data_table.Examination: euthymic, no extrapyramidal signs, no fine tremor
data_table.Investigations: valproate level 500 micromol/L (350-700); LFTs, FBC, creatinine within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate medication-management plan?

options.text: Continue valproate with high-dose folic acid 5 mg daily during planning and pregnancy
options.rationale: Folic acid supplementation does not mitigate valproate's spina bifida and developmental risk; valproate-related neurodevelopmental harm and 10 percent major malformation rate persist despite folate. (Source: RANZCP Mood Disorders CPG; TGA Valproate Pregnancy Prevention)
source_refs: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines for Mood Disorders

options.text: Continue valproate until pregnancy confirmed, then cease and switch to lamotrigine
options.rationale: Major teratogenic effects of valproate occur in the early first trimester before pregnancy is often confirmed; stopping at that point is too late to prevent neural-tube defects. (Source: TGA Valproate Pregnancy Prevention Program)

options.text: Reduce valproate to 500 mg daily during planning to minimise teratogenicity risk overall
options.rationale: Although risk is dose-related, no dose of valproate is considered safe in pregnancy and the 500 mg dose is also associated with neurodevelopmental harm; switching the agent is preferred. (Source: TGA Valproate Pregnancy Prevention Program)

options.text: Cross-titrate from valproate to lithium with cardiology echo screen and pre-conception planning
options.rationale: Lithium is the preferred mood stabiliser for bipolar I in women planning pregnancy because of valproate's 10 percent major malformation rate and substantial neurodevelopmental impact. The plan acknowledges Ebstein anomaly risk (approximately 1 in 1000) via fetal echo at 18 to 20 weeks. (Source: COPE Perinatal Mental Health Guideline; RANZCP Mood Disorders CPG)
source_refs: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines for Mood Disorders

options.text: Stop valproate immediately and commence high-dose olanzapine 20 mg nightly indefinitely
options.rationale: Abrupt valproate cessation risks rapid relapse, and olanzapine 20 mg long-term carries substantial metabolic burden; cross-titration with a mood stabiliser is preferred. (Source: RANZCP Mood Disorders CPG)
source_refs: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines for Mood Disorders

explanation.summary: Sodium valproate causes major congenital malformation in around 10 percent of exposed pregnancies (especially neural-tube defects) and neurodevelopmental impairment in around 30 to 40 percent. TGA imposes a Pregnancy Prevention Program (PPP) requiring annual risk acknowledgement and effective contraception in all women of childbearing potential. When pregnancy is planned, switching to a safer mood stabiliser before conception is the standard approach. Lithium is the preferred option for bipolar I with risk of Ebstein anomaly approximately 1 in 1000, fetal echo at 18 to 20 weeks. Lamotrigine is an alternative for bipolar depression-predominant illness. Stopping valproate during pregnancy is too late to prevent first-trimester teratogenicity.
key_points: Valproate has 10 percent major malformation rate and substantial neurodevelopmental risk
Switch agent before conception, not at pregnancy confirmation
Lithium preferred for bipolar I (Ebstein risk approximately 1 in 1000) with fetal echo at 18 to 20 wk
TGA Pregnancy Prevention Program requires annual risk acknowledgement
explanation.pearls: Valproate in women of childbearing potential: switch to lithium or lamotrigine before conception; folic acid does not mitigate the 10 percent malformation rate.

sources.label: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines for Mood Disorders

subtopic_detail: Lithium continuation in pregnancy for bipolar I
stem:
A 31-year-old woman with bipolar I disorder is referred to the perinatal mental health clinic at 6 weeks gestation in her first pregnancy. She has been stable on lithium 900 mg nightly for four years after a severe manic episode that required involuntary admission. She has had two further close calls with mood escalation, both of which resolved promptly when her lithium dose was adjusted upward.

She reports unplanned but very welcomed pregnancy and is anxious about her medication. Her current lithium level is 0.7 mmol/L (target 0.6 to 0.8). She has booked with a community midwife and has a supportive partner and family. Her last menstrual period was 6 weeks ago. She has no other medications and the pregnancy ultrasound at 6 weeks confirmed a viable intrauterine pregnancy.

data_table.Vital signs: within normal limits
data_table.Examination: euthymic mood, no fine tremor, no peripheral oedema
data_table.Investigations: lithium level 0.7 mmol/L (target 0.6-0.8); creatinine and TSH within normal limits; viable 6-wk IUP on ultrasound

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management of her lithium during pregnancy?

options.text: Cease lithium immediately and substitute olanzapine 10 mg nightly throughout pregnancy
options.rationale: Lithium discontinuation in pregnancy carries roughly 70 percent relapse risk in bipolar I; switching to olanzapine alone may not match lithium's efficacy in her established disease and exposes the fetus to two drugs in sequence. (Source: COPE Perinatal Mental Health Guideline)

options.text: Continue lithium at lowest effective dose, divide doses, and arrange fetal echo at 18 to 20 weeks
options.rationale: Ebstein anomaly risk on first-trimester lithium is approximately 1 in 1000 (background 1 in 20,000); the absolute risk is far outweighed by relapse risk after stopping. RANZCP/COPE recommend continuation at lowest effective dose, divided dosing to minimise peak levels, and fetal echo at 18 to 20 weeks. (Source: COPE Perinatal Mental Health Guideline; RANZCP Mood Disorders CPG)
source_refs: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines for Mood Disorders

options.text: Reduce lithium dose by 50 percent immediately to mitigate first-trimester teratogenic risk
options.rationale: Halving the dose risks subtherapeutic levels and relapse without meaningfully reducing the Ebstein risk, which is most strongly tied to peak rather than trough levels; divided dosing rather than total reduction is preferred. (Source: COPE Perinatal Mental Health Guideline)

options.text: Cross-titrate lithium to lamotrigine over 4 weeks during the first trimester
options.rationale: Lamotrigine is preferred for bipolar depression-predominant illness, not the bipolar I with mania-predominant pattern she has. Switching late in the first trimester would expose the fetus to overlapping drugs without justification. (Source: RANZCP Mood Disorders CPG)
source_refs: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines for Mood Disorders

options.text: Continue lithium unchanged with no additional monitoring beyond routine antenatal care
options.rationale: Lithium clearance rises as pregnancy progresses, requiring level monitoring monthly then more frequently in the third trimester, plus dose-timing adjustments around delivery. Routine antenatal care alone is inadequate. (Source: COPE Perinatal Mental Health Guideline)

explanation.summary: Continuing lithium in pregnancy in a woman with severe bipolar I disorder is the default Australian position because the relapse risk after discontinuation (approximately 70 percent within 6 months) substantially outweighs the absolute teratogenic risk. Ebstein anomaly risk increases from background 1 in 20,000 to approximately 1 in 1000 with first-trimester exposure. Management is continuation at the lowest effective dose, divided dosing to limit peak levels, monthly serum levels (increasing in the third trimester as clearance rises), fetal echo at 18 to 20 weeks, and a clear plan around delivery (lithium hold 24 to 48 hours before induction or caesarean to limit toxicity from acute volume shifts).
key_points: Relapse risk after lithium discontinuation: approximately 70 percent in 6 months
Ebstein anomaly risk: approximately 1 in 1000 on first-trimester lithium
Continue at lowest effective dose with divided dosing; fetal echo at 18 to 20 weeks
Lithium hold 24 to 48 hours pre-delivery; monthly levels increasing in third trimester
explanation.pearls: Stopping lithium in pregnancy carries approximately 70 percent relapse risk in bipolar I; continue at lowest effective dose with divided dosing, monthly levels, and fetal echo at 18 to 20 weeks.

sources.label: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines for Mood Disorders

subtopic_detail: Serotonin syndrome from linezolid plus SSRI
stem:
A 58-year-old woman is admitted with a 36-hour history of confusion, sweating, and shaking limbs. She has a longstanding history of major depressive disorder and has been on escitalopram 20 mg daily for two years. Eight days ago she was started on linezolid 600 mg twice daily for a multi-drug-resistant skin and soft tissue infection in the orthopaedic ward.

On examination she is agitated and confused, with pulse 124, blood pressure 170 by 96 mmHg, respiratory rate 22, SpO2 98 percent on room air, temperature 39.0 degrees Celsius. There is sustained ankle clonus bilaterally, generalised hyperreflexia, ocular clonus, and intermittent tremor. Pupils are 6 mm bilaterally. Muscle tone is increased but not lead-pipe rigid. Creatine kinase is 480 U/L (less than 200). White cell count 11.0 x10^9/L (4-11) and CRP 18 mg/L (less than 5).

data_table.Vital signs: HR 124, BP 170/96, RR 22, SpO2 98% room air, temperature 39.0 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: agitated, sustained ankle clonus bilaterally, hyperreflexia, ocular clonus, mydriasis, increased tone without lead-pipe rigidity

lead_in: What is the most appropriate combination of immediate management actions?

options.text: Continue escitalopram and linezolid, IV cefazolin and dantrolene for presumed NMS
options.rationale: Sustained clonus, hyperreflexia, mydriasis, and short interval after a serotonergic-drug interaction strongly favour serotonin syndrome over NMS, which usually presents with lead-pipe rigidity and hyporeflexia evolving over days. Continuing escitalopram and linezolid would worsen symptoms. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic; Hunter Serotonin Toxicity Criteria)

options.text: Cease escitalopram and linezolid, IV benzodiazepines, active cooling, oral cyproheptadine 12 mg
options.rationale: This case meets Hunter criteria for serotonin syndrome (spontaneous clonus, or inducible clonus plus agitation plus diaphoresis, or ocular clonus plus tremor plus hyperreflexia). Linezolid is a non-selective MAOI that precipitates serotonin syndrome with SSRIs. Withdraw both agents, support with benzodiazepines and cooling, and add cyproheptadine 12 mg oral as serotonin antagonist. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic; Hunter Serotonin Toxicity Criteria)

options.text: Cease escitalopram only, continue linezolid, IV haloperidol 5 mg for agitation control
options.rationale: Both drugs must be ceased because their interaction is causal. Haloperidol can worsen serotonin syndrome by adding dopaminergic blockade and lowering the seizure threshold, and is not first-line for agitation here. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Cease linezolid only, continue escitalopram, paracetamol and IV fluids for fever control
options.rationale: Antipyretics alone do not address the cause and continuing escitalopram delays recovery; serotonin-mediated hyperthermia responds poorly to paracetamol. Both drugs need to stop. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Cease both drugs, give IV bromocriptine 2.5 mg eight hourly and supportive care only
options.rationale: Bromocriptine is a dopaminergic agonist used in NMS, not serotonin syndrome; in serotonin syndrome it adds no benefit and risks worsening agitation. Cyproheptadine is the serotonin-specific antagonist. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

explanation.summary: Serotonin syndrome from a drug-drug interaction between an SSRI and another serotonergic agent (linezolid is a non-selective monoamine oxidase inhibitor, tramadol, fentanyl, MDMA, tryptans) presents within hours to days of the new agent. The Hunter Criteria diagnose toxicity when a serotonergic agent has been taken and any one of: spontaneous clonus, inducible clonus plus agitation or diaphoresis, ocular clonus plus agitation or diaphoresis, tremor plus hyperreflexia, or hypertonia with temperature above 38 degrees with ocular or inducible clonus. Management is cessation of all serotonergic drugs, IV benzodiazepines, active cooling for hyperthermia above 39 degrees, and cyproheptadine 12 mg oral then 2 mg every 2 hours up to 32 mg/24 h as a serotonin antagonist.
key_points: Linezolid plus SSRI causes serotonin syndrome through MAOI activity
Hunter criteria: spontaneous clonus or inducible clonus plus agitation/diaphoresis or ocular clonus combinations
Serotonin syndrome: hyperreflexia + clonus + mydriasis (vs NMS: rigidity + hyporeflexia + diaphoresis)
Cyproheptadine 12 mg oral then 2 mg every 2 hours as serotonin antagonist
explanation.pearls: Linezolid is a non-selective MAOI and precipitates serotonin syndrome with SSRIs; treat with cessation, benzodiazepines, cooling, and cyproheptadine 12 mg orally.

subtopic_detail: Refractory delirium tremens despite high-dose diazepam
stem:
A 54-year-old man with chronic alcohol dependence is admitted with severe alcohol withdrawal 48 hours after his last drink. He is on a symptom-triggered diazepam regimen using the CIWA-Ar scale, has received 180 mg of diazepam orally over the past 8 hours, and additional 20 mg IV doses in the past hour.

He remains agitated with visual hallucinations of insects on the walls, tremor, and disorientation to place and time. Vital signs are pulse 138, blood pressure 172 by 102 mmHg, respiratory rate 24, SpO2 95 percent on room air, temperature 38.4 degrees Celsius. There is no rigidity. He has received pabrinex (high-potency parenteral B and C vitamins). Magnesium and phosphate were replaced 6 hours ago and remain within normal limits. His CIWA-Ar score is 28 (severe). Liver function shows AST 88 U/L (less than 40), ALT 55 U/L (less than 40), bilirubin 24 micromol/L, INR 1.3.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 138, BP 172/102, RR 24, SpO2 95% room air, temperature 38.4 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: tremor, visual hallucinations of insects, disoriented to place and time, no rigidity
data_table.Investigations: CIWA-Ar 28 (severe); AST 88, ALT 55, bilirubin 24, INR 1.3; magnesium and phosphate within normal limits; cumulative diazepam 200 mg in 8 h

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next pharmacological step?

options.text: IV haloperidol 5 mg with paracetamol 1 g for symptomatic agitation and fever
options.rationale: Haloperidol does not treat the GABA-deficit driving withdrawal and lowers the seizure threshold; it is not the right next step in benzodiazepine-refractory withdrawal. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Addiction Medicine)

options.text: IV dexmedetomidine infusion 0.4 microgram/kg/h with continued benzodiazepine infusion
options.rationale: Dexmedetomidine reduces sympathetic surge but does not treat the GABA deficit underlying delirium tremens, and is therefore considered adjunctive only after primary GABAergic control. It is not first choice in refractory withdrawal. (Source: ANZICS recommendations)

options.text: Oral baclofen 10 mg three times daily and continue current diazepam protocol
options.rationale: Baclofen has a role in long-term abstinence support but acute oral baclofen has slow onset and modest effect, and would not control acute delirium tremens in this severity. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Addiction Medicine)

options.text: Switch to oxazepam 60 mg every 2 hours and continue symptom-triggered scoring intervals
options.rationale: Cross-tapering one benzodiazepine for another at higher dose simply repeats the failed mechanism; in benzodiazepine resistance the response is to add a second GABA modulator with different pharmacology, not change the agent. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Addiction Medicine)

options.text: IV phenobarbital 130 to 260 mg loading dose, then titrated to symptom control
options.rationale: Benzodiazepine-refractory severe alcohol withdrawal requires escalation to a second GABA-A modulator. IV phenobarbital (loading dose 130 to 260 mg, repeated to symptom control with airway watch) is the recognised Australian addiction-medicine step before propofol intubation. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Addiction Medicine; ANZICS recommendations)

explanation.summary: Severe alcohol withdrawal that does not respond to escalating benzodiazepines (typically defined as more than 200 mg of diazepam in a few hours without response, or CIWA-Ar persistently above 20 despite high doses) is treated by adding a second GABA-A modulator with different binding kinetics. Phenobarbital is the Australian addiction-medicine step (130 to 260 mg IV loading dose, repeated to control, with airway monitoring). Adjuncts include magnesium and phosphate replacement, parenteral thiamine before any glucose, and treatment of co-existing infection. Propofol with intubation is the final escalation when phenobarbital is insufficient. Dexmedetomidine and antipsychotics are adjuncts but do not address the GABA deficit.
key_points: Benzodiazepine-refractory DT escalates to phenobarbital as second GABA-A agent
Phenobarbital IV loading 130 to 260 mg, repeated to symptom control
Continue thiamine, magnesium, phosphate; treat occult infection
Antipsychotics and dexmedetomidine are adjuncts not substitutes
explanation.pearls: Benzodiazepine-refractory delirium tremens: IV phenobarbital 130 to 260 mg loading dose, repeated to control; antipsychotics lower the seizure threshold and are not GABA-active.

stem:
A 28-year-old man with first-episode psychosis was commenced on olanzapine 10 mg nightly six weeks ago by the early psychosis team. His psychotic symptoms have settled, his sleep has improved, and he is back at his apprenticeship. He has gained 3 kg since starting and is generally well. He attends your community mental health clinic for routine review.

Baseline bloods taken when olanzapine was started showed fasting glucose 4.8 mmol/L (3.9 to 5.4), HbA1c 5.2%, total cholesterol 4.2 mmol/L, LDL 2.4 mmol/L, triglycerides 1.0 mmol/L. ECG showed a QTc of 410 ms. Weight at baseline was 78 kg; today 81 kg. There is no personal or family history of diabetes.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse 76 /min, blood pressure 124/78 mmHg, respiratory rate 14 /min, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.6 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: BMI 27 kg/m^2; no signs of EPS, akathisia, or tardive dyskinesia
data_table.Investigations: ongoing weekly weight checks since commencement

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next monitoring schedule?

options.text: Recheck metabolic bloods only if he gains more than 7% of his baseline weight
options.rationale: Weight gain triggers extra review, but routine 12-week metabolic monitoring is scheduled regardless of weight under RANZCP. Many patients develop dyslipidaemia or insulin resistance before substantial weight change. (Source: RANZCP Adult Antipsychotic Monitoring Statement)

options.text: Repeat fasting glucose, lipids, and weight at 12 weeks then yearly thereafter
options.rationale: RANZCP and the Maudsley Guidelines recommend baseline, 12-week, and then yearly metabolic monitoring (fasting glucose or HbA1c, lipids, weight, BP, waist circumference) for all patients on second-generation antipsychotics, with more frequent weight checks during the first three months. Olanzapine and clozapine have the highest metabolic burden of the second-generation agents. (Source: RANZCP Adult Antipsychotic Monitoring Statement)

options.text: Switch to quetiapine to reduce metabolic risk and recheck at one year
options.rationale: Switching is not indicated in a patient stable and responding well after 6 weeks of olanzapine. Monitoring is the next step; switching is reserved for significant or intolerable metabolic decline despite lifestyle intervention. (Source: RANZCP Adult Antipsychotic Monitoring Statement)

options.text: Add metformin 500 mg twice daily prophylactically to prevent metabolic syndrome
options.rationale: Metformin is considered for olanzapine- or clozapine-associated weight gain after it occurs and lifestyle measures fail; it is not routinely prescribed prophylactically at week 6 in a normoglycaemic patient. (Source: RANZCP Adult Antipsychotic Monitoring Statement)

options.text: Repeat the ECG every 3 months indefinitely while he remains on olanzapine
options.rationale: Routine 3-monthly ECG is not required for olanzapine. ECG is checked at baseline and repeated if dose-related QTc concerns arise or with high-QTc agents like ziprasidone. The metabolic profile is the priority for olanzapine. (Source: RANZCP Adult Antipsychotic Monitoring Statement)

explanation.summary: RANZCP, the Maudsley Guidelines, and Therapeutic Guidelines Psychotropic all recommend a structured metabolic monitoring schedule for second-generation antipsychotics: baseline, 12 weeks, then yearly for fasting glucose or HbA1c, fasting lipids, weight, waist circumference, and BP. Olanzapine and clozapine carry the highest metabolic burden; aripiprazole and lurasidone the lowest. Lifestyle counselling starts at initiation; metformin can be added in established or progressive weight gain or pre-diabetes. ECG is baseline plus reassessment with QT-prolonging agents.
key_points: Baseline, 12-week, then yearly metabolic monitoring is RANZCP standard
Weight checks more frequent (often weekly to monthly) in the first 3 months
Olanzapine and clozapine carry the highest metabolic burden
Metformin for weight gain or pre-diabetes after lifestyle intervention; not prophylactic
explanation.pearls: Second-gen antipsychotic monitoring: baseline, 12-week, then yearly fasting glucose/HbA1c, lipids, weight, BP, waist. Weight checks more often in first 3 months. Metformin for established weight gain or pre-diabetes after lifestyle intervention.

stem:
A 52-year-old woman with chronic schizophrenia stable on aripiprazole attends your community mental health clinic. She has smoked 25 cigarettes per day since age 18 and wants to quit because of new chronic obstructive pulmonary disease. She has tried nicotine patches twice in the past with limited success.

Her mental state is stable. She has no current depressive features, no suicidal thoughts, and no recent psychotic relapse. She has no past history of seizures or anorexia. She has no significant cardiovascular history. She is keen on a more aggressive pharmacological approach this time, supported by her case manager. She has no contraindications to systemic medication on review of her current chart.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse 78 /min, blood pressure 132/82 mmHg, respiratory rate 16 /min, SpO2 96% on room air, temperature 36.6 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: no nicotine staining of fingers visible (she wears gloves), no oral mucosal lesions
data_table.Investigations: spirometry confirms COPD; FEV1 65% predicted; FBC, UEC, LFT within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first-line pharmacotherapy?

options.text: Bupropion SR 150 mg daily increasing to 150 mg twice daily after a week
options.rationale: Bupropion is effective but carries a seizure risk in eating disorders and uncontrolled epilepsy, and has more drug interactions than varenicline. Varenicline has stronger evidence in stable schizophrenia per EAGLES. (Source: RACGP Smoking Cessation Guideline)

options.text: Varenicline 1 mg twice daily after one-week escalation, quit date in week 2
options.rationale: Varenicline has the highest abstinence rates in the RACGP Smoking Cessation Guideline and is suitable in stable psychiatric illness. The EAGLES trial showed no excess neuropsychiatric adverse events compared with placebo, patch, or bupropion. Dose escalates over week 1 (0.5 mg daily x3 days, 0.5 mg bd x4 days, then 1 mg bd) with a target quit date in week 2. (Source: RACGP Smoking Cessation Guideline)

options.text: Combination patch plus oral nicotine replacement therapy with behavioural support
options.rationale: Combination NRT is a reasonable option and is also first-line in RACGP, but in a 25-a-day smoker with prior patch failure and stable psychiatric illness, varenicline has the greatest abstinence effect. (Source: RACGP Smoking Cessation Guideline)

options.text: Off-label nortriptyline 75 mg nightly for smoking cessation support
options.rationale: Nortriptyline is second-line at best and not registered for smoking cessation in Australia. Side effects (anticholinergic, QT) limit utility. (Source: RACGP Smoking Cessation Guideline)

options.text: Clonidine 75 micrograms twice daily titrated to symptoms of nicotine withdrawal
options.rationale: Clonidine has weak evidence for smoking cessation and is not recommended as first-line. Hypotension and sedation limit acceptability. (Source: RACGP Smoking Cessation Guideline)

explanation.summary: First-line pharmacotherapy for tobacco smoking cessation in Australia includes varenicline, combination nicotine replacement therapy (patch plus short-acting), and bupropion. Varenicline has the highest abstinence effect in network meta-analyses and is now considered safe in stable psychiatric illness following the EAGLES trial. Dose escalates over week 1 with a target quit date in week 2; treatment continues for 12 weeks. Behavioural support (Quitline, brief intervention) doubles efficacy. Bupropion is avoided in eating disorders and uncontrolled epilepsy. NRT alone is appropriate for lighter smokers and where varenicline is contraindicated.
key_points: Varenicline 1 mg twice daily after week-1 escalation; 12-week course
EAGLES trial: no excess neuropsychiatric adverse events in stable psychiatric illness
Bupropion avoided in eating disorders and uncontrolled epilepsy
Combination NRT (patch plus short-acting) is also first-line
explanation.pearls: Smoking cessation first-line: varenicline 1 mg twice daily (after week-1 escalation), combination NRT, or bupropion. EAGLES showed varenicline is safe in stable psychiatric illness. Always pair with Quitline or behavioural support.

stem:
A 23-year-old woman is referred to your community mental health team following a third presentation in 12 weeks for superficial wrist lacerations after arguments with her partner. She describes intense rage, chronic emptiness, and frantic efforts to avoid being left when relationships strain. She has had three boyfriends and two best friends in two years.

Her mood swings throughout each day between euphoric and tearful. There are no fixed delusions, no command hallucinations, no manic episodes lasting beyond an afternoon, and no full depressive episodes. She has tried two SSRIs over 18 months with limited benefit. She has no substance dependence currently. The team formulation lands on borderline personality disorder by DSM-5-TR criteria.

data_table.Vital signs: within normal limits
data_table.Examination: mental state: dysphoric, intermittently tearful, reactive affect, no psychosis, no current suicidal intent though chronic suicidal ideation
data_table.Investigations: no acute medical issues

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first-line treatment?

options.text: Switch the SSRI to venlafaxine extended release as an alternative antidepressant trial
options.rationale: Antidepressants help comorbid depression but do not target BPD symptoms specifically. Repeated antidepressant switching in the absence of a clear depressive episode does not address the core problem. (Source: NHMRC BPD Guideline)
source_refs: NHMRC Clinical Practice Guideline for the Management of Borderline Personality Disorder

options.text: Commence olanzapine 5 mg nightly to stabilise mood and behaviour
options.rationale: Antipsychotics are not first-line in BPD and have modest effects on a narrow symptom range (cognitive perceptual, anger). NHMRC explicitly cautions against using them as a substitute for structured psychotherapy. (Source: NHMRC BPD Guideline)
source_refs: NHMRC Clinical Practice Guideline for the Management of Borderline Personality Disorder

options.text: Commence sodium valproate 500 mg twice daily for mood stabilisation
options.rationale: Sodium valproate has weak and inconsistent evidence in BPD; it is teratogenic and not appropriate for a young woman of reproductive age unless pregnancy is reliably prevented. NHMRC does not endorse it as first-line. (Source: NHMRC BPD Guideline)
source_refs: NHMRC Clinical Practice Guideline for the Management of Borderline Personality Disorder

options.text: Plan a brief inpatient admission to contain the behaviour after each episode
options.rationale: Brief crisis-driven admissions can reinforce dependence on inpatient care without addressing core deficits. NHMRC supports community-based structured psychotherapy and only short admissions for acute risk that cannot otherwise be managed. (Source: NHMRC BPD Guideline)
source_refs: NHMRC Clinical Practice Guideline for the Management of Borderline Personality Disorder

options.text: Refer for a structured psychological therapy such as dialectical behaviour therapy
options.rationale: RANZCP and NHMRC guidance identify structured psychological therapies (dialectical behaviour therapy, mentalisation-based therapy, schema-focused therapy, transference-focused therapy) as first-line for borderline personality disorder. Pharmacotherapy is adjunctive for specific symptom clusters, never primary. (Source: NHMRC Clinical Practice Guideline for the Management of Borderline Personality Disorder)
source_refs: NHMRC Clinical Practice Guideline for the Management of Borderline Personality Disorder

explanation.summary: Borderline personality disorder is treated primarily with structured psychological therapy under the NHMRC guideline, RANZCP, and NICE. Evidence-based options include dialectical behaviour therapy (DBT), mentalisation-based therapy (MBT), schema-focused therapy (SFT), and transference-focused psychotherapy (TFP). Pharmacotherapy is adjunctive, used for specific comorbidities (depression, psychosis, mood instability) and discontinued if not clearly helpful. Admission is reserved for acute risk that cannot otherwise be managed safely.
key_points: Structured psychological therapy is first-line in BPD (DBT, MBT, SFT, TFP)
Pharmacotherapy is adjunctive, targeting specific symptom clusters only
Avoid valproate in women of reproductive age unless contraception is reliable
Brief planned admissions for crisis only; avoid long inpatient stays
explanation.pearls: BPD first-line: structured psychological therapy (DBT, MBT, schema, TFP). Pharmacotherapy adjunctive only. Avoid valproate in women of reproductive age. Crisis admissions kept brief and planned.

sources.label: NHMRC Clinical Practice Guideline for the Management of Borderline Personality Disorder

stem:
A 24-year-old woman with a known diagnosis of bipolar I disorder is brought to the emergency department by her family for being mute, immobile in unusual postures, and not eating or drinking for 36 hours. Her mother says she stopped responding two days ago after stopping her lithium and quetiapine three weeks ago to start a master's degree.

On examination she stares ahead, follows commands occasionally, holds her arm wherever you place it for over 30 seconds, and grimaces. There are no focal neurological signs. She is afebrile. Family report no recent infection, no head injury, no street drug use, and no withdrawal symptoms. There is no rigidity, no autonomic instability, and no fever to suggest neuroleptic malignant syndrome.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse 88 /min, blood pressure 122/76 mmHg, respiratory rate 14 /min, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.8 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Bush-Francis Catatonia Rating Scale: stupor, mutism, waxy flexibility, posturing, grimacing; no rigidity, no clonus, no fever
data_table.Investigations: FBC, UEC, CK 220 U/L (40 to 240), TSH 1.6 mIU/L, glucose 5.0 mmol/L; CT head non-contrast normal; urine drug screen negative

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Order an immediate lumbar puncture to exclude autoimmune encephalitis
options.rationale: Autoimmune encephalitis is on the differential but a primary psychiatric catatonia with a clear precipitant (medication cessation) and normal CT and inflammatory markers does not mandate LP before the lorazepam challenge. LP is considered if challenge fails or red flags emerge. (Source: RANZCP Catatonia Statement)

options.text: Commence haloperidol 5 mg IM now to treat the underlying psychosis
options.rationale: Antipsychotics, particularly typical agents, can worsen catatonia and precipitate neuroleptic malignant syndrome. They are avoided until catatonia is broken with benzodiazepines or ECT. (Source: RANZCP Catatonia Statement)

options.text: Restart lithium at the prior maintenance dose to reverse the mood episode driver
options.rationale: Restarting lithium is appropriate as a longer-term plan but does not address the acute catatonic state. Catatonia carries risks of dehydration, deep vein thrombosis, and aspiration that need same-day intervention. (Source: RANZCP Catatonia Statement)

options.text: Trial IM or IV lorazepam 1 to 2 mg with reassessment of catatonia scale at 30 minutes
options.rationale: A lorazepam challenge is the standard diagnostic and initial therapeutic test for catatonia. An improvement of 50% or more on the Bush-Francis scale within 30 to 60 minutes confirms benzodiazepine-responsive catatonia and directs further treatment with scheduled lorazepam, often 6 to 24 mg per day in divided doses. (Source: RANZCP Catatonia Statement)

options.text: Refer for urgent ECT before any pharmacological intervention is given
options.rationale: ECT is the next step if the lorazepam challenge fails or for malignant catatonia. Benzodiazepines come first as both diagnostic and therapeutic. (Source: RANZCP Catatonia Statement)

explanation.summary: Catatonia is a syndromic diagnosis recognised across primary psychiatric (mood, psychotic) and medical causes (autoimmune encephalitis, metabolic, infective). The Bush-Francis Catatonia Rating Scale is the standard assessment. A lorazepam challenge of 1 to 2 mg IM or IV with reassessment in 30 to 60 minutes is both diagnostic and the first therapeutic step. Maintenance lorazepam (6 to 24 mg per day, occasionally higher) is then titrated. ECT is the second-line treatment for non-responders and the first-line for malignant catatonia (with autonomic instability and hyperthermia). Antipsychotics are avoided until catatonia has resolved.
key_points: Lorazepam 1 to 2 mg IM or IV with reassessment at 30 to 60 minutes is the diagnostic challenge
Maintenance lorazepam 6 to 24 mg per day in divided doses for responders
Avoid antipsychotics until catatonia resolves; risk of NMS and worsening
ECT is second-line and first-line for malignant catatonia
explanation.pearls: Catatonia: lorazepam 1 to 2 mg IM or IV challenge, reassess Bush-Francis at 30 to 60 minutes. Responders go to 6 to 24 mg per day in divided doses. ECT is second-line and first-line for malignant catatonia. Avoid antipsychotics until resolution.

stem:
A 38-year-old man with major depressive disorder is brought to the emergency department by his housemate with restlessness, sweating, and tremor that began six hours ago. His housemate says he ran out of sertraline two weeks ago and was started on phenelzine three days ago by his private psychiatrist after multiple SSRI failures. He took his usual dose this morning then took two of his housemate's tramadol 50 mg tablets for a sore back.

On arrival he is agitated, has spontaneous clonus in both legs (sustained for several seconds), brisk deep tendon reflexes, ocular clonus, and diaphoresis. There is no muscle rigidity. His pupils are dilated.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse 134 /min, blood pressure 168/96 mmHg, respiratory rate 26 /min, SpO2 98% on room air, temperature 38.6 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: agitated, spontaneous lower limb clonus, ocular clonus, hyperreflexia (4+) more pronounced in lower limbs, dilated pupils, diaphoresis, no lead-pipe rigidity
data_table.Investigations: CK 380 U/L (40 to 240); UEC normal; ABG within normal limits; ECG sinus tachycardia QTc 430 ms; venous lactate 2.1 mmol/L

lead_in: What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.text: Serotonin syndrome from MAOI plus tramadol with incomplete SSRI washout
options.rationale: The Hunter Serotonin Toxicity Criteria are met (spontaneous clonus, plus agitation, sweating, and hyperthermia). The combination of phenelzine (irreversible MAOI) plus tramadol (serotonergic) plus an inadequate sertraline washout (less than 2 weeks) is classic. Lower limb hyperreflexia, ocular clonus, and dilated pupils favour serotonin syndrome over NMS. (Source: Hunter Serotonin Toxicity Criteria; Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Neuroleptic malignant syndrome with autonomic instability and rigidity
options.rationale: NMS presents with lead-pipe rigidity, bradyreflexia, and an indolent onset over days, typically after antipsychotic initiation or dose increase. This patient has hyperreflexia and clonus and no antipsychotic exposure. (Source: Hunter Criteria; Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Anticholinergic toxidrome from tramadol's noradrenergic and serotonergic effects
options.rationale: Anticholinergic toxicity features dry skin and mucous membranes, urinary retention, and a flushed face, not the diaphoresis and clonus here. Tramadol can have anticholinergic effects but the dominant picture is serotonergic. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology)

options.text: Thyroid storm precipitated by recent infection and tramadol use
options.rationale: Thyroid storm causes hypermetabolic state but typically with goitre, atrial fibrillation, and bradyreflexia. The classic combination of agitation, spontaneous clonus, ocular clonus, and diaphoresis points to serotonin syndrome. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

options.text: Sympathomimetic toxidrome from concurrent stimulant intoxication
options.rationale: Stimulant intoxication can produce agitation, hypertension, and tachycardia but does not classically produce lower-limb-dominant clonus or ocular clonus. The medication history is the discriminator. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology)

explanation.summary: Serotonin syndrome is diagnosed clinically using the Hunter Serotonin Toxicity Criteria: in the setting of a serotonergic agent, the presence of spontaneous clonus, OR inducible clonus with agitation or diaphoresis, OR ocular clonus with agitation or diaphoresis, OR tremor and hyperreflexia, OR hypertonia plus temperature above 38 degrees Celsius with ocular or inducible clonus, is diagnostic. The pattern of hyperreflexia, lower-limb-predominant clonus, mydriasis, and acute onset distinguishes it from NMS (rigidity, bradyreflexia, days to develop). MAOI plus tramadol or other serotonergic agent is a particularly high-risk combination, requiring a 2-week SSRI washout before introducing an MAOI.
key_points: Hunter Criteria use spontaneous or inducible clonus, ocular clonus, hyperreflexia, agitation, diaphoresis, hyperthermia
Serotonin syndrome: hyperreflexia, lower-limb-dominant clonus, mydriasis, acute onset
NMS: lead-pipe rigidity, bradyreflexia, indolent onset, antipsychotic exposure
MAOI plus tramadol or SSRI without 2-week washout is a high-risk combination
