explanation.pearls: Hunter Criteria for serotonin syndrome: spontaneous clonus, OR inducible clonus with agitation/diaphoresis, OR ocular clonus with agitation/diaphoresis, OR tremor and hyperreflexia, OR hypertonia plus T>38 with clonus. Lower limb dominance and mydriasis distinguish from NMS. MAOI plus tramadol is classic.

stem:
A 64-year-old man with bipolar I disorder on lithium for 15 years presents to the emergency department brought by his daughter with confusion, slurred speech, and tremor that has worsened over a week. She mentions he had a chest infection 10 days ago and was started on an unknown medication by a locum GP. He has remained on his lithium 750 mg twice daily.

On arrival he is drowsy and disoriented to time. He has coarse tremor in both hands, gait ataxia when assisted up, and brisk deep tendon reflexes. There is no fever and no focal neurology. His past medical history includes hypertension on perindopril and chronic kidney disease stage 3.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse 64 /min, blood pressure 152/94 mmHg, respiratory rate 14 /min, SpO2 97% on room air, temperature 36.7 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: drowsy, dysarthric, coarse bilateral hand tremor, gait ataxia, brisk reflexes
data_table.Investigations: lithium level 3.4 mmol/L (0.4 to 1.0); creatinine 180 micromol/L (45 to 90, baseline 110); sodium 138 mmol/L; potassium 4.2 mmol/L; ECG: sinus bradycardia with flattened T waves

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Administer activated charcoal 50 g via a nasogastric tube now
options.rationale: Activated charcoal does not bind lithium and has no role in lithium toxicity. It is not recommended in any toxicology guideline for this indication. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology)

options.text: IV 0.9% sodium chloride at 200 mL/hr alone and recheck the level in 6 hours
options.rationale: Saline alone is appropriate for mild toxicity in normal renal function but is insufficient in CKD with AKI, encephalopathy, and a level over 2.5 mmol/L. EXTRIP supports dialysis in this scenario. (Source: EXTRIP)

options.text: Arrange urgent haemodialysis after IV 0.9% sodium chloride is commenced
options.rationale: EXTRIP consensus recommends haemodialysis for lithium toxicity when the level exceeds 4.0 mmol/L, OR exceeds 2.5 mmol/L with significant impaired consciousness, seizures, life-threatening arrhythmia, OR exceeds 2.5 mmol/L with renal impairment that will impair clearance. This patient meets the third criterion: level 3.4 with CKD stage 3 and acute kidney injury, plus altered mental status. IV saline is started while dialysis is arranged. (Source: EXTRIP Workgroup Lithium Recommendations)

options.text: Withhold lithium and recheck levels in 24 hours without other intervention
options.rationale: Watchful waiting in a patient with encephalopathy, AKI, and a level of 3.4 mmol/L risks deterioration, seizures, and arrhythmia. Active clearance is needed. (Source: EXTRIP)

options.text: Administer sodium polystyrene sulfonate to lower the lithium level
options.rationale: Sodium polystyrene sulfonate has been investigated for lithium binding but is not endorsed as primary therapy. EXTRIP supports haemodialysis as the definitive extracorporeal removal modality. (Source: EXTRIP)

explanation.summary: Lithium toxicity occurs by reduced renal clearance (NSAIDs, ACE inhibitors, dehydration, AKI), dose error, or deliberate overdose. EXTRIP recommendations for haemodialysis are: any lithium level over 4.0 mmol/L, OR over 2.5 mmol/L with significant impaired consciousness, seizures, life-threatening arrhythmia, OR over 2.5 mmol/L with renal impairment that will prevent clearance within 36 hours. Saline IV at 1.5 to 2 times maintenance is given while dialysis is arranged. Rebound rises after dialysis (intracellular shifts) require recheck and may need re-dialysis. The classic clinical triad is coarse tremor, ataxia, and altered mental status.
key_points: Haemodialysis if level over 4.0 mmol/L, OR over 2.5 mmol/L with encephalopathy, seizures, arrhythmia, OR renal impairment
IV 0.9% sodium chloride at 1.5 to 2 times maintenance while dialysis is arranged
Activated charcoal does NOT bind lithium
Expect rebound levels after dialysis from intracellular redistribution
explanation.pearls: Lithium toxicity dialysis (EXTRIP): level over 4.0 mmol/L, OR over 2.5 mmol/L with encephalopathy/seizures/arrhythmia, OR over 2.5 mmol/L with renal impairment. Saline IV at 1.5 to 2 times maintenance bridges to dialysis. Activated charcoal does NOT bind lithium.

stem:
A 29-year-old engineer presents to your practice asking about adult ADHD assessment. He describes lifelong difficulty starting and finishing tasks, frequent forgetfulness, fidgeting through meetings, and a pattern of late submissions throughout university and at work. School reports from age 8 noted disorganisation and inattention; he completed his degree but struggled. He has no history of mood or psychotic disorder, no substance dependence, no head injury, and no medical illness on review.

His cardiovascular history is unremarkable. His resting pulse is 72 /min and BP 122/78 mmHg. He has no personal or family history of structural heart disease, sudden death under 40, or unexplained syncope. His full mental state and neurological examination today are unremarkable.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse 72 /min, blood pressure 122/78 mmHg, respiratory rate 14 /min, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.6 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: no abnormal findings; cardiovascular examination unremarkable
data_table.Investigations: thyroid function, FBC, UEC all within normal limits; ECG sinus rhythm rate 72 with no abnormalities

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Reassure adult-onset ADHD is rare and offer CBT for organisation skills only
options.rationale: ADHD is by definition a developmental disorder with symptoms from childhood, and adult presentation reflecting previously unrecognised lifelong difficulty is common. Dismissing the assessment misses a treatable condition. (Source: Australian ADHD Guideline)
source_refs: Australian Evidence-Based Clinical Practice Guideline for ADHD

options.text: Trial methylphenidate 10 mg twice daily in the practice and review in 2 weeks
options.rationale: GPs cannot initiate stimulants without specialist authority under state Schedule 8 legislation. Initiation requires specialist diagnosis. (Source: Australian ADHD Guideline)
source_refs: Australian Evidence-Based Clinical Practice Guideline for ADHD

options.text: Commence atomoxetine 40 mg daily and titrate up to 80 mg over 2 weeks
options.rationale: Atomoxetine is non-stimulant but still requires authority initiation. Adult ADHD diagnosis must be specialist-confirmed before any first-line medication. (Source: Australian ADHD Guideline)
source_refs: Australian Evidence-Based Clinical Practice Guideline for ADHD

options.text: Refer for neuropsychological testing as the diagnostic gold standard
options.rationale: Neuropsychological testing supplements clinical assessment but is not the diagnostic standard. ADHD is a clinical diagnosis based on developmental history, current impairment across settings, and DSM-5-TR criteria. (Source: Australian ADHD Guideline)
source_refs: Australian Evidence-Based Clinical Practice Guideline for ADHD

options.text: Refer to a psychiatrist or paediatrician with stimulant authority for diagnosis
options.rationale: Adult ADHD diagnosis in Australia requires confirmation by an appropriately credentialed specialist (psychiatrist, paediatrician, or in some states neurologist) with stimulant prescribing authority. Stimulants are Schedule 8 and need state authority. GPs co-prescribe under a shared-care plan once initiated. (Source: Australian Evidence-Based Clinical Practice Guideline for ADHD)
source_refs: Australian Evidence-Based Clinical Practice Guideline for ADHD

explanation.summary: The 2022 Australian Evidence-Based Clinical Practice Guideline for ADHD sets out a structured pathway: GP triage with collateral history and screening (ASRS), then specialist referral for diagnostic confirmation by a psychiatrist, paediatrician, or, in some states, neurologist with stimulant prescribing authority. Stimulant initiation (methylphenidate or dexamfetamine) requires Schedule 8 authority and ECG and cardiovascular screening before initiation. Driving counselling, comorbidity screening (anxiety, depression, substance use), and informed consent on diversion risks are required. GPs continue maintenance under shared-care arrangements.
key_points: Adult ADHD diagnosis requires specialist confirmation by a psychiatrist or paediatrician
Stimulants are Schedule 8 and need state authority before initiation
Cardiovascular screen (history and ECG) before stimulant initiation
GPs continue maintenance under shared-care arrangements
explanation.pearls: Adult ADHD: GP screens (ASRS) and refers; specialist (psychiatrist, paediatrician, sometimes neurologist) confirms diagnosis and initiates stimulant under Schedule 8 authority. CV screen and ECG before initiation; GP shared-care maintenance.

sources.label: Australian Evidence-Based Clinical Practice Guideline for ADHD

subtopic_detail: Sodium valproate in women of childbearing age
stem:
A 28-year-old woman with bipolar I disorder attends your psychiatry outpatient clinic for review. She has been stable on sodium valproate 1000 mg daily for 4 years with no relapses. She tells you that she and her partner are planning a pregnancy in the next 6 months. She is not currently using contraception.

She has a documented history of three manic episodes prior to commencing valproate, the last with a brief admission under the Mental Health Act for risk of harm to others. She has not had a depressive episode since valproate initiation. She has no comorbid medical conditions. She has not previously trialled lithium or lamotrigine.

data_table.Examination: well-groomed, euthymic mood, no thought disorder, no psychotic features, normal cognition, BMI 24, no neurological signs
data_table.Investigations: current valproate level 78 micromol/L (therapeutic 350-700 not routinely targeted), full blood count and liver function within normal limits, urine pregnancy test negative today, beta-hCG not done

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Continue valproate and add high-dose folate 5 mg daily, reviewing in pregnancy if it occurs in the next 6 months
options.rationale: Same problem as above; the teratogenicity of valproate extends well beyond neural tube defects and is not mitigated by folate. (Source: TGA valproate-containing medicines safety communications)

options.text: Continue valproate at current dose and provide written advice on neural tube defect risk plus high-dose folate
options.rationale: Folate supplementation does not abolish the substantial teratogenic risk from valproate. AU regulators have restricted valproate use in WCBA and a pregnancy planning consultation should pivot to a safer agent. (Source: TGA valproate-containing medicines safety communications)

options.text: Cease valproate over 4 weeks and commence lithium 400 mg nocte plus Pregnancy Prevention Program until conception planned
options.rationale: Sodium valproate is contraindicated in women of childbearing potential unless conditions of the AU Pregnancy Prevention Program are met because the absolute risk of major congenital malformations (around 10 percent) and neurodevelopmental disorders (around 30 to 40 percent) is high. Lithium is preferred for relapse prevention in bipolar I disorder with manic predominance, with much lower teratogenic risk and reversible Ebstein anomaly concern weighed against ongoing manic relapse risk. (Source: RANZCP Mood Disorders CPG; TGA valproate-containing medicines safety communications)

options.text: Switch valproate directly to lamotrigine 25 mg daily with stepwise titration as the primary maintenance choice
options.rationale: Lamotrigine is recommended for bipolar depression prevention rather than manic relapse prevention. Given her history of manic episodes and absence of depressive episodes on valproate, lithium is the preferred long-term agent. (Source: RANZCP Mood Disorders CPG)

options.text: Cease valproate immediately and trial olanzapine 10 mg nocte as monotherapy maintenance instead of mood stabilisers
options.rationale: Abrupt cessation of valproate without an overlap risks destabilisation. Olanzapine is an option for acute mania but lithium has superior maintenance evidence for bipolar I with manic predominance and is the preferred long-term agent. (Source: RANZCP Mood Disorders CPG)

explanation.summary: Sodium valproate is associated with up to 10 percent risk of major congenital malformations and 30 to 40 percent risk of neurodevelopmental disorders in exposed children. TGA restrictions require adherence to a Pregnancy Prevention Program for use in women of childbearing potential. Pre-conception planning should switch to a safer agent rather than wait for a positive pregnancy test. Lithium is preferred for bipolar I with manic predominance and has lower (but not zero) teratogenic risk.
key_points: Valproate WCBA risk: around 10 percent major malformations, 30 to 40 percent neurodevelopmental disorders.
Pre-conception switch should be planned, not at the time of positive pregnancy test.
Lithium is preferred for manic-predominant bipolar I maintenance during pregnancy planning.
Lamotrigine is preferred for bipolar depression prevention.
explanation.pearls: Switch valproate to lithium 400 mg nocte for a woman planning pregnancy with manic-predominant bipolar I disorder; folate does not mitigate the 10 percent malformation and 30 to 40 percent neurodevelopmental risks of valproate.

subtopic_detail: Tricyclic antidepressant overdose - sodium bicarbonate threshold
stem:
A 34-year-old man is brought to the emergency department by ambulance 90 minutes after ingesting an unknown quantity of his amitriptyline tablets in a suicide attempt. He has a history of treatment-resistant depression and recurrent self-harm. He is drowsy, with intermittent confusion. The ambulance team note he had two brief generalised seizures on the way in that resolved without treatment.

In the resus bay the ECG shows sinus tachycardia at 132 /min with a QRS width of 130 milliseconds and a terminal R wave in aVR of 4 mm. The blood pressure is 92/56 mmHg. He is alert to voice and protecting his airway for now. Capillary blood glucose is 5.4 mmol/L. The poisons information service has been called.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse 132 /min, blood pressure 92/56 mmHg, respiratory rate 22 /min, SpO2 96% on room air, temperature 36.7 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: drowsy but rousable to voice, GCS 13, dry mucous membranes, dilated pupils, reduced bowel sounds, urinary retention on bladder scan, no focal neurology
data_table.Investigations: ECG sinus tachycardia QRS 130 ms terminal R wave in aVR 4 mm, venous blood gas pH 7.32 pCO2 36 mmHg lactate 2.4 mmol/L, sodium 138 mmol/L (135-145), potassium 4.2 mmol/L (3.5-5.0)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Intravenous lidocaine 1 mg/kg as a bolus for the wide-complex tachycardia and ongoing sodium channel blockade
options.rationale: Class IB antiarrhythmics are second-line after bicarbonate fails in TCA cardiotoxicity. Class IA agents (procainamide) are contraindicated because they compound sodium channel blockade. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines Toxicology)

options.text: Intravenous magnesium sulfate 2 g over 10 minutes for the QRS widening and the risk of ventricular arrhythmia
options.rationale: Magnesium sulfate is the antidote for torsades de pointes and refractory ventricular arrhythmias, not for sodium channel blockade-driven QRS widening. The mechanism here is wrong target. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines Toxicology)

options.text: Activated charcoal 50 g via nasogastric tube as primary gastrointestinal decontamination for the tricyclic ingestion
options.rationale: Activated charcoal is reserved for ingestions within 1 to 2 hours in a patient with a protected airway; this patient is drowsy and at risk of aspiration. Cardiotoxicity treatment with bicarbonate is the upstream priority. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines Toxicology)

options.text: Intravenous sodium bicarbonate 1 to 2 mmol/kg over 5 minutes targeting pH 7.45 to 7.55 and QRS below 100 ms
options.rationale: TCA cardiotoxicity is driven by fast sodium channel blockade. ECG features predicting toxicity are QRS above 100 milliseconds and a terminal R wave in aVR above 3 mm. Sodium bicarbonate (1 to 2 mmol/kg bolus, repeat as needed, targeting pH 7.45 to 7.55) overcomes the channel blockade and is the first-line cardiotoxicity treatment. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines Toxicology; ANZCOR ALS for poisoning)

options.text: Intravenous flumazenil 0.2 mg as a bolus to reverse the central nervous system depression and protect the airway
options.rationale: Flumazenil is contraindicated in mixed overdose because it can precipitate seizures in a patient with sodium channel blockade and low seizure threshold from the TCA itself. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines Toxicology)

explanation.summary: TCA cardiotoxicity is driven by sodium channel blockade and manifests with QRS widening and a tall terminal R wave in aVR. Sodium bicarbonate (1 to 2 mmol/kg, targeting serum pH 7.45 to 7.55 and QRS below 100 milliseconds) is the first-line treatment. Activated charcoal and antiarrhythmics are second-line; class IA agents are contraindicated.
key_points: ECG predictors of TCA toxicity: QRS above 100 ms, terminal R in aVR above 3 mm.
Sodium bicarbonate: 1 to 2 mmol/kg bolus, target pH 7.45 to 7.55.
Lidocaine is second-line after bicarbonate; class IA antiarrhythmics are contraindicated.
Flumazenil is contraindicated in mixed overdose because of seizure risk.
explanation.pearls: TCA overdose with QRS above 100 ms or terminal R in aVR above 3 mm needs IV sodium bicarbonate 1 to 2 mmol/kg titrated to pH 7.45 to 7.55; flumazenil and class IA antiarrhythmics are contraindicated.

stem:
A 24-year-old man with treatment-resistant schizophrenia is on day 19 of a clozapine titration on the inpatient ward. He is currently on clozapine 200 mg daily and tolerating it. On routine surveillance bloods today (week 3 of the AU clozapine monitoring protocol) his troponin I has risen from less than 5 ng/L two days ago to 86 ng/L (less than 14). He reports mild chest tightness for the last day, which he attributed to anxiety.

His CRP is 38 mg/L (under 5), creatine kinase is 240 U/L (45-250), and ECG shows sinus tachycardia at 112 /min with no acute changes. He has had no fever. His haematology and metabolic surveillance bloods are otherwise unremarkable. The clozapine clinic registrar is contactable; the next clozapine dose is due in 4 hours.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse 112 /min, blood pressure 116/72 mmHg, respiratory rate 18 /min, SpO2 98% on room air, temperature 36.9 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: alert and oriented, mild chest tightness on direct questioning, no peripheral oedema, no S3 or murmur, lungs clear, no focal neurology
data_table.Investigations: troponin I 86 ng/L (under 14), CRP 38 mg/L (under 5), creatine kinase 240 U/L (45-250), ECG sinus tachycardia 112 /min no acute changes, NT-proBNP not yet returned

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Arrange a routine outpatient stress echocardiogram in 2 weeks and continue current clozapine therapy
options.rationale: Outpatient stress echo on a non-urgent timeline does not address the acute risk of fulminant myocarditis. The pathway demands urgent inpatient cardiology review. (Source: Clozapine Implementation Tool)

options.text: Continue clozapine at the same dose and repeat troponin and CRP in 48 hours to confirm a sustained rise
options.rationale: A confirmed troponin and CRP rise during the high-risk window is itself the trigger to act, not to monitor for further worsening. Continued exposure to clozapine while myocarditis is evolving is potentially fatal. (Source: Clozapine Implementation Tool)

options.text: Increase the clozapine dose to 250 mg to overcome the dose-related side effects with clinical review in 1 week
options.rationale: Increasing clozapine in the context of biochemical evidence of myocarditis is unsafe and contradicts the cessation pathway. (Source: Clozapine Implementation Tool)

options.text: Commence empirical intravenous methylprednisolone 1 g daily for 3 days for autoimmune-mediated myocarditis
options.rationale: Glucocorticoids are not standard initial therapy for clozapine-induced myocarditis. Cessation of clozapine, supportive care, and cardiology assessment are first. Steroid use is limited to specific eosinophilic or autoimmune subgroups guided by specialist input. (Source: Clozapine Implementation Tool)

options.text: Withhold the next clozapine dose, arrange urgent echocardiogram and cardiology review for suspected clozapine-induced myocarditis
options.rationale: Clozapine-induced myocarditis typically presents in the first 4 to 6 weeks of treatment. The Australian protocol monitors troponin and CRP weekly in this window. Rising troponin (over twice the upper reference) plus raised CRP triggers cessation, urgent echocardiogram, and cardiology review. Delaying creates risk of fulminant myocarditis. (Source: Clozapine Implementation Tool; RANZCP psychotropic monitoring guidance)

explanation.summary: Clozapine-induced myocarditis is most likely in the first 4 to 6 weeks of treatment. The Australian protocol monitors troponin and CRP weekly during this window. A rise in troponin to twice the upper reference plus a raised CRP, with or without symptoms, mandates withholding clozapine and urgent cardiology and echocardiographic assessment. Rechallenge after recovery is uncommon and specialist-led.
key_points: High-risk window: first 4 to 6 weeks of clozapine.
Trigger to act: troponin above twice upper reference plus raised CRP.
Withhold clozapine, urgent echocardiogram, cardiology review.
Rechallenge is specialist-led and uncommon.
explanation.pearls: Rising troponin (over twice upper reference) plus raised CRP in the first 4 to 6 weeks of clozapine titration triggers immediate cessation and urgent echocardiogram and cardiology review; do not continue dosing or wait for a second confirmation.

stem:
A 26-year-old man is brought to the emergency department by police on a mental health emergency apprehension for assessment. He has a 5-year history of paranoid schizophrenia and is not engaged with community follow-up. He is shouting, pacing, threatening staff, and refusing oral medication. Verbal de-escalation by the senior nurse and you has not been effective. Other patients in the corridor are being moved.

He has no documented allergies. He has no history of seizures or QT prolongation. He has not received any sedating medication in the last 24 hours according to his MyHealthRecord summary. He is well-built and appears to have used substances; toxicology screen is pending. The hospital-wide code grey team has been activated and the patient is being safely restrained by security with adequate personnel for safe parenteral medication administration.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse 124 /min, blood pressure 142/86 mmHg, respiratory rate 22 /min, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 37.0 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: agitated, threatening, hyperverbal, no focal neurology, dilated pupils, well-perfused, no recent injury identified
data_table.Investigations: ECG sinus tachycardia QTc 410 ms, capillary blood glucose 6.4 mmol/L, toxicology screen pending, breath alcohol zero

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate pharmacological intervention?

options.text: Intramuscular olanzapine 10 mg into the deltoid as monotherapy with no concurrent IM benzodiazepine within 1 hour
options.rationale: AU guidance for acute behavioural disturbance recommends IM olanzapine 10 mg as a first-line monotherapy parenteral agent. Concurrent IM benzodiazepine (within 1 hour) is avoided because of synergistic respiratory depression. Continuous monitoring of airway, SpO2, BP, and conscious state is mandatory after parenteral antipsychotic. (Source: RANZCP Acute behavioural disturbance guidance; SA Health rapid tranquillisation framework)

options.text: Intramuscular olanzapine 10 mg plus intramuscular lorazepam 2 mg into the same deltoid for synergistic sedation
options.rationale: Co-administration of IM olanzapine and IM benzodiazepine within 1 hour is contraindicated because of synergistic respiratory depression and reported deaths. Where additional sedation is needed, the second agent is given orally or by a different timing pathway. (Source: SA Health rapid tranquillisation framework)

options.text: Intramuscular haloperidol 10 mg into the deltoid because of the broader evidence base in chronic psychotic disorders
options.rationale: High-dose IM haloperidol carries higher risk of acute dystonia, QT prolongation, and torsades. AU guidance prefers second-generation IM antipsychotics (olanzapine, ziprasidone) where available. If haloperidol is used, the dose is typically 5 mg with promethazine. (Source: RANZCP Acute behavioural disturbance guidance)

options.text: Intramuscular midazolam 10 mg into the deltoid as monotherapy for rapid onset and reasonably short duration of action
options.rationale: IM midazolam achieves rapid sedation but carries significant respiratory depression risk and lacks specific antipsychotic effect. It is not first-line for primary acute behavioural disturbance secondary to psychosis. (Source: RANZCP Acute behavioural disturbance guidance)

options.text: Intravenous droperidol 10 mg as a slow bolus over 2 minutes as the first parenteral agent for behavioural control
options.rationale: IV droperidol is used in some EDs for acute behavioural disturbance but requires reliable IV access, which is hazardous to obtain in a violently agitated patient. IM route is preferred when restraint and access are limited. (Source: RANZCP Acute behavioural disturbance guidance)

explanation.summary: Acute behavioural disturbance in a psychiatric emergency is managed with verbal de-escalation, environmental measures, and pharmacological intervention if needed. AU guidance favours IM olanzapine 10 mg as first-line monotherapy with continuous monitoring of airway, respiration, and conscious state. Concurrent IM benzodiazepine within 1 hour is contraindicated due to synergistic respiratory depression.
key_points: First-line IM: olanzapine 10 mg monotherapy.
Do not give IM olanzapine and IM benzodiazepine within 1 hour of each other.
Continuous airway, SpO2, BP and conscious state monitoring is mandatory.
Haloperidol 5 mg + promethazine is an alternative when olanzapine is unavailable.
explanation.pearls: IM olanzapine 10 mg as monotherapy with continuous monitoring is first-line for acute behavioural disturbance in adults; do not co-administer IM benzodiazepine within 1 hour because of synergistic respiratory depression.

stem:
A 17-year-old girl is brought to the paediatric emergency department by her general practitioner with concerns about anorexia nervosa. She has restricted intake for 9 months and lost 18 kg from a BMI of 22 to a current BMI of 14.6. Her resting heart rate is 38 /min and lying blood pressure is 88/52 mmHg. She had a syncopal episode at school yesterday. She acknowledges restriction but says she is fine.

Electrolytes show sodium 132 mmol/L, potassium 2.9 mmol/L, magnesium 0.62 mmol/L, phosphate 0.68 mmol/L. ECG shows sinus bradycardia with a QTc of 478 milliseconds and no ischaemic changes. She has not menstruated in 6 months. Her parents are present and engaged. There is no overt suicidality.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse 38 /min, blood pressure 88/52 mmHg lying, respiratory rate 16 /min, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 35.8 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: BMI 14.6, dry mucous membranes, capillary refill 3 seconds, lanugo over the back, acrocyanosis, no peripheral oedema, alert and conversing
data_table.Investigations: sodium 132 mmol/L (135-145), potassium 2.9 mmol/L (3.5-5.0), magnesium 0.62 mmol/L (0.70-1.00), phosphate 0.68 mmol/L (0.75-1.50), ECG sinus bradycardia QTc 478 ms

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Admit directly to a child and adolescent mental health inpatient unit for psychiatric stabilisation as the sole pathway
options.rationale: Mental health units may not have cardiac monitoring and electrolyte infusion capability needed for the medical instability. Medical ward admission precedes or runs concurrently with mental health care. (Source: ANZAED Eating disorders guidelines)

options.text: Refer for outpatient family-based treatment with weekly weight monitoring and electrolyte review in 1 week time
options.rationale: Outpatient family-based treatment is the standard psychotherapy for paediatric anorexia, but this patient has multiple medical instability criteria and cannot be safely managed in the community without medical stabilisation first. (Source: ANZAED Eating disorders guidelines)

options.text: Discharge with oral potassium and magnesium supplementation and review by general practitioner within 3 days
options.rationale: Discharge in the presence of severe bradycardia, hypotension, QT prolongation, and electrolyte derangement risks sudden cardiac death. Medical admission is required first. (Source: ANZAED Eating disorders guidelines)

options.text: Admit to a paediatric medical ward for cardiac monitoring, electrolyte replacement and supervised structured refeeding
options.rationale: Anorexia with bradycardia under 50 /min, hypotension, QTc prolongation, electrolyte derangement, and BMI below 16 meets multiple medical instability criteria for admission per the AU eating disorders MEED-aligned framework. Supervised structured refeeding with phosphate replacement prevents refeeding syndrome. Cardiac monitoring detects arrhythmia driven by hypokalaemia and hypomagnesaemia. (Source: ANZAED Eating disorders guidelines; MEED-aligned RCH guidance)

options.text: Commence high-calorie refeeding at 50 kcal/kg/day immediately to address the long-standing nutritional deficit fully
options.rationale: Aggressive refeeding precipitates refeeding syndrome (hypophosphataemia, hypokalaemia, hypomagnesaemia, thiamine deficiency, cardiac failure). MEED-aligned AU guidance recommends starting at 20 to 30 kcal/kg/day with thiamine prophylaxis and daily electrolyte monitoring for the first week. (Source: ANZAED Eating disorders guidelines)

explanation.summary: Medical instability criteria for admission in anorexia nervosa include heart rate below 50 /min, systolic blood pressure below 90 mmHg, QTc prolongation, severe electrolyte disturbance, and BMI below 16. Refeeding starts cautiously (20 to 30 kcal/kg/day) with thiamine prophylaxis and daily electrolytes for the first week to prevent refeeding syndrome. Family-based outpatient treatment is the longer-term framework.
key_points: Medical admission criteria: HR under 50, BP under 90 systolic, QTc prolongation, electrolyte derangement, BMI under 16.
Start refeeding at 20 to 30 kcal/kg/day with thiamine 200 to 300 mg daily.
Daily phosphate, potassium, magnesium for the first week of refeeding.
Cardiac monitoring while bradycardic and QT prolonged.
explanation.pearls: Medical admission for anorexia is triggered by bradycardia under 50, hypotension, QTc prolongation, or electrolyte derangement; refeed at 20 to 30 kcal/kg/day with thiamine and daily electrolytes to prevent refeeding syndrome per ANZAED.

stem:
A 62-year-old woman with bipolar I disorder on lithium 1000 mg nocte for 12 years is brought to the emergency department by her daughter with 3 days of confusion, coarse tremor of the hands, and unsteadiness. She started ramipril 5 mg daily for newly diagnosed hypertension 10 days ago. Daughter says she has been drinking less than usual in a heatwave.

In the resus bay she is confused, has horizontal nystagmus, coarse tremor, and broad-based gait. Tendon reflexes are brisk with sustained ankle clonus. Lithium level is 2.6 mmol/L (therapeutic 0.6 to 1.0 in maintenance), creatinine 168 micromol/L (baseline 88 four months ago), sodium 142 mmol/L, potassium 4.0 mmol/L. ECG is in sinus rhythm with non-specific T wave flattening. She is haemodynamically stable.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse 92 /min, blood pressure 132/82 mmHg, respiratory rate 18 /min, SpO2 98% on room air, temperature 37.1 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: confused (orientated to person only), horizontal nystagmus, coarse tremor of both hands, ankle clonus sustained, broad-based gait, no focal weakness
data_table.Investigations: lithium 2.6 mmol/L (therapeutic 0.6-1.0), creatinine 168 micromol/L (baseline 88), eGFR 28 mL/min/1.73 m^2, sodium 142 mmol/L (135-145), potassium 4.0 mmol/L (3.5-5.0)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Administer activated charcoal 50 g via nasogastric tube to bind any unabsorbed lithium remaining in the gut lumen
options.rationale: Activated charcoal does not bind lithium effectively because lithium is a small cation. It also exposes a confused patient to aspiration risk. (Source: EXTRIP recommendations for lithium poisoning)

options.text: Withhold lithium and commence intravenous 0.9 percent saline at 250 mL/hour with daily lithium and creatinine checks
options.rationale: Saline diuresis alone does not match the clearance achievable with dialysis when there is renal impairment. The patient has neurological signs and a level above 2.5 mmol/L with reduced eGFR, which meet dialysis indication. (Source: EXTRIP recommendations for lithium poisoning)

options.text: Discuss urgent haemodialysis with the renal team and commence intravenous 0.9 percent saline at maintenance rate
options.rationale: Acute on chronic lithium toxicity with neurological features and impaired renal function meets EXTRIP haemodialysis criteria: lithium above 4.0 mmol/L regardless of symptoms, or above 2.5 mmol/L with reduced renal function or severe neurological features. The renal impairment from ACE inhibitor introduction and volume depletion precipitated the toxicity. Saline maintains volume status; lithium clears via dialysis. (Source: EXTRIP recommendations for lithium poisoning)

options.text: Administer intravenous flumazenil 0.2 mg as a bolus to reverse the confusion and gait disturbance from suspected sedation
options.rationale: Flumazenil reverses benzodiazepines; it has no role in lithium toxicity and could precipitate seizures if the patient has unrecognised polypharmacy. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines Toxicology)

options.text: Stop the recently introduced ramipril and continue current lithium dose with rechecks of creatinine and level in 24 hours
options.rationale: Stopping the ACE inhibitor addresses the precipitant but does not address the acute toxicity. The patient has neurological signs requiring active intervention now. (Source: EXTRIP recommendations for lithium poisoning)

explanation.summary: Acute on chronic lithium toxicity meets EXTRIP haemodialysis criteria when the level is above 4.0 mmol/L regardless of symptoms, or above 2.5 mmol/L with reduced renal function or severe neurological features. Common precipitants are renal-impairing medications (ACE inhibitors, NSAIDs, thiazides) and dehydration. Treatment combines urgent dialysis, volume resuscitation, and identification of the precipitant.
key_points: EXTRIP dialysis criteria: lithium above 4.0 mmol/L OR above 2.5 with renal impairment or severe neurology.
ACE inhibitors, NSAIDs, and thiazides reduce lithium clearance.
Dehydration in heat reduces clearance further.
Saline alone is inadequate when dialysis criteria are met.
explanation.pearls: Lithium 2.6 mmol/L with renal impairment and neurological features meets EXTRIP haemodialysis criteria; saline alone is inadequate and ACE inhibitors and NSAIDs are common precipitants.

stem:
A 28-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department by ambulance two hours after a witnessed overdose. Her partner found an empty pack of dothiepin 75 mg tablets (originally 25 tablets) and a half empty bottle of red wine. She is drowsy with a Glasgow Coma Score of 11. She has had no seizures pre-hospital. There is no history of cardiac disease.

On arrival a 12-lead ECG shows sinus tachycardia at 128, a QRS duration of 132 milliseconds with a rightward terminal R wave in aVR of 4 millimetres, and a QTc of 480 milliseconds. Her pupils are dilated, mouth is dry, and bladder palpable. Auscultation is clear. Capillary glucose 5.2 mmol/L. There is no focal neurology. Vital signs are below.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse rate 128, blood pressure 96/58, respiratory rate 14, SpO2 97 percent on room air, temperature 36.4 degrees
data_table.Investigations: venous blood gas pH 7.34, lactate 2.4 mmol/L, potassium 3.6 mmol/L, sodium 137 mmol/L, urinary urine drug screen positive for tricyclics, paracetamol level pending

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Intravenous flumazenil 200 micrograms to reverse co-ingested benzodiazepine sedation and improve airway control
options.rationale: Flumazenil precipitates seizures in TCA overdose by removing the protective benzodiazepine effect on a pro-convulsant brain; it is specifically contraindicated. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology and Wilderness)

options.text: Intravenous 8.4 percent sodium bicarbonate 1 to 2 mmol/kg bolus and repeat to target QRS under 100 ms and pH 7.50 to 7.55
options.rationale: QRS prolongation above 100 milliseconds and the R wave in aVR of 3 mm or more are markers of sodium channel blockade and predict seizures and ventricular arrhythmia. Sodium bicarbonate provides both a sodium load (overwhelms blockade) and alkalinisation (increases protein binding) and is the first line intervention. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology and Wilderness)

options.text: Intravenous amiodarone 300 mg over 20 minutes to treat the broad complex tachycardia and prevent ventricular arrhythmia
options.rationale: Class Ia, Ic, and III antiarrhythmics further block sodium channels or prolong QT in TCA overdose and may precipitate arrest. Sodium bicarbonate is the antiarrhythmic of choice here. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology and Wilderness)

options.text: Activated charcoal 50 g via nasogastric tube now without prior airway protection given the rising drowsiness
options.rationale: Activated charcoal is contraindicated without a protected airway in a patient with a falling GCS; risk of aspiration outweighs benefit at two hours post-ingestion. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology and Wilderness)

options.text: Intravenous magnesium sulfate 2 g over 20 minutes to address the prolonged QTc and prevent torsades de pointes
options.rationale: Magnesium addresses torsades de pointes but is not the priority while sodium channel blockade continues. Bicarbonate addresses both QRS and QTc by reversing the sodium channel block. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology and Wilderness)

explanation.summary: Tricyclic antidepressant overdose causes sodium channel blockade (QRS widening, R wave in aVR over 3 mm, ventricular arrhythmia), anticholinergic syndrome, alpha-1 blockade (hypotension), and seizures. Treatment is sodium bicarbonate 1 to 2 mmol/kg IV bolus repeated to target QRS less than 100 ms and arterial pH 7.50 to 7.55, intubation if GCS falls below 9 or seizures occur, benzodiazepines (not phenytoin) for seizures, and noradrenaline for refractory hypotension. Intravenous lipid emulsion is considered for cardiac arrest unresponsive to standard measures. Flumazenil is contraindicated.
key_points: QRS > 100 ms predicts seizures; QRS > 160 ms predicts ventricular arrhythmia
R wave in aVR > 3 mm is a sensitive marker of sodium channel blockade
Sodium bicarbonate 1 to 2 mmol/kg IV bolus, target QRS < 100 ms and pH 7.50 to 7.55
Benzodiazepines (not phenytoin) for TCA seizures
Flumazenil contraindicated; activated charcoal only if airway protected and within 1 to 2 hours
explanation.pearls: Intravenous lipid emulsion 20 percent at 1.5 mL/kg over 1 minute then 0.25 mL/kg/min may rescue refractory cardiac arrest in lipophilic TCA toxicity - sequester the drug in the lipid phase.

stem:
A 27-year-old long-haul truck driver presents to a community psychiatry clinic for assessment of suspected attention deficit hyperactivity disorder. He has had chronic difficulties with concentration, planning, finishing tasks, and emotional regulation since primary school. He has accumulated three speeding infringements and two near-miss incidents at work in the past 18 months. The screening Adult ADHD Self Report Scale and a collateral history from his mother are highly consistent with combined-type ADHD; structured clinical interview confirms the diagnosis.

He has no history of psychosis, no current substance use disorder, no cardiac disease, blood pressure 122/78, and a normal baseline ECG. He drinks two standard drinks twice a week. He is keen to start medication so he can keep his commercial driver's licence. He has been informed that his diagnosis has driving implications.

data_table.Investigations: ECG within normal limits, blood pressure 122/78, urinary drug screen negative, full blood count and liver function within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Commence bupropion 150 mg daily as a stimulant alternative with no driver licensing notification required of him
options.rationale: Bupropion is not first line for ADHD in Australia and the driving notification requirement is triggered by the diagnosis, not by the drug class. (Source: RANZCP Adult ADHD Guideline)

options.text: Commence atomoxetine 40 mg daily and reassure him that no driver licensing notification is required at present
options.rationale: Notification of a new ADHD diagnosis is mandatory for commercial driver license holders under Austroads regardless of medication choice. Atomoxetine is a non-stimulant second line option, not first line. (Source: Austroads Assessing Fitness to Drive)

options.text: Refer for cognitive behavioural therapy alone and avoid pharmacotherapy because of the commercial driving implications
options.rationale: CBT is adjunctive but does not match the effect size of stimulants in adult ADHD. Withholding pharmacotherapy from a symptomatic adult on the basis of driving risk is paternalistic and not supported by guideline. (Source: RANZCP Adult ADHD Guideline)

options.text: Commence modafinil 100 mg daily as an off-label alternative to stimulants for adult attention deficit hyperactivity disorder
options.rationale: Modafinil is not recommended for ADHD in Australian guidelines and is approved for narcolepsy and shift work sleep disorder. Stimulants remain first line. (Source: RANZCP Adult ADHD Guideline)

options.text: Commence dexamfetamine 5 mg twice daily under psychiatry authority and notify the state driver licensing authority
options.rationale: Long acting or short acting psychostimulants (dexamfetamine, methylphenidate, lisdexamfetamine) are first line for adult ADHD; in Australia they are S8 medicines requiring psychiatry-led prescription. Under Austroads 'Assessing Fitness to Drive', a commercial driver with a new ADHD diagnosis must notify the licensing authority and is generally fit to drive only on stable treatment with documented benefit. (Source: RANZCP Adult ADHD Guideline)

explanation.summary: Adult ADHD treatment in Australia combines stimulant pharmacotherapy (dexamfetamine, methylphenidate, lisdexamfetamine) with psychoeducation and CBT. Stimulants are Schedule 8 drugs and prescribing is restricted to psychiatrists or paediatricians under state and territory authority. Atomoxetine and guanfacine are non-stimulant options. Under Austroads 'Assessing Fitness to Drive', a commercial driver with a new ADHD diagnosis is required to notify the driver licensing authority; private drivers are not generally required to notify but the doctor is expected to advise the patient on safe driving and impairment. Stable treatment with documented response usually allows return to commercial driving.
key_points: Stimulants (methylphenidate, dexamfetamine, lisdexamfetamine) are first line
Atomoxetine, guanfacine are non-stimulant options
S8 medicines: psychiatry / paediatric authority prescribing in Australia
Austroads: commercial drivers must notify; private drivers advised by doctor
Baseline ECG, BP, weight monitoring during titration
explanation.pearls: Lisdexamfetamine has a smoother pharmacokinetic profile than dexamfetamine because it is a prodrug requiring red cell hydrolysis to release dexamfetamine - this caps the rate of release and reduces euphoric peak, supporting once daily dosing.

stem:
A 21-year-old university student is brought to a community psychiatric assessment service by his parents with a three week history of paranoid ideation, persecutory beliefs about being followed by a state intelligence agency, and second person auditory hallucinations criticising him. He has been using high potency cannabis daily for the past four months around exam stress. He has used no other illicit substances on urine drug screen and serology.

There is no history of head injury, neurological disease, or thyroid disorder. He has a maternal uncle with chronic schizophrenia. He has stopped attending lectures and his sleep is reversed. Mental state examination shows a tense young man, suspicious, with thought disorder including loosening of associations. He has no insight. The parents say he was 'completely well' four months ago and his GP letter confirms no prior psychiatric contact.

data_table.Investigations: urine drug screen positive for cannabinoids only, full blood count within normal limits, thyroid function within normal limits, CRP 2 mg/L, syphilis serology negative, HIV serology negative, vitamin B12 and folate within normal limits, computed tomography of the brain within normal limits

lead_in: Which one of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Diagnose cannabis induced psychotic disorder, prescribe risperidone 1 mg twice daily for five days, discharge to GP review
options.rationale: Even if cannabis induced psychosis is the working diagnosis, three weeks of fixed persecutory beliefs, second person auditory hallucinations, and thought disorder in a 21-year-old with family history warrant assertive specialist follow up rather than GP review. Premature discharge risks treatment dropout and decompensation. (Source: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guideline for Schizophrenia)
source_refs: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guideline for Schizophrenia

options.text: Apply for an involuntary admission order under the Mental Health Act without offering voluntary admission first to him
options.rationale: Voluntary admission should be offered first if the patient has capacity and agrees. Involuntary admission is reserved for refusal in a person at risk of harm to self or others. (Source: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guideline for Schizophrenia)
source_refs: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guideline for Schizophrenia

options.text: Commence high dose oral olanzapine 20 mg daily and arrange clozapine clinic review at four weeks for resistant symptoms
options.rationale: Clozapine is reserved for treatment resistance (failure of two adequate trials of other antipsychotics). High dose olanzapine in a stimulant naive young man exposes him to weight gain, metabolic syndrome, and sedation. (Source: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guideline for Schizophrenia)
source_refs: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guideline for Schizophrenia

options.text: Admit voluntarily under early psychosis service for trial of an oral second generation antipsychotic and substance counselling
options.rationale: First episode psychosis with persistent positive symptoms beyond a few days of abstinence cannot be reliably labelled cannabis induced until at least one month of cannabis abstinence shows symptom resolution. Early Psychosis Prevention and Intervention Centre (EPPIC) model favours assertive specialist follow up, low dose oral second generation antipsychotic, and integrated substance use treatment. (Source: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guideline for Schizophrenia)
source_refs: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guideline for Schizophrenia

options.text: Defer pharmacotherapy and observe abstinent in a residential rehabilitation unit for two weeks before any antipsychotic
options.rationale: Three weeks of psychotic symptoms after presentation already exceeds the two week abstinence window that would support a substance induced diagnosis. Withholding antipsychotic medication delays symptom resolution. (Source: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guideline for Schizophrenia)
source_refs: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guideline for Schizophrenia

explanation.summary: Differentiating substance induced from primary psychosis in a young person with cannabis use and a positive family history is clinically difficult and often requires longitudinal observation. The RANZCP and Orygen early psychosis pathway favours treating as first episode psychosis if symptoms persist beyond a month of abstinence (or earlier if a clear primary disorder is suspected) using low dose oral second generation antipsychotic, integrated substance use treatment, and assertive case management. About one in three cannabis induced psychoses convert to schizophrenia within three years.
key_points: Persistence of psychosis beyond one month of cannabis abstinence supports primary psychosis
Around 30 percent of cannabis induced psychoses convert to schizophrenia within 3 years
Low dose oral second generation antipsychotic is first line (e.g. risperidone, aripiprazole, olanzapine)
Integrated substance treatment within early psychosis service
Family history of schizophrenia roughly doubles conversion risk
explanation.pearls: Among cannabis users with a first episode psychosis, around 30 percent meet criteria for schizophrenia within three years on Australian early psychosis cohort follow up - assertive engagement during this window predicts long term function.

sources.label: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guideline for Schizophrenia

stem:
A 48-year-old woman attends general practice for assistance with quitting smoking. She has smoked 25 cigarettes per day for 30 years, has had three previous unaided quit attempts that lasted between two days and three weeks, and her Heaviness of Smoking Index is 6. She has had two depressive episodes in the past treated with sertraline, the last episode resolving 18 months ago. She has stable hypertension on perindopril.

She has had one generalised tonic-clonic seizure at age 19 attributed to alcohol withdrawal at the time and has not had another. She is not pregnant. She has tried 21 mg nicotine patches in the past without success and dislikes nicotine gum. She has commercial driver's licence requirements at work. She is keen to use the most effective option supported by Australian guidelines and has heard about varenicline.

data_table.Investigations: blood pressure 142/86, weight 78 kg, full blood count and liver function within normal limits, urinary pregnancy test negative, ECG within normal limits

lead_in: Which one of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Commence varenicline 0.5 mg daily for 3 days, 0.5 mg twice daily for 4 days, then 1 mg twice daily for 12 weeks
options.rationale: Varenicline is the most effective monotherapy for smoking cessation (number needed to treat about 8 versus placebo at 12 months) and is first line in Australia. Past depression treated and resolved is not a contraindication; previous concerns about neuropsychiatric harm were not borne out by the EAGLES trial. (Source: RACGP: Supporting Smoking Cessation)

options.text: Commence bupropion sustained release 150 mg daily for 3 days then 150 mg twice daily for 7 to 12 weeks as monotherapy
options.rationale: Bupropion is contraindicated by prior seizure (even alcohol withdrawal seizure historically) because it lowers the seizure threshold. It is also less effective than varenicline and combination NRT. (Source: RACGP: Supporting Smoking Cessation)

options.text: Re-prescribe 21 mg nicotine patches as sole therapy and reassure that previous failure does not predict future failure
options.rationale: Single agent patches at high dependence have lower efficacy than combination NRT (patch plus short acting form) or varenicline. Repeating a previously failed strategy without intensifying is unlikely to succeed. (Source: RACGP: Supporting Smoking Cessation)

options.text: Refer for nicotine vaping as a harm reduction strategy and avoid any prescription smoking cessation pharmacotherapy
options.rationale: Nicotine vaping is a second line option in Australia under prescription where first line agents have failed or are not suitable. It is not first line and is not preferred over varenicline. (Source: RACGP: Supporting Smoking Cessation)

options.text: Recommend an Allen Carr style behavioural change program alone without any pharmacotherapy and review in three months
options.rationale: Behavioural support is encouraged but works best in combination with pharmacotherapy in highly dependent smokers (Heaviness of Smoking Index 5 or more). Withholding pharmacotherapy underuses an evidence based intervention. (Source: RACGP: Supporting Smoking Cessation)

explanation.summary: Australian smoking cessation pharmacotherapy is led by varenicline (number needed to treat about 8 versus placebo at 12 months), followed by combination nicotine replacement therapy (patch plus short acting), then monotherapy NRT, then bupropion. Behavioural support plus pharmacotherapy roughly doubles cessation rates compared with either alone. Bupropion is contraindicated by seizure history, current or past eating disorder, MAOI use within two weeks, and severe hepatic impairment. Nicotine vaping is second line under prescription where first line agents have failed or are not suitable.
key_points: Varenicline first line - NNT ~8 at 12 months
Combination NRT (patch + short acting) second line (NNT ~11)
Bupropion third line - contraindicated by seizures, eating disorders, MAOI
Past resolved depression NOT a contraindication to varenicline (EAGLES trial)
Behavioural support plus pharmacotherapy roughly doubles cessation
explanation.pearls: EAGLES trial (4 arm RCT in 8000 smokers with and without psychiatric history) found no excess of neuropsychiatric adverse events with varenicline compared with placebo, patch, or bupropion - past depression alone is no longer a contraindication.

subtopic_detail: Schizoaffective versus bipolar with psychotic features
stem:
A 32-year-old woman is admitted to an acute psychiatric ward in her fourth presentation in five years. The current episode features one month of elevated mood, reduced need for sleep, grandiose delusions of being a celebrity, and pressure of speech, with persecutory voices saying she will be killed. The euphoria resolved with oral olanzapine 20 mg and lithium 1 g daily over 10 days but the persecutory voices persist three weeks after mood symptoms have settled.

Review of her records shows two previous mood episodes (one manic, one major depressive) and one inter-episode period of four months when she had paranoid delusions and second person hallucinations in the absence of any mood symptoms. She is medication adherent. There is no substance misuse. Cognition is intact. She is currently euthymic on mental state examination and her current PANSS shows persistent positive symptoms.

data_table.Investigations: blood lithium level 0.8 mmol/L, full blood count and thyroid function within normal limits, urinary drug screen negative, CT brain within normal limits

lead_in: Which one of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

options.text: Paranoid schizophrenia with secondary mood symptoms from psychotic decompensation
options.rationale: Schizophrenia is diagnosed when mood symptoms are present for a minority of the active and residual illness, which is not the case in someone with two prior major mood episodes plus the current manic episode. (Source: RANZCP Mood Disorders)

options.text: Bipolar I disorder with mood congruent psychotic features during the manic episode
options.rationale: Bipolar I with psychotic features requires that psychotic symptoms occur only during mood episodes. The documented four month inter-episode psychotic period rules this out. (Source: RANZCP Mood Disorders)

options.text: Schizoaffective disorder, bipolar type, with persistent inter-episode psychotic symptoms
options.rationale: The DSM-5 criterion for schizoaffective disorder requires a major mood episode concurrent with criterion A schizophrenia symptoms, plus at least two weeks of psychotic symptoms in the absence of mood symptoms during the lifetime course. The four month period of psychosis without mood symptoms satisfies this. (Source: RANZCP Schizoaffective Disorder)

options.text: Delusional disorder persecutory type with concurrent bipolar I and current manic episode
options.rationale: Delusional disorder requires non-bizarre delusions without prominent hallucinations and minimal functional impairment outside the delusion - inconsistent with the prominent hallucinations and functional decline here. Comorbidity with bipolar I is rarely diagnosed and would not capture the cross sectional picture. (Source: RANZCP Mood Disorders)

options.text: Substance induced psychotic and mood disorder despite negative urinary drug screen
options.rationale: Negative urinary drug screen and absence of substance misuse history exclude a substance induced disorder. The longitudinal pattern across five years is incompatible with intoxication or withdrawal phenomena. (Source: RANZCP Mood Disorders)

explanation.summary: Schizoaffective disorder requires (a) a major mood episode concurrent with schizophrenia criterion A symptoms, (b) at least two weeks of psychotic symptoms in the absence of mood symptoms at some time in the lifetime course, and (c) mood symptoms present for a majority of the active and residual illness. The 'bipolar type' subtype is given when manic episodes have occurred, the 'depressive type' when only major depressive episodes have occurred. Treatment combines mood stabiliser (lithium or sodium valproate) with an antipsychotic and structured psychosocial care; clozapine is considered for treatment resistance.
key_points: Schizoaffective: major mood episode plus criterion A schizophrenia, plus 2 or more weeks of psychosis without mood
Bipolar with psychotic features: psychosis only during mood episodes
Schizophrenia: mood symptoms are a minority of active/residual illness
Treatment: mood stabiliser plus antipsychotic; clozapine for treatment resistance
Diagnosis can shift across the course; longitudinal history is essential
explanation.pearls: Two weeks of psychotic symptoms in the absence of any mood episode at any point in the lifetime course is the boundary criterion that distinguishes schizoaffective disorder from bipolar I with psychotic features - mine the chart for inter-episode periods to establish this.

stem:
A 56-year-old man with bipolar I disorder has been on lithium 1000 mg daily for 22 years. He is psychiatrically well, has had no manic episodes in 12 years on lithium plus aripiprazole 5 mg, and is followed in shared care between psychiatry and general practice. He has hypertension on perindopril (added two years ago) and no diabetes. He drinks one glass of red wine four nights a week. His eGFR has been monitored every six months.

The most recent eGFR is 38 mL/min/1.73 m^2, falling from 54 a year ago and 72 two years ago. Lithium level today is 0.9 mmol/L. Thyroid stimulating hormone is 4.2 mU/L. Corrected calcium is 2.62 mmol/L (2.10-2.60). 24 hour urinary protein is 0.4 g (less than 0.15). He has no symptoms of polyuria, polydipsia, or tremor. The renal physician you spoke with suggested coming off lithium would not necessarily reverse the decline.

data_table.Investigations: lithium 0.9 mmol/L, eGFR 38 mL/min/1.73 m^2 declining from 54 then 72, thyroid stimulating hormone 4.2 mU/L, corrected calcium 2.62 mmol/L, parathyroid hormone 9.4 pmol/L (1.6-6.9), 24 hour urinary protein 0.4 g, blood pressure 138/82, urinary drug screen not performed

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Continue lithium 1000 mg daily and recheck eGFR in six months without specialist renal medicine input
options.rationale: Progressive eGFR decline through stage 3b CKD on a known nephrotoxin warrants psychiatric and renal multidisciplinary review with a documented plan to switch or taper, not passive monitoring. (Source: RANZCP Bipolar Guideline)

options.text: Halve the lithium dose and target a serum level of 0.4 mmol/L to reduce nephrotoxicity over the next year
options.rationale: Dose reduction below 0.6 mmol/L generally loses prophylactic efficacy and does not reliably halt renal decline. Multidisciplinary planning toward alternative agents is preferred. (Source: RANZCP Bipolar Guideline)

options.text: Stop lithium today to halt further renal damage and substitute high dose sodium valproate from tomorrow morning
options.rationale: Abrupt cessation of lithium after long term use carries up to 50 percent risk of mood relapse within 12 months. A planned slow taper is preferred. (Source: RANZCP Bipolar Guideline)

options.text: Increase fluid intake to four litres daily and continue lithium at the same dose without specialist referral
options.rationale: Volume loading does not reverse established chronic interstitial nephritis from lithium and may risk hyponatraemia. The dose should not stay the same in CKD stage 3b without weighing alternatives. (Source: RANZCP Bipolar Guideline)

options.text: Coordinate joint psychiatry and renal medicine review for a slow lithium taper to sodium valproate or lamotrigine
options.rationale: Australian psychiatric guidance advises planned multidisciplinary review when eGFR falls under 60 and especially under 45, weighing relapse risk against renal benefit; a slow taper over 3 to 6 months with an alternative mood stabiliser is preferred. Abrupt cessation risks relapse and may not reverse renal decline beyond stage 3b. (Source: RANZCP Bipolar Guideline)

explanation.summary: Long term lithium use carries cumulative renal risk through chronic tubulointerstitial nephritis and nephrogenic diabetes insipidus. Surveillance every six months should include eGFR, lithium level, thyroid stimulating hormone, calcium and parathyroid hormone (lithium induced hyperparathyroidism), and urinalysis. eGFR below 60 prompts shared care with renal medicine; below 45 prompts active discussion of cessation versus continuation, weighing 50 percent twelve month relapse risk if stopped abruptly. Lithium induced hyperparathyroidism is treated by lithium cessation where possible or parathyroidectomy.
key_points: 6 monthly: eGFR, Li level, TSH, calcium/PTH, urinalysis
eGFR < 60: shared care with renal medicine
eGFR < 45: actively discuss cessation versus continuation
Slow taper over 3 to 6 months reduces relapse risk
Lithium induced hyperparathyroidism: high calcium with high or inappropriately normal PTH
explanation.pearls: Hypercalcaemia plus inappropriately normal or high PTH in a patient on long term lithium is lithium induced hyperparathyroidism - around 10 percent prevalence after 10 years of lithium therapy, and the parathyroid hyperplasia often does not reverse on lithium withdrawal.

stem:
A 19-year-old man with a six month prodromal history of social withdrawal and odd beliefs is brought to a psychiatric assessment unit by his family. Over the past five days he has stopped eating and drinking, has been mute, and adopts unusual postures for hours at a time. He has not been on any medication in the past year. He has no fever, no rigidity, and no autonomic instability. Vital signs are within normal limits.

On examination he is awake with eyes open but unresponsive to verbal commands. Posturing is present (he holds his arm in the air when placed there for at least 30 seconds). There is waxy flexibility on passive movement, mutism, negativism (resists eye opening), and grimacing. The remainder of the neurological examination cannot be completed due to negativism. There is no neck stiffness. Computed tomography of the brain and a metabolic screen are unremarkable.

data_table.Investigations: venous blood gas pH 7.42, sodium 138 mmol/L, potassium 4.0 mmol/L, urea 4.6 mmol/L, creatine kinase 142 U/L (<200), thyroid stimulating hormone within normal limits, urinary drug screen negative, computed tomography of the brain within normal limits, urinalysis sterile

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Commence intravenous haloperidol 5 mg every 6 hours to treat the underlying suspected schizophrenic psychosis directly
options.rationale: Antipsychotics are relatively contraindicated as first line in catatonia because of the risk of precipitating neuroleptic malignant syndrome (NMS) and worsening catatonic features. Benzodiazepines are first line. (Source: RANZCP Catatonia Guideline)

options.text: Lorazepam 2 mg intramuscular bolus and reassess catatonic features at 15 minutes, then oral lorazepam 6 to 12 mg daily
options.rationale: Lorazepam 1 to 2 mg IV or IM is both diagnostic and therapeutic in catatonia: around 70 percent of cases show measurable improvement in Bush Francis catatonia rating score within 15 to 30 minutes. Lack of response prompts urgent consideration of electroconvulsive therapy. (Source: RANZCP Catatonia Guideline)

options.text: Arrange urgent electroconvulsive therapy under general anaesthesia without trial of pharmacotherapy as the first step
options.rationale: ECT is second line after lorazepam (and may be first line in life-threatening malignant catatonia with autonomic instability), but trialling lorazepam first is standard in non-malignant catatonia. ECT is also indicated when there is no response within 24 to 48 hours. (Source: RANZCP Catatonia Guideline)

options.text: Commence intravenous flumazenil 200 micrograms to exclude benzodiazepine intoxication as a cause of unresponsiveness
options.rationale: Flumazenil is contraindicated when a seizure risk exists, may precipitate seizures, and addresses a different clinical picture from catatonia. The urinary drug screen excludes benzodiazepine intoxication here. (Source: RANZCP Catatonia Guideline)

options.text: Commence intravenous dantrolene 2 mg/kg to treat presumed neuroleptic malignant syndrome with rigidity and autonomic signs
options.rationale: NMS requires recent exposure to dopamine antagonists, hyperthermia, rigidity, autonomic instability, and a raised creatine kinase - none of which are present here. Dantrolene has no role in non-malignant catatonia. (Source: RANZCP Catatonia Guideline)

explanation.summary: Catatonia is a clinically diagnosed syndrome (Bush Francis Catatonia Rating Scale: 3 or more of 14 features) that complicates schizophrenia, mood disorders, and a range of medical conditions including autoimmune encephalitis. First line treatment is the lorazepam challenge (1 to 2 mg IV or IM with assessment at 15 minutes); around 70 percent improve dramatically. If lorazepam fails or malignant catatonia develops (hyperthermia, autonomic instability), ECT is the next step. Antipsychotics are relatively contraindicated because they may precipitate NMS. Always look for an underlying cause: autoimmune encephalitis (NMDA receptor), HIV, encephalitis, lupus.
key_points: Bush Francis Catatonia Rating Scale: 3 or more of 14 features
Lorazepam 1 to 2 mg IV or IM (diagnostic and therapeutic - 70 percent response)
ECT for refractory catatonia or malignant catatonia
Avoid antipsychotics first line (precipitate NMS)
Screen for autoimmune (NMDA receptor encephalitis), HIV, lupus, metabolic
explanation.pearls: Malignant catatonia (catatonia with hyperthermia, autonomic instability, and rigidity) is clinically indistinguishable from neuroleptic malignant syndrome - the differentiator is dopamine antagonist exposure history; treatment is electroconvulsive therapy and supportive ICU care regardless.

stem:
A 35-year-old man with bipolar I disorder has been on lithium carbonate 1000 mg daily for eight years with steady-state levels around 0.7 mmol/L on annual monitoring. His general practitioner prescribed ibuprofen 400 mg three times daily two weeks ago for new shoulder pain.

He now presents to a metropolitan emergency department with three days of coarse tremor, persistent nausea and vomiting, unsteady gait, and his partner reports he has become mildly confused over the last 24 hours. He has had no falls. He takes no other medications and has not started any new herbal supplements. He has continued his lithium tablets through the illness. He has no chronic kidney disease history and his last creatinine three months ago was 78 micromol/L.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse rate 92, blood pressure 134/82, respiratory rate 18, SpO2 99 percent on room air, temperature 36.8 degrees
data_table.Investigations: serum lithium 1.8 mmol/L (0.6-0.8), sodium 138 mmol/L (135-145), potassium 4.4 mmol/L (3.5-5.0), creatinine 122 micromol/L (60-110), eGFR 48 mL/min/1.73 m squared, ECG sinus rhythm with flattened T waves

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Stop lithium and ibuprofen, commence intravenous 0.9 percent saline for volume expansion, and contact the renal team to arrange urgent haemodialysis
options.rationale: Lithium level 1.8 with neurological features and impaired renal function meets criteria for moderate-to-severe lithium toxicity. NSAIDs reduce renal lithium clearance through prostaglandin-mediated vasoconstriction. Haemodialysis is indicated for level greater than 4 mmol/L, or 2.5 to 4 with severe symptoms or renal failure, or 1.5 to 2.5 with significant neurological involvement. (Source: AMH: Lithium)

options.text: Continue lithium at the current dose, switch ibuprofen to paracetamol 1 g four times daily, and recheck the lithium level in 24 hours at clinic review
options.rationale: Continuing lithium at this level with neurological involvement risks deterioration including seizures, arrhythmias, and irreversible neurological injury. Immediate cessation is required. (Source: AMH: Lithium)

options.text: Reduce lithium dose to 500 mg daily, continue ibuprofen at half dose with a proton pump inhibitor for gastric protection
options.rationale: Dose reduction without cessation does not address acute toxicity, and continued NSAID exposure will perpetuate the renal clearance impairment. (Source: AMH: Lithium)

options.text: Stop lithium for 48 hours then restart at 500 mg, switch mood stabiliser to sodium valproate, and continue ibuprofen as prescribed by the general practitioner
options.rationale: Premature restart before level clears risks rebound toxicity. Switching to valproate is a longer-term consideration rather than acute management of a toxic level. (Source: AMH: Lithium)

options.text: Switch lithium to a sustained release preparation and add ondansetron 8 mg three times daily for vomiting and supportive oral rehydration solution
options.rationale: Sustained-release lithium does not reduce toxicity; it changes the kinetics. The acute step is to remove lithium, not to reformulate it. (Source: AMH: Lithium)

explanation.summary: Lithium toxicity is precipitated commonly by dehydration, NSAID use (reduced renal prostaglandin-mediated vasodilation), ACE inhibitor or thiazide initiation, and acute kidney injury. Management is immediate cessation of lithium and precipitating drug, intravenous saline for volume expansion, and consideration of haemodialysis for severe toxicity (level above 4, or 2.5 to 4 with severe symptoms or renal failure, or 1.5 to 2.5 with significant neurological signs). Coarse tremor and ataxia indicate moderate toxicity.
key_points: Common precipitants: NSAID, ACE inhibitor, thiazide, dehydration, AKI
Symptoms: coarse tremor, ataxia, confusion, vomiting, dysarthria, seizures (severe)
Haemodialysis if level > 4, or 2.5-4 with severe symptoms or renal failure
Stop lithium plus precipitating drug, give intravenous saline
Long-term follow-up: thyroid, parathyroid, and renal function monitoring
explanation.pearls: Ibuprofen reduces lithium clearance by around 25 percent through prostaglandin-mediated renal vasoconstriction and can push a previously therapeutic patient into toxicity within days; routine paracetamol is the preferred analgesic on lithium.

stem:
A 28-year-old man with treatment-resistant schizophrenia has been taking clozapine for four weeks after two previous trials of risperidone and olanzapine with persistent psychotic symptoms. He is now on clozapine 250 mg daily with significant reduction in auditory hallucinations and improved engagement at his community clinic. He has no fever, no sore throat, no rash, and no recent infection.

He has had weekly full blood counts since starting clozapine through the registry-monitored program. His latest result today shows white cells 4.2 and absolute neutrophil count 2.0. He is asking the consultant psychiatrist what monitoring schedule applies for the next year and how it relates to his current results. He has no other medical comorbidities and takes no other medications. He understands the requirement for ongoing blood tests and is happy to comply with the schedule.

data_table.Investigations: white cells 4.2 x10^9/L (4-11), absolute neutrophil count 2.0 x10^9/L (2.0-7.5), haemoglobin 142 g/L (130-180), platelets 230 x10^9/L (150-400), CRP 3 mg/L (<5), trough clozapine level 380 micrograms/L (350-600 therapeutic)

lead_in: Which monitoring schedule is correct?

options.text: Increase to twice weekly full blood count for the next four weeks given the borderline neutrophil count and continue treatment unchanged
options.rationale: Counts of 2.0 are at the lower limit of the green zone and do not trigger increased monitoring frequency. Twice weekly is not a routine clozapine monitoring interval. (Source: TGA Clozapine Risk Management Plan)

options.text: Continue weekly full blood count until 18 weeks of clozapine, then four-weekly indefinitely while the patient remains on clozapine
options.rationale: The Australian clozapine registry protocol requires weekly haematological monitoring for the first 18 weeks (highest risk period for agranulocytosis), then four-weekly thereafter for the duration of therapy. (Source: TGA Clozapine Risk Management Plan)

options.text: Switch to monthly full blood count from week five given stable counts and good clinical response with no adverse effects in the first month
options.rationale: Monthly monitoring is not appropriate before 18 weeks because the highest risk of agranulocytosis is within the first 18 weeks of treatment. (Source: TGA Clozapine Risk Management Plan)

options.text: Stop clozapine immediately and switch to oral olanzapine 20 mg at night because the absolute neutrophil count is at the lower limit of normal
options.rationale: Absolute neutrophil count of 2.0 is at the lower border of the green zone and does not require cessation. The red zone (cease clozapine and admit) is below 1.5. (Source: TGA Clozapine Risk Management Plan)

options.text: Continue weekly full blood count indefinitely as a routine policy for all patients prescribed clozapine throughout their treatment course
options.rationale: Weekly indefinite monitoring is not the registry protocol and over-burdens the patient. Frequency steps down after 18 weeks of stable counts. (Source: TGA Clozapine Risk Management Plan)

explanation.summary: Clozapine is regulated through a national TGA risk management plan because of the risk of agranulocytosis and other haematological events. Australian protocol requires weekly full blood count for the first 18 weeks of treatment (highest risk window), then four-weekly indefinitely while the patient remains on clozapine. Trigger thresholds use the absolute neutrophil count: green zone (>= 2.0) continue, amber (1.5-1.99) twice weekly, red (< 1.5) cease and admit.
key_points: Weekly FBC for first 18 weeks of clozapine
Then four-weekly indefinitely
Green: ANC >= 2.0; amber: 1.5-1.99; red: < 1.5
Red zone: cease clozapine, admit, haematology referral
Also monitor for myocarditis (first 4 weeks): troponin, CRP, ECG
explanation.pearls: Agranulocytosis risk on clozapine peaks within the first 18 weeks (around 0.8 percent cumulative incidence) then falls; this is why the Australian registry steps weekly monitoring down to four-weekly only after week 18.

stem:
A 35-year-old man with major depressive disorder has been taking paroxetine 40 mg daily for two years. He stopped the medication five days ago without consulting his general practitioner because he felt better and thought he no longer needed it. His mood has been stable for the past six months on the medication.

He now presents to his general practitioner with five days of dizziness on standing, sensations he describes as electric brain shocks, persistent nausea, agitation, and difficulty sleeping. He denies any suicidal ideation and his mood is currently good. He has had no fever, no abdominal pain, and no new medications. He does not use alcohol or recreational drugs. His blood pressure and other observations are normal. He is keen to know what his treating doctor recommends he do next.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse rate 84, blood pressure 122/76, respiratory rate 16, SpO2 99 percent on room air, temperature 36.8 degrees

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Reassure him that discontinuation symptoms typically resolve spontaneously within 24 hours and continue total cessation with general supportive care
options.rationale: Untreated paroxetine discontinuation syndrome usually persists for one to three weeks (paroxetine has a short half-life and high discontinuation rate). Reassurance alone is inadequate. (Source: RANZCP Mood Disorders CPG)

options.text: Commence fluoxetine 20 mg daily as a bridging therapy for one week and stop the fluoxetine completely without further taper
options.rationale: Bridging with fluoxetine is sometimes used for severe discontinuation syndrome but seven days is too short, increases fluoxetine accumulation, and does not address the underlying need for a gradual taper. (Source: RANZCP Mood Disorders CPG)

options.text: Commence venlafaxine 75 mg daily as an alternative serotonin-noradrenaline reuptake inhibitor to provide ongoing maintenance therapy
options.rationale: Switching antidepressant class is not the answer to discontinuation symptoms and venlafaxine has a similar or worse discontinuation profile than paroxetine. (Source: RANZCP Mood Disorders CPG)

options.text: Restart paroxetine 40 mg daily and then taper by twenty five percent of the dose every two to four weeks over several months
options.rationale: The recommended approach is to restart at the original dose and then taper slowly (typically 25 percent reduction every 2 to 4 weeks) over months. Paroxetine has the worst discontinuation profile of common SSRIs and requires the slowest taper. (Source: RANZCP Mood Disorders CPG)

options.text: Add lorazepam 1 mg three times daily for symptomatic management of agitation and insomnia and continue paroxetine cessation
